explanations.b: Reynolds number is a flow-similarity parameter unrelated to smoke color in flow visualization.
explanations.c: Cd is meaningful at whatever Reynolds number it is measured at; there is no single universally required Re value.
explanations.d: Blockage ratio and Reynolds number are independent pieces of information; reporting one does not substitute for the other.

questions.prompt: What is a mount tare run, and why is it required?

options.text: A run measuring the empty support strut's own drag, subtracted from later readings, since the mount holding the model adds drag that is not the model's
A run at double the normal tunnel speed to check for turbulence
A calibration of the tunnel's temperature sensor
An optional step only needed for lift measurements, not drag

explanations.a: Correct — the sting or wire supporting the model in the flow generates its own drag; a tare run measures that support-only drag so it can be subtracted from the model-plus-support reading, isolating the model's true drag.
explanations.b: A tare run is about isolating support-structure drag, not about testing at a different speed or checking turbulence.
explanations.c: Tare runs concern mechanical/aerodynamic drag isolation, not temperature sensor calibration (matched dynamic pressure handles density/temperature effects separately).
explanations.d: Mount tare correction is needed for drag measurements just as much as lift measurements; it is not optional or lift-specific.

questions.prompt: A classroom tunnel model has a frontal area that is 8% of the test-section area. What does this figure represent, and is it acceptable?

options.text: The blockage ratio; acceptable, since it falls under the roughly 5–10% guideline where tunnel walls do not significantly inflate measured drag
The Reynolds number; unacceptable because it is far too low
The lift coefficient; irrelevant to a drag study
The mount tare correction; acceptable regardless of value

explanations.a: Correct — this is the blockage ratio (model frontal area as a fraction of test-section area); staying under roughly 5–10% keeps wall-constraint effects from artificially inflating the measured drag, so 8% is within the acceptable range.
explanations.b: Reynolds number is a speed/size/viscosity ratio, not an area ratio; an 8% figure in this context describes blockage, not Re.
explanations.c: Lift coefficient is a force ratio, not an area ratio, and is not what an 8% figure here describes.
explanations.d: Mount tare correction is a subtracted drag value from a separate run, not a percentage of test-section area.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a trustworthy classroom drag-crisis experiment on a sphere, from first to last.

items.text: Choose a question the tunnel can resolve (e.g., trip-strip effect on sphere Cd) and check blockage ratio is under roughly 5–10%
Run a mount tare test to measure the empty support's own drag
Run bare-sphere and tripped-sphere configurations several times each at matched dynamic pressure q
Report Cd with its test Reynolds number, error bars from repeat runs, and the scaling limitation relative to full-scale Re

questions.explanation: A sound study first picks a resolvable question and checks blockage is acceptable, then establishes the tare correction before taking data, then collects repeated matched-q runs for each configuration, and finally reports results with Reynolds number, error bars, and an explicit statement of what the test Re does and does not let you claim about full scale.

units.label: Confined Flow Fundamentals and the Laminar Solution

lessons.label: Why a Pipe Is Not a Free Stream

sections.heading: The fluid is surrounded, not streaming past
sections.body: Everything in external aerodynamics — a wing, a car, a cyclist — sits inside an effectively infinite fluid with a well-defined free-stream velocity far from the body. Internal flow flips that picture: the wall wraps completely around the fluid, there is no undisturbed region to reference, and nothing 'arrives' at a pipe the way air arrives at an airfoil. Motion through a duct is driven from inside the flow itself, by an imposed pressure difference between inlet and outlet, not by an oncoming stream meeting an obstacle. A pump, a reservoir head, or a compressor sets up delta_p across the length L, and the fluid moves because the wall confines it into a single admissible direction. This is the branch's core reframing: internal-flow problems are posed in terms of driving pressure and flow rate, not in terms of angle of attack or freestream Mach number.

sections.heading: Continuity in a duct: Q, mass flow, and area
sections.body: Mass conservation for steady incompressible flow reduces to a single control-volume statement: volumetric flow rate Q = V*A is constant along the duct, and mass flow rate mdot = rho*Q. This holds station to station even where the cross-sectional area A itself varies along the duct's length — a converging nozzle section, a sudden expansion, a tapered fitting — because no fluid can accumulate between two fixed stations in steady flow. So for any two stations 1 and 2 along the same duct, Q1 = Q2 gives V1*A1 = V2*A2: wherever the duct narrows, the bulk velocity must rise in exact proportion, and wherever it widens, the bulk velocity must fall. A nozzle that halves the flow area, for instance, doubles the bulk velocity passing through it, with no extra assumption needed beyond incompressibility. This is the internal-flow analog of the streamtube argument used in external flow, except here the 'streamtube' is the pipe wall itself, so there is no ambiguity about where the control volume boundary sits.

sections.heading: Point velocity versus bulk velocity
sections.body: No-slip at the wall means the local point velocity u(r) is zero at r = R and maximum at the centerline — it is never uniform across the section. Because most engineering questions (how much fluid arrives, how long does filling take) care about total delivery rather than the local profile shape, internal-flow analysis defines a bulk (mean, or area-averaged) velocity V = (1/A) * integral of u dA over the cross-section, chosen so that V*A reproduces the true Q. V is a bookkeeping velocity, not a velocity any fluid particle actually has, and every downstream formula in this unit (Reynolds number, head loss, Hagen-Poiseuille) is written in terms of V, not the unmeasurable u(r) at some arbitrary radius.

lessons.workedExample: A 2 cm-diameter (A = 3.14e-4 m^2) pipe carries water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3) at Q = 1.5 L/s = 1.5e-3 m^3/s. Bulk velocity V = Q/A = 1.5e-3 / 3.14e-4 = 4.78 m/s, and mass flow mdot = rho*Q = 1.5 kg/s. Even though the true velocity profile u(r) ranges from 0 at the wall to some centerline maximum well above 4.78 m/s, every practical question here — fill time for a 200 L tank (133 s), pump sizing, downstream Reynolds number — uses the single bulk value V, because that is what the pressure difference driving the flow actually controls through Q = V*A.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is this a free-stream problem or a confined problem?' to check whether a student has loaded the right mental model before writing any equation. A project that treats a pipe like a wing in a wind tunnel — talking about angle of attack, or expecting an undisturbed upstream region — signals confusion at the setup stage that no amount of correct arithmetic later can fix. A student who instead says 'flow here is driven by the pressure drop across the duct, and I'm using the area-averaged velocity because that's what continuity and my flow meter actually give me' has correctly separated the two branches of fluid dynamics before doing any calculation.

questions.prompt: What primarily drives fluid motion through a confined duct, in contrast to external flow over a body?

options.text: An oncoming free-stream velocity far from the duct
An imposed pressure difference between inlet and outlet
The angle of attack of the duct wall
Gravity acting on the duct material itself

explanations.a: There is no free stream in internal flow — the wall surrounds the fluid everywhere, so there is no undisturbed upstream region to define one.
explanations.b: Correct — a pump, reservoir head, or compressor sets up a pressure difference delta_p across the duct length, and that pressure gradient is what pushes the fluid through.
explanations.c: Angle of attack is an external-aerodynamics concept describing a body's orientation to a free stream; it has no meaning for flow confined inside a duct.
explanations.d: Gravity can contribute an elevation-head term in some ducts, but it is not the general driver of internal flow — pressure difference is.

questions.prompt: Why does internal-flow analysis define a bulk (area-averaged) velocity V instead of just using the point velocity u(r)?

options.text: Because u(r) is uniform across the pipe so V equals u(r) everywhere anyway
Because no-slip makes u(r) vary from zero at the wall to a maximum at the centerline, and V = (1/A)*integral(u dA) is the single value that reproduces the true Q = V*A
Because point velocity cannot be defined mathematically inside a pipe
Because bulk velocity is always numerically equal to the maximum centerline velocity

explanations.a: No-slip guarantees u(r) is not uniform — it is zero at the wall and peaks at the centerline, so this option contradicts the physics.
explanations.b: Correct — u(r) varies across the section, so engineers use the area-averaged V, defined so that V*A reproduces the actual volumetric flow rate Q, as the practical bookkeeping velocity.
explanations.c: Point velocity is perfectly well-defined at any radius; the issue is that it varies with r, not that it cannot be defined.
explanations.d: V is always less than the centerline maximum for a non-uniform profile; the two are equal only in the idealized case of perfectly uniform (plug) flow.

questions.prompt: A 2 cm-diameter pipe (A = 3.14e-4 m^2) carries water at Q = 1.5e-3 m^3/s. What is the bulk velocity V?

options.text: About 0.21 m/s
About 4.78 m/s
About 47.8 m/s
About 1.5 m/s

explanations.a: This is A/Q inverted, not V = Q/A; dividing area by flow rate gives the wrong quantity and wrong units.
explanations.b: Correct — V = Q/A = 1.5e-3 / 3.14e-4 ≈ 4.78 m/s, exactly as computed in the worked example.
explanations.c: This is off by a factor of 10 from the correct division of Q by A.
explanations.d: This is just Q's numeric value in different units mistaken for V; it ignores dividing by the cross-sectional area entirely.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct description in confined pipe flow.

right.text: Equals V*A for a fixed cross-section
Equals rho*Q
The area average (1/A)*integral(u dA), chosen to reproduce Q
Zero at the wall, maximum at the centerline due to no-slip

questions.explanation: Q = V*A by continuity, mdot = rho*Q by definition of mass flow, V is the area-averaged velocity constructed so V*A reproduces Q, and u(r) is the true local profile that no-slip forces to zero at the wall while peaking at the centerline.

lessons.label: Heads, the Energy Equation and Head Loss

sections.heading: From Bernoulli to the real, lossy pipe
sections.body: Ideal Bernoulli's equation (p/(rho*g) + V^2/(2g) + z = constant) assumes frictionless, inviscid flow along a streamline — an assumption no real pipe satisfies, since viscosity is exactly what makes the fluid stick to the wall. Real internal-flow analysis instead uses the extended energy equation between two sections 1 and 2: p1/(rho*g) + alpha1*V1^2/(2g) + z1 + h_pump = p2/(rho*g) + alpha2*V2^2/(2g) + z2 + h_turbine + h_L. Every term has units of length ('head') because dividing energy per unit weight by rho*g converts joules per newton into meters, which is why engineers speak of pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head rather than raw energy. h_pump adds head (a pump), h_turbine removes head (a turbine extracting work), and h_L is head lost to friction — always positive, always subtracted, never recoverable.

sections.heading: The correction factor alpha: why V^2/2g alone isn't quite right
sections.body: Because kinetic energy depends on velocity squared, and the true profile u(r) is not uniform, the average of u^2 across the section is not equal to V^2 (the square of the average). The kinetic-energy correction factor alpha fixes this: true KE flux = alpha*rho*Q*V^2/2, with alpha = (1/A)*integral((u/V)^3 dA). For the parabolic laminar profile derived later in this unit, alpha works out to exactly 2.0 — a large correction, because the profile is very non-uniform. For turbulent flow, the profile is much flatter (fuller) near the wall, so alpha is close to 1.0, typically about 1.05. Using alpha = 1 for laminar flow is a common source of error in student energy-balance calculations, understating kinetic head by a factor of two.

sections.heading: Head loss and the two grade lines
sections.body: h_L represents irreversible conversion of useful mechanical (pressure + kinetic + potential) energy into internal energy (heat) via viscous friction — it can never be negative and can never be recovered downstream. The standard diagnostic picture is two lines drawn along the pipe: the energy grade line (EGL), plotting total head p/(rho*g) + alpha*V^2/(2g) + z, which always slopes downward in the flow direction (steeper where losses are concentrated, e.g. at fittings) except for a jump up at a pump; and the hydraulic grade line (HGL), plotting just p/(rho*g) + z, which sits exactly one velocity head (alpha*V^2/2g) below the EGL — moving closer to the EGL where the pipe widens (velocity head falls) and dropping further below it where the pipe narrows (velocity head rises). Sketching EGL and HGL before computing anything catches sign errors and identifies where a pipe might run at sub-atmospheric pressure (risking cavitation, specifically at a narrowing where the HGL dips lowest) long before the algebra would reveal it.

lessons.workedExample: Water flows from a reservoir surface (V1 ≈ 0, p1 = 0 gauge, z1 = 20 m) through a pipe with no pump or turbine to a discharge point (z2 = 0 m, p2 = 0 gauge, V2 = 6 m/s, turbulent so alpha2 ≈ 1.05). The energy equation gives 20 = 1.05*(6^2)/(2*9.81) + h_L, so 20 = 1.93 + h_L, giving h_L = 18.07 m. If a student mistakenly used alpha = 1.0, they would compute velocity head as 1.83 m instead of 1.93 m — a small but systematic 5% underestimate of the kinetic term, and a 50% underestimate (exactly half the correct kinetic head) if the flow were actually laminar (alpha = 2.0) rather than turbulent.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to sketch the EGL and HGL for their setup because it is the fastest way to tell whether they understand energy accounting versus having memorized a formula. A student who draws the EGL as flat, or has it rise without a pump, reveals they don't grasp that h_L is strictly irreversible. A student who correctly picks alpha = 2.0 for a laminar capillary flow and alpha ≈ 1.05 for a turbulent process line — rather than defaulting to 1.0 everywhere — demonstrates they understand that kinetic energy flux depends on the actual shape of the velocity profile, not just its mean.

questions.prompt: In the extended energy equation, why does h_L always appear as a term that reduces available head, never as one that can be negative?

options.text: Because it represents irreversible conversion of mechanical energy to heat via viscous friction, which cannot spontaneously reverse
Because pipes are always oriented so elevation decreases
Because pumps always add more head than friction removes
Because h_L is defined as the negative of the pressure head

explanations.a: Correct — h_L is the head lost irreversibly to viscous dissipation (heat), and the second law prevents that dissipated energy from spontaneously converting back into useful mechanical head.
explanations.b: Pipe orientation affects the elevation head term z, not h_L, which is a friction loss independent of whether the pipe runs uphill or downhill.
explanations.c: Whether a pump's added head exceeds friction losses is a case-by-case system design question, not a reason h_L itself must stay positive.
explanations.d: h_L is a friction-loss term separate from and unrelated in sign to the pressure head p/(rho*g).

questions.prompt: What is the kinetic-energy correction factor alpha for fully developed laminar (parabolic) pipe flow?

explanations.a: alpha = 1.0 applies only to a perfectly uniform (plug) profile, which laminar flow is not.
explanations.b: 1.05 is the typical turbulent value, where the flatter near-wall profile makes the correction small, not the laminar value.
explanations.c: Correct — the parabolic laminar profile is highly non-uniform, and integrating (u/V)^3 across it yields exactly alpha = 2.0.
explanations.d: alpha cannot be less than 1.0 for any physically realizable profile, since (u/V)^3 averaged is always at least as large as the cube of the average by convexity.

questions.prompt: Water drains from a reservoir (z1 = 20 m, V1 ≈ 0, p1 = p2 = 0 gauge) to a point at z2 = 0 m with turbulent exit velocity V2 = 6 m/s (alpha2 = 1.05) and no pump/turbine. What is the head loss h_L?

explanations.a: This ignores the velocity head entirely, as if all 20 m of elevation head became loss with none converted to kinetic energy.
explanations.b: Correct — velocity head is 1.05*(6^2)/(2*9.81) = 1.93 m, so h_L = 20 - 1.93 = 18.07 m, matching the worked example.
explanations.c: This is the velocity head itself, not the head loss — it's the term being subtracted, not the result.
explanations.d: This would come from doubling the velocity head subtraction, which does not follow from the energy balance.

questions.prompt: Match each grade-line concept to its correct description.

left.text: Vertical gap between EGL and HGL
Effect of a pump on the EGL

right.text: Plots p/(rho*g) + alpha*V^2/(2g) + z; always slopes downward except at a pump
Plots just p/(rho*g) + z
Equal to the velocity head, alpha*V^2/(2g)
Causes an upward jump in the EGL

questions.explanation: The EGL tracks total head and only drops (friction) or jumps up (a pump adding energy); the HGL omits the velocity-head term and so sits one velocity head below the EGL at every station; a pump is the one feature that raises the EGL rather than letting it fall.

lessons.label: Reynolds Number Inside a Pipe

sections.heading: The pipe-flow Reynolds number and its practical bands
sections.body: Specialized to internal flow, the Reynolds number is Re = rho*V*D/mu = V*D/nu, using the bulk velocity V and the pipe diameter D as the characteristic length. It compares inertial forces (which want to keep disturbances growing) to viscous forces (which want to damp them out). Decades of pipe experiments converge on three practical bands: below about Re = 2300 the flow is reliably laminar — smooth, layered, no mixing across streamlines; between roughly 2300 and 4000 lies a transitional band where the flow is unpredictable, intermittently switching between laminar and turbulent patches (called puffs or slugs) depending on entrance conditions, wall roughness, and vibration; above about Re = 4000 the flow is turbulent — chaotic, three-dimensional, and efficiently mixing across the cross-section.

sections.heading: Thresholds, not physical constants
sections.body: It is tempting to treat Re = 2300 as a hard physical law, but it is really an engineering threshold describing what happens in an ordinary pipe with the small disturbances (roughness, inlet turbulence, vibration) any real installation has. Osborne Reynolds himself, in his landmark 1883 dye-streak experiments, showed that with an extraordinarily smooth, disturbance-free glass tube and a calm, vibration-isolated inlet, laminar flow could persist to Reynolds numbers far above 4000 — sometimes cited well past 10,000. The instability that eventually triggers turbulence is genuinely present at lower Re too, but it needs a large enough disturbance to trigger it; a pristine lab setup removes those disturbances and pushes transition later. For any real engineering pipe — with a valve, an elbow, or ordinary manufacturing roughness upstream — 2300–4000 remains the reliable practical band, which is why every plumbing and process-design handbook uses it.

sections.heading: Reynolds number governs the rest of the unit
sections.body: Every remaining lesson in this unit is organized around which side of these thresholds a flow sits on: the entrance length scaling, the existence (or not) of the Hagen-Poiseuille parabolic solution, and the friction-factor formula all branch on Re. A single dimensionless number, computed from three or four measurable quantities, tells you which physical regime — and which set of equations — applies before you do anything else. Take friction factor as a concrete example: for laminar flow, f = 64/Re is exact, so at Re = 2000 (still laminar) f = 64/2000 = 0.032. Push the same pipe to Re = 100,000 (turbulent, smooth wall) and a standard turbulent correlation gives f in roughly the 0.017-0.02 range — a different formula entirely, not just a different number plugged into the same one. Using the laminar f = 64/Re formula on a turbulent flow, or a turbulent correlation on a laminar one, gives a wrong answer even with perfectly correct arithmetic, because Re selects which physics — and which equation — is in play before any numbers go in.

lessons.workedExample: Four systems, same formula, wildly different regimes. Garden hose: D = 0.016 m, V ≈ 1.5 m/s, water nu = 1e-6 m^2/s, giving Re = 1.5*0.016/1e-6 = 24,000 — solidly turbulent, which is why hose flow feels chaotic and noisy. A 4 mm capillary tube: D = 0.004 m, V = 0.1 m/s, same water nu, giving Re = 0.1*0.004/1e-6 = 400 — laminar, well below 2300. The human aorta at peak systole: diameter ~2.5 cm, peak blood velocity driving Re up to roughly 4000 — right at the laminar-turbulent threshold, which is why brief, transient turbulent-like disturbances during peak systole are a recognized physiological phenomenon. A crude-oil pipeline: D = 0.9 m, V ≈ 1.5 m/s, oil nu ≈ 1e-5 m^2/s (oil is far more viscous than water), giving Re = 1.5*0.9/1e-5 = 135,000 — still turbulent despite the oil's higher viscosity, because the pipeline's huge diameter and flow speed dominate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to compute Re for their own setup because it is the single fastest sanity check on whether the student picked the right governing equations. A student who reports a laminar-flow result (say, from Hagen-Poiseuille) for a Re = 20,000 system has silently applied the wrong physics, and a judge who does the mental Re estimate in ten seconds will catch it immediately. The stronger answer also distinguishes '2300 is a practical threshold for ordinary disturbed pipes' from '2300 is a hard physical law' — citing Reynolds's own 1883 result that pristine, vibration-free tubes stay laminar far higher shows the student understands transition as disturbance-triggered instability, not a magic number.

questions.prompt: Which characteristic length is used in the pipe-flow Reynolds number Re = rho*V*D/mu?

options.text: The pipe length L
The pipe diameter D
The entrance length L_e
The wall roughness height

explanations.a: Pipe length appears in head-loss and pressure-drop formulas, but it is not the characteristic length in the Reynolds number itself.
explanations.b: Correct — internal-flow Reynolds number uses the diameter D as the characteristic length, since it sets the scale of the velocity profile and the distance over which viscous effects act.
explanations.c: Entrance length is itself a quantity that depends on Re (see the next lesson); it is not an input to computing Re.
explanations.d: Roughness height matters for the friction factor in turbulent flow, but it is not part of the standard Reynolds-number definition.

questions.prompt: A 4 mm capillary carries water (nu = 1e-6 m^2/s) at V = 0.1 m/s. What is Re, and what regime does it indicate?

options.text: Re = 400, laminar
Re = 4000, transitional
Re = 40,000, turbulent
Re = 40, laminar

explanations.a: Correct — Re = V*D/nu = 0.1*0.004/1e-6 = 400, well below 2300, so the flow is laminar, matching the worked example.
explanations.b: This overstates Re by a factor of 10; the arithmetic gives 400, not 4000.
explanations.c: This overstates Re by a factor of 100.
explanations.d: This understates Re by a factor of 10; correctly dividing gives 400, not 40.

questions.prompt: Osborne Reynolds's 1883 dye-streak experiments showed that laminar flow in a pristine, vibration-free glass tube could persist far above Re = 4000. What does this imply about the 2300–4000 transitional band?

options.text: The 2300–4000 band is a fixed physical constant that never changes under any conditions

The band is a practical threshold for ordinary disturbed pipes; transition is triggered by disturbances, so removing them (roughness, vibration, inlet turbulence) pushes the onset of turbulence to much higher Re
Reynolds's result proves the transitional band does not exist at all
The band only applies to gases, not liquids

explanations.a: Reynolds's own experiment contradicts this — a sufficiently smooth, disturbance-free tube pushed transition well past 4000, so the band is not a universal constant.
explanations.b: Correct — the underlying instability exists at lower Re too, but needs a disturbance large enough to trigger it; ordinary pipes with roughness and inlet turbulence transition in the 2300–4000 band, while a pristine setup delays transition.
explanations.c: The transitional band is real and well documented for ordinary engineering pipes; Reynolds's result refines its interpretation rather than eliminating it.
explanations.d: Reynolds's classic experiments used water in glass tubes; the result concerns disturbance sensitivity generally, not a gas-versus-liquid distinction.

questions.prompt: A crude-oil pipeline has D = 0.9 m, V = 1.5 m/s, and oil kinematic viscosity nu = 1e-5 m^2/s (ten times water's). What regime is this flow in?

options.text: Laminar, because oil is much more viscous than water
Turbulent, because Re = 1.5*0.9/1e-5 = 135,000, well above 4000 despite the higher viscosity
Transitional, right at the 2300–4000 boundary
Impossible to determine without knowing the pipeline's total length

explanations.a: Higher viscosity alone does not guarantee laminar flow — the large diameter and flow speed can still push Re well into the turbulent range, as the arithmetic shows.
explanations.b: Correct — Re = 135,000, matching the worked example; the pipeline's large diameter and speed dominate over the oil's tenfold-higher viscosity.
explanations.c: 135,000 is more than 30 times the top of the transitional band, not close to its boundary.
explanations.d: Reynolds number depends on V, D, and nu, not on total pipeline length; it can be computed from the given values alone.

lessons.label: Entrance Length and Fully Developed Flow

sections.heading: Boundary layers growing inward from the wall
sections.body: Fluid entering a pipe from a reservoir or a straight duct arrives with a nearly uniform velocity profile across the whole cross-section. The instant it touches the wall, no-slip forces the velocity there to zero, and a viscous boundary layer begins growing inward from the wall, just as it would over a flat plate. Outside that thin layer, an inviscid 'core' still moves at close to the original uniform speed, and because the core carries less and less of the flow as the boundary layers thicken, continuity forces the core to accelerate. This growth continues until the boundary layers from all sides of the pipe meet at the centerline — at that point the viscous influence of the wall has diffused all the way across the section, and the velocity profile stops changing shape from station to station.

sections.heading: Fully developed flow: what stops changing
sections.body: Once the profile shape becomes invariant with downstream distance x (du/dx = 0 for the velocity profile itself, though the fluid is still accelerating along streamlines within that fixed shape), the flow is called fully developed. A key consequence is that the pressure gradient dp/dx becomes constant along the pipe in this region — all of the pressure drop is now doing the same job at every station, balancing wall friction against a fluid moving at constant profile shape, rather than partly going into reshaping the profile. This is the regime in which the clean, closed-form solutions of this unit — the Hagen-Poiseuille parabola, the f = 64/Re friction factor — are derived; they describe fully developed flow specifically, not the entrance region.

sections.heading: How far the entrance region extends
sections.body: The distance from the inlet to where the profile is considered fully developed is the entrance length L_e, and it scales very differently for laminar and turbulent flow. For laminar flow, the commonly used engineering correlation is L_e/D ≈ 0.05*Re (other references, using a slightly different theoretical fit, cite ≈0.06*Re — the two conventions agree to within about 20%) — at the upper laminar limit of Re = 2300, that gives L_e/D ≈ 115, meaning the entrance region can occupy over a hundred diameters of pipe. For turbulent flow, the more vigorous cross-stream mixing accelerates development dramatically: L_e/D ≈ 4.4*Re^(1/6), which for typical turbulent pipe Reynolds numbers works out to roughly 10 to 60 diameters — an order of magnitude shorter, relatively, than the laminar case, because turbulent eddies mix momentum across the section far faster than viscous diffusion alone.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs water at Re = 2000 (laminar) through a D = 1 cm tube and places a pressure tap 20 cm (20 diameters) from the inlet to measure friction factor. The laminar entrance length is L_e/D ≈ 0.05*2000 = 100, or L_e = 100 cm — five times longer than where the tap sits. At 20 diameters the profile is still developing: the core is still accelerating and the wall shear (and therefore the local pressure gradient) is steeper than the fully developed value, because part of the pressure drop there is still going into reshaping the velocity profile rather than purely balancing friction. The student's measured friction factor will read artificially high, and the error disappears only if the tap is moved past roughly 100 diameters or the theoretical fully developed dp/dx is used instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes entrance length because it is the most common invisible flaw in a student pressure-drop or friction-factor measurement: the equipment works, the pressure gauge reads a real number, but if the tap sits inside the developing region the number does not mean what the student thinks it means. A student who can state 'my tap is at 20 diameters, but at Re = 2000 the laminar entrance length is about 100 diameters, so my reading is contaminated by developing flow' has diagnosed a systematic bias a superficial analysis would never catch. The right fix — moving the tap downstream, or accounting for the extra entrance pressure drop — is a strong sign of real experimental fluency.

questions.prompt: Order the physical events, from pipe inlet to fully developed flow.

items.text: Fluid enters the pipe with a nearly uniform velocity profile
No-slip forces velocity to zero at the wall; a viscous boundary layer begins growing inward
The inviscid core, carrying a shrinking share of the flow, accelerates as the boundary layers thicken
Boundary layers from all sides meet at the centerline
The velocity profile shape stops changing with downstream distance; dp/dx becomes constant

questions.explanation: Flow enters uniform, no-slip immediately starts a wall boundary layer, the shrinking inviscid core accelerates by continuity, the boundary layers eventually merge at the centerline, and beyond that point the profile shape and pressure gradient both become constant — the fully developed state.

questions.prompt: At Re = 2300 (the upper laminar limit), approximately how many pipe diameters does the laminar entrance length span, using L_e/D ≈ 0.05*Re?

options.text: About 11.5 diameters
About 115 diameters
About 1150 diameters
About 2300 diameters

explanations.a: This is off by a factor of 10 from 0.05*2300.
explanations.b: Correct — 0.05*2300 = 115, so the laminar entrance region can occupy over a hundred diameters before the profile is fully developed.
explanations.c: This overstates the correlation by a factor of 10.
explanations.d: This mistakes Re itself for L_e/D; the 0.05 scaling factor must be applied.

questions.prompt: Why is the turbulent entrance length, relative to diameter, generally much shorter than the laminar one at comparable Reynolds numbers?

options.text: Turbulent flow has lower viscosity than laminar flow
Turbulent eddies mix momentum across the cross-section far faster than viscous diffusion alone can in laminar flow
Turbulent pipes are always shorter than laminar pipes
Turbulent flow has no boundary layer at the wall

explanations.a: Viscosity is a fluid property independent of whether the flow happens to be laminar or turbulent at a given condition.
explanations.b: Correct — vigorous turbulent eddies transport momentum across the section much faster than slow molecular viscous diffusion, so the profile develops in far fewer diameters (roughly 10-60D versus 0.05*Re for laminar).
explanations.c: Entrance length is a fraction of pipe length development, not a statement about total installed pipe length.
explanations.d: Turbulent flow still has a thin viscous sublayer at the wall; it is not the absence of a wall layer that shortens development, but faster cross-stream mixing.

questions.prompt: A student places a pressure tap 20 diameters from the inlet of a laminar (Re = 2000) pipe to compute a friction factor. What is the practical consequence?

options.text: No consequence, since 20 diameters is well past the entrance length of 100 diameters
The measured friction factor reads artificially high, because the tap sits inside the still-developing region where the pressure gradient is steeper than the fully developed value
The measured friction factor reads artificially low
The result is unaffected because friction factor only depends on Re, not on tap location

explanations.a: This has it backwards — at Re = 2000, L_e/D ≈ 0.05*2000 = 100, so 20 diameters is well inside the developing region, not past it.
explanations.b: Correct — inside the entrance region, part of the pressure drop is reshaping the profile, making the local gradient steeper than the fully developed dp/dx, which biases a friction-factor measurement high.
explanations.c: The developing-region gradient is steeper, not shallower, than fully developed, so the bias runs high, not low.
explanations.d: Friction factor correlations like f = 64/Re assume fully developed flow; measuring inside the entrance region violates that assumption and biases the result regardless of the true Re.

lessons.label: Hagen-Poiseuille: Deriving Laminar Pipe Flow

sections.heading: A force balance on a cylindrical fluid element
sections.body: Consider fully developed, steady, laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a straight circular tube of radius R. Because the flow is fully developed, the profile no longer changes with axial position and there is no radial velocity component — fluid moves only in the axial direction. Because the flow is also axisymmetric, nothing depends on the angular position around the tube. Together these two facts collapse what could be a full three-dimensional problem into a one-dimensional balance along the radius alone. Isolate a thin cylindrical fluid element of radius r and length L, coaxial with the pipe. Two forces act on its surfaces along the flow direction: pressure pushing it forward, delta_p*(pi*r^2), and viscous shear tau resisting on its outer curved surface, tau*(2*pi*r*L). Because the flow is fully developed (no acceleration), these must balance: delta_p*(pi*r^2) = tau*(2*pi*r*L), giving tau(r) = (delta_p/L)*(r/2) — shear stress grows linearly from zero at the centerline to a maximum at the wall.

sections.heading: Integrating with Newton's law of viscosity
sections.body: For a Newtonian fluid, shear stress and the velocity gradient are related by tau = -mu*du/dr, not tau = +mu*du/dr. The minus sign is required to keep the two quantities consistent: tau(r) derived above is positive for r > 0, but u(r) decreases outward from the centerline to zero at the wall, so du/dr is negative — without the minus sign, a positive tau would force du/dr positive, which is backwards. Substituting tau(r) = (delta_p/L)*(r/2) gives -mu*du/dr = (delta_p/L)*(r/2), so du/dr = -(delta_p)/(2*mu*L)*r. Integrating once: u(r) = -(delta_p)/(4*mu*L)*r^2 + C. The no-slip condition u(R) = 0 fixes the constant, giving the parabolic velocity profile u(r) = (delta_p)/(4*mu*L)*(R^2 - r^2), or equivalently u(r) = u_max*(1 - r^2/R^2) where u_max = (delta_p*R^2)/(4*mu*L) occurs at r = 0.

sections.heading: From the profile to Q, V, and the friction factor
sections.body: Integrating u(r) over the cross-section, Q = integral of u(r)*2*pi*r dr from 0 to R. Substituting the profile u(r) = (delta_p)/(4*mu*L)*(R^2 - r^2) gives Q = integral from 0 to R of [(delta_p)/(4*mu*L)*(R^2 - r^2)]*2*pi*r dr, and pulling the constants out front leaves Q = (delta_p*pi)/(2*mu*L) * integral from 0 to R of (R^2*r - r^3) dr. That integral evaluates term by term to R^2*r^2/2 - r^4/4, and at the upper limit r = R this is R^4/2 - R^4/4 = R^4/4. So Q = (delta_p*pi)/(2*mu*L) * (R^4/4) = pi*delta_p*R^4/(8*mu*L), which is the Hagen-Poiseuille law; converting R = D/2 gives the equivalent diameter form Q = pi*delta_p*D^4/(128*mu*L) — flow rate scales with the fourth power of diameter, the single most consequential fact in this unit. Dividing by area gives the bulk velocity V = Q/(pi*R^2) = u_max/2: the mean velocity of a parabolic profile is exactly half its peak. Rearranging Hagen-Poiseuille to solve for delta_p and substituting into the definition of the Darcy friction factor f = (delta_p/L)*(D/(rho*V^2/2)) produces f = 64/Re — laminar friction factor depends on Reynolds number alone, with no dependence on wall roughness, unlike the turbulent case.

lessons.workedExample: A capillary viscometer forces glycerin (mu = 1.0 Pa*s) through a D = 2 mm, L = 0.5 m tube under delta_p = 8000 Pa. Q = pi*delta_p*D^4/(128*mu*L) = pi*8000*(1.6e-11)/(128*1.0*0.5) = pi*(1.28e-7)/64 ≈ 6.28e-9 m^3/s, a tiny flow of about 6.3 microliters per second — exactly the scale a fine capillary should produce under modest pressure. Dividing by the cross-sectional area A = pi*R^2 ≈ 3.14e-6 m^2 gives V = Q/A ≈ 2.0 mm/s, and u_max = 2*V ≈ 4.0 mm/s. This is exactly the geometry Hagen used in 1839 and Poiseuille refined through the 1840s: force a viscous liquid through a fine capillary and measure Q against delta_p to back out mu, decades before Navier and Stokes's theory was reconciled with these empirical results.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to derive, not just quote, Hagen-Poiseuille because the derivation is where the physics lives: the linear shear-stress balance, the no-slip boundary condition, and the D^4 scaling all fall out of a single force balance plus Newton's law of viscosity. A student who can only recite Q = pi*delta_p*D^4/(128*mu*L) cannot explain why doubling the diameter increases flow sixteenfold, while a student who walks through the force balance can. Naming Hagen (1839) and Poiseuille (1840s) as independent experimentalists who found this law empirically, well before the underlying theory was fully reconciled, also signals real command of the history behind the equation, not just the formula.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Hagen-Poiseuille derivation.

items.text: Balance pressure force delta_p*(pi*r^2) against viscous shear tau*(2*pi*r*L) on a cylindrical fluid element
Substitute Newton's law tau = -mu*du/dr into the shear-stress relation
Integrate and apply no-slip (u = 0 at r = R) to get the parabolic profile u(r) = u_max*(1 - r^2/R^2)
Integrate u(r) over the cross-section to get Q = pi*delta_p*D^4/(128*mu*L)
Substitute Q into the Darcy friction-factor definition to obtain f = 64/Re

questions.explanation: The derivation starts from a force balance giving shear stress vs. radius, brings in Newton's law of viscosity to relate shear to the velocity gradient, integrates with the no-slip condition to get the parabolic profile, integrates that profile over the area to get Q, and finally converts Q into the dimensionless friction factor f = 64/Re.

questions.prompt: How does the bulk (mean) velocity V relate to the centerline maximum velocity u_max in fully developed laminar pipe flow?

options.text: V = u_max (they are equal)
V = u_max/2
V = u_max/4
V = 2*u_max

explanations.a: This would only hold for a uniform (plug) profile; the parabolic laminar profile is not uniform.
explanations.b: Correct — integrating the parabolic profile over the circular area and dividing by that area gives V = u_max/2, exactly half the centerline peak.
explanations.c: This is off by a factor of 2 from the correct area-averaged result.
explanations.d: V cannot exceed u_max for a profile that peaks at the centerline; the mean of a decreasing function from its own maximum must be smaller, not larger.

questions.prompt: In the Hagen-Poiseuille law Q = pi*delta_p*D^4/(128*mu*L), what happens to Q if the diameter D is doubled while delta_p, mu, and L are held fixed?

options.text: Q doubles
Q quadruples
Q increases by a factor of 16
Q is unaffected by diameter

explanations.a: This assumes a linear dependence on D, but Q depends on D^4, not D^1.
explanations.b: This assumes Q depends on D^2, but the correct exponent is 4.
explanations.c: Correct — because Q scales with D^4, doubling D multiplies Q by 2^4 = 16, the single most consequential fact in the Hagen-Poiseuille relation.
explanations.d: Q is extremely sensitive to diameter, not independent of it — this is exactly why bore metrology matters so much for capillary experiments.

questions.prompt: What is historically notable about how the Hagen-Poiseuille law was first established?

options.text: It was derived purely from the Navier-Stokes equations before any experiments were run
Hagen (1839) and Poiseuille (1840s) each found the law experimentally and independently, decades before the underlying theory was fully reconciled
It was discovered simultaneously by Reynolds and Bernoulli in the 18th century
It has never been experimentally verified and remains purely theoretical

explanations.a: The historical order ran the other way — the empirical law came first, from capillary-tube experiments, with theoretical reconciliation following later.
explanations.b: Correct — Hagen (1839) and Poiseuille, working through the 1840s, independently found the D^4 relationship experimentally using capillary-tube setups, before the equation's derivation from the Navier-Stokes equations was fully connected to their results.
explanations.c: Neither Reynolds nor Bernoulli is credited with this specific law; Reynolds's landmark contribution (covered elsewhere in this unit) concerns the transition to turbulence, not this laminar solution.
explanations.d: The law is one of the most thoroughly experimentally verified results in fluid mechanics, starting with Hagen's and Poiseuille's own 19th-century measurements.

lessons.label: The Fine Print: Where Poiseuille Breaks

sections.heading: Every assumption is a place the equation can fail
sections.body: Q = pi*delta_p*D^4/(128*mu*L) was derived under a specific stack of assumptions, and each one is a real system where it can quietly fail: steady flow (no pulsing or ramping), incompressible fluid, Newtonian fluid (constant mu, independent of shear rate), fully developed flow (past the entrance length), laminar flow (Re below ~2300), no-slip at the wall, and a rigid, straight, circular tube. Treat the derivation as a checklist before applying the formula to any real system, not as a universal law of pipe flow.

sections.heading: Fluids that break the Newtonian assumption
sections.body: Blood is the canonical failure case: it is shear-thinning (viscosity drops as shear rate rises, due to red-cell deformation and aggregation) and its effective viscosity even depends on tube diameter — the Fahraeus-Lindqvist effect, in which apparent viscosity falls as vessel diameter shrinks below roughly 300 micrometers, because red cells migrate toward the centerline and leave a cell-free plasma layer near the wall. Polymer solutions and paints show similar shear-thinning behavior. For any of these, plugging measured mu into Hagen-Poiseuille as if it were a constant gives a systematically wrong Q-versus-delta_p curve; a proper analysis needs a non-Newtonian constitutive model (e.g., Casson or power-law) integrated the same way the Newtonian case was.

sections.heading: Unsteady, microscale, and compliant failures
sections.body: Pulsatile flow — blood driven by a beating heart, or any pump with a duty cycle — violates the steady-flow assumption; the relevant dimensionless group is the Womersley number, introduced by Womersley in 1955, which compares the pulsation frequency's unsteady inertia to viscous forces and tells you whether the instantaneous profile still looks parabolic (low Womersley number) or lags badly behind the pressure signal (high Womersley number, as in the aorta). At the microchannel scale, apparent slip at the wall and surface-tension-dominated effects can violate no-slip itself. Compliant tubing (a blood vessel, a soft silicone hose) violates the rigid-tube assumption because the tube diameter itself responds to the local pressure, coupling the flow equation to the wall's elastic mechanics rather than letting D stay fixed.

sections.heading: The D^4 sensitivity makes metrology the whole experiment
sections.body: Because Q depends on D^4, a small measurement error in bore diameter is amplified fourfold in relative terms: a 2% error in D produces roughly an 8% error in predicted Q (since a 1+x fractional change in D gives approximately 1+4x in D^4 for small x). This is why capillary-tube viscosity experiments live or die on how precisely the bore diameter is known — a cheaply manufactured or slightly out-of-round capillary can dominate the total experimental error budget more than any other single source.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures apparent blood viscosity in a 150-micrometer glass capillary and gets a value noticeably lower than the bulk viscosity measured in a wide 3 mm tube with a standard viscometer. Assuming a data error, they discard the capillary result. In fact this is the expected Fahraeus-Lindqvist effect: below roughly 300 micrometers, red blood cells migrate toward the centerline, leaving a thin cell-free plasma layer that lubricates the wall region and lowers apparent viscosity as diameter shrinks. The 'wrong' data point is the real physics — the fix is not throwing it out but reporting it as evidence that Hagen-Poiseuille's constant-viscosity assumption breaks down for blood at small vessel scales, and citing the vessel-diameter dependence explicitly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees Hagen-Poiseuille applied to blood, a microchannel, or a soft tube will immediately ask which assumption the student checked before applying it. A student who says 'I used mu = 3.5 mPa*s for blood without checking shear-thinning' has applied a formula outside its validity range and will be pressed on it; a student who says 'blood is shear-thinning and shows the Fahraeus-Lindqvist effect below about 300 micrometers, so I used an apparent viscosity appropriate to my vessel diameter, or a Casson model instead' demonstrates they understand the equation's assumptions as boundaries, not decoration. Naming the D^4 sensitivity and its metrology consequence is an equally strong signal of rigor.

questions.prompt: Match each Hagen-Poiseuille assumption to the real-world system that violates it.

right.text: Blood, which is shear-thinning
Pulsatile flow driven by a beating heart
A compliant blood vessel or soft silicone hose
Microchannel flow, where apparent wall slip can occur

questions.explanation: Blood's shear-thinning violates the constant-viscosity Newtonian assumption; a beating heart's pulsatile drive violates steady flow; a compliant vessel's diameter response to pressure violates the rigid-tube assumption; and microchannel apparent slip violates no-slip itself.

questions.prompt: What is the Fahraeus-Lindqvist effect?

options.text: Apparent blood viscosity increases as vessel diameter shrinks below 300 micrometers
Apparent blood viscosity falls as vessel diameter shrinks below roughly 300 micrometers, because red cells migrate toward the centerline and leave a cell-free plasma layer near the wall
Blood becomes Newtonian at small vessel diameters
Pressure drop becomes independent of flow rate in small vessels

explanations.a: This states the opposite of the actual effect — apparent viscosity falls, not rises, as diameter shrinks in this regime.
explanations.b: Correct — as vessel diameter drops below roughly 300 micrometers, red cells concentrate toward the centerline, leaving a lubricating cell-free plasma layer near the wall that lowers apparent viscosity.
explanations.c: Blood remains non-Newtonian (shear-thinning) at small diameters; the Fahraeus-Lindqvist effect describes a diameter-dependent apparent viscosity, not a shift to Newtonian behavior.
explanations.d: The effect concerns apparent viscosity's dependence on diameter, not a decoupling of pressure drop from flow rate.

questions.prompt: The Womersley number, introduced in 1955, is used to characterize which kind of flow?

options.text: Steady laminar flow in a rigid straight tube
Pulsatile flow, comparing unsteady inertia from the pulsation frequency to viscous forces
Turbulent flow transition in smooth pipes
Shear-thinning of non-Newtonian fluids at steady state

explanations.a: Steady laminar flow in a rigid tube is exactly the regime Hagen-Poiseuille already covers; the Womersley number is not needed there.
explanations.b: Correct — the Womersley number compares unsteady (pulsation-driven) inertial forces to viscous forces, telling you whether an instantaneous velocity profile still looks parabolic or lags the driving pressure signal, as in the pulsatile aorta.
explanations.c: Laminar-to-turbulent transition is characterized by the ordinary Reynolds number, not the Womersley number.
explanations.d: Shear-thinning under steady conditions is captured by non-Newtonian constitutive models like Casson or power-law, not by the Womersley number, which is specifically about unsteadiness.

questions.prompt: Because Q scales with D^4 in Hagen-Poiseuille, roughly what error in predicted Q results from a 2% error in measured bore diameter D?

options.text: About 2%
About 4%
About 8%
About 16%

explanations.a: This treats Q as if it scaled linearly with D (D^1), but it scales with D^4.
explanations.b: This treats Q as if it scaled with D^2, not D^4.
explanations.c: Correct — for a small fractional error x in D, the fractional error in D^4 is approximately 4x, so a 2% diameter error becomes roughly an 8% flow error, which is why bore metrology dominates the error budget in capillary experiments.
explanations.d: This would require an 8x scaling factor rather than the correct 4x from the D^4 dependence.

lessons.label: Wall Shear, Friction Velocity and the Pressure-Drop Link

sections.heading: From a manometer reading to a wall stress
sections.body: The same force balance used to derive Hagen-Poiseuille — delta_p*(pi*R^2) balancing the total wall shear force tau_w*(2*pi*R*L) on a fully developed control volume the full radius of the pipe — holds regardless of whether the flow inside is laminar or turbulent, because it is just momentum conservation on the fluid as a whole, not a statement about the velocity profile's shape. Setting the two forces equal and solving gives tau_w = (D/4)*(delta_p/L). This is the exact bridge between something a student can directly measure — delta_p across a known length L, read off a manometer or two pressure taps — and the wall shear stress, which cannot be measured directly at all. Because it comes from a pure force balance rather than the laminar solution, it applies equally to laminar and turbulent fully developed flow.

sections.heading: Friction velocity as the natural velocity scale
sections.body: Wall shear stress has units of pressure (force per area), so dividing by density and taking a square root converts it into a velocity: u* = sqrt(tau_w/rho), the friction velocity (also called the shear velocity). u* is not a velocity any fluid particle has — it is a derived scale — but it turns out to be the natural yardstick for near-wall behavior: distances non-dimensionalized as y*= y*u*/nu and velocities as u+ = u/u* are the coordinates in which the law of the wall and the viscous sublayer thickness are universally described, in both pipes and boundary layers generally. Every later lesson on turbulent near-wall structure in this branch is built on u*, so recognizing where it comes from — directly from tau_w, which itself comes directly from a measurable delta_p — matters now.

sections.heading: The Darcy/Fanning trap
sections.body: Two friction factors are both in common use, differing by exactly a factor of 4, and conflating them is the single most common factor-of-four error in student pipe-flow reports. The Darcy (Darcy-Weisbach) friction factor f_D is defined so that h_L = f_D*(L/D)*(V^2/(2g)), and for laminar flow f_D = 64/Re, as derived earlier in this unit. The Fanning friction factor f_F is defined directly from wall shear as f_F = tau_w/(rho*V^2/2), and for laminar flow f_F = 16/Re. The relationship is f_D = 4*f_F. Mechanical and civil engineering references (and most US textbooks) default to Darcy; chemical engineering references often default to Fanning. Before using any friction-factor chart or correlation, a student must confirm which one it reports — mixing them silently multiplies (or divides) a computed head loss by 4.

lessons.workedExample: A pipe run has D = 0.05 m, L = 10 m, and a measured pressure drop delta_p = 4000 Pa in water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3). Wall shear: tau_w = (D/4)*(delta_p/L) = (0.05/4)*(4000/10) = 0.0125*400 = 5.0 Pa. Friction velocity: u* = sqrt(tau_w/rho) = sqrt(5.0/1000) = sqrt(0.005) ≈ 0.0707 m/s. If a student then looks up a friction factor of 0.032 from a Moody chart (which reports Darcy f_D) but mistakenly plugs it into a Fanning-based head-loss formula, they would compute a head loss 4 times too large — the exact factor-of-four trap this lesson exists to prevent.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what's your wall shear stress?' after a student reports only a pressure drop is testing whether the student knows the two are connected by an exact, derivable relationship (tau_w = (D/4)*(delta_p/L)), not two independent measurements. A judge who then asks 'is that friction factor Darcy or Fanning?' is testing for the single most common numerical error in this whole subfield — a factor of 4 that silently corrupts every downstream head-loss or pump-sizing calculation. A student who states both relationships correctly, and explains why f_D = 4*f_F rather than treating the two as interchangeable, has shown real command of the friction-factor bookkeeping that most reports get wrong.

questions.prompt: Why does tau_w = (D/4)*(delta_p/L) apply to both laminar and turbulent fully developed pipe flow?

options.text: Because it is derived from the parabolic laminar velocity profile, which happens to also describe turbulent flow
Because it comes from a pure force balance (momentum conservation on the whole fluid column), not from any assumption about the velocity profile's shape
Because turbulent flow has no wall shear stress, so the formula trivially applies
It does not apply to turbulent flow; a separate formula is required

explanations.a: The parabolic profile is specific to laminar flow and was not used to derive this force balance; using it as the justification is incorrect.
explanations.b: Correct — balancing total pressure force against total wall shear force on a fully developed control volume is a statement of momentum conservation alone, independent of whether the interior profile is laminar or turbulent.
explanations.c: Turbulent flow has real, generally larger, wall shear stress than laminar flow at the same conditions; the formula still connects it to the measurable pressure drop.
explanations.d: The relationship holds for turbulent fully developed flow just as it does for laminar, precisely because it does not depend on profile shape.

questions.prompt: A pipe has D = 0.05 m, L = 10 m, and measured delta_p = 4000 Pa. What is the wall shear stress tau_w?

options.text: 0.5 Pa
5.0 Pa
50 Pa
20 Pa

explanations.a: This is off by a factor of 10 from the correct value.
explanations.b: Correct — tau_w = (D/4)*(delta_p/L) = (0.05/4)*(4000/10) = 0.0125*400 = 5.0 Pa, matching the worked example.
explanations.c: This is off by a factor of 10 in the other direction.
explanations.d: This results from omitting the factor of 1/4 in the formula (using D*(delta_p/L) directly).

questions.prompt: What is the friction velocity u* for tau_w = 5.0 Pa in water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3)?

options.text: About 0.0707 m/s
About 0.707 m/s
About 5.0 m/s
About 0.005 m/s

explanations.a: Correct — u* = sqrt(tau_w/rho) = sqrt(5.0/1000) = sqrt(0.005) ≈ 0.0707 m/s, matching the worked example.
explanations.b: This is off by a factor of 10 from the correct square root.
explanations.c: This mistakes tau_w itself, in different units, for the friction velocity.
explanations.d: This is the value of tau_w/rho before taking the square root, not the friction velocity itself.

questions.prompt: If the Fanning friction factor for laminar flow is f_F = 16/Re, what is the corresponding Darcy friction factor, and by what factor do they differ?

options.text: f_D = 16/Re; they are identical
f_D = 64/Re; Darcy is 4 times the Fanning value
f_D = 4/Re; Darcy is 1/4 the Fanning value
f_D = 256/Re; Darcy is 16 times the Fanning value

explanations.a: The two friction factors are not identical; conflating them is exactly the factor-of-four error this lesson warns against.
explanations.b: Correct — the general relationship f_D = 4*f_F applied to f_F = 16/Re gives f_D = 64/Re, matching the Darcy laminar friction factor derived earlier in this unit from Hagen-Poiseuille.
explanations.c: This inverts the relationship; f_D is 4 times f_F, not one-fourth of it.
explanations.d: This applies a factor of 16, not the correct factor of 4, between the two definitions.

units.label: Turbulent Pipe Flow, Darcy-Weisbach and the Law of the Wall

lessons.label: What Changes When the Flow Goes Turbulent

sections.heading: Two flow regimes, one pipe
sections.body: Osborne Reynolds's 1883 dye experiment showed that the same pipe can carry two qualitatively different flows depending only on a dimensionless speed: Re = VD/nu. Below roughly Re = 2300 a thin dye streak stays a smooth, straight line all the way down the pipe — laminar flow, where fluid moves in parallel layers and momentum crosses streamlines only by molecular viscosity. Above that threshold the streak wavers, breaks into intermittent puffs, and eventually smears across the whole cross-section within centimeters — turbulence, where chaotic three-dimensional eddies do the mixing. The transition Reynolds number is not a hard wall; with a very smooth pipe and quiet inlet, laminar flow can persist to Re near 10,000, but any real disturbance trips it near 2300.

sections.heading: Decomposing the velocity field
sections.body: Turbulence is analyzed with Reynolds decomposition: the instantaneous velocity u is split into a time-averaged mean u-bar plus a fluctuation u', so u = u-bar + u'. Plugging that split into the Navier-Stokes equations and averaging produces an extra term in the mean-flow momentum balance, the Reynolds stress, -rho*<u'v'> (the overbar denotes a time average of the product of the streamwise and wall-normal fluctuations). Physically this is an apparent shear stress: turbulent eddies swap fluid parcels across the velocity gradient, carrying high-momentum fluid inward and low-momentum fluid outward far more effectively than molecular diffusion does in a laminar flow. Because eddies transport momentum so efficiently across most of the pipe, the mean velocity profile flattens into a blunt, near-uniform core with a thin high-shear region pinned at the wall — a sharp contrast to the smooth parabola of laminar flow.

sections.heading: The measurable consequence: a different friction exponent
sections.body: That extra momentum transport shows up directly in how pressure drop scales with flow rate. In laminar flow, the Hagen-Poiseuille result gives Delta-p proportional to V to the first power — double the flow rate, double the pressure drop. Once the flow turns turbulent, the added Reynolds-stress dissipation makes Delta-p climb faster than linearly, roughly V^1.75 in the smooth-pipe turbulent regime and approaching V^2 as roughness or Reynolds number increases. A student who measures pressure drop at several flow rates and plots log(Delta-p) against log(V) can read the regime directly off the slope of that line: about 1 means laminar, about 1.75 to 2 means turbulent.

lessons.workedExample: Consider water (nu ~ 1x10^-6 m^2/s) in a 2 cm pipe. At Re = 1500 (V ~ 0.075 m/s) the flow is laminar: Hagen-Poiseuille gives Delta-p/L proportional to V exactly, and the velocity profile is a smooth parabola with centerline speed twice the mean. Raise the flow rate tenfold to Re = 15000 (V ~ 0.75 m/s): turbulent eddies now dominate momentum transport, the profile flattens into a blunt core with a thin high-shear wall layer, and Delta-p/L no longer scales linearly. An experimenter measuring pressure drop at several turbulent flow rates would find a log-log slope near 1.75-1.8 (the Blasius regime) instead of the laminar slope of 1.0.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this transition because it reveals whether a student understands turbulence as a physical mechanism (extra momentum transport by eddies, quantified by the Reynolds stress) rather than a vague label for 'chaotic flow.' A strong answer connects the Reynolds decomposition to the flattened velocity profile and then to the measurable friction-exponent shift from V^1 to roughly V^1.75-2 — a prediction the student could actually test with a flow rig and a pressure gauge. A weak answer says turbulence just 'has more mixing' without tying that mixing to a stress term or a testable exponent.

questions.prompt: In Reynolds decomposition, u = u-bar + u', what does u' represent?

options.text: The instantaneous fluctuation of velocity about the time-averaged mean
The velocity at the pipe centerline
The difference between laminar and turbulent critical Reynolds numbers
The mean velocity averaged over the whole pipe cross-section

explanations.a: Correct — u' is the turbulent fluctuation, the instantaneous deviation from the time-averaged mean u-bar; squaring and cross-multiplying these fluctuations produces the Reynolds stresses.
explanations.b: The centerline velocity is a spatial location, not a decomposition term; it has its own mean and fluctuating parts.
explanations.c: The critical Reynolds number is a threshold value (~2300), unrelated to the decomposition of velocity into mean and fluctuating parts.
explanations.d: That describes u-bar, the mean part of the decomposition, not u', which is the fluctuation.

questions.prompt: Physically, what does the Reynolds stress -rho*<u'v'> represent in a turbulent pipe flow?

options.text: An apparent shear stress from eddies transporting momentum across the mean velocity gradient
The static pressure difference between the pipe inlet and outlet
The viscous stress exerted by the fluid's molecular viscosity alone
The kinetic energy lost to heat during laminar flow

explanations.a: Correct — the correlated fluctuations u' and v' arise because eddies exchange fluid parcels across the mean shear, and this momentum exchange acts exactly like an extra shear stress in the averaged momentum equation.
explanations.b: Static pressure drop along the pipe is captured by Delta-p, a separate quantity driven partly by Reynolds stresses but not identical to them.
explanations.c: Molecular viscous stress is the laminar (mu*du/dy) term; Reynolds stress is the additional turbulent term that appears only after averaging fluctuating flow.
explanations.d: Reynolds stress exists specifically because the flow is turbulent, not laminar, and it represents momentum transport, not a direct heat-loss term.

questions.prompt: How does pressure drop Delta-p scale with mean velocity V in laminar versus turbulent pipe flow?

options.text: Delta-p ~ V^1 in laminar flow; Delta-p ~ V^1.75 to V^2 in turbulent flow
Delta-p ~ V^2 in laminar flow; Delta-p ~ V^1 in turbulent flow
Delta-p is independent of V in both regimes
Delta-p ~ V^1 in both laminar and turbulent flow

explanations.a: Correct — Hagen-Poiseuille gives a linear Delta-p ~ V in laminar flow, while the added Reynolds-stress dissipation in turbulent flow makes Delta-p climb faster than linearly, roughly V^1.75 to V^2.
explanations.b: This reverses the actual scaling; the linear relationship belongs to laminar flow, not turbulent.
explanations.c: Pressure drop always increases with flow speed in a real pipe; it is never independent of V.
explanations.d: The linear V^1 scaling holds only for laminar flow; turbulence adds extra momentum dissipation that steepens the exponent.

questions.prompt: Order these observations of Reynolds's dye-streak experiment as the pipe's Reynolds number increases.

items.text: Re ~ 1000 — the dye forms a single straight, unwavering line down the pipe axis
Re ~ 2300 — the dye line begins to waver and break into intermittent puffs
Re ~ 15000 — dye disperses across the entire cross-section within a short distance

questions.explanation: As Reynolds number rises from a low laminar value through the transitional threshold and into the fully turbulent range, the dye streak goes from perfectly ordered, to intermittently unstable, to fully mixed by chaotic eddies — the visual signature of the laminar-to-turbulent transition Reynolds documented in 1883.

lessons.label: The Darcy-Weisbach Equation

sections.heading: Building h_f from dimensional analysis
sections.body: Head loss in a straight pipe depends on pressure drop Delta-p, density rho, mean velocity V, diameter D, length L, viscosity mu, and roughness epsilon — seven variables built from three fundamental dimensions (mass, length, time). The Buckingham Pi theorem says these seven variables collapse into 7 - 3 = 4 independent dimensionless groups: a pressure coefficient Delta-p/(rho*V^2), the length ratio L/D, the Reynolds number Re = rho*V*D/mu, and the relative roughness epsilon/D. Because pressure drop in a straight, fully developed pipe is observed to scale linearly with L/D, that group can be pulled out front, leaving a single dimensionless friction factor f that must depend only on the two remaining groups: f = phi(Re, epsilon/D). That one relationship — an unknown function of two dimensionless numbers — is the entire logical basis for the Moody chart: every curve on it is just phi evaluated at a fixed epsilon/D as Re varies.

sections.heading: The Chezy-Weisbach-Darcy lineage
sections.body: The equation's name reflects three separate contributions across nearly a century. Antoine Chezy, working on open-channel flow in the 1770s, proposed V = C*sqrt(R*S), an empirical resistance formula relating velocity to channel slope and a resistance coefficient C. Julius Weisbach in 1845 proposed the modern head-loss form for closed pipes, h_f = f*(L/D)*(V^2/2g), introducing f as a dimensionless coefficient to be determined experimentally. Henry Darcy spent the 1850s running extensive pipe-friction experiments — published in 1857 — that supplied the systematic data showing f depends on roughness as well as flow condition. The combined name credits Weisbach's functional form and Darcy's experimental grounding of f.

sections.heading: Rearranging for design, and a common trap
sections.body: Because h_f = f*(L/D)*V^2/(2g), the same relation rearranges directly for whichever quantity a design problem asks for: solve for Delta-p = rho*g*h_f once h_f is known, substitute V = Q/A = 4Q/(pi*D^2) to get h_f in terms of flow rate Q, or hold h_f and Q fixed and solve iteratively for D (f itself depends on Re, which depends on V, which depends on D, so diameter-sizing problems are solved by iteration or a chart, not algebra alone). One trap worth naming explicitly: chemical engineers often use the Fanning friction factor f_F, defined so that f_Fanning = f_Darcy/4. Plugging a Fanning value into the Darcy-Weisbach formula (or vice versa) silently produces an answer off by a factor of four.

lessons.workedExample: Water flows at V = 2 m/s through a 100 m length of 10 cm cast-iron pipe (epsilon ~ 0.26 mm, so epsilon/D ~ 0.0026). At the resulting Re ~ 2x10^5, the Moody chart gives f ~ 0.026. Then h_f = f*(L/D)*V^2/(2g) = 0.026*(100/0.1)*(2^2)/(2*9.81) = 0.026*1000*4/19.62 ~ 5.30 m. Converting to a pressure drop: Delta-p = rho*g*h_f = 1000*9.81*5.30 ~ 52,000 Pa, or about 52 kPa over the 100 m run — a number a student could compare directly against a measured pressure-gauge reading on a real test rig.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing the Darcy-Weisbach equation wants to see that a student can derive f = phi(Re, epsilon/D) from first principles (dimensional analysis) rather than treating the Moody chart as a black box, and that they know which friction factor convention their chart or software uses. The giveaway of real understanding is a student who can rearrange the same equation for Delta-p, Q, or D depending on what the experiment measured, and who catches a factor-of-four error if Fanning and Darcy friction factors get mixed — a mistake that silently doubles or halves a reported pressure loss.

questions.prompt: Buckingham Pi analysis on Delta-p, rho, V, D, L, mu, and epsilon (7 variables, 3 fundamental dimensions) produces 4 dimensionless groups. After pulling out the L/D term (since Delta-p scales linearly with L/D for straight pipe flow), what does the Darcy friction factor f depend on?

options.text: Only the pipe length L
Only the fluid density rho
Reynolds number Re and relative roughness epsilon/D
Only the pipe diameter D

explanations.a: L was already factored out into the separate L/D group; f itself does not depend on absolute length.
explanations.b: Density appears inside the Reynolds number (Re = rho*V*D/mu), not as an independent dependence of f.
explanations.c: Correct — after removing the L/D group, dimensional analysis leaves exactly two remaining dimensionless groups, Re and epsilon/D, so f = phi(Re, epsilon/D) is the most general form consistent with dimensional homogeneity.
explanations.d: Diameter appears inside both Re and epsilon/D, not as an independent variable outside those groups.

questions.prompt: How is the Fanning friction factor f_Fanning related to the Darcy friction factor f_Darcy used in h_f = f*(L/D)*(V^2/2g)?

options.text: f_Fanning = f_Darcy / 4
f_Fanning = f_Darcy * 4
They are identical
f_Fanning = f_Darcy^2

explanations.a: Correct — the Fanning factor is defined from wall shear stress directly and comes out to one-quarter of the Darcy value; mixing the two into the wrong formula produces a friction loss off by a factor of four.
explanations.b: This inverts the actual relationship; Fanning is the smaller of the two, not four times larger.
explanations.c: They differ by exactly a factor of 4 by definition, which is precisely why confusing them is a classic sizing error.
explanations.d: The relationship is a simple linear factor of 4, not a square.

questions.prompt: Match each historical figure to their contribution to the Darcy-Weisbach lineage.

right.text: Empirical open-channel resistance formula, V = C*sqrt(R*S)
Proposed the head-loss functional form h_f = f*(L/D)*(V^2/2g)
Extensive pipe-friction experiments (published 1857) showing f's dependence on roughness

questions.explanation: Chezy's 1770s formula addressed open-channel flow resistance; Weisbach in 1845 proposed the closed-pipe head-loss form still used today; Darcy's 1850s experiments (published in 1857) supplied the systematic roughness data that made f a usable engineering quantity.

questions.prompt: Given h_f = f*(L/D)*(V^2/2g) and V = 4Q/(pi*D^2), how does h_f scale with pipe diameter D at fixed flow rate Q, length L, and friction factor f?

options.text: h_f is independent of D
h_f scales as 1/D
h_f scales as 1/D^5
h_f scales as D^2

explanations.a: Diameter appears both directly in L/D and through V, which itself depends on D^2, so h_f is strongly diameter-dependent, not independent of it.
explanations.b: This misses that V itself scales as 1/D^2, so V^2 contributes an additional D^-4 on top of the D^-1 from L/D.
explanations.c: Correct — substituting V = 4Q/(pi*D^2) into h_f = f*(L/D)*(V^2/2g) gives h_f proportional to Q^2/D^5: one factor of 1/D from L/D and 1/D^4 from V^2, combining to D^-5.
explanations.d: This has the wrong sign and wrong power; h_f decreases sharply, not increases, as D grows.

lessons.label: Turbulent Velocity Profiles and the Power Law

sections.heading: An empirical curve, not a derivation
sections.body: The one-seventh power law, u/u_max = (y/R)^(1/n), describes how turbulent pipe velocity rises from the wall (y = 0) to the centerline (y = R). Ludwig Prandtl proposed the exponent n = 7 for the moderate-Reynolds-number range where his student Paul Blasius's smooth-pipe friction correlation also held, roughly Re between 4000 and 10^5. It was never derived from momentum balance the way the laminar parabola is from the Navier-Stokes equations; it is a curve fit chosen because it reproduces measured profiles reasonably well and is easy to integrate. Critically, n is not fixed: as Reynolds number rises the profile grows blunter and n climbs, from about 6 near the low end of the turbulent range up toward about 10 at the very high Reynolds numbers Johann Nikuradse's 1930s pipe experiments reached.

sections.heading: What the exponent buys you: mean velocity and correction factors
sections.body: Integrating the power-law profile over the pipe's circular cross-section gives a closed-form ratio of mean to maximum velocity, V/u_max = 2n^2 / [(n+1)(2n+1)]. For n = 7 this works out to about 0.82; as n rises toward 10 at higher Reynolds number the ratio climbs toward about 0.87 — both comfortably inside the commonly quoted 0.8-0.87 range, and both far blunter than the laminar parabola's fixed ratio of 0.5. The same integration yields the kinetic-energy correction factor alpha (used in the mechanical energy equation) of roughly 1.03-1.11 for turbulent flow, typically taken as about 1.05 — much closer to the ideal uniform-flow value of 1.0 than the laminar value of 2.0, which is exactly what a blunt, nearly flat turbulent core implies.

sections.heading: Where the fit breaks: unphysical endpoints
sections.body: The power law's convenience comes at the cost of getting the physics wrong at both ends of the domain. Because the exponent 1/n is less than 1, the derivative du/dy diverges as y approaches 0, predicting an infinite velocity gradient — and therefore infinite wall shear stress — right at the wall, where the true physics is the opposite: a thin viscous sublayer where shear stress is finite and set by molecular viscosity. At the centerline the fit predicts exactly zero slope, which happens to be correct by symmetry but for the wrong reason — the power law has no mechanism connecting to the actual outer-layer wake physics. The lesson is practical: use the power law to integrate bulk quantities like mean velocity or momentum flux, but never to infer wall shear stress or near-wall behavior — that requires the law of the wall covered next.

lessons.workedExample: A turbulent pipe flow has a measured centerline velocity u_max = 10 m/s. At a moderate Reynolds number where n = 7, the power-law formula gives V/u_max = 2(7)^2 / [(8)(15)] = 98/120 = 0.817, so the mean velocity is about 8.17 m/s. If the same pipe were run at a much higher Reynolds number where the profile blunts further to n = 10, the ratio becomes 2(10)^2/[(11)(21)] = 200/231 = 0.866, giving a mean velocity of about 8.66 m/s for the same 10 m/s centerline speed — a direct, calculable illustration of how the profile flattens as n grows with Reynolds number, even holding u_max fixed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about the power law wants to know whether a student treats it as a physically derived law or, correctly, as a convenient empirical fit with known limits. The strong answer names the specific failure — infinite predicted wall-shear gradient at y = 0 — and explains that the fit is used for integrated quantities like mean velocity or momentum flux, not for wall stress. A student who quotes 'one-seventh power law' without knowing n changes with Reynolds number, or who tries to compute wall shear stress directly from it, has memorized a formula without understanding what it can and cannot do.

questions.prompt: Why is the power-law velocity profile u/u_max = (y/R)^(1/n) described as 'wrong as physics' near the wall?

options.text: It predicts negative velocity near the wall
Its derivative diverges as y approaches 0, implying infinite wall shear stress instead of the finite value set by viscosity
It predicts the centerline velocity is lower than the wall velocity
It only applies to laminar flow, not turbulent flow

explanations.a: The profile is well-behaved and non-negative everywhere on [0, R]; the problem is in the slope, not the sign of velocity.
explanations.b: Correct — because the exponent 1/n is less than one, du/dy blows up as y goes to zero, incorrectly predicting infinite shear stress at the wall rather than the finite, viscosity-set value that actually occurs in the real viscous sublayer.
explanations.c: The profile correctly increases monotonically from zero at the wall to u_max at the centerline; it does not invert this order.
explanations.d: The power law is specifically an empirical fit for turbulent pipe profiles; laminar flow instead follows an exact parabolic solution from the Navier-Stokes equations.

questions.prompt: Using V/u_max = 2n^2/[(n+1)(2n+1)] with n = 7, what is the ratio of mean velocity to centerline velocity?

options.text: About 0.50
About 0.82
About 1.00
About 0.25

explanations.a: 0.50 is the laminar parabolic profile's V/u_max ratio, not the turbulent power-law value.
explanations.b: Correct — plugging n = 7 gives 2(49)/(8*15) = 98/120 = 0.817, matching the blunt, near-uniform turbulent profile.
explanations.c: A ratio of 1.00 would mean the velocity is uniform across the whole pipe with no wall shear at all, which is unphysical.
explanations.d: 0.25 is far too low for any real pipe-flow profile, laminar or turbulent.

questions.prompt: How does the turbulent kinetic-energy correction factor alpha (~1.03-1.11, typically ~1.05) compare to the laminar value?

options.text: It is much closer to 1.0 than the laminar value of 2.0, reflecting the blunter turbulent profile
It is identical to the laminar value of 2.0
It is larger than the laminar value
Alpha does not apply to turbulent flow
