questions.prompt: Per Wagner's function, an airfoil reaches roughly 90% of its steady-state lift only after traveling approximately:

options.text: Eight chord-lengths
One-tenth of a chord-length
Exactly one chord-length
It never exceeds 50% in any finite time

explanations.a: Correct — the classic result from Wagner's indicial response is that roughly eight chord-lengths of travel are needed to build circulatory lift to about 90% of the eventual steady value.
explanations.b: A tenth of a chord-length is far too short; lift is still close to its initial ~50% jump at that point.
explanations.c: One chord-length is well short of the distance needed; the buildup toward 90% is gradual over several chord-lengths.
explanations.d: Lift does rise past 50% over time, asymptotically approaching 100%; it does not stay capped at the initial jump value.

lessons.label: Measuring Unsteadiness: Reduced Frequency, Strouhal and Added Mass

sections.heading: Reduced frequency: is quasi-steady theory even allowed?
sections.body: The Wagner-function lesson showed that lift lags behind instantaneous circulation after a sudden start; reduced frequency k is the single dimensionless number engineers use to decide, before doing any hard analysis, whether that lag matters for a given oscillating motion. For an airfoil of chord c oscillating (pitching or plunging) at frequency f in a freestream U, k = pi*f*c/U compares how far the airfoil moves in one oscillation cycle to its own chord length. Small k means the airfoil sweeps through many chord-lengths per cycle, so the flow has time to re-equilibrate and quasi-steady aerodynamics (computing lift from the instantaneous angle of attack, as if it were always steady) is a good approximation; large k means the motion is fast relative to the flow's ability to respond, and the wake memory captured by functions like Wagner's dominates. The commonly used thresholds are k < 0.05 for flow that may be treated as quasi-steady and k > 0.2 for flow that is strongly unsteady, with the 0.05-0.2 band a transitional regime where neither simplification is safe.

sections.heading: Strouhal number: the vortex shedding clock
sections.body: A different kind of unsteadiness arises when a bluff body (a cylinder, a strut, a stalled airfoil) sheds vortices periodically into its wake rather than responding to imposed motion — the von Kármán vortex street. The Strouhal number St = f*D/U, where D is a characteristic cross-stream dimension and f is the shedding frequency, nondimensionalizes that shedding rate. For a circular cylinder across a wide range of Reynolds numbers, St sits remarkably close to 0.2, a near-universal empirical constant discovered by Vincenc Strouhal in 1878 (originally studying wires singing in the wind) and refined through the twentieth century — knowing St lets an engineer predict shedding frequency (and thus resonance risk, as in vortex-induced-vibration lock-in of a chimney stack or slender mast, where shedding frequency locks onto the structure's natural frequency) directly from geometry and speed without running a full unsteady simulation. (The 1940 Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse is popularly cited as this kind of shedding resonance, but the standard modern analysis attributes it to self-excited aeroelastic torsional flutter, a distinct mechanism from simple vortex-shedding lock-in.)

sections.heading: Added mass: the fluid a body drags along
sections.body: The third parameter, added (or apparent) mass, is not about a frequency at all but about inertia: any body accelerating through a fluid must also accelerate a surrounding volume of fluid with it, and that entrained fluid resists the acceleration just as the body's own mass does. For an airfoil executing a sudden pitch or plunge, part of the immediate force jump seen in Wagner's indicial response (the roughly 50% at the instant of starting) is this apparent-mass contribution, not circulatory lift at all — it is present from t = 0 because it requires no time for a wake or bound circulation to develop, unlike the circulatory part. Classifying unsteadiness by cause matters for later work: periodic unsteadiness (regular oscillation or shedding, characterized by k or St), transient unsteadiness (a one-time step or gust, characterized by an indicial function like Wagner's), and turbulent unsteadiness (broadband, chaotic fluctuation with no single dominant frequency) each demand different analysis tools, and naming which one a later problem involves is the first step in solving it.

lessons.workedExample: A small wind-turbine blade section of chord c = 0.3 m operates in a freestream U = 15 m/s while the blade flaps at f = 0.5 Hz due to tower-shadow interaction. Reduced frequency k = pi*f*c/U = pi*0.5*0.3/15 ≈ 0.031, below the 0.05 quasi-steady threshold, so a quasi-steady aerodynamic model is defensible for this flapping. Separately, a cylindrical mast of diameter D = 0.05 m stands in the same wind: using St ≈ 0.2, the expected vortex-shedding frequency is f = St*U/D = 0.2*15/0.05 = 60 Hz — an engineer would then check that 60 Hz is far from the mast's structural natural frequency to avoid a vortex-shedding lock-in resonance (the kind of coupling that plagues chimney stacks and slender masts, distinct from the aeroelastic flutter that brought down Tacoma Narrows).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is your flow quasi-steady, and how do you know?' to test whether a student picked a modeling assumption or merely inherited one from a textbook example. The strong answer computes k = pi*f*c/U (or St = f*D/U for a shedding problem) for their actual geometry and speed, states which regime it falls in, and names which of the three unsteadiness categories — periodic, transient, or turbulent — their phenomenon belongs to. A student who cannot compute k for their own setup has not verified the single assumption their whole aerodynamic model depends on.

questions.prompt: Reduced frequency k = pi*f*c/U for an oscillating airfoil is used to decide:

options.text: The airfoil's lift-to-drag ratio at cruise
Whether quasi-steady aerodynamic theory is a valid approximation for the motion
The Reynolds number of the flow
The maximum structural load the airfoil can bear

explanations.a: Lift-to-drag ratio is an aerodynamic efficiency metric unrelated to the unsteadiness classification k provides.
explanations.b: Correct — k compares oscillation frequency to flow-crossing time (via chord and freestream speed) to determine whether the flow can be treated as quasi-steady or is strongly unsteady.
explanations.c: Reynolds number nondimensionalizes inertial-to-viscous forces using a length scale and viscosity; it is a distinct parameter from reduced frequency.
explanations.d: Structural load limits are a materials/structures question, not something reduced frequency addresses.

questions.prompt: Per the thresholds given, a flow with reduced frequency k = 0.35 should be treated as:

options.text: Quasi-steady, since k is a small number
Strongly unsteady, since k exceeds the 0.2 threshold
Impossible to classify without also knowing the Strouhal number
In the ambiguous transitional band between 0.05 and 0.2

explanations.a: k = 0.35 is well above the 0.05 quasi-steady cutoff, so it cannot be treated as quasi-steady regardless of feeling 'small' in absolute terms.
explanations.b: Correct — k = 0.35 exceeds the k > 0.2 threshold for strongly unsteady flow, where wake memory (e.g., Wagner-type lag) dominates and quasi-steady theory fails.
explanations.c: Reduced frequency alone is sufficient to classify oscillatory unsteadiness against the stated thresholds; Strouhal number addresses a different (shedding) problem.
explanations.d: 0.35 lies above the 0.05-0.2 transitional band, squarely in the strongly-unsteady regime, not within the ambiguous zone.

questions.prompt: Match each dimensionless/physical parameter to what it characterizes.

right.text: Whether an oscillating airfoil's motion can be treated with quasi-steady aerodynamics
The periodic vortex-shedding frequency behind a bluff body (near 0.2 for a cylinder)
The fluid inertia a body must accelerate along with itself, contributing to instantaneous force even before circulation builds

questions.explanation: Reduced frequency governs whether oscillatory motion can be approximated as quasi-steady; the Strouhal number nondimensionalizes bluff-body vortex-shedding frequency (near 0.2 for a cylinder, per Strouhal's 1878 work); added mass captures the immediate inertial force from accelerating surrounding fluid, distinct from circulatory (Wagner-type) lift buildup.

questions.prompt: Which type of unsteadiness would best describe a wing suddenly encountering a single sharp wind gust, then returning to steady flight?

options.text: Periodic unsteadiness
Transient unsteadiness
Turbulent unsteadiness
None of these categories apply to gusts

explanations.a: Periodic unsteadiness describes regular, repeating oscillation or shedding (characterized by k or St), not a single one-time event.
explanations.b: Correct — a single gust is a one-time step-like disturbance, the defining case of transient unsteadiness, analyzed with an indicial (step-response) function such as Wagner's.
explanations.c: Turbulent unsteadiness is broadband, chaotic fluctuation with no single dominant event or frequency, unlike one discrete gust.
explanations.d: A single gust fits cleanly into the transient category, one of the three named classifications.

units.label: Vortex Shedding and the Karman Vortex Street

lessons.label: How a Vortex Street Forms

sections.heading: Two shear layers that cannot both survive
sections.body: Put a cylinder in a stream fast enough to separate flow, and two shear layers peel off its sides, one spinning clockwise, one counterclockwise. Naively you might expect them to roll up into two steady, symmetric vortices sitting behind the body forever. They cannot: J. E. Gerrard's 1966 paper on the formation region showed the process is inherently unstable. As each shear layer rolls into a growing vortex, that vortex's own circulation reaches across the wake centerline and entrains fluid from the opposite shear layer. The entrained fluid carries opposite-sign vorticity, and once enough of it arrives the growing vortex effectively cuts off its own feed. Starved of further circulation, it detaches and is swept downstream, while the far shear layer, no longer being drawn on, now dominates and begins rolling up its own vortex on the other side. The cycle then repeats, alternating side to side, and this is the mechanism, not any external vibration or acoustic forcing, that produces the alternating Karman vortex street.

sections.heading: Formation length and base pressure
sections.body: Gerrard defined the formation length as the distance downstream of the body at which a shed vortex reaches its full strength and detaches, typically on the order of one to two cylinder diameters for a circular cylinder in the laminar-to-subcritical range. A short formation length means the shear layers curve back and interact quickly, which correlates with a lower (more negative) base pressure coefficient behind the body, higher shedding frequency, and higher form drag. A long formation length means weaker cross-wake entrainment, higher base pressure, and quieter, lower-drag shedding. This is why any change that alters formation length, a splitter plate, a change in Reynolds number, boundary-layer trips, immediately shows up in both the drag and the tone of the wake.

sections.heading: A global instability of the near wake
sections.body: The crucial conceptual point is that vortex shedding is a self-sustained, global instability of the near-wake flow, not a forced response to some outside periodic input. The near wake behaves like an absolutely unstable oscillator: any small asymmetry, inevitable in a real flow, grows because the entrainment feedback described above amplifies it, and the system settles into a stable limit-cycle oscillation at a well-defined frequency. This is why shedding appears even in a perfectly steady free-stream and why it can synchronize with (lock onto) an external vibration of the right frequency, a phenomenon called lock-in, without being caused by one.

lessons.workedExample: A student places a splitter plate, a thin flat fin, along the wake centerline directly behind a rod in a water tunnel. With the plate in place, each shear layer can no longer curve inward far enough to reach the opposite layer, so cross-wake entrainment is blocked, the feedback loop that cuts off vortex growth is broken, and periodic shedding is suppressed almost entirely, leaving two long, stable, steady vortices instead of an alternating street. This is direct evidence that shedding is driven by cross-wake shear-layer interaction, exactly Gerrard's formation-region mechanism, and not by anything happening far downstream or upstream.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why does the wake alternate instead of just forming two steady vortices?" is testing whether a student can explain shedding as a wake-internal feedback instability rather than reciting "vortices form and get shed" as if it were self-evident. The strong answer names the mechanism, one growing vortex draws in and gets cut off by the opposite-sign shear layer, connects formation length to base pressure and drag, and can predict that blocking cross-wake interaction (a splitter plate) suppresses shedding. That prediction is the tell that the student understands the loop, not just the label.

questions.prompt: In Gerrard's (1966) formation-region model, what actually stops a growing vortex from continuing to grow?

options.text: It runs out of downstream space
It entrains opposite-sign vorticity from the far shear layer, which cuts off its own supply
The free-stream turbulence dissipates it
The cylinder's boundary layer stops feeding vorticity after one rotation

explanations.a: Downstream space is not the limiting factor; the cutoff happens within the compact formation region near the body.
explanations.b: Correct — the growing vortex reaches across the wake and draws in opposite-sign vorticity from the other shear layer, which cancels its own supply and forces it to detach.
explanations.c: Free-stream turbulence is not required for shedding; it occurs even in very clean, low-turbulence flows.
explanations.d: The boundary layer continuously supplies vorticity to the shear layer; the cutoff is due to cross-wake entrainment, not a supply timeout at the cylinder.

questions.prompt: A shorter formation length is associated with which combination of effects?

options.text: Higher base pressure and lower drag
Lower (more negative) base pressure, higher shedding frequency, and higher drag
No change in drag, only a change in tone
Suppressed shedding entirely

explanations.a: This describes the opposite case, a long formation length with weaker interaction.
explanations.b: Correct — a short formation length means faster, stronger shear-layer interaction, which lowers base pressure, raises shedding frequency, and increases form drag.
explanations.c: Formation length change affects both the mean pressure field (drag) and the frequency, not tone alone.
explanations.d: Suppressed shedding is what a splitter plate does by blocking interaction; a short formation length is the opposite, strong interaction.

questions.prompt: Why is calling vortex shedding an 'externally forced' oscillation misleading?

options.text: Because shedding never occurs in a perfectly steady free-stream
Because it is a self-sustained global instability of the near wake, arising from internal feedback rather than an outside periodic driver
Because shedding frequency is random and unpredictable
Because it only happens when the body itself vibrates

explanations.a: Shedding does occur in a steady free-stream; that is exactly the point, it is self-generated.
explanations.b: Correct — the near wake acts as an absolutely unstable oscillator whose own entrainment feedback amplifies small asymmetries into a periodic limit cycle, with no external forcing required.
explanations.c: Shedding has a well-defined, predictable frequency (captured by the Strouhal number), not random behavior.
explanations.d: Body vibration can lock onto shedding (lock-in) but is not required for shedding to occur in the first place.

questions.prompt: Match each wake feature to its correct description.

right.text: Distance downstream where a shed vortex reaches full strength and detaches
The rolled-up sheet of vorticity peeling off one side of the body
A fin along the wake centerline that blocks cross-wake entrainment and suppresses shedding
Synchronization of shedding frequency to an external vibration near the natural shedding rate

questions.explanation: Formation length is the detachment distance; the shear layer is the vorticity sheet from separation; a splitter plate blocks the cross-wake entrainment that drives shedding; lock-in is synchronization with, not the cause of, an external vibration.

lessons.label: Reynolds-Number Regimes of the Cylinder Wake

sections.heading: From creeping flow to the twin-vortex bubble
sections.body: The same circular cylinder produces qualitatively different wakes depending only on Reynolds number, Re = UD/nu, so geometry alone never tells you what a wake looks like; regime does. Below Re of about 5, the flow is creeping and attached, no separation at all, streamlines close smoothly around the back. As Re rises past about 5, the boundary layer separates and two steady, symmetric, counter-rotating vortices form and stay attached to the base, a stable recirculating twin-vortex bubble that grows longer with Re. This bubble persists, still steady, up to roughly Re 40.

sections.heading: The Hopf bifurcation into periodic shedding
sections.body: Near Re of about 47, the steady twin-vortex wake becomes unstable to small perturbations and the flow transitions, through a classic Hopf bifurcation, into self-sustained periodic vortex shedding: the wake begins oscillating at a single well-defined frequency with an amplitude that grows continuously from zero as Re exceeds this critical value, the textbook signature of a supercritical Hopf bifurcation: quantitatively, the shedding amplitude grows as the square root of the distance above the critical Reynolds number, amplitude proportional to sqrt(Re - Re_c) with Re_c of about 47, the same square-root scaling law that shows up in every supercritical Hopf bifurcation, from this wake to laser onset to Rayleigh-Benard convection. From roughly Re 47 to 190, the shed vortices remain essentially two-dimensional, laminar, and highly organized, the cleanest Karman vortex streets seen in any regime.

sections.heading: Going three-dimensional, then turbulent, then the drag crisis
sections.body: Around Re 190, the wake loses spanwise uniformity: mode A instability appears, large-scale spanwise waviness with a wavelength of roughly three to four diameters, and vortex dislocations, points where shedding along the span falls briefly out of phase. Near Re 230 to 260, a second, finer-scale instability, mode B, with wavelength around one diameter, takes over as the dominant three-dimensional pattern; this transition sequence was mapped in detail by C. H. K. Williamson's work through the 1990s. From roughly Re 300 up to the low 10^5 range (the subcritical regime), the wake is fully turbulent while the boundary layer on the cylinder itself is still laminar at separation. The drag coefficient stays close to 1.2 throughout this whole subcritical range. Then near Re of 2 to 4 x 10^5 comes the drag crisis: the laminar boundary layer, right at the edge of transitioning, is tripped into turbulence before it separates; a turbulent boundary layer resists adverse pressure gradients better, so separation is delayed, the wake narrows sharply, and drag coefficient collapses from about 1.2 to about 0.3 almost discontinuously, while the Strouhal number simultaneously jumps up toward about 0.45.

lessons.workedExample: A golf ball and a smooth cue ball, similar size, are dropped through the same air at speeds that put both around Re 10^5, comfortably subcritical for a smooth sphere. The smooth ball sits well below its drag crisis, high drag, wide laminar-separation wake. The golf ball's dimples trip its boundary layer to turbulent early, effectively shifting its own drag crisis down to a lower Reynolds number, so at the same Re 10^5 the dimpled ball has already collapsed to low drag, exactly the smooth-cylinder story of laminar separation giving way to a delayed turbulent separation, engineered on purpose rather than reached by raising speed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the Re ladder because it is the single best test of whether a student understands that the cylinder wake is not one fixed pattern but a sequence of distinct instabilities, each with its own trigger. A student who can state that shedding onset is a Hopf bifurcation near Re 47, that 3D transition happens through named modes A and B, and that the drag crisis is a laminar-to-turbulent boundary-layer effect (not a wake effect) shows they grasp cause and effect, not just a list of numbers. The giveaway of shallow understanding is treating 'high Reynolds number' as one undifferentiated bucket.

questions.prompt: Order these cylinder-wake states from lowest to highest Reynolds number.

items.text: Creeping attached flow, no separation
Steady twin-vortex recirculation bubble
Laminar, 2D periodic vortex shedding
Mode B three-dimensional instability
Drag crisis (Cd collapse)

questions.explanation: The sequence runs creeping flow below Re~5, a steady twin-vortex bubble to Re~40, laminar 2D shedding from Re~47 to ~190 (after mode A appears near 190 and mode B near 230-260), and finally the drag crisis far higher near Re 2-4x10^5.

questions.prompt: What physically causes the drag crisis near Re 2-4x10^5?

options.text: The wake becomes perfectly laminar again
The cylinder's boundary layer transitions to turbulent before separating, delaying separation and narrowing the wake
Vortex shedding stops entirely
The free stream becomes compressible

explanations.a: The opposite happens; the boundary layer becomes turbulent, and the wake itself is already turbulent well before this point.
explanations.b: Correct — a turbulent boundary layer resists the adverse pressure gradient longer, delaying separation, narrowing the wake and cutting form drag roughly from Cd 1.2 to 0.3.
explanations.c: Shedding continues; the Strouhal number actually jumps toward about 0.45 at the drag crisis rather than shedding stopping.
explanations.d: Compressibility is irrelevant at these Reynolds numbers and speeds; the mechanism is purely a boundary-layer transition effect.

questions.prompt: The onset of periodic vortex shedding near Re~47 is best described as:

options.text: A discontinuous jump with the oscillation appearing at full amplitude immediately
A supercritical Hopf bifurcation, with oscillation amplitude growing continuously from zero above the critical Re
A random, non-repeating transition with no defined critical Re
Caused by acoustic resonance in the test section

explanations.a: A discontinuous full-amplitude jump is not what is observed; amplitude grows smoothly from zero, the hallmark of a supercritical bifurcation.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the textbook signature of a supercritical Hopf bifurcation: a well-defined critical Re with continuously growing oscillation amplitude beyond it.
explanations.c: The critical Re (~47) is well-defined and reproducible, not random.
explanations.d: The instability is intrinsic to the near-wake flow, not driven by acoustics in the facility.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes mode A from mode B three-dimensional instability in the cylinder wake?

options.text: Mode A has a longer spanwise wavelength (~3-4 diameters) and appears near Re~190; mode B has a shorter wavelength (~1 diameter) and appears near Re~230-260
Mode A only occurs above the drag crisis
Mode B is two-dimensional while mode A is three-dimensional
They are two names for the same instability

explanations.a: Correct — mode A (larger-scale spanwise waviness with vortex dislocations, ~3-4 diameter wavelength) sets in near Re 190, and mode B (finer-scale, ~1 diameter wavelength) becomes dominant near Re 230-260.
explanations.b: Both mode A and mode B occur far below the drag crisis, which is orders of magnitude higher in Re.
explanations.c: Both modes A and B are three-dimensional instabilities; the 2D regime is the earlier, lower-Re laminar shedding range.
explanations.d: They are distinct instabilities with different wavelengths and different onset Reynolds numbers, mapped separately in Williamson's transition studies.

lessons.label: Strouhal Number and Shedding Frequency

sections.heading: A dimensionless clock for the wake
sections.body: The Strouhal number, St = fD/U, packages shedding frequency f, body diameter D, and free-stream speed U into a single dimensionless ratio, and it is the key fact that makes vortex shedding useful rather than just interesting: for a circular cylinder St stays remarkably close to 0.2 over a huge span of Reynolds numbers, roughly 300 to 2x10^5, the entire subcritical regime. That constancy means shedding frequency scales almost linearly with speed for a fixed body, f is proportional to U, which is exactly what turns a shedding cylinder into a usable flow sensor: measure f and D, and you get U directly, no calibration curve needed across that whole range.

sections.heading: Roshko's fitted relations
sections.body: St is not perfectly flat outside that plateau. Anatol Roshko's 1954 NACA study of turbulent wakes from vortex streets fit the Re-dependence with two relations. In the stable range (roughly Re 40 to 150, before the wake becomes fully turbulent) St = 0.212(1 - 21.2/Re). In the transition range that follows (roughly Re 150 to 300, where the wake is becoming irregular before settling into the subcritical plateau) St = 0.212(1 - 12.7/Re). Both curves approach the same asymptotic value, 0.212, close to the commonly quoted 0.2, as Re grows and the 1/Re correction term shrinks toward zero; the correction terms simply capture the extra viscous drag on the vortex formation process at these still-modest Reynolds numbers.

sections.heading: Working the formula both directions
sections.body: Because St = fD/U rearranges trivially, f = StU/D, U = fD/St, D = fU/St, a single measured quantity unlocks the other two, given St from the regime the flow is in. This is the arithmetic every vortex flowmeter and every anemometry lab exercise runs on: fix D and read f electronically (with a hot-wire or a pressure tap sensing the alternating side forces) to back out U in real time. The number itself is named for Vincenc Strouhal, a Czech physicist who in 1878 studied the tones sung by wires stretched in the wind, measuring how the pitch of the aeolian tone scaled with wire diameter and wind speed; that experiment is the direct ancestor of the ratio used here, and the same singing-wire phenomenon is picked up in full later in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: A 10 mm diameter rod sits in a 10 m/s air stream, comfortably in the St~0.2 plateau (Re here is around 6700, well within 300 to 2x10^5). Predicted shedding frequency: f = St*U/D = 0.2 * 10 / 0.01 = 200 Hz. Now invert the problem: a hot-wire downstream of an unknown rod in a 20 m/s flow measures a tone at 800 Hz. Using St = 0.2, D = St*U/f = 0.2*20/800 = 0.005 m, a 5 mm rod. This is literally how a vortex flowmeter works in industrial pipelines: a fixed bluff-body shedder of known D is placed in the line, and the measured shedding frequency is converted straight to flow velocity via U = fD/St.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about the Strouhal number is testing two things at once: can the student do the dimensional arithmetic cleanly in either direction, and do they know the number is not a universal constant but a regime-dependent, empirically fit quantity with named limits (Roshko's two relations, the plateau near 0.2, the drag-crisis jump to ~0.45 elsewhere in this unit). A student who plugs f=StU/D correctly but insists St=0.2 is exact and universal has memorized a formula without understanding that Roshko had to fit curves because Re-dependence is real at lower Reynolds numbers.

questions.prompt: A 10 mm rod is placed in a 10 m/s air stream, well within the St~0.2 plateau. What is the predicted vortex shedding frequency?

options.text: 20 Hz
200 Hz
0.2 Hz

explanations.a: This would result from dividing by U instead of multiplying, or a units slip; check f = St*U/D = 0.2*10/0.01.
explanations.b: Correct — f = St*U/D = 0.2 * 10 m/s / 0.01 m = 200 Hz.
explanations.c: This overshoots by a factor of 10; check that D was converted from mm to meters (0.01 m, not 0.1 m).
explanations.d: This is St itself, not a frequency; the formula requires multiplying by U/D, not just quoting St.

questions.prompt: A hot-wire downstream of an unknown rod in a 20 m/s flow measures a shedding tone of 800 Hz. Using St = 0.2, what is the rod diameter?

options.text: 5 mm
50 mm
0.5 mm
8 mm

explanations.b: This is off by a factor of 10; check the arithmetic 0.2*20/800 carefully.
explanations.c: This is off by a factor of 10 in the other direction.
explanations.d: This does not follow from D = St*U/f with the given numbers; recompute directly.

questions.prompt: Over which Reynolds number range does St stay close to a constant ~0.2 for a circular cylinder?

options.text: Roughly 1 to 5
Roughly 300 to 2x10^5
Only exactly at Re = 47
Above Re = 10^7

explanations.a: This range is the creeping-flow / early-separation regime, well below periodic shedding, so St~0.2 does not even apply.
explanations.b: Correct — the subcritical plateau where St is nearly Reynolds-number-independent near 0.2 spans roughly Re 300 to 2x10^5.
explanations.c: Re = 47 is the shedding-onset bifurcation point, not the plateau; St there is close to but not exactly 0.2 and is still Re-dependent per Roshko's fit.
explanations.d: Above roughly 2x10^5 the drag crisis intervenes and St jumps toward 0.45, so the constant-0.2 plateau no longer holds.

questions.prompt: Match each Roshko (1954) relation or quantity to its correct role.

right.text: Fitted relation for the stable range (roughly Re 40-150)
Fitted relation for the transition range (roughly Re 150-300)
Asymptotic value both fitted curves approach as Re grows
The defining dimensionless-frequency ratio itself

questions.explanation: Roshko fit separate curves for the stable and transition Reynolds-number ranges, both converging toward 0.212 at higher Re, while St = fD/U is the underlying dimensionless definition those curves describe.

lessons.label: Bluff Bodies, Base Pressure and Shape Effects

sections.heading: Fixed versus free separation points
sections.body: A circular cylinder has a free separation point: where the boundary layer detaches depends on Reynolds number, because it depends on how far a laminar or turbulent boundary layer can fight the adverse pressure gradient around the curved surface, which is exactly why its Strouhal number and drag both shift with regime (covered in the previous lesson). A square cylinder, by contrast, has fixed separation, the flow detaches cleanly at the sharp leading corners regardless of Reynolds number, because a sharp corner forces separation independent of boundary-layer state. Fixed-separation bodies therefore show Strouhal numbers and drag coefficients that are far more Reynolds-number-insensitive than the circular cylinder's own free-separation wake: a square cylinder sheds at St around 0.13, and a flat plate held broadside (normal) to the flow sheds at St around 0.15, both nearly constant across a wide speed range because the geometry, not the boundary layer, decides where the flow leaves the body.

sections.heading: Shape sets the wake, and the wake sets the drag
sections.body: Wider effective separation, meaning separation points far apart and a wide wake, produces high form drag; narrow, aft-shifted separation reduces it. A sphere, unlike a 2D cylinder, sheds three-dimensional hairpin-shaped vortex loops rather than a straight alternating street, because its axisymmetric wake structure has no single spanwise direction to organize into 2D rollers. A well-designed streamlined fairing, a teardrop cross-section with a long, gradually tapering tail, delays and can nearly eliminate separation altogether: with no organized alternating shear layers to feed a von Karman instability, periodic shedding is suppressed and the tone disappears along with most of the drag, exactly the design logic behind streamlined struts, fairings on cables, and helical strakes wrapped around smokestacks and marine risers.

sections.heading: Base pressure coefficient is the wake, quantified
sections.body: The base pressure coefficient, Cpb = (pbase - pinf)/(0.5*rho*U^2), measures how far below free-stream pressure the body's back surface sits. Because pressure integrated around a bluff body's surface is what produces form drag (skin friction is comparatively minor for these shapes), a more negative Cpb translates almost directly into higher drag: this is why base pressure is treated as the single most diagnostic measurement of a bluff-body wake, low base pressure means a strong, close-formed wake and high drag, and higher (less negative) base pressure means a longer formation region, weaker wake, and lower drag. Measuring Cpb with a single pressure tap at the rear of a model is a cheap, powerful proxy for a full drag balance.

lessons.workedExample: Three models of the same frontal width are tested in the same wind tunnel: a circular cylinder, a square cylinder, and a teardrop fairing. The circular cylinder shows St~0.2 and a fairly negative Cpb; the square cylinder, despite having sharp fixed-separation corners, shows a lower St~0.13 but an even more negative Cpb and higher drag, because its flat face and sharp-cornered wake are simply wider than the circular cylinder's; the teardrop fairing shows no periodic tone at all and a Cpb close to zero, because its tapering tail lets the boundary layer stay attached almost to the trailing edge, leaving no organized shear layers to shed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe shape effects because it is easy to memorize that 'circles shed vortices' and never generalize the underlying cause, fixed versus free separation, to other geometries. The strong answer explains why a square cylinder's Strouhal number barely moves with speed (sharp corners fix separation) while a circular cylinder's does (boundary-layer state decides separation), and connects a measured base pressure directly to predicted drag without needing a force balance. That connection, pressure measurement standing in for a drag measurement, is the applied insight a fair project can actually use.

questions.prompt: Why is a square cylinder's Strouhal number much less sensitive to Reynolds number than a circular cylinder's?

options.text: Square cylinders do not shed vortices at all
Sharp corners fix the separation point geometrically, independent of boundary-layer state, unlike a circular cylinder's free separation
Square cylinders are always tested at a single fixed speed
The Strouhal number is undefined for non-circular shapes

explanations.a: Square cylinders do shed periodically, at St around 0.13.
explanations.b: Correct — a sharp corner forces separation regardless of whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent, removing the Reynolds-number sensitivity that a circular cylinder's free separation point has.
explanations.c: St is measured across a range of speeds for any shape; the insensitivity is a physical property of fixed separation, not a testing artifact.
explanations.d: St = fD/U applies to any bluff body, circular or not; it is a general dimensionless shedding frequency.

questions.prompt: Why does a sphere produce hairpin-shaped vortex loops instead of a straight, 2D alternating street?

options.text: Spheres never shed vortices
The axisymmetric wake has no single spanwise direction to organize a straight 2D roller pattern
Spheres always operate past the drag crisis
Hairpin loops only occur in compressible flow

explanations.a: Spheres do shed, just in a three-dimensional hairpin pattern rather than a 2D street.
explanations.b: Correct — a 2D cylinder has a spanwise axis along which a straight, alternating street can organize; a sphere's axisymmetric geometry has no such preferred direction, producing 3D hairpin loops instead.
explanations.c: Hairpin shedding occurs well below the drag crisis; it is a geometric effect of axisymmetry, not a high-Re effect.
explanations.d: This is an incompressible-flow phenomenon tied to geometry, unrelated to compressibility.

questions.prompt: A more negative base pressure coefficient (Cpb) on a bluff body generally indicates:

options.text: Lower form drag
Higher form drag, since a strong, closely-formed wake pulls the base pressure well below free-stream
No relationship to drag at all
That the body has a streamlined tail

explanations.a: This is backwards; more negative base pressure corresponds to higher, not lower, drag.
explanations.b: Correct — since pressure drag dominates form drag on bluff bodies, a lower (more negative) base pressure means a stronger low-pressure wake pulling harder on the back of the body, raising drag.
explanations.c: Base pressure is treated as the primary diagnostic proxy for bluff-body drag precisely because the relationship is strong.
explanations.d: A streamlined tail (like a teardrop fairing) produces a base pressure close to zero, not strongly negative.

questions.prompt: Why does a teardrop-shaped fairing suppress periodic vortex shedding almost entirely?

options.text: It has no boundary layer
Its gradually tapering tail keeps the boundary layer attached nearly to the trailing edge, leaving no organized alternating shear layers to feed the instability
It only works at Re below 5
It increases the base pressure coefficient's magnitude to make shedding stronger

explanations.a: Every real body in a viscous fluid develops a boundary layer; the fairing does not eliminate it, it keeps it attached longer.
explanations.b: Correct — delaying separation to near the trailing edge removes the two well-separated, strong shear layers that Gerrard's mechanism needs to feed alternating vortex growth, suppressing the tone.
explanations.c: Streamlined fairings are used across a wide range of practical Reynolds numbers, not only in creeping flow.
explanations.d: A fairing pushes Cpb toward zero (less negative), the opposite of strengthening shedding.

lessons.label: The Aeolian Tone and Singing Wires

sections.heading: From alternating force to sound
sections.body: Every shed vortex leaves the body carrying circulation of one sign, and by Newton's third law the body feels an equal and opposite reaction force each time. Because the vortices alternate side to side, that reaction force fluctuates transversely at the shedding frequency f = St*U/D, a lift force oscillating side to side rather than a steady drag. A fluctuating force pressed against the surrounding air radiates sound, and because the mechanism is a force acting at a point (the body) rather than a mass source, the radiation pattern is a dipole, strongest broadside to the flow and weak fore-aft. This tone, produced purely by vortex shedding with no vibrating string or reed involved, is called the aeolian tone, after Aeolus, the Greek keeper of the winds, and it is the whistling, humming, or singing sound of wind past a thin wire, branch, or antenna.

sections.heading: Curle's surface-source formulation
sections.body: The rigorous acoustic theory for sound generated by a solid body in a flow comes from M. J. Lighthill's 1952 acoustic-analogy framework, extended by N. Curle in 1955 to include the effect of solid boundaries: Curle showed the surface force fluctuations (exactly the alternating lift from shedding) act as an effective dipole source, and worked out how its radiated sound depends on the unsteady surface pressure distribution. This is the formal justification for why vortex shedding, not just resonance, is a genuine acoustic source, and it is the theoretical basis engineers use to predict and quiet everything from wind-turbine blade tips to car radio antennas.

sections.heading: A whole family of everyday singing wakes
sections.body: The same physics shows up wherever wind crosses a thin, roughly cylindrical object: telephone and power lines singing in a steady breeze, the deliberately tuned strings of an aeolian harp left to hum in an open window, the drone of a car's roof rack crossbars at highway speed, and the slap and hum of a boat's rope halyard against a mast in gusty wind. In every case the tone rises with wind speed because f is proportional to U at fixed D and St, and the loudness rises far faster than the tone: for a compact dipole source, radiated acoustic power scales roughly as U^6, so doubling the wind speed raises the sound power by roughly a factor of 64, which is why a gentle breeze past a wire is barely audible while a stiff wind past the same wire is a loud, unmistakable whine.

lessons.workedExample: A 3 mm diameter telephone wire hums in a 15 m/s crosswind. Using the Strouhal plateau St~0.2, predicted tone: f = St*U/D = 0.2*15/0.003 = 1000 Hz, close to a 1 kHz whistle, audibly high and piercing, matching what people actually hear from singing wires in strong wind. If the wind then gusts up to 30 m/s, double the speed, the tone rises proportionally to about 2000 Hz, but the acoustic power rises far more steeply, by roughly 2^6 = 64 times, so the wire goes from a faint hum to a loud shriek even though the frequency only doubled.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about the aeolian tone is checking whether a student connects an everyday sound to the same shedding mechanism taught elsewhere in this unit, rather than treating acoustics as an unrelated topic. The strong answer computes f=StU/D correctly for a real object, names the dipole radiation pattern and its physical cause (alternating transverse force, per Curle's 1955 surface-source theory), and can explain why loudness rises so much faster than pitch as wind speed increases, the U^6 power scaling. A student who only says 'wind makes wires vibrate' has missed that the vortex shedding is the cause of both the force and the sound.

questions.prompt: A 3 mm wire hums in a 15 m/s crosswind, with shedding near the St~0.2 plateau. What tone frequency is predicted?

options.text: 100 Hz
0.2 Hz

explanations.a: This understates the result by roughly a factor of 10; recheck the diameter conversion from mm to meters.
explanations.c: This overstates the result by a factor of 10.
explanations.d: This is simply St itself, not a frequency; St must be multiplied by U/D.

questions.prompt: Why does the aeolian tone radiate as an acoustic dipole rather than a monopole?

options.text: Because the source is a fluctuating force on the body (Curle's surface-source result), not a fluctuating mass flow
Because the wind is subsonic
Because vortex shedding only occurs at night
Because the wire is thin

explanations.a: Correct — a monopole comes from a fluctuating volume/mass source, while a dipole comes from a fluctuating force; the alternating transverse lift force from shedding is exactly the force source Curle's 1955 extension of Lighthill's theory describes.
explanations.b: Subsonic flow is the normal condition for aeolian tones but does not by itself determine monopole versus dipole character; that depends on the type of source.
explanations.c: Time of day is irrelevant to the acoustic radiation mechanism.
explanations.d: Wire thinness affects the frequency (via D) but not why the source is a dipole rather than a monopole.

questions.prompt: If wind speed past a singing wire doubles, roughly how does the radiated sound power change, given a compact dipole source scales as U^6?

options.text: It doubles
It increases by roughly a factor of 64
It stays the same
It increases by roughly a factor of 4

explanations.a: Doubling would only apply if power scaled linearly with U, but the dipole scaling is U^6, much steeper.
explanations.b: Correct — for a compact dipole, power scales as U^6, so doubling U multiplies power by 2^6 = 64.
explanations.c: Power is strongly speed-dependent for a dipole source, not constant.
explanations.d: A factor of 4 would correspond to U^2 scaling, which describes dynamic pressure, not dipole acoustic power.

questions.prompt: What physically produces the fluctuating force that generates the aeolian tone?

options.text: The steady drag force on the body
The alternating transverse (lift) reaction force as vortices of alternating sign are shed from opposite sides
Friction between the wire and the wind
Resonance of the wire's own material stiffness, unrelated to the flow

explanations.a: Steady drag does not fluctuate at the shedding frequency and is not the acoustic source here.
explanations.b: Correct — each shed vortex produces an equal-and-opposite reaction force on the body, and because shedding alternates sides, this force oscillates transversely at f = St*U/D, driving the dipole sound.
explanations.c: Simple friction does not produce a periodic tone at a well-defined frequency; the mechanism is the alternating vortex-induced force.
explanations.d: The aeolian tone occurs even for a perfectly rigid, non-resonant cylinder; material resonance can amplify it (as in true structural singing) but is not required to produce the tone itself.

lessons.label: Reading a Wake: Momentum Deficit and Decay

sections.heading: The wake is a missing-momentum bookkeeping problem
sections.body: A body immersed in a stream slows the fluid that passes near it: skin friction and pressure drag both act by robbing streamwise momentum from the flow, and that missing momentum shows up directly downstream as a velocity deficit, a dip in streamwise velocity across the wake compared to the undisturbed free stream. Because momentum is conserved, integrating that deficit across the wake's cross-section gives the total streamwise momentum the body removed per unit time, which by Newton's second law equals the drag force the fluid exerted on the body. This is the control-volume argument behind the classic momentum-deficit method: D = rho * integral of u(U - u) dA across a wake plane far enough downstream that the static pressure has returned to free-stream, where u is the local wake velocity and U is the free-stream speed.

sections.heading: Near wake versus far wake
sections.body: Close behind a bluff body (the near wake), the flow is dominated by the discrete, organized structure of the Karman vortex street itself, distinct velocity peaks and troughs tracing individual vortex cores, and static pressure has not yet fully recovered to free-stream, so applying the simple momentum-deficit formula there overestimates drag. Farther downstream (the far wake, typically tens of diameters back), the discrete vortices have diffused and merged through viscous mixing and turbulent transport into a smooth, single-troughed velocity-deficit profile; pressure has equilibrated, and the momentum-deficit integral gives an accurate drag estimate. As you move further downstream still, the wake widens (grows wider as a power law with distance) while its centerline velocity deficit shrinks, because the same missing momentum spreads across an ever-larger cross-section, conserving the integral even as the local deficit shape flattens.

sections.heading: From organized vortices to self-similar turbulence
sections.body: Far enough downstream, the periodic vortex street itself is no longer visible: viscous diffusion and turbulent mixing erase the discrete rollers, and the wake settles into a smooth, self-similar turbulent shear layer whose deficit profile, once rescaled by local wake width and centerline deficit, looks the same at every downstream station, a universal shape independent of the exact body that generated it. This self-similar decay is why a wake traverse taken with a single-point probe, a pitot-static tube or a hot-wire, stepped across the wake at one downstream station, is enough to recover drag without ever touching a force balance: measure the velocity profile, apply the momentum-deficit integral, and the drag force falls out directly.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants the drag on a small cylinder in a wind tunnel but has no force balance. They traverse a pitot tube across the wake 20 diameters downstream, well into the far wake where pressure has recovered, recording velocity at 1 cm intervals. They numerically integrate rho*u(U-u) across the traverse, U being the free-stream reading from a pitot outside the wake. The resulting number is the drag force per unit span directly, matching what a force balance would read, because the momentum lost by the fluid equals the force the fluid exerted back on the body. Doing the same traverse only 2 diameters back (deep in the near wake, still showing individual vortex peaks and incomplete pressure recovery) would overestimate drag, illustrating why downstream station matters.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing wake measurement wants to see whether a student understands drag as a momentum-accounting result, not just something a load cell spits out. The strong answer explains why the traverse must be taken far enough downstream for pressure to recover, states the momentum-deficit integral in words even without symbols, and knows that the wake widens while the centerline deficit shrinks as the same missing momentum spreads out, which is why the method still works dozens of diameters back even though the near-wake vortex structure is long gone by then.

questions.prompt: Why does the momentum-deficit method require measuring the wake far enough downstream rather than right behind the body?

options.text: Because the near wake has no velocity deficit at all
Because near-wake static pressure has not yet recovered to free-stream, so the simple deficit integral overestimates drag there
Because probes cannot physically fit close to a body
Because the free stream is undefined near the body

explanations.a: The near wake has the largest velocity deficit of anywhere in the flow, driven by the organized vortex structure.
explanations.b: Correct — the simple momentum-deficit formula assumes free-stream static pressure across the measurement plane; that assumption only holds once pressure has equilibrated downstream, in the far wake.
explanations.c: This is a practical concern in some setups but not the physical reason the method requires a far-wake station.
explanations.d: Free-stream conditions are still well-defined outside the wake even close to the body; the issue is pressure recovery within the wake itself.

questions.prompt: As the wake develops further downstream, what happens to its width and centerline velocity deficit?

options.text: Both grow together
The wake widens while the centerline deficit shrinks, conserving the total momentum deficit
The wake narrows while the deficit grows
Both stay exactly constant

explanations.a: If both grew, the integrated momentum deficit (and thus apparent drag) would keep increasing downstream, which is not physical for steady flow.
explanations.b: Correct — the same missing momentum spreads across a widening cross-section, so the wake grows wider while its peak (centerline) deficit shrinks, keeping the integrated momentum deficit constant.
explanations.c: This is the reverse of the observed behavior.
explanations.d: The wake visibly spreads and its peak deficit visibly decays with downstream distance; neither stays constant.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for the far wake to become 'self-similar'?

options.text: The wake exactly repeats the near-wake vortex pattern at every station
Once rescaled by local wake width and centerline deficit, the velocity-deficit profile has the same shape at every downstream station
The wake becomes perfectly laminar again
The drag force changes at every downstream station

explanations.a: The discrete organized vortex structure of the near wake is exactly what has been erased by the time the far wake becomes self-similar.
explanations.b: Correct — self-similarity means the profile shape is universal once normalized by local scales, even though the absolute width and deficit magnitude both change with distance.
explanations.c: The far wake is turbulent, not laminar; self-similarity describes a statistical turbulent structure, not a return to laminar flow.
explanations.d: The integrated drag force is conserved (constant) downstream once pressure has recovered; it is the local velocity profile shape, not the force, that becomes self-similar.

questions.prompt: A single-point pitot or hot-wire traverse across a far wake, combined with the momentum-deficit integral, can recover which quantity without a force balance?

options.text: The body's lift coefficient
The body's drag force
The body's surface temperature
The shedding frequency only

explanations.a: Lift is a transverse force not captured by a streamwise momentum-deficit traverse in general.
explanations.b: Correct — integrating rho*u(U-u) across a far-wake velocity profile directly yields the drag force per unit span, by conservation of streamwise momentum.
explanations.c: Velocity traverses give no thermal information.
explanations.d: Shedding frequency can be extracted from a time-resolved probe signal, but it is a separate quantity from the drag obtained via the momentum-deficit integral of the mean profile.

lessons.label: Drafting and Slipstreaming: Riding Another Body's Wake

sections.heading: Lower dynamic pressure, lower drag, for the trailing body
sections.body: The velocity-deficit region behind any body, the wake described in the previous lesson, is by definition slower-moving fluid than the free stream. Drag on a bluff or streamlined body scales with dynamic pressure, 0.5*rho*U^2, using the local relative speed the body actually experiences. A trailing body positioned inside that deficit region therefore sits in air (or water) that is already moving closer to its own speed, so the relative velocity between the trailing body and the surrounding fluid is reduced, cutting its dynamic pressure and, with it, its drag. This is drafting or slipstreaming: riding in the sheltered, momentum-depleted wake of a leading body.

sections.heading: The leading body benefits too
sections.body: The benefit is not one-directional. A trailing body sitting close behind partially fills in the low-pressure base region right behind the leading body, the same base pressure discussed earlier in this unit, raising that base pressure back toward free-stream and reducing the leading body's own form drag. This is why elite cyclists riding in a tight paceline still see the lead rider's power output measurably drop compared to riding fully alone, and why professional cycling teams rotate the lead position deliberately: both riders in a close pair save energy, just unevenly, with the trailing rider saving substantially more.

sections.heading: Numbers, and the safety cost
sections.body: Wind-tunnel and field studies of cycling put the drag saving for a rider positioned roughly one bike-length behind a single leading rider at roughly 25 to 40 percent, a very large effect given that aerodynamic drag is the dominant resistance for a cyclist above modest speeds. The same physics scales up to highway trucking: automated truck platooning trials (following distances of a few meters, held automatically) have measured fuel savings on the order of 10 percent for a trailing truck and smaller but real savings for the lead truck, enough that platooning is pursued commercially for fleet fuel economy. But riding in someone else's wake has a real safety cost: the flow there is unsteady rather than the clean laminar-ish stream ahead of the leader, so a drafting body experiences buffeting, fluctuating side loads from the leader's own shed vortices, meaning reduced control margin, and it also loses the visual and stopping-distance buffer of open road, which is why platooning systems require automated, fast-reacting control and why cyclists drafting too closely are exposed to sudden collisions if the wheel ahead brakes or wobbles.

lessons.workedExample: A cyclist riding solo at 35 km/h experiences essentially the full free-stream dynamic pressure on their frontal area. A second cyclist tucks in one bike-length behind; because that position sits in the lead rider's velocity-deficit wake, the trailing rider's effective relative airspeed is reduced enough to cut their aerodynamic drag by roughly 30 percent, near the middle of the commonly measured 25 to 40 percent range, at the same road speed, meaning they can either hold the same pace for noticeably less power or hold a higher pace for the same power. Meanwhile the lead rider, whose base region is now partly filled by the trailing rider's presence, sees a smaller but real drag reduction too, which is the physical reason pacelines rotate the lead rather than one rider doing all the work.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about drafting wants to see the wake concept applied, not just recited: can a student explain drafting as a direct consequence of the velocity-deficit region lowering relative dynamic pressure, connect the leading body's benefit to base pressure recovery from earlier in the unit, and cite a real, bounded figure (the 25-40 percent cycling range) rather than a vague 'it helps.' The strongest answers also flag the safety tradeoff unprompted, unsteady buffeting and reduced stopping margin, showing the student sees drafting as an engineering tradeoff, not a free lunch.

questions.prompt: Why does a trailing body positioned in a leading body's wake experience lower drag?

options.text: The leading body blocks all air resistance completely
The wake's velocity-deficit region reduces the relative speed between the trailing body and the surrounding fluid, lowering its dynamic pressure
The trailing body becomes lighter
Vortex shedding stops entirely behind the leading body

explanations.a: Drag is reduced substantially, not eliminated; the trailing body still experiences real aerodynamic drag, just less of it.
explanations.b: Correct — since drag scales with dynamic pressure based on relative velocity, sitting in slower-moving wake fluid directly cuts the trailing body's dynamic pressure and drag.
explanations.c: Aerodynamic drag reduction has nothing to do with mass or weight.
explanations.d: Vortex shedding continues; drafting exploits the mean velocity deficit of the wake, and the resulting unsteady vortex structure is actually the source of the buffeting hazard discussed in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Roughly what drag reduction does a cyclist see riding about one bike-length behind a single leading rider?

options.text: About 2-5 percent
About 25-40 percent
About 90 percent
Drag actually increases

explanations.a: This underestimates the effect; the measured cycling drafting benefit is much larger than a few percent.
explanations.b: Correct — wind-tunnel and field studies put the saving for a rider roughly one bike-length behind a single leader at roughly 25 to 40 percent.
explanations.c: This overstates the effect; drag is substantially reduced, not nearly eliminated.
explanations.d: The trailing rider's drag decreases, not increases, due to the reduced relative dynamic pressure in the wake.

questions.prompt: Why does the leading body also gain a (smaller) drag benefit from a trailing body riding close behind?

options.text: The trailing body partially fills the leader's low-pressure base region, raising base pressure back toward free-stream and reducing the leader's form drag
The trailing body pushes the leader forward directly
The leader's boundary layer becomes laminar
There is no benefit to the leading body

explanations.a: Correct — this ties directly to base pressure from earlier in the unit: a trailing body sitting close behind raises the leader's base pressure, cutting its form drag.
explanations.b: There is no meaningful direct push; the mechanism is aerodynamic (pressure), not a contact or momentum-transfer push.
explanations.c: Boundary-layer state on the leader is not what changes here; it is the base-pressure field behind the leader that shifts.
explanations.d: The leading body does measurably benefit, which is why paceline riders rotate the lead position rather than one rider bearing the full cost alone.

questions.prompt: What is the primary safety cost of riding in another body's wake, beyond the drag benefit?

options.text: Increased top speed with no downside
Unsteady buffeting from the leader's shed vortices, reducing control authority and stopping/reaction margin
Guaranteed engine or muscle failure
Complete loss of steering control at all times

explanations.a: There is a real downside, unsteady wake flow, not just a free speed benefit.
explanations.b: Correct — the wake carries fluctuating side loads from the leader's own vortex shedding, so a following body (cyclist or platooning truck) experiences buffeting and has less margin to react to a sudden change ahead.
explanations.c: This overstates the effect; the hazard is reduced control margin and unsteady loading, not guaranteed mechanical failure.
explanations.d: Control is degraded, not completely and permanently lost; automated platooning systems specifically compensate for this with fast control loops.

units.label: Measuring Unsteady Flow

lessons.label: Hot-Wire Anemometry for Time-Resolved Velocity

sections.heading: Constant temperature vs. constant current
sections.body: A hot-wire probe is a few-micron metal filament, welded across two support needles, heated electrically above the fluid temperature; convective cooling by the passing flow is what gets measured. There are two ways to drive it. Constant-current anemometry (CCA) pushes a fixed current through the wire and reads the voltage as its resistance (and temperature) drifts with cooling — simple electronics, but the wire's own thermal inertia limits how fast it can respond. Constant-temperature anemometry (CTA) instead wraps the wire in a Wheatstone-bridge feedback loop that instantly adjusts the current to hold resistance, and therefore temperature, fixed; the bridge does the work the wire's thermal mass otherwise couldn't, which is why CTA dominates modern unsteady-flow work. The overheat ratio — operating resistance divided by cold resistance, typically set around 1.5-1.8 — trades sensitivity (higher overheat, stronger signal) against thermal stress on the filament.

sections.heading: King's law and calibration
sections.body: The physics linking voltage to velocity is forced-convection heat transfer off a heated cylinder in crossflow, analyzed by King (1914): E^2 = A + B*U^n, with the exponent n empirically close to 0.5 for typical hot-wire operating conditions. A, B, and n are not looked up — they are fit for each individual wire by exposing it to a set of known velocities (a calibration jet checked against a pitot-static reference) and least-squares fitting the E-U pairs. Because the relationship is nonlinear and wire-specific, every probe needs its own calibration, and that calibration drifts with fluid temperature: the wire's cooling depends on the temperature difference to the fluid, so a lab that warms up 3-4 degrees C over an afternoon quietly shifts the E-U curve unless temperature is compensated or the wire is recalibrated.

sections.heading: Why hot wire wins on bandwidth, and where it fails
sections.body: A roughly 5-micron tungsten or platinum wire with CTA feedback delivers flat frequency response out to a few tens of kHz — well beyond the reach of pressure transducers fighting tubing resonance or load cells fighting mount vibration — which is exactly why hot wire is the default instrument for resolving vortex-shedding tones and the turbulent energy cascade above them. Its central failure is directional ambiguity: the wire senses only the magnitude of cooling, not the sign of velocity, so it cannot distinguish forward flow from reversed flow. In a recirculating near-wake or a separated/stalled region, a single wire reports a rectified-looking signal that folds negative velocity onto positive. The fix is to add wires: an X-wire (two wires crossed at an angle, commonly 90 degrees) resolves two velocity components with sign within a valid acceptance cone; a triple-wire array adds the third component. Beyond directionality, fine wires are fragile — they break from dust, seeding particles, or accidental contact with the model — so a running experiment budgets for wire replacement and recalibration.

lessons.workedExample: A student calibrates a single CTA hot wire against a pitot-static reference at six speeds from 3 to 18 m/s and fits King's law, getting n = 0.46. They place the wire three diameters downstream of a 1 cm cylinder in a 6 m/s stream, where a Strouhal number near 0.2 predicts shedding around 120 Hz. Sampling at 5 kHz — far inside the wire's tens-of-kHz bandwidth — the spectrum shows one clean, narrow peak at about 118 Hz, confirming vortex shedding is being resolved rather than aliased. Moving the same wire into the near-wake recirculation bubble right behind the cylinder, the time trace turns lumpy and the spectrum smears: the wire is intermittently seeing reversed flow it cannot sign correctly, and the fix is to swap in an X-wire before trusting any velocity number from that location.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about hot-wire technique because it is the instrument students most often use without understanding what it actually senses. A student who only says "it measures velocity" hasn't engaged with the method. One who can state that the signal is a nonlinear heat-loss voltage requiring per-wire King's-law calibration, name the overheat ratio and temperature drift as sources of error, and specifically flag that a single wire cannot see flow direction in a recirculating wake — describing the X-wire fix — demonstrates they understand both why the tool was chosen (bandwidth) and where its readings can quietly lie.

questions.prompt: King's law relating hot-wire voltage to flow velocity has the form:

options.text: E = A + B*U, a simple linear relationship
E^2 = A + B*U^n, with n empirically near 0.5
U = A*E^2 + B, velocity as a linear function of squared voltage
E = A*log(U) + B, a logarithmic relationship

explanations.a: The heat-loss physics is not linear in E; squaring the voltage is what linearizes the relationship against velocity to first order.
explanations.b: Correct — King's (1914) forced-convection analysis gives E^2 = A + B*U^n, with n typically close to 0.5, fit per wire by calibration against a known-velocity reference.
explanations.c: This inverts the roles incorrectly and is not the empirical form used for calibration.
explanations.d: Hot-wire heat transfer is a power-law relationship in velocity, not a logarithmic one.

questions.prompt: Why does constant-temperature anemometry (CTA) achieve much higher frequency response than constant-current anemometry (CCA)?

options.text: CTA uses a thicker wire that heats up faster
The CTA feedback bridge instantly adjusts current to hold resistance fixed, bypassing the wire's own thermal inertia
CTA probes are always X-wires, which sample twice as fast
CCA is actually faster, but CTA is cheaper to build

explanations.a: CTA wires are typically as fine as CCA wires (around 5 microns); the speed advantage is electronic, not from wire thickness.
explanations.b: Correct — the Wheatstone-bridge feedback loop in CTA continuously drives current to keep the wire's resistance (temperature) constant, so the electronics respond fast even though the wire's own thermal mass is slow to change.
explanations.c: Wire count (single vs. X-wire) is about resolving velocity components, not about frequency response.
explanations.d: CTA is the faster of the two, which is exactly why it is preferred for shedding and turbulence spectra.

questions.prompt: A single hot wire placed in a recirculating near-wake region gives an unreliable reading mainly because:

options.text: It senses only the magnitude of cooling, not the sign of velocity, so it cannot distinguish forward from reversed flow
Its frequency response is too slow to see recirculation
The overheat ratio is always set incorrectly for wakes
King's law does not apply below 5 m/s

explanations.a: Correct — heat loss depends on flow speed past the wire regardless of direction, so a single wire cannot sign the velocity, producing a rectified-looking signal in reversing flow.
explanations.b: Bandwidth (tens of kHz) is not the limitation here; the problem is directional ambiguity, not speed of response.
explanations.c: Overheat ratio affects sensitivity and thermal stress generally, not specifically wake directionality.
explanations.d: King's law calibration range is a separate, solvable issue and not the reason recirculating flow confuses a single wire.

questions.prompt: Match each hot-wire limitation to its fix or cause.

left.text: Cannot tell forward from reversed flow
Calibration curve shifts over a session

right.text: Add a second (or third) wire: X-wire or triple-wire array
Ambient/fluid temperature change alters heat loss; recalibrate or compensate
Micron-scale wire is fragile against dust, seeding particles, or contact

questions.explanation: Directional ambiguity is resolved by adding wires (X-wire for two components, triple-wire for three); calibration drift traces back to the temperature dependence of convective heat loss and is fixed by recalibration or temperature compensation; and breakage is simply the price of a filament fine enough to give tens-of-kHz bandwidth.

lessons.label: Time-Resolved and Phase-Locked PIV

sections.heading: Two ways to build up a picture of an unsteady wake
sections.body: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) tracks seeded tracer particles across paired camera frames separated by a known laser-pulse interval, cross-correlating small interrogation windows to build a velocity field — the modern form traces to Adrian's foundational reviews in the early 1990s. Resolving an unsteady wake with PIV can go two ways. Time-resolved PIV uses a high-repetition-rate laser (kilohertz-class, e.g. diode-pumped Nd:YLF) and a high-speed camera to capture a continuous movie of the flow, so a single run shows the wake evolving in real time — powerful, but the hardware is expensive and record length is limited by camera memory. Phase-locked PIV instead uses ordinary low-repetition-rate double-pulse equipment (a 10 Hz Nd:YAG system is standard) but fires it only at a fixed phase of the shedding cycle, triggered off a reference signal such as a hot-wire zero-crossing or a shaft encoder pulse; repeating over many cycles builds a phase-averaged flow field at that instant of the cycle for a fraction of the cost.

sections.heading: Setting the timing: sampling rate and pulse separation
sections.body: For time-resolved PIV to actually resolve shedding rather than alias it, the frame rate should give at least roughly 10 frames per shedding cycle, so a 120 Hz shedding tone needs on the order of 1200+ Hz acquisition — comparable in spirit to the oversampling margin used for any periodic unsteady signal. Within each frame pair, the laser pulse separation is set by the expected particle displacement: too short and particles barely move, burying the signal in cross-correlation noise; too long and fast-moving particles leave the interrogation window entirely (or, worse, out-of-plane motion carries them out of the laser sheet), so the separation is tuned to put the expected displacement at roughly a quarter of the interrogation window.

sections.heading: Seeding fidelity and computing vorticity from a noisy field
sections.body: PIV only measures the tracer particles' motion, so the particles must actually follow the flow. Fidelity is governed by the Stokes number, the ratio of particle response time to a flow timescale; a low-Stokes-number tracer (sub-micron oil droplets or DEHS in air, hollow glass spheres or titanium dioxide in water) relaxes to the local fluid velocity fast enough that its trajectory is a faithful proxy for the flow's — a Stokes number well below 1 is the target, and coarse or dense seeding particles simply lag the flow, especially through the sharp velocity gradients inside a vortex core. Once a velocity field is in hand, vorticity is computed by spatially differentiating it (curl of the in-plane velocity), and differentiation amplifies noise — a velocity field with modest random error can produce a vorticity field that is visibly speckled unless the raw data is smoothed or interpolated onto a finer, validated grid first.

lessons.workedExample: A team studies a cylinder shedding at 120 Hz behind their benchtop tunnel. With only a 10 Hz double-pulse laser available, they cannot resolve the cycle directly, so they wire a hot wire in the wake as a phase reference: each time its signal crosses zero on the rising edge, it triggers one PIV image pair after a programmed delay. By sweeping that delay across one full shedding period (about 8.3 ms) in small steps and averaging ~50 image pairs per delay setting, they reconstruct a phase-averaged vortex-shedding cycle — effectively a slow-motion movie built from many separate cycles — at a fraction of the cost of a kilohertz time-resolved system, though they lose the ability to see cycle-to-cycle variability that a true time-resolved run would capture.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes PIV timing choices because it is where students either show they engineered the measurement or just borrowed a lab's default settings. A strong answer explains why the frame rate or trigger scheme was matched to the known (or estimated) shedding frequency rather than picked arbitrarily, names the Stokes number as the reason their tracer particles were chosen, and — critically — recognizes that a vorticity field is a derivative of noisy data, so a clean-looking vorticity plot without any mention of smoothing or validation is a red flag, not a strength.

questions.prompt: For time-resolved PIV to adequately resolve a 120 Hz vortex-shedding cycle, the camera frame rate should be roughly:

options.text: 120 Hz, matching the shedding frequency exactly
At least ~1200 Hz, giving on the order of 10 frames per shedding cycle
60 Hz, half the shedding frequency
Any rate above 10 Hz is sufficient

explanations.a: Sampling exactly at the shedding frequency captures the same phase every time and would not resolve the cycle's evolution at all.
explanations.b: Correct — aiming for roughly 10 frames per shedding cycle gives enough temporal resolution to actually trace the cycle's evolution, not just detect that shedding is occurring.
explanations.c: Sampling below the shedding frequency risks aliasing the periodic motion into a false, much lower apparent frequency.
explanations.d: A 10 Hz rate is far too coarse relative to a 120 Hz event; it would only occasionally catch a nearly-random phase of the cycle.

questions.prompt: What does phase-locked PIV trade away compared to true time-resolved PIV?

options.text: Spatial resolution of each individual image
The ability to see cycle-to-cycle variability, since each phase is built from an average over many separate cycles
The ability to measure velocity at all, only vorticity
Nothing; it is strictly superior in every way

explanations.a: Phase-locked PIV typically uses the same camera resolution as any double-pulse PIV setup; spatial resolution is not the trade-off.
explanations.b: Correct — because each phase is assembled from many separate shedding cycles triggered at the same relative phase, natural cycle-to-cycle variation is averaged away, unlike a true time-resolved recording of one continuous cycle.
explanations.c: Phase-locked PIV still measures velocity fields directly; vorticity is computed afterward from either technique's velocity data.
explanations.d: It is cheaper and uses standard equipment, but it explicitly sacrifices seeing individual-cycle variability.

questions.prompt: Why does the Stokes number matter when choosing PIV seeding particles?

options.text: It determines how bright the particles appear under laser illumination
A low Stokes number means the particle's response time is fast enough that it faithfully follows the flow, including through steep gradients like a vortex core
It sets the required laser pulse separation directly
It only matters for water flows, not air flows

explanations.a: Brightness is governed by particle size, scattering properties, and laser power, not by the Stokes number.
explanations.b: Correct — the Stokes number compares particle response time to a flow timescale; well below 1 means the tracer relaxes to local fluid velocity quickly enough to be trusted as a faithful proxy, especially through sharp gradients.
explanations.c: Pulse separation is set by expected particle displacement across the interrogation window, a related but distinct timing choice.
explanations.d: Stokes number is a general tracer-fidelity criterion that applies to seeding in both air and water PIV.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of setting up a phase-locked PIV measurement of a shedding cylinder wake.

items.text: Establish a periodic reference signal (e.g. hot wire or encoder) tied to the shedding cycle
Program a trigger delay corresponding to the desired phase within the cycle
Fire the double-pulse laser and camera at that delay, repeated over many cycles
Ensemble-average the resulting image pairs into a phase-averaged velocity field
Step the delay across the full cycle and repeat, to reconstruct the whole phase-averaged cycle

questions.explanation: A phase reference is established first so triggering is possible at all; a delay picks the target phase; the laser/camera fire repeatedly at that fixed delay across many cycles; those repeats are averaged into one phase-averaged field; then the whole process is swept across delays to reconstruct the full cycle.

lessons.label: Unsteady Force, Pressure and Vibration Signals

sections.heading: Measuring fluctuating force: load cells and balances
sections.body: Vortex shedding produces an oscillating side-force (lift) on a bluff body at the shedding frequency and a smaller drag fluctuation at twice that frequency, and two instrument families capture it. Piezoelectric load cells (crystal elements that generate charge proportional to applied force, e.g. Kistler-style sensors) have very high stiffness and bandwidth, making them well suited to fast force transients, but they cannot hold a true static (zero-frequency) reading because the charge slowly leaks away — fine for oscillating aerodynamic loads, unusable for steady mean force. Strain-gauge balances, by contrast, measure the tiny elastic deflection of a calibrated structure and hold a DC reading indefinitely, but their lower stiffness caps their usable bandwidth well below a piezoelectric cell's.

sections.heading: The trap that dominates real unsteady-force data: structural resonance
sections.body: The single biggest pitfall in unsteady-force measurement is that the model is never rigidly grounded — it sits on a sting or a balance with its own mass and stiffness, so the whole mounted system has natural (structural) frequencies of its own. If one of those structural modes lies anywhere near the vortex-shedding frequency, the sting rings like a tuning fork and the measured force spectrum shows a large peak that is mechanical vibration, not aerodynamic lift.
