The only defense is to identify the mount's natural frequencies before trusting any spectral peak as aerodynamic: a tap test (or hammer test) — striking the unloaded model and recording its free-decay response — reveals the sting/balance's own resonant frequencies, which must then be checked against, and kept well clear of, the expected shedding frequency range.

sections.heading: Pressure, sound, and structural motion
sections.body: Unsteady surface pressure is read with pressure transducers, but if the sensor sits at the end of a length of tubing connecting it to a surface tap (common when the transducer itself cannot fit at the surface), that tubing has its own acoustic resonance — a Helmholtz-type resonance set by the tube's length, diameter, and any connected cavity volume — which can amplify or distort the pressure signal near its resonant frequency exactly the way the sting mount distorts force data; short, stiff tubing or an in-situ (flush-mounted) transducer avoids it. The periodic vortex shedding behind a wire or slender body also radiates sound at the shedding frequency, the aeolian tone (named for Aeolus, the wind god, and studied quantitatively by Strouhal in 1878), which a microphone can pick up as a clean, non-intrusive frequency marker. Finally, accelerometers mounted directly on a model measure its own vibration response, essential for vortex-induced-vibration (VIV) studies where the structure's motion feeds back into the flow.

lessons.workedExample: A team mounts a cylinder on a slender sting attached to a piezoelectric load cell and measures a strong spectral peak at 145 Hz, which they initially report as the vortex-shedding lift frequency. Before trusting it, they run a tap test: with the tunnel off, they strike the sting and record its free-decay vibration, finding a natural frequency of 143 Hz — essentially the same peak. Repeating the wind-on test at several tunnel speeds shows the "shedding" peak staying locked at 143-145 Hz regardless of speed, confirming it is sting resonance being excited by broadband buffeting, not true Strouhal shedding (which should scale with velocity). They stiffen the sting mount, shifting its natural frequency above 400 Hz, and only then does the measured peak track linearly with tunnel speed as expected for aerodynamic shedding.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the sting-resonance trap because it is the single most common way an unsteady-force science-fair project silently reports a wrong result with high confidence. A student who ran a tap test before the wind-on run, and can explain that a true aerodynamic peak should move with flow speed while a structural peak stays fixed, has done the diagnostic that separates real data from an artifact. A student who reports a spectral peak as "the shedding frequency" without ever having characterized their mount's own resonance has skipped the step that most experienced experimentalists consider non-negotiable.

questions.prompt: Why can't a piezoelectric load cell hold a reliable steady (DC) force reading?

options.text: It has too much stiffness to respond to any force at all
The charge generated by the piezoelectric element slowly leaks away, so a constant applied force does not produce a lasting signal
It can only be powered for a few seconds at a time
Piezoelectric cells can only measure pressure, not force

explanations.a: High stiffness is what gives piezoelectric cells their excellent high-frequency response; it is not the reason they drop static readings.
explanations.b: Correct — piezoelectric charge output decays over time under a constant load, so these sensors excel at fast, oscillating forces but cannot substitute for a strain-gauge balance when a true mean (steady) force is needed.
explanations.c: This is not a real limitation of piezoelectric sensors; the issue is charge decay under static load, not a power duration limit.
explanations.d: Piezoelectric elements are used for both force and pressure sensing; that is not what limits their DC response.

questions.prompt: A student sees a strong spectral peak in their sting-mounted force data. What single test should be run before calling that peak aerodynamic vortex shedding?

options.text: Repeat the exact same run again to check repeatability
A tap (hammer) test on the unloaded mount, to identify the sting/balance's own natural frequencies
Increase the sampling rate
Switch from a piezoelectric cell to a microphone

explanations.a: Repeatability alone does not distinguish a structural resonance (which repeats consistently) from a true aerodynamic peak.
explanations.b: Correct — a tap test with the flow off reveals the mount's own structural natural frequencies, which must be checked against the shedding frequency range before any peak can be trusted as aerodynamic.
explanations.c: Sampling rate affects whether a peak can be resolved at all (Nyquist/aliasing), not whether an already-resolved peak is structural or aerodynamic in origin.
explanations.d: A microphone measures radiated sound, a useful independent cross-check, but it does not itself identify the sting's structural resonance.

questions.prompt: How can a true aerodynamic shedding peak be distinguished from a structural (sting) resonance peak across a range of tunnel speeds?

options.text: The aerodynamic peak's frequency scales with flow speed; the structural peak stays fixed near the mount's natural frequency regardless of speed
The structural peak always has a higher amplitude
The aerodynamic peak only appears at exactly one flow speed
There is no way to distinguish them without replacing the sting entirely

explanations.a: Correct — Strouhal shedding frequency scales linearly with flow velocity, while a structural resonance is a fixed property of the mount's mass and stiffness and stays put as speed changes, which is exactly the diagnostic used to unmask sting resonance.
explanations.b: Amplitude alone does not reliably distinguish the two sources; frequency behavior versus speed is the diagnostic.
explanations.c: Vortex shedding occurs across a range of speeds, with frequency tracking speed, not appearing at only one point.
explanations.d: Sweeping tunnel speed and checking whether the peak frequency moves is a non-destructive diagnostic that does not require modifying the rig first.

questions.prompt: Match each unsteady-flow measurement to the instrument that captures it.

left.text: A model's own vibration response (e.g. in a VIV study)
Unsteady surface pressure at a tap

right.text: Piezoelectric load cell or strain-gauge balance
Microphone
Accelerometer mounted on the model
Pressure transducer (flush-mounted or via short tubing)

questions.explanation: Fluctuating force is measured by piezoelectric or strain-gauge sensors; the radiated aeolian tone is captured non-intrusively by a microphone; a vibrating model's own motion is measured by an accelerometer; and unsteady surface pressure is read by a pressure transducer, ideally flush-mounted or connected by short tubing to avoid resonance.

lessons.label: Sampling an Unsteady Signal Correctly

sections.heading: Nyquist, and how aliasing lies to you
sections.body: Any digitized signal — hot-wire voltage, pressure, force — must be sampled at least twice the frequency of the fastest real content it contains, the Nyquist criterion (Nyquist 1928, formalized for sampling theory by Shannon in 1949). Violate it and the signal does not simply blur: a frequency component above half the sampling rate folds down and reappears disguised as a false low frequency, aliasing. A concrete case: a 500 Hz shedding tone sampled at 800 Hz (Nyquist frequency 400 Hz) does not vanish — it reflects off the 400 Hz boundary and reappears at |800-500| = 300 Hz, a fabricated peak that looks entirely legitimate on a spectrum plot. The only real defense is an analog anti-alias low-pass filter placed ahead of the ADC, cutting off content above the Nyquist frequency before digitization; filtering after the fact cannot remove an alias because by then the fake and real frequencies are indistinguishable.

sections.heading: Record length: resolution versus stationarity
sections.body: The frequency resolution of a spectrum computed from a finite record of length T is df = 1/T — a 1-second record can only resolve peaks 1 Hz apart, so distinguishing a 118 Hz shedding tone from a nearby 122 Hz sideband needs at least a quarter-second of clean data (df <= 4 Hz means T >= 0.25 s), and in practice a bit more to account for spectral leakage from windowing. But recording longer is not free: the flow must stay statistically stationary (mean speed, turbulence level, shedding frequency not drifting) across the whole record, or the spectrum smears frequency content that was never simultaneously present into one another. A wind tunnel whose motor speed creeps as it warms up, or a water channel whose head tank slowly drains, can quietly violate stationarity over a multi-minute record, so record length is chosen as the longest window that still fits inside a genuinely steady condition.

sections.heading: Ensemble averaging and phase references
sections.body: A single record's spectral estimate is noisy — each frequency bin's power estimate has high random variance even with a long record — so a converged, trustworthy spectrum comes from averaging many independent shorter records (segments, or repeated runs) together; the estimate's variance falls roughly as the reciprocal of the number of ensembles averaged, so going from a handful of segments to several dozen meaningfully cleans up the spectrum (this is the logic behind Welch's method of spectral estimation). A related but separate choice is a trigger or phase reference — a hot-wire zero-crossing, a shaft encoder pulse, or any other repeatable marker in the cycle — needed whenever the goal is not just a spectrum but a phase-averaged waveform, since averaging raw unsynchronized records together would simply cancel out the periodic content instead of reinforcing it.

lessons.workedExample: A student samples a hot-wire signal at 800 Hz to look for vortex shedding, expecting a peak near 500 Hz based on Strouhal scaling. The spectrum instead shows a strong peak at 300 Hz. Rather than reporting "shedding at 300 Hz," they recognize 800 Hz gives a Nyquist frequency of only 400 Hz — too low to safely capture a real 500 Hz signal — and that 500 Hz aliases to exactly |800-500| = 300 Hz. They resample at 2000 Hz (comfortably above twice 500 Hz) with an anti-alias filter set below 1000 Hz ahead of the ADC, and the true peak appears at 498 Hz. They then record five 2-second segments rather than one 10-second segment, since the tunnel's speed control has a slow 15-second drift cycle, and average the five segment spectra together for a cleaner, still-stationary result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about sampling rate choice because aliasing is invisible on the resulting plot — a fabricated peak looks exactly as clean as a real one, which makes it the easiest way to report a confidently wrong frequency. A student who explains their sampling rate relative to the expected (or a conservatively high assumed) frequency, mentions an anti-alias filter ahead of the digitizer, and can justify why they chose a given record length against both frequency resolution and flow stationarity, is showing they understand that a spectrum is only as trustworthy as the sampling decisions behind it — not just a button pressed in software.

questions.prompt: A signal contains a real 500 Hz component but is sampled at only 800 Hz. Where does that content appear in the resulting spectrum?

options.text: It is removed entirely and does not appear
It appears correctly at 500 Hz, just with lower amplitude
It folds down and appears as a false peak at 300 Hz
It appears doubled, at both 500 Hz and 1000 Hz

explanations.a: Undersampled content does not disappear; it reappears disguised at a different, false frequency.
explanations.b: 800 Hz sampling gives a Nyquist frequency of only 400 Hz, below 500 Hz, so the true frequency cannot be represented correctly at all.
explanations.c: Correct — content above the Nyquist frequency (400 Hz here) folds back below it; a 500 Hz component appears at |800-500| = 300 Hz, a fabricated peak indistinguishable from a real one.
explanations.d: Aliasing folds the frequency to one false location, not to two.

questions.prompt: Why must an anti-alias filter be applied before the ADC digitizes the signal, rather than filtered out afterward in software?

options.text: Software filters are always less accurate than analog filters
Once aliasing has occurred, the fake low-frequency peak is indistinguishable from a real signal at that frequency, so it cannot be identified or removed after the fact
It is a regulatory requirement for all digital instruments
It reduces the total file size of the recorded data

explanations.a: Both analog and digital filters can be accurate; that is not the reason for the ordering requirement.
explanations.b: Correct — aliasing happens at the moment of sampling; the resulting false frequency is mathematically identical to a real signal at that frequency, so no amount of post-processing can separate them after digitization.
explanations.c: This is a signal-processing necessity, not a regulatory rule.
explanations.d: File size is unrelated to why the filter must come before digitization.

questions.prompt: A 1-second record and a 5-second record are both used to compute a spectrum. What is the main trade-off in choosing the longer record?

options.text: Better frequency resolution (df = 1/T), but greater risk that the flow condition drifted and the record is no longer stationary
Worse frequency resolution, but a cleaner-looking plot
No difference; record length does not affect a spectrum
The longer record eliminates the need for an anti-alias filter

explanations.a: Correct — frequency resolution improves as df = 1/T with longer records, but the flow must stay stationary across the whole window, and a longer record is more likely to span a drift in mean speed or condition.
explanations.b: Longer records improve, not worsen, frequency resolution; the trade-off runs the other way.
explanations.c: Record length directly sets frequency resolution via df = 1/T, so it very much matters.
explanations.d: Anti-alias filtering addresses sampling rate versus signal content, a separate concern from record length.

questions.prompt: Why average many shorter segments together rather than trusting the spectrum from one long record alone?

options.text: A single record's spectral estimate has high random variance per frequency bin; averaging multiple independent segments reduces that variance for a more converged, trustworthy spectrum
Averaging segments improves the frequency resolution beyond what any single segment could achieve
It is only necessary when using a hot wire, not other sensors
It removes the need for a phase or trigger reference entirely

explanations.a: Correct — each segment's spectral estimate is noisy; averaging several independent segments (as in Welch's method) reduces that estimator variance, giving a smoother, more reliable spectrum.
explanations.b: Frequency resolution is set by each segment's own length (df = 1/T); averaging shorter segments together does not recover the resolution of one long record — it is a separate trade-off.
explanations.c: Ensemble averaging for spectral convergence applies generally to any sampled unsteady signal, not just hot-wire data.
explanations.d: A phase/trigger reference is a separate requirement, needed specifically for phase-averaged waveforms, not replaced by ensemble averaging of a spectrum.

lessons.label: Seeing the Unsteady Wake: Visualization Methods

sections.heading: Marking the flow: smoke, dye, and bubbles
sections.body: The classic way to make an unsteady wake visible in air is the smoke-wire technique: a thin wire coated with oil is flash-heated electrically, vaporizing the oil into a sheet of fine parallel smoke filaments that the flow then carries and distorts, revealing the vortex street downstream. A smoke rake — an array of small tubes feeding smoke from an external generator — does the same job when a heated wire would disturb a delicate flow. In water channels the equivalent is dye injected from a fine tube or slot at a fixed point, or the hydrogen-bubble technique, where a thin wire electrolyzes the water and a stream of tiny hydrogen bubbles marks the flow either continuously (as streaklines) or as pulsed timelines when the current is switched on and off rhythmically. Soap-film tunnels — a vertical, gravity-driven soap film only microns thick — give an almost purely two-dimensional flow and have been used since the 1980s-90s to study 2D vortex streets and turbulence directly, because the film's thinness suppresses the third dimension that always complicates real bluff-body wakes.

sections.heading: Freezing the motion: cameras and strobes
sections.body: None of these tracer methods are useful without a way to capture the pattern fast enough. A high-speed camera records a continuous sequence through the shedding cycle, at the cost of expensive hardware and large data volumes. A cheaper alternative is a strobe light timed (or phase-locked) to the known shedding frequency, so a single flash catches the wake at the same relative phase on every shedding cycle, or a slowly detuned strobe can be used to make the vortex pattern appear to march slowly, revealing its evolution to the naked eye — the same phase-triggering logic used in phase-locked PIV, but with a light source and a camera instead of a laser.

sections.heading: The interpretation trap: streaklines are not streamlines
sections.body: The single most common misreading of a smoke or dye photo is treating it as a snapshot of the instantaneous velocity field. In steady flow, three classic flow-visualization curves — streamlines (curves everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity field), pathlines (the trajectory traced by one fluid particle over time), and streaklines (the locus, at one instant, of every particle that has ever passed through a fixed injection point) — all coincide, so the distinction rarely matters. In unsteady flow, such as a shedding wake, they do not coincide at all: a continuous smoke or dye plume from a fixed point is a streakline, built from particles that entered the flow at many different past times and each felt a different, evolving velocity field along the way. It records history, not an instant. Reading the vortex spacing off a smoke photograph and calling it "the velocity field at this moment" is exactly the error this distinction is meant to prevent.

lessons.workedExample: A student photographs a smoke-wire visualization of a cylinder wake and confidently reports "the instantaneous velocity field shows vortices spaced 8 cm apart, so the local velocity here is X." A judge points out the smoke filaments are a streakline: each visible strand is smoke that left the wire at a different past instant and has been advected and rolled up by the wake's evolving velocity field ever since, so the photograph encodes flow history integrated over roughly the last several shedding cycles, not the velocity field at the moment of the flash. To actually recover an instantaneous velocity field, the student would need PIV (which computes velocity from particle displacement between two close-spaced instants) rather than reading spacing off a single continuous-injection smoke image.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to explain their smoke or dye photo because it is the fastest way to check whether they understand what flow visualization actually records. Nearly every student who has not been taught the streamline/pathline/streakline distinction will describe a smoke photo as showing "the velocity" at that instant; a student who correctly identifies it as a streakline — built from many past injection times — and explains why that differs from an instantaneous streamline or an individual particle's pathline, demonstrates real command of unsteady-flow kinematics rather than a plausible-sounding but wrong reading of a pretty picture.

questions.prompt: In an unsteady flow, a continuous stream of smoke or dye released from one fixed point traces out a:

options.text: Streamline
Pathline
Streakline
Timeline

explanations.a: A streamline is a curve tangent to the instantaneous velocity field at one moment; it is a mathematical construct, not what a continuous smoke plume traces.
explanations.b: A pathline is the trajectory of a single particle followed over time, not the pattern formed by continuously injected tracer from a fixed point.
explanations.c: Correct — the locus, at one instant, of every particle that has ever passed through a fixed injection point is by definition a streakline, and that is exactly what a continuous smoke or dye plume shows.
explanations.d: A timeline (as in the pulsed hydrogen-bubble technique) marks a set of particles released at the same instant, not a continuously injected plume.

questions.prompt: Why do streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines coincide in steady flow but diverge in unsteady flow?

options.text: They never actually coincide, even in steady flow
In steady flow the velocity field does not change over time, so a particle's path, the tangent curve to the field, and the accumulated injection trace all trace the same fixed geometry
Streaklines only exist in unsteady flow
The distinction only matters for compressible flows

explanations.a: In steady flow they do coincide exactly; this is a standard, well-established result.
explanations.b: Correct — with a time-invariant velocity field, every particle that ever passes through a given point follows the same subsequent path, so pathlines, streaklines, and the instantaneous streamline pattern all collapse onto the same curves.
explanations.c: Streaklines can be defined in any flow; they simply happen to coincide with the other two curve types when the flow is steady.
explanations.d: The distinction is about time-dependence (unsteadiness), not compressibility.

questions.prompt: Match each flow-visualization technique to its working medium or method.

right.text: Oil-coated wire flash-heated to vaporize into smoke filaments (air)
Fine wire electrolyzes water, releasing tiny bubbles that mark streaklines or timelines
A microns-thick gravity-driven film gives a near-2D flow for studying vortex streets
A light flash timed to the shedding cycle freezes the same relative phase on every cycle

questions.explanation: The smoke-wire technique flash-heats an oil-coated wire into smoke filaments; the hydrogen-bubble technique electrolyzes water at a fine wire; a soap-film tunnel's thinness suppresses the third dimension for near-2D vortex-street study; and phase-triggered strobe imaging times a flash to the shedding cycle to freeze the same phase repeatedly, the same logic phase-locked PIV uses with a laser.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants an actual instantaneous velocity field of a shedding wake, not just a picture of tracer patterns. Which technique directly provides that?

options.text: A continuous dye plume photographed once
PIV, which computes velocity from tracer displacement between two closely spaced instants
A smoke-wire photo with a longer exposure time
A soap-film tunnel viewed with the naked eye

explanations.a: A continuous dye plume is a streakline, which encodes flow history from many past injection times, not an instantaneous velocity field.
explanations.b: Correct — PIV measures particle displacement across a short, known time interval between two frames and divides by that interval, directly producing an instantaneous (or near-instantaneous) velocity field rather than a history-integrated tracer pattern.
explanations.c: A longer exposure only blurs the streakline further; it does not convert a tracer pattern into a velocity measurement.
explanations.d: Viewing a soap film by eye shows tracer or interference patterns, not a quantitative instantaneous velocity field without further measurement (e.g. PIV applied to the film).

lessons.label: Rigs for Unsteady and Vibration Experiments

sections.heading: Free vibration vs. forced oscillation
sections.body: Two rig families dominate vortex-induced-vibration (VIV) research. An elastically mounted cylinder rig suspends a test cylinder on springs (often riding on low-friction air bearings) so it is free to oscillate transverse to the flow; as flow speed increases toward the point where shedding frequency nears the system's natural structural frequency, the cylinder locks into large-amplitude self-sustained oscillation — the lock-in phenomenon studied extensively since Feng's foundational 1968 experiments and refined by Khalak and Williamson's low-mass-damping work in the late 1990s, which mapped distinct wake vortex patterns (labeled modes like 2S and 2P by Williamson and Roshko in 1988) against oscillation amplitude and frequency. A forced-oscillation rig instead drives the cylinder through a prescribed motion at a chosen amplitude and frequency using a motor, and measures the resulting fluid force directly — trading the self-excited realism of a free rig for the ability to map force coefficients (including the fluid-added-mass and damping contributions) systematically across a parameter grid a free rig would only sample where lock-in happens to occur.

sections.heading: Measuring structural damping: free-decay log decrement
sections.body: Before a VIV rig's data can be trusted, its own structural damping — how quickly it would settle after a disturbance with no flow at all — must be quantified. The standard method is a free-decay test: displace the elastically mounted cylinder and release it, then record the decaying oscillation amplitude. The logarithmic decrement compares the natural log of successive peak amplitudes, and dividing by 2*pi gives the damping ratio; this single number sets the baseline against which any flow-induced damping or excitation is measured, and it is exactly the same tap-test logic used to characterize a sting's structural resonance before trusting a force spectrum as aerodynamic.

sections.heading: Making the wake actually two-dimensional
sections.body: Nearly every idealized vortex-shedding result assumes a two-dimensional wake, but a real finite-length cylinder is not two-dimensional — flow spills around its free ends, and that end effect can propagate inward and contaminate shedding behavior over a large fraction of the span unless it is controlled. Three geometry rules manage this: end plates (flat discs or plates capping the cylinder ends) block the end-spillage flow and are close to mandatory on any short test cylinder; a span-to-diameter ratio above roughly 20 keeps end effects confined to a small fraction of the total span even without end plates; and tunnel blockage — the model's frontal area as a fraction of the test-section cross-section — kept under roughly 5-10% avoids the accelerated flow and altered pressure field a too-large model induces in a confined test section. A classroom rig that ignores all three can produce shedding data that looks clean but describes a three-dimensional, wall-contaminated flow rather than the idealized 2D vortex street being taught.

lessons.workedExample: A classroom team builds a low-cost VIV rig: a 1 cm diameter, 25 cm long wooden rod (span-to-diameter ratio 25, comfortably above the 20 rule of thumb) fitted with cardboard end plates, suspended across a narrow water channel by two lengths of fishing line acting as springs, restricted to move only transverse to the flow by guide rails. They tape a phone to the rod's mount to use its accelerometer as the vibration sensor. First, with the channel drained, they pull the rod aside and release it, recording the free decay on the phone's accelerometer log and computing a damping ratio from the logarithmic decrement of three successive peaks. Then, with water flowing, they sweep flow speed slowly and watch oscillation amplitude spike sharply over a narrow speed range — lock-in — right where the Strouhal shedding frequency crosses the rod's own natural frequency measured in the dry test.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes rig geometry because it is where a plausible-looking VIV or shedding result quietly stops being two-dimensional, or stops being a clean structural measurement. A student who can justify their span-to-diameter ratio, mention end plates or explain why they were omitted, state their tunnel's blockage fraction, and describe having measured structural damping by free decay before ever turning the flow on, is showing the same root-cause discipline the sting tap-test demands elsewhere in unsteady measurement — controlling the rig, not just running it.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an elastically mounted (free-vibration) VIV rig and a forced-oscillation rig?

options.text: The free rig lets the cylinder oscillate on its own under fluid forces (including self-excited lock-in); the forced rig drives a prescribed motion with a motor to directly map force coefficients
Only the forced-oscillation rig can measure vortex shedding at all
The free rig requires a much larger tunnel than the forced rig
They are two names for the same setup

explanations.a: Correct — a free rig responds naturally to fluid forces and can lock in near resonance, showing self-excited amplitude; a forced rig imposes a chosen motion via a motor, trading that self-excited realism for systematic coverage of the amplitude-frequency parameter space.
explanations.b: Both rig types can be used to study vortex-shedding-driven phenomena; the difference is in how the cylinder's motion is generated, not whether shedding occurs.
explanations.c: Tunnel size requirements depend on the model and blockage limits, not on whether the rig is free or forced.
explanations.d: They are distinct rig types with different mechanisms and different information they yield.

questions.prompt: The logarithmic-decrement method, applied to a free-decay test with no flow, is used to measure:

options.text: The vortex-shedding frequency
The rig's own structural damping ratio
The Strouhal number of the cylinder
The tunnel blockage ratio

explanations.a: Shedding frequency requires flow and is measured from the flow-on spectrum, not a no-flow free-decay test.
explanations.b: Correct — comparing the natural log of successive free-decay peak amplitudes (divided by 2*pi) gives the structural damping ratio, the baseline needed before any flow-induced effect can be identified.
explanations.c: Strouhal number relates shedding frequency, body size, and flow speed; it requires flow, unlike a no-flow decay test.
explanations.d: Blockage ratio is a purely geometric quantity (model frontal area versus tunnel cross-section), unrelated to a decay-based damping measurement.

questions.prompt: Which combination of design choices best protects a wake-measurement rig from three-dimensional end effects and tunnel-wall contamination?

options.text: A short cylinder with no end plates and a model that fills most of the tunnel cross-section
End plates on the cylinder, a span-to-diameter ratio above roughly 20, and blockage kept under roughly 5-10%
A longer test section with no other changes
A higher flow speed to overpower end effects

explanations.a: This combination maximizes exactly the problems (end spillage and wall-induced flow acceleration) the design rules exist to avoid.
explanations.b: Correct — end plates block end-spillage flow, a span-to-diameter ratio above about 20 confines any residual end effect to a small fraction of the span, and blockage under roughly 5-10% avoids wall-induced flow acceleration; together they keep the wake close to the idealized two-dimensional case.
explanations.c: Test-section length does not address spanwise end effects or blockage, the two specific contamination mechanisms described.
explanations.d: Flow speed does not correct geometric contamination; end effects and blockage persist across speeds set by geometry, not velocity.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a classroom team should take to build and validate a low-Re elastically mounted VIV rig.

items.text: Mount the cylinder on springs (e.g. fishing line) with end plates sized for span-to-diameter above ~20
Attach a vibration sensor (e.g. phone accelerometer) to the mount
With no flow, displace and release the cylinder to record free decay and compute the damping ratio
Turn on flow and sweep speed slowly, watching for the lock-in amplitude spike

questions.explanation: The rig's geometry (springs, end plates, span-to-diameter ratio) must be built first; a sensor is attached to actually record motion; structural damping is characterized with a no-flow free-decay test before any flow-induced behavior is trusted; only then is flow introduced and swept to observe lock-in against the already-known structural natural frequency.

units.label: Reading Unsteady Signatures

lessons.label: From Time Trace to Spectrum

sections.heading: Bin width, windowing, and why raw FFTs lie
sections.body: An FFT turns N samples taken at sample rate fs into frequency bins spaced Δf = fs/N: a longer record gives finer frequency resolution, but a raw periodogram's variance does not shrink just because you recorded longer — more samples at fixed record length only add more bins, not more independent looks at each one. Windowing matters because the FFT implicitly assumes the recorded chunk repeats forever; if the signal does not contain a whole number of cycles, the wrap-around creates a discontinuity that smears energy from the true peak into neighboring bins — spectral leakage. A rectangular window (i.e., no tapering) has the narrowest peak but the worst leakage; a Hann or Hamming window tapers the record's edges to zero, trading a slightly wider peak for much lower leakage sidelobes. Welch's method (Welch, 1967) fixes the variance problem directly: split the record into overlapping segments (commonly 50% overlap), window and FFT each one, then average the resulting power spectra — more segments buys lower-variance estimates at the cost of coarser frequency resolution per segment.

sections.heading: Reading the fingerprint on log axes
sections.body: Power spectral density is plotted on log frequency and log power (or dB) because shedding and turbulence span orders of magnitude on both axes. Organized, laminar-regime shedding shows a narrow, sharp peak at the Strouhal frequency f_s plus weaker harmonics at 2f_s and 3f_s — the harmonics appear because a fixed probe crosses vortices from both shear layers each cycle, distorting the otherwise periodic signal away from a pure sinusoid. A turbulent or higher-Reynolds-number wake instead shows a broadened hump: the peak's Q (center frequency divided by bandwidth) drops as jitter and three-dimensional cell structure along the span smear the frequency from cycle to cycle. Farther from the shedding-dominated band, energy cascades into a self-similar inertial range where Kolmogorov's (1941) −5/3 law holds, appearing as a straight line of slope −5/3 on log-log axes.

sections.heading: Telling a shedding peak from an impostor
sections.body: Not every sharp line is fluid physics. Mains hum sits at a fixed electrical line frequency (50 or 60 Hz) and its harmonics, regardless of flow speed — the giveaway is that it refuses to move when U changes, whereas a genuine shedding peak scales with speed through St = fD/U. A structural resonance (a probe stem or mounting sting's natural frequency) is likewise fixed in frequency and often shows up strongly on an accelerometer channel, not just the flow-sensing channel. The reliable test is to sweep U and replot frequency versus U (or St versus Re): a real shedding line moves proportionally, while an electrical or structural artifact stays parked.

lessons.workedExample: A student sets a hot-wire behind a D = 0.04 m cylinder at U = 8 m/s, samples at fs = 2000 Hz with N = 4096 points per segment (Δf ≈ 0.49 Hz), applies a Hann window, and averages 8 overlapping Welch segments. The PSD shows a sharp peak at 40 Hz with a weaker harmonic near 80 Hz — matching the predicted f_shed = St·U/D = 0.2·8/0.04 = 40 Hz. A second, unmoving spike sits at 60 Hz. Dropping U to 6 m/s should move the shedding peak to 30 Hz — it does — but the 60 Hz spike stays exactly at 60 Hz, confirming it is mains hum, not flow physics.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the spectrum because it separates a student who eyeballed 'a peak' from one who can defend the processing chain: why that window, why Welch averaging instead of one long FFT, and why the axes are log. The tell of real understanding is diagnosing a candidate peak by re-running the sweep and checking that frequency scales with velocity — a student who instead reports a fixed-frequency spike as 'the shedding frequency' without checking it against a second flow speed has not actually verified the physics.

questions.prompt: What specifically causes spectral leakage when computing an FFT of a recorded signal?

options.text: Sampling at too high a rate
A discontinuity at the record's wrap-around point when it does not contain a whole number of signal cycles
Using too many samples in the record
The signal having a DC offset

explanations.a: Sample rate sets the Nyquist limit and affects aliasing, not leakage.
explanations.b: Correct — the FFT assumes the record repeats periodically; a non-integer number of cycles creates an artificial jump at the seam, and that jump's energy smears into neighboring frequency bins as leakage.
explanations.c: More samples changes resolution and variance, not leakage by itself.
explanations.d: A DC offset just adds energy at 0 Hz; it does not by itself cause leakage into other bins.

questions.prompt: Why does Welch's method average multiple overlapping segments instead of computing one FFT over the whole record?

options.text: To increase frequency resolution beyond what one FFT could give
To reduce the statistical variance of the power spectrum estimate, at the cost of coarser frequency resolution
To remove mains hum automatically
To eliminate the need for a window function

explanations.a: The opposite — splitting into segments coarsens resolution (each segment is shorter than the whole record).
explanations.b: Correct — a single raw periodogram is a statistically inconsistent estimator; averaging several independent (or overlapping) segments trades resolution for lower variance in the PSD estimate.
explanations.c: Welch averaging does nothing to distinguish electrical artifacts from flow physics; that requires the velocity-sweep test.
explanations.d: Each segment in Welch's method is still windowed before its FFT.

questions.prompt: A spectral peak stays at exactly 60 Hz no matter what the flow speed is set to. What does this indicate?

options.text: It is the vortex-shedding frequency at that particular speed
It is likely an electrical (mains hum) or structural-resonance artifact, not flow physics
It is the second harmonic of shedding
It confirms the flow has entered the inertial range

explanations.a: A true shedding peak must scale with velocity through St = fD/U; a fixed-frequency peak fails that test.
explanations.b: Correct — mains hum and structural resonances sit at fixed frequencies set by the electrical grid or the mounting hardware, independent of flow speed, which is exactly why they don't move on a speed sweep.
explanations.c: A harmonic of shedding would also scale with speed, tracking 2× the fundamental.
explanations.d: The inertial range is a broadband −5/3 slope region, not a fixed narrow peak.

questions.prompt: Match each spectral feature to what it indicates.

left.text: Sharp narrow peak plus weak harmonics
Broadened, low-Q hump around the shedding frequency
Straight line of slope −5/3 on log-log axes
Narrow peak that does not shift when flow speed changes

right.text: Organized, near-periodic vortex shedding
Turbulent or jittery shedding with cycle-to-cycle frequency variation
Kolmogorov inertial-range turbulence cascade
Mains hum or structural resonance, not flow physics

questions.explanation: A sharp peak with harmonics is the signature of organized periodic shedding; a broadened hump reflects turbulent modulation of the shedding process; a −5/3 log-log slope is Kolmogorov's inertial-range cascade; and a peak that ignores flow speed is an electrical or structural artifact rather than a fluid-dynamic signal.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Welch's method for estimating a power spectral density.

items.text: Split the recorded time series into overlapping segments
Apply a window function (e.g., Hann) to each segment
Compute the FFT (periodogram) of each windowed segment
Average the periodograms across all segments

questions.explanation: Welch's method segments the record (with overlap), windows each segment to suppress leakage, computes each segment's periodogram, then averages the periodograms together to reduce estimator variance at the cost of per-segment frequency resolution.

lessons.label: Strouhal Collapse and Scaling Up

sections.heading: Why nondimensionalizing collapses the data
sections.body: The Strouhal number St = fD/U is the dimensionless shedding frequency. Dynamic similarity says that two geometrically similar bodies at matched Reynolds number Re = UD/ν produce matched dimensionless behavior — including St — regardless of the absolute size or speed involved. That is why a small model tested in a wind tunnel at whatever speed reproduces the full-scale Re can hand you a value of St that then rescales, via f = St·U/D, to predict the full-scale shedding frequency at the full-scale D and operating U. Over a wide band of subcritical Reynolds numbers for a circular cylinder — roughly 300 to 2×10^5 — St plateaus near 0.2; Roshko's (1954) cylinder-wake measurements are the classic source establishing this near-constant regime.

sections.heading: Where the collapse breaks
sections.body: The plateau ends at the drag crisis. Around Re ≈ 3×10^5–3.5×10^5, the cylinder's boundary layer transitions from laminar to turbulent before separating, pushing the separation points aft, shrinking the wake, and crashing the drag coefficient from roughly 1.2 to about 0.3 — documented in Achenbach's (1968) detailed surface-pressure and drag measurements. Through the critical and supercritical regimes the organized periodic shedding is disrupted: the spectral peak nearly vanishes in the critical range, then re-emerges at a higher St (often 0.3–0.5) in the supercritical range before settling back down at very high Re. A single St(Re) value from a model test is only trustworthy if the model and the full-scale case sit in the same Re regime; straddling the drag crisis breaks the collapse outright. Sharp-edged bodies fail differently: because separation is pinned at a fixed geometric corner rather than migrating with boundary-layer state, St becomes nearly Re-independent but takes a shape-specific value — a square cylinder held broadside sheds near St ≈ 0.12–0.13, well below the circular cylinder's ≈0.2 — so a circular-cylinder St cannot be borrowed for a rectangular stack or bridge deck.

sections.heading: Using it: lock-in-risk screening
sections.body: Given a model-derived St (confirmed to be in the same Re regime as the full-scale case) and the full-scale diameter D, sweep the design wind-speed range from U_min to U_max, compute f_shed = St·U/D at both ends, and check whether that band brackets any structural natural frequency f_n from a modal test or FE model. If f_n falls inside [f_shed(U_min), f_shed(U_max)], some wind speed within the operating envelope will drive shedding frequency and structural frequency to coincide — a lock-in-risk flag calling for added damping, strakes, or a redesigned f_n, not proof of failure on its own.

lessons.workedExample: A model chimney test gives St = 0.2, confirmed to be in the same subcritical Re regime as the real structure. The full-scale chimney has D = 2 m and a design wind-speed range of U = 5–15 m/s, giving f_shed = St·U/D ranging from 0.2·5/2 = 0.5 Hz to 0.2·15/2 = 1.5 Hz. A shaker test measures the chimney's first bending mode at f_n = 1.0 Hz — which falls inside [0.5, 1.5] Hz, flagging lock-in risk. Solving f_shed = f_n for the exact wind speed gives U = f_n·D/St = 1.0·2/0.2 = 10 m/s, a wholly ordinary operating wind speed, so the design needs mitigation such as helical strakes or added damping.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because St = 0.2 is easy to memorize and easy to misapply. A judge wants to see the student confirm that the model test and the full-scale case sit in the same Reynolds-number regime (not straddling the drag crisis) before reusing St, and then actually compute the wind speed at which lock-in risk occurs rather than stopping at 'the frequencies are close.' Reciting St ≈ 0.2 without checking the Re regime or running the screening calculation is the signature of a student who memorized the number but not what it is a similarity parameter for.

questions.prompt: What does the Strouhal number St = fD/U represent, and why does it let you scale a model test up to full scale?

options.text: It is the dimensionless shedding frequency; matching Re between model and full scale keeps St the same, so f = St·U/D rescales correctly
It is the drag coefficient nondimensionalized by dynamic pressure
It is a fixed universal constant equal to 0.2 for every bluff body at every Reynolds number
It only applies to flows inside pipes, not external bluff-body wakes

explanations.a: Correct — St is the dimensionless shedding frequency, and dynamic similarity at matched Re means a model test's St transfers directly to the full-scale case via f = St·U/D.
explanations.b: That describes the drag coefficient, C_D, not the Strouhal number.
explanations.c: St ≈ 0.2 only holds over a limited subcritical Re range for circular cylinders; it changes at the drag crisis and differs entirely for other shapes.
explanations.d: St is a general dimensionless-frequency parameter used across bluff-body wake flows, not restricted to internal pipe flow.

questions.prompt: Match each flow regime or body shape to its Strouhal-number behavior.

left.text: Circular cylinder, critical Re near the drag crisis (~3×10^5)
Sharp-edged body (e.g., square cylinder), any Re

right.text: St plateaus near 0.2
Shedding disorganized; spectral peak nearly disappears
St jumps higher, often 0.3–0.5
St nearly Re-independent but shape-specific (e.g., ≈0.12–0.13 for a square cylinder)

questions.explanation: The subcritical plateau near St ≈ 0.2 (Roshko, 1954) breaks down at the drag crisis (Achenbach, 1968) where organized shedding briefly disappears, then St re-emerges higher in the supercritical range. Sharp-edged bodies separate at a fixed geometric corner rather than a Re-dependent boundary-layer point, giving a nearly Re-independent but shape-specific St.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a lock-in-risk screening using a model-test-derived Strouhal number.

items.text: Measure St from a model test in the same Reynolds-number regime as the full-scale case
Compute f_shed = St·U/D at both ends of the full-scale design wind-speed range
Obtain the structure's natural frequency f_n from a modal test or FE model
Check whether f_n falls within the computed f_shed band; flag lock-in risk if so

questions.explanation: The screening starts from a Re-matched St, projects it to the full-scale shedding-frequency band across the design wind-speed range, brings in the independently measured structural natural frequency, and finally checks whether the two overlap.

questions.prompt: For the chimney worked example (St = 0.2, D = 2 m, f_n = 1.0 Hz), at what wind speed does f_shed exactly equal f_n?

options.text: 5 m/s
10 m/s
15 m/s
20 m/s

explanations.a: At U = 5 m/s, f_shed = 0.2·5/2 = 0.5 Hz, not 1.0 Hz.
explanations.b: Correct — solving f_n = St·U/D for U gives U = f_n·D/St = 1.0·2/0.2 = 10 m/s, which lies within the 5–15 m/s design range.
explanations.c: At U = 15 m/s, f_shed = 0.2·15/2 = 1.5 Hz, not 1.0 Hz.
explanations.d: 20 m/s is outside the stated design wind-speed range and still gives f_shed = 2.0 Hz, not 1.0 Hz.

questions.prompt: Why can't a Strouhal number measured for a circular cylinder be reused, unmodified, to predict shedding from a square cross-section stack?

options.text: Because square cross-sections do not shed vortices at all
Because separation on a sharp-edged shape is pinned at a fixed corner rather than at a Reynolds-number-dependent boundary-layer point, giving it its own shape-specific St
Because the Strouhal number is only defined for Re above the drag crisis
Because square stacks never experience wind loading

explanations.a: Sharp-edged bodies do shed vortices, often quite strongly, just at a different St than a circular cylinder.
explanations.b: Correct — a circular cylinder's separation point migrates with the boundary layer's laminar-to-turbulent state (Re-dependent), while a sharp-edged body's separation is geometrically fixed at the corner, giving a different, largely Re-independent St value.
explanations.c: St is defined and useful across the full Re range, including well below the drag crisis.
explanations.d: Square stacks are routinely exposed to wind loading and vortex-induced excitation, which is exactly why the shape-specific St matters.

lessons.label: Reading Lock-In and Amplitude-Response Plots

sections.heading: Reduced velocity and three branches of amplitude
sections.body: Reduced velocity U* = U/(f_n·D) is a dimensionless flow speed normalized by the structure's natural frequency and diameter — it tells you how many diameters the flow travels per structural oscillation period. Plotting normalized vibration amplitude A*/D (peak-to-peak or RMS) against U* reveals the branch structure of vortex-induced vibration. Feng's (1968) pioneering elastically-mounted cylinder experiments, at relatively high mass-damping, found two branches: an initial branch where amplitude rises steeply as U* enters the synchronization range, and a lower branch of reduced, roughly constant amplitude through the rest of lock-in. Khalak and Williamson's (1999) later high-precision, low mass-damping experiments revealed a third, previously hidden upper branch sitting between initial and lower — low mass-damping systems jump from the initial branch to a higher-amplitude upper branch (commonly exceeding A*/D ≈ 0.8–1.0) before dropping to the lower branch and eventually desynchronizing.

sections.heading: Hysteresis, the synchronization band, and the frequency plot
sections.body: The initial-to-upper and upper-to-lower transitions are typically hysteretic: sweeping U* upward versus downward gives different transition points, a signature of a bistable nonlinear system rather than a single-valued response. This hysteresis has a concrete mechanism behind it: Williamson and Roshko (1988), mapping the near-wake vortex pattern across a grid of forced oscillation amplitude and frequency, found the wake switches discretely between a 2S mode (two single vortices shed per cycle, one from each shear layer) and a 2P mode (two vortex pairs shed per cycle). The initial-to-upper branch jump corresponds to a 2S-to-2P wake-mode switch, and the upper-to-lower jump corresponds to a 2P-to-2S switch back; because each wake mode stays locally stable over a range of amplitude and phase before the switch triggers, the switch point differs depending on whether U* is increasing or decreasing, producing the observed hysteresis. The synchronization (lock-in) band — the U* range where oscillation frequency stays clamped near f_n — spans roughly U* ≈ 4–8 for a circular cylinder, widening as mass-damping decreases. The companion plot of oscillation frequency f (or f/f_n) versus U* shows the wake abandoning the ordinary Strouhal relationship: outside lock-in, f follows f = St·U/D, a straight rising line; inside the synchronization band, f flattens and clamps to f_n regardless of U, only rejoining the Strouhal line once the body desynchronizes at the band's upper edge.

sections.heading: The Griffin plot: peak amplitude vs mass-damping
sections.body: Compiling peak lock-in amplitude A*/D against a combined mass-damping parameter across many independent experiments produces the Griffin plot: amplitude falls off roughly monotonically as mass-damping increases, since heavier or more heavily damped structures vibrate less. But the compiled data show wide scatter — a factor of two or three spread at a given mass-damping value — because Reynolds number, turbulence intensity, surface roughness, aspect ratio, and end conditions all shift the curve independently of mass-damping. The Griffin plot is therefore a useful design screening tool, not a precise predictor: mass-damping alone does not pin down peak amplitude.

lessons.workedExample: A lab cylinder (D = 0.03 m, f_n = 2 Hz, low mass-damping) is swept from U* = 2 to U* = 10 by increasing tunnel speed. Below U* = 4, A*/D stays near 0.05 (negligible). At U* = 4 it jumps to the initial branch (A*/D ≈ 0.4); by U* = 5 it jumps again to the upper branch, peaking near A*/D ≈ 0.9; by U* = 7 it drops to the lower branch (A*/D ≈ 0.5); beyond U* = 8 it desynchronizes back toward zero. Repeating the sweep in reverse, from U* = 10 downward, shows the upper-to-lower transition occurring at a different point (around U* = 6 instead of 7) — direct evidence of hysteresis. Meanwhile the f/f_n plot stays flat at 1.0 across U* = 4–8, diverging from the rising Strouhal line that governs frequency outside that band.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because peak amplitude alone is a shallow answer to 'does this structure experience vortex-induced vibration.' A student who ran the sweep in only one direction has missed the hysteresis that is central to the phenomenon; one who can name the initial, upper, and lower branches, and connect the flat f/f_n plateau to lock-in rather than to the Strouhal line, has actually engaged with the structure of the response rather than reporting a single peak reading.

questions.prompt: What does the reduced velocity U* = U/(f_n·D) physically represent?

options.text: The ratio of drag force to lift force on the structure
How many diameters the flow travels per period of the structure's natural oscillation
The Reynolds number of the flow around the structure
The structural damping ratio

explanations.a: U* is a kinematic ratio of flow speed to structural frequency and length scale, not a force ratio.
explanations.b: Correct — U* normalizes flow speed by the structural natural frequency and diameter, giving a dimensionless measure of how far the flow moves per oscillation cycle.
explanations.c: Reynolds number is Re = UD/ν, a ratio of inertial to viscous forces, not a frequency-normalized speed.
explanations.d: Damping ratio is a separate structural property; it appears in the mass-damping parameter, not in U* itself.

questions.prompt: Match each amplitude-response branch to its description.

right.text: Amplitude rises steeply as U* enters the synchronization range
Highest amplitude branch, seen only in low mass-damping systems (Khalak & Williamson, 1999)
Reduced, roughly constant amplitude before desynchronization

questions.explanation: The initial branch is the steep rise entering lock-in; the upper branch, only revealed by low mass-damping experiments, carries the highest amplitude; the lower branch is a reduced, roughly steady amplitude that persists until desynchronization.

questions.prompt: What does hysteresis between an increasing-U* sweep and a decreasing-U* sweep indicate about vortex-induced vibration?

options.text: The measurement equipment was miscalibrated
The amplitude response is a single-valued function of U* that the equipment failed to capture
The system is bistable — the branch transitions depend on sweep history/direction, not on U* alone
The cylinder was not rigidly mounted

explanations.a: Hysteresis is a real, repeatable feature of VIV response, not a calibration artifact.
explanations.b: The opposite — hysteresis means the response is NOT single-valued in U* alone; it depends on which branch the system was already on.
explanations.c: Correct — different transition points on increasing versus decreasing sweeps show the response is bistable/history-dependent, a hallmark of the nonlinear branch structure.
explanations.d: Mounting rigidity affects f_n and damping, but hysteresis itself reflects the nonlinear dynamics of the lock-in transitions, not a mounting defect.

questions.prompt: In the companion frequency plot (f/f_n vs U*), what does a flat region at f/f_n ≈ 1 indicate?

options.text: The vortex shedding frequency has locked to the structural natural frequency, abandoning the Strouhal relationship
Vortex shedding has stopped entirely
The flow has become laminar
St has increased to exactly 1.0

explanations.a: Correct — inside the synchronization band the vibrating body forces the shedding frequency to track f_n, flattening the plot instead of following the rising f = St·U/D Strouhal line.
explanations.b: Shedding continues during lock-in; it is exactly what drives the vibration, not what stops it.
explanations.c: Lock-in is a vortex-induced vibration phenomenon at typical bluff-body Reynolds numbers, not a laminarization of the flow.
explanations.d: The flat region means f equals f_n, not that St itself becomes 1.0; St is a separate dimensionless parameter.

questions.prompt: The Griffin plot shows a factor-of-two-to-three scatter in peak amplitude at a given mass-damping value. What does this scatter imply?

options.text: Mass-damping is irrelevant to VIV amplitude
Mass-damping alone is a useful screening parameter but not a precise predictor — Reynolds number, turbulence, roughness, and end conditions also matter
All the underlying experiments were flawed
Amplitude depends only on Reynolds number, not on mass-damping at all

explanations.a: The overall downward trend with mass-damping shows it does matter — just not as the sole variable.
explanations.b: Correct — the general trend (higher mass-damping, lower amplitude) holds, but the spread shows additional factors like Re, turbulence intensity, surface roughness, aspect ratio, and end conditions also shift peak amplitude at fixed mass-damping.
explanations.c: The scatter reflects genuine additional physical variables across differing experimental setups, not systematic experimental error.
explanations.d: The Griffin plot's whole premise is a trend against mass-damping, so mass-damping clearly has a first-order effect even amid the scatter.

lessons.label: Phase-Averaging and Conditional Sampling

sections.heading: Building one cycle from thousands
sections.body: A hot-wire or PIV record behind a bluff body contains thousands of shedding cycles buried in turbulent noise. Phase averaging exploits the periodicity directly: pick a reference signal correlated with the shedding process itself — often the same probe, a nearby pressure tap, or a dedicated wake reference — and define a fiducial phase point in each cycle, commonly the positive-going zero-crossing of the (band-pass filtered) reference signal. Every subsequent sample, or for PIV every full velocity/vorticity field acquired in sync with that reference, is tagged with its phase angle φ within its cycle (0°–360°) and sorted into phase bins, typically 12 to 36 across one cycle. Averaging all samples that land in the same bin, across all recorded cycles, produces one phase-resolved value per bin — stitched together, one clean representative cycle of the shedding motion, with incoherent turbulent scatter averaged out while the periodic structure that a plain average would destroy is preserved.

sections.heading: Triple decomposition
sections.body: This is formalized by Hussain and Reynolds' (1970) triple decomposition of the instantaneous velocity: u(x,t) = U(x) + ũ(x,φ) + u′(x,t) — a time-mean part U, a phase-locked coherent periodic part ũ that repeats with the shedding cycle, and a random turbulent part u′ that does not correlate with phase. Phase averaging directly computes ⟨u⟩(x,φ) = U(x) + ũ(x,φ), the ensemble average at fixed phase; subtracting the ordinary time-mean U(x) isolates ũ, the coherent vortex signature, cleanly separated from the incoherent turbulence for the first time. This separation matters beyond visualization: Cantwell and Coles' (1983) phase-averaged near-wake study used it to build a coherent Reynolds-stress and energy budget of the wake, contrasting a coherent production term built from gradients of ũ — the rate at which the mean flow feeds energy into the organized vortex motion — against an incoherent turbulent-production term built from u′ — the rate at which random turbulence extracts energy from the mean flow. Comparing the two terms showed the coherent structures, not the background turbulence, dominate momentum and energy transport in the near wake.

sections.heading: Why the ordinary time average erases the street
sections.body: At a fixed point behind the body, vortices from the top and bottom shear layers pass by with opposite-sign vorticity at regular phase intervals. A plain, unconditioned time average sums these alternating-sign contributions over many cycles, and they cancel — leaving only a smooth mean wake profile (essentially two merging shear layers) with no trace of the discrete alternating vortices. Conditioning the average on phase, instead of collapsing across all phases, is what prevents that cancellation and lets the coherent vortex pattern survive averaging. Every vortex-street visualization built from averaged data — phase-locked streaklines, phase-averaged vorticity contours — depends on this conditioning; a raw time-average of the same data never shows the street at all.

lessons.workedExample: PIV is recorded behind a D = 0.02 m cylinder at U = 5 m/s, with shedding at f_s ≈ 50 Hz. The camera runs at 1 kHz, uncorrelated with shedding, capturing 500 snapshots at effectively random phases across many cycles. A synchronized hot-wire reference in the near wake tags each PIV frame with its phase, sorted into 24 bins of 15° each (360°/24 = 15°). Averaging vorticity fields within each bin reveals the classic staggered street: alternating clockwise and counterclockwise vortex cores convecting downstream. Averaging the same 500 frames without phase conditioning instead produces a smooth, vortex-free, symmetric wake-deficit profile — identical raw data, but the vortices only appear once the average is conditioned on phase.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because a naive time-averaged PIV field of a wake looks nothing like a vortex street, and a student who just says 'we averaged the images' has not explained why. The tell of real understanding is being able to describe the reference-signal-plus-phase-binning procedure concretely, and to use the vocabulary of triple decomposition — coherent versus random — to explain why unconditioned averaging specifically cancels alternating-sign vortices rather than just 'blurring' the picture.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the reference signal in phase averaging?

options.text: To measure the mean drag force on the body
To define a fiducial phase point per cycle so every sample or field can be tagged with its phase and sorted into bins
To filter out all turbulence from the flow before recording
To synchronize the camera's frame rate to exactly the shedding frequency

explanations.a: The reference signal establishes phase timing, not force; drag would require a separate force measurement.
explanations.b: Correct — a correlated reference signal (e.g., a hot-wire zero-crossing) gives the fiducial phase point needed to tag and bin every subsequent sample or field by phase.
explanations.c: Phase averaging does not remove turbulence from the physical flow; it statistically separates the coherent part from the random part after the fact.
explanations.d: The camera can run at any (even uncorrelated) rate — phase averaging works precisely because phase is assigned after acquisition via the reference signal, not by synchronizing frame rate.

questions.prompt: Match each term in the triple decomposition u(x,t) = U(x) + ũ(x,φ) + u′(x,t) to its meaning.

right.text: Time-mean flow
Phase-locked, periodic (coherent) part that repeats with the shedding cycle
Random turbulent part that does not correlate with phase

questions.explanation: Hussain and Reynolds' (1970) triple decomposition splits the instantaneous velocity into a time-mean, a phase-locked coherent periodic component, and a random turbulent residual that phase averaging cannot organize.

questions.prompt: Why does an unconditioned (ordinary) time average of wake velocity erase the vortex street?

options.text: Because time averaging always requires more samples than are typically available
Because alternating-sign contributions from top- and bottom-shear-layer vortices, summed across all phases, cancel out at a fixed point
Because vortices only exist for a few milliseconds and decay before any averaging can capture them
Because time averaging amplifies noise relative to signal

explanations.a: Sample count affects statistical convergence, not the fundamental cancellation mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct — vortices of opposite sign pass a fixed point at regular phase intervals; averaging across all phases sums these opposite contributions and they cancel, leaving only the smooth mean wake.
explanations.c: Vortices persist and convect over many diameters downstream; their disappearance from a time average is a cancellation effect, not decay.
explanations.d: Averaging generally reduces noise relative to a repeating signal; the issue here is cancellation of the coherent signal itself when phase is ignored.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the phase-averaging procedure.

items.text: Acquire a reference signal simultaneously with the flow measurement
Define a fiducial phase point (e.g., a zero-crossing) in the reference signal
Tag each sample or field with its phase angle and sort into phase bins
Average all samples within each bin across all recorded cycles

questions.explanation: Phase averaging requires a simultaneous reference signal, a defined fiducial phase point within each cycle, phase tagging and binning of every subsequent sample or field, and finally averaging within each bin across all cycles to build one representative cycle.

questions.prompt: In the worked PIV example, 360° of one shedding cycle is divided into 24 phase bins. How wide is each bin?

explanations.c: Correct — 360° divided into 24 equal bins gives 15° per bin, matching the worked example.
explanations.d: 360°/24 = 15°; 30° would correspond to only 12 bins.

lessons.label: Correlation, Coherence and Convection Velocity

sections.heading: Spanwise correlation length
sections.body: The two-point correlation coefficient R(Δz) = ⟨u′(z,t)u′(z+Δz,t)⟩/u′_rms² is measured with two spanwise-separated hot-wires or PIV planes behind a bluff body. Integrating R(Δz) over Δz gives an integral length scale L_z — the spanwise correlation length, roughly how many diameters of span shed vortices in step before phase drifts apart. For a stationary circular cylinder at subcritical Reynolds number, L_z is short — commonly cited figures fall in the 3–6 D range, as reviewed by Norberg (2003) — because three-dimensional instabilities (vortex dislocations, oblique shedding cells) continually break phase coherence along an unforced span. Once the cylinder is allowed to vibrate and lock-in occurs, this changes sharply: the structural motion imposes a single coherent forcing along the whole span, and correlation length grows dramatically — often to many diameters, effectively spanning the whole instrumented length — because the body now organizes the wake rather than the wake organizing itself.

sections.heading: Convection velocity from cross-spectral phase
sections.body: Placing two probes at the same spanwise position but different streamwise stations in the near wake and computing the cross-spectrum between their signals gives a phase φ(f). For a coherent structure convecting downstream at velocity U_c, phase increases linearly with frequency: φ(f) = 2πfΔx/U_c, so the slope dφ/df yields U_c = 2πΔx/(dφ/df) directly. In cylinder wakes, this convection velocity for shed vortices typically comes out around 0.8–0.9 of the freestream velocity U∞ — slower than the free stream because the vortices form and travel through the lower-momentum wake-deficit region rather than the outer flow.

sections.heading: Coherence and the missing lift
sections.body: Squared coherence γ²(f) = |S_xy(f)|²/(S_xx(f)S_yy(f)) measures, frequency by frequency, how linearly related two signals are, bounded from 0 (unrelated) to 1 (perfectly related). At the shedding frequency, coherence between separated points stays high while the wake is organized and falls toward zero at frequencies dominated by uncorrelated turbulence — a direct, quantitative readout of how organized the wake still is. This spanwise decorrelation explains a classic discrepancy: two-dimensional strip theory, which assumes shedding is perfectly in phase along the entire span, predicts a much larger fluctuating (RMS) lift coefficient than what real finite-span cylinders actually show. Because shedding is only correlated over the few-diameter length L_z, forces from different spanwise segments partially cancel when integrated over a real span, so measured fluctuating lift comes out well below the 2D prediction — Norberg's (2003) review compiles RMS lift coefficients that vary strongly with aspect ratio and end conditions precisely because of this correlation-length averaging effect, not a change in 2D shedding strength itself.

lessons.workedExample: A stationary D = 0.025 m cylinder in a subcritical flow (Re ≈ 10^4) is instrumented with two spanwise-separated hot-wires. The correlation R(Δz) drops to 0.5 by Δz ≈ 3D and to near zero by Δz ≈ 6D, giving an integral length L_z ≈ 4D. The same cylinder is then mounted on soft springs and driven into lock-in at U* ≈ 5; repeating the spanwise correlation measurement shows R staying above 0.8 even at the largest separation tested (10D) — correlation length has grown past the whole test section because the body's motion now drives the wake coherently. Separately, two streamwise hot-wires spaced 1D apart in the near wake give a cross-spectral phase slope corresponding to U_c ≈ 0.85·U∞.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because it is the direct explanation for why measured fluctuating lift on a real structure is much smaller than a naive 2D calculation predicts — a gap that trips up students who only think in two dimensions. A student who can state a correlation length in diameters, describe how it grows once the body vibrates, and connect that growth to partial cancellation of spanwise force has engaged with the mechanism; one who describes the wake as merely 'messy' or '3D' without a quantitative correlation-length argument has not.

questions.prompt: What does the spanwise correlation length L_z quantify?

options.text: The distance downstream at which vortices fully dissipate
The distance along the span over which vortex shedding stays in phase before decorrelating
The wavelength of the vortex street in the streamwise direction
The diameter of the cylinder itself

explanations.a: Streamwise dissipation distance is a different quantity; L_z is measured along the span, not downstream.
explanations.b: Correct — L_z is the integral of the spanwise two-point correlation coefficient, quantifying how far along the span shedding stays phase-coherent before three-dimensional effects break it apart.
explanations.c: Streamwise vortex spacing is set by the shedding frequency and convection velocity, not by spanwise correlation.
explanations.d: L_z is typically expressed in units of diameters (e.g., 4D), but it is a separate, measured length scale, not the diameter itself.

questions.prompt: What typically happens to spanwise correlation length when a cylinder is allowed to vibrate and enters lock-in?

options.text: It shrinks toward zero as the vibration disrupts the wake
It stays exactly the same as the stationary case
It grows dramatically, often spanning most or all of the instrumented length, because the body's motion now organizes the wake
It becomes undefined because shedding stops during lock-in

explanations.a: Lock-in increases organization along the span rather than disrupting it further.
explanations.b: Correlation length changes substantially between the stationary and lock-in cases, as shown in the worked example.
explanations.c: Correct — structural motion imposes a single coherent forcing along the whole span, so correlation length grows dramatically compared to the few-diameter length seen on a stationary cylinder.
explanations.d: Shedding continues (and is enhanced in organization) during lock-in; it does not stop.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for obtaining vortex convection velocity from two streamwise probes.

items.text: Place two probes at the same spanwise location but different streamwise stations, separated by Δx
Record simultaneous time series from both probes
Compute the cross-spectrum and extract the phase φ(f) between the two signals
Fit the slope dφ/df and compute U_c = 2πΔx/(dφ/df)

questions.explanation: Convection velocity requires two streamwise-separated simultaneous measurements, a cross-spectral phase computed between them, and finally the linear phase-versus-frequency slope converted into a convection speed.

questions.prompt: Why is the measured fluctuating (RMS) lift coefficient on a real, finite-span cylinder typically much less than two-dimensional strip theory predicts?

options.text: Because 2D strip theory overestimates the shedding frequency
Because shedding is only correlated over a few diameters of span, so forces from different spanwise segments partially cancel when integrated over the full length
Because real cylinders have lower drag than idealized 2D cylinders
Because lift only exists near the ends of a finite cylinder

explanations.a: The discrepancy is about force magnitude from spanwise cancellation, not about shedding frequency prediction.
explanations.b: Correct — 2D strip theory assumes perfect in-phase shedding along the whole span, but real shedding only stays correlated over L_z (a few diameters), so integrating over a longer span sums partially out-of-phase segments that partially cancel.
explanations.c: Drag and lift are separate quantities; this discrepancy is specific to the fluctuating lift force tied to spanwise correlation, not overall drag.
explanations.d: Lift-generating shedding occurs along the whole span; the reduction comes from decorrelation, not from lift being localized to the ends.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to what it measures or how it is obtained.

right.text: Integral of the spanwise two-point correlation coefficient over separation distance
= 2πΔx/(dφ/df), from the cross-spectral phase slope between two streamwise stations
Frequency-resolved, 0-to-1 measure of how linearly related two signals are

questions.explanation: Spanwise correlation length comes from integrating the spanwise correlation coefficient; convection velocity comes from the slope of cross-spectral phase versus frequency between streamwise-separated probes; coherence is a frequency-resolved, normalized measure of how linearly two signals relate, bounded between 0 and 1.

lessons.label: Modal Decomposition and Reduced-Order Reading

sections.heading: POD: energy-ranked coherent structures
sections.body: Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, introduced to turbulence by Lumley (1967), decomposes a flow field's fluctuations into an orthogonal set of spatial modes ranked by how much fluctuating kinetic energy each captures — mode 1 captures the most, mode 2 the largest remainder, and so on, with orthogonality guaranteed by construction (an eigen-decomposition of the two-point spatial covariance). Applied to a cylinder-wake dataset, vortex shedding dominates the fluctuation energy so overwhelmingly that the leading pair of POD modes together captures it — and critically, the pair appears in spatial quadrature, roughly 90° out of phase, because a single static spatial pattern cannot represent a traveling wave of vortices; it takes two orthogonal patterns combined with two oscillating time coefficients to reconstruct something that travels. Noack et al.'s (2003) widely cited low-dimensional-model study of the transient cylinder wake showed this leading pair capturing most of the fluctuation energy at fixed Reynolds number, but that a naive Galerkin model built from just that pair fails to track the mean-flow deformation during the transient from unstable steady state to limit-cycle shedding — motivating an added, non-oscillatory 'shift mode' to follow the changing mean flow.

sections.heading: DMD: frequency-tagged modes
sections.body: Dynamic Mode Decomposition, formalized by Schmid (2010), instead extracts modes each tied to a single temporal frequency and growth or decay rate — an eigenvalue of a linear operator fit to the sequence of snapshots — connecting to Koopman-operator theory for nonlinear systems (Rowley et al., 2009). Unlike POD's energy ranking, DMD ranks by dynamical significance: a mode that is dynamically dominant but energetically modest can be found directly and tagged with its exact frequency, useful when a physically important but low-energy mode (a weak secondary instability, say) would otherwise sit buried far down a POD energy ranking.

sections.heading: Limits: a basis is not physics
sections.body: It is tempting to treat POD or DMD modes as literal physical mechanisms because they look vortex-like, but both are mathematical bases — energy-optimal for POD, frequency-diagonal for linearized dynamics for DMD — fit to one particular dataset. The modes depend on the domain, the snapshot sampling, and the flow regime used to compute them, so a reduced-order model built from modes extracted at one operating condition (one Re, one U∞) can fail silently, producing plausible-looking but wrong output, when extrapolated to a regime it never saw — exactly the mean-flow-deformation failure Noack's shift mode was built to patch. A related, purely time-frequency tool, the spectrogram (a sliding-window FFT over time), is often used alongside modal decomposition to read a non-stationary signal directly: a startup transient shows the shedding frequency and amplitude ramping up as the wake spins up from rest, and a speed sweep shows the shedding frequency tracking continuously along the Strouhal line — except where it flattens into a lock-in plateau, visible as a horizontal band on the spectrogram.

lessons.workedExample: A simulation of a 2D cylinder wake at Re = 100, in its post-transient limit cycle, produces 500 velocity snapshots spanning several shedding periods. POD on this dataset finds the first two modes capturing about 95% of the fluctuating energy combined (roughly split evenly), visually resembling alternating vortex pairs shifted by a quarter wavelength — about 90° in phase — with their time coefficients oscillating as a sine/cosine pair at the shedding frequency. DMD applied to the same dataset returns a leading complex-conjugate mode pair tagged with a frequency matching the shedding frequency and a near-zero growth rate, consistent with a stable limit cycle.
