Taking snapshots across the startup transient instead and building a spectrogram shows the shedding frequency ramping from near 0 at t = 0 up to the converged value over roughly 40 shedding periods, as the wake instability grows and saturates.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because it is easy to show a colorful POD or DMD mode plot without understanding what it actually claims. The tell of real understanding is explaining why a traveling vortex street needs two modes in quadrature rather than one, naming the energy-versus-frequency tradeoff between POD and DMD, and — most tellingly — stating the regime the modes or reduced-order model were fit to and whether the student validated it there or naively extrapolated it elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why does representing a traveling vortex street with POD require a pair of modes rather than a single mode?

options.text: Because POD always returns modes in pairs by mathematical definition
Because a single static spatial pattern cannot represent a traveling wave; two orthogonal patterns in spatial quadrature, combined with oscillating time coefficients, are needed
Because the simulation used two separate cameras
Because vortex shedding produces exactly two vortices per cycle

explanations.a: POD does not always return paired modes; pairing here is a consequence of the traveling-wave structure of shedding, not a general rule.
explanations.b: Correct — a traveling wave needs two orthogonal spatial patterns roughly 90° apart combined with oscillating (sine/cosine-like) time coefficients to reconstruct motion; one static mode alone cannot do this.
explanations.c: POD is computed from the snapshot dataset regardless of how many cameras or sensors produced it; camera count is unrelated to the pairing.
explanations.d: Shedding does alternate top/bottom vortices, but that is not why POD specifically needs a mode pair — the pairing comes from the traveling-wave representation requirement.

questions.prompt: How does DMD's mode ranking differ from POD's?

options.text: DMD ranks modes by dynamical significance (frequency/growth rate), while POD ranks by fluctuating energy captured
DMD and POD always produce identical rankings for any dataset
DMD ranks modes alphabetically by label
POD ranks modes by frequency, while DMD ranks by energy

explanations.a: Correct — POD's ranking is by energy captured (an eigen-decomposition of the covariance), while DMD ties each mode to a specific frequency and growth/decay rate from a fitted linear operator.
explanations.b: The two methods use different criteria and generally produce different mode orderings and even different mode shapes.
explanations.c: Mode ranking is based on physical/mathematical criteria (energy or dynamics), not arbitrary labeling.
explanations.d: This reverses the actual assignment — POD is energy-ranked, DMD is frequency/growth-rate-tagged.

questions.prompt: What is the primary limitation of a reduced-order model (e.g., a Galerkin model) built from POD or DMD modes?

options.text: It requires more computing power than the original simulation
The modes and the model built from them are fit to the specific dataset/regime used; extrapolating to a different regime can fail silently
It can only be applied to two-dimensional flows
It cannot represent oscillatory behavior at all

explanations.a: Reduced-order models are specifically built to be cheaper than the original simulation, not more expensive.
explanations.b: Correct — modes are a basis fit to one domain, sampling, and flow regime; a model built from them can look plausible yet be wrong when applied outside that regime, as with the mean-flow-deformation failure motivating Noack's shift mode.
explanations.c: POD and DMD are applied to 3D flows as well as 2D flows; dimensionality is not the core limitation described here.
explanations.d: The leading POD/DMD pair specifically represents oscillatory (traveling-wave) behavior; that is exactly what they are good at capturing within their fitted regime.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or model component to what it reveals about a wake.

right.text: Energy-ranked spatial modes, with the shedding pair dominant and in quadrature
Frequency- and growth-rate-tagged modes from a fitted linear operator
Time-resolved frequency content, revealing startup transients or lock-in plateaus during a speed sweep
Added non-oscillatory mode that tracks mean-flow deformation missed by the leading POD pair alone

questions.explanation: POD ranks spatial modes by energy, with the shedding pair usually dominant and in quadrature; DMD tags modes with frequency and growth/decay rate from a linear operator fit; a spectrogram shows time-resolved frequency content useful for transients and speed sweeps; and Noack's shift mode is an added, non-oscillatory component that tracks mean-flow deformation the leading POD pair alone cannot capture.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that lead to a POD-based reduced-order model failing silently outside its fitted regime.

items.text: Collect flow snapshots at one operating condition (one Reynolds number, one U∞)
Compute POD modes ranked by fluctuating energy from that snapshot set
Build a Galerkin reduced-order model using the leading energy-ranked modes
Apply the model to a different operating regime it was never fit to, and observe it produce plausible but wrong output

questions.explanation: The failure mode starts with snapshots from a single regime, proceeds through energy-ranked POD modes and a Galerkin model built from them, and only becomes apparent when that model is extrapolated to a regime outside the one it was fit to, where it can fail silently rather than obviously.

units.label: Landmark Work and Open Debates

lessons.label: Strouhal, Benard, Karman: Who Found the Street

sections.heading: Strouhal's singing wire, 1878
sections.body: Vincenz Strouhal, working in Würzburg, Germany as an assistant to physicist Friedrich Kohlrausch in 1878 (Strouhal would not become a physics professor in his native Bohemia, at Prague, until 1884), studied the tone a taut wire sings in wind (the 'aeolian tone', named for Aeolus, Greek god of wind). He found the pitch scaled with wind speed over wire diameter, giving the dimensionless group now written St = fD/U, where f is the shedding frequency, D the diameter, and U the flow speed. Strouhal did not know the tone came from shed vortices; Lord Rayleigh's 1879-80 follow-up connected the pitch to periodic flow separation behind the wire and tied it to the older mystery of the aeolian harp. St itself stayed near 0.2 for a cylinder across a wide speed range, a fact later work would explain.

sections.heading: Benard's photographs, 1908
sections.body: Henri Benard, in France, photographed the alternating, staggered vortex pattern shed behind an obstacle in a moving fluid around 1908, years before any stability theory existed for it. Because Benard had the pattern on film first, French-language literature to this day calls the structure the 'allee de Benard-von Karman' (Benard-Karman street), and Benard pressed a priority claim once Karman's theory made the pattern famous. The dispute is genuine and unresolved by consensus: Benard supplies the first clear observation, Karman supplies the first theory of why the pattern is stable at all.

sections.heading: Karman and Rubach's stability analysis, 1911-12
sections.body: At Gottingen in 1911-12, Theodore von Karman, with Hermann Rubach, modeled the wake as two infinite rows of idealized point vortices and asked which row spacing survives small perturbations. A symmetric arrangement is always unstable; a staggered arrangement is unstable for almost every spacing ratio h/a (row spacing over in-row vortex spacing) except one: h/a = cosh^-1(sqrt(2))/pi, approximately 0.281, which alone is neutrally stable. That single number, checkable against photographs of real wakes, is why the pattern bears Karman's name.

sections.heading: Why the theory is admired and distrusted at once
sections.body: The catch, raised almost immediately and repeated by every honest textbook since, is that Karman's result is fragile. It is inviscid, two-dimensional, and built from idealized point vortices with no core size, no viscosity, and no mechanism for the vortices to form in the first place; 'neutrally stable' at exactly one ratio means small disturbances neither grow nor decay in the linear theory, which is a razor's edge, not the robust persistence real streets show for hundreds of diameters downstream. Real streets are viscous, three-dimensional, and self-sustained by continuous shedding from the body, none of which the 1912 analysis includes.

lessons.workedExample: A telephone wire 2 mm in diameter hums in a 10 m/s crosswind. Using St approximately equal to 0.2 for this Reynolds-number range, the shedding frequency is f = St*U/D = 0.2*10/0.002 = 1000 Hz, an audible tone -- exactly the aeolian-tone effect Strouhal measured in 1878. A photograph of the wake taken far downstream would let a student measure the staggered rows' spacing ratio directly and check it against Karman and Rubach's predicted h/a = 0.281; real wakes typically come out close but not exact, because viscosity and finite vortex cores relax the idealized point-vortex constraint.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'so who actually discovered the vortex street, Benard or Karman?' is testing whether a student can hold two true things at once: Benard photographed the pattern first, and Karman explained why one specific spacing survives at all. The strong answer names both, dates both (1908 versus 1911-12), and adds the harder point that Karman's tidy 0.281 result is a fragile, idealized, neutrally-stable case that does not by itself explain why real streets persist so robustly -- showing the student understands the difference between describing a phenomenon and proving why it exists.

questions.prompt: What does the Strouhal number St = fD/U relate?

options.text: Shedding frequency, body diameter, and flow speed
Fluid density and viscosity only
Wake row spacing and vortex core size
Lift coefficient and angle of attack

explanations.a: Correct -- St is the dimensionless group Strouhal defined from his 1878 aeolian-tone measurements: shedding frequency f, characteristic diameter D, and flow speed U.
explanations.b: Density and viscosity combine into the Reynolds number, a separate dimensionless group that sets the flow regime, not St directly.
explanations.c: Row spacing ratio (h/a) is the quantity from Karman and Rubach's 1911-12 stability analysis, a different number from St.
explanations.d: Lift coefficient and angle of attack belong to steady airfoil aerodynamics, unrelated to the shedding-frequency relation Strouhal measured.

questions.prompt: In Karman and Rubach's point-vortex stability analysis, which staggered row-spacing ratio (h/a) is neutrally stable?

options.text: 1.000, a square arrangement
Approximately 0.281
0.500, exactly half the in-row spacing
There is no stable ratio -- all staggered arrangements are unstable

explanations.a: A square (unstaggered) arrangement is unstable in the analysis, not the stable case.
explanations.b: Correct -- h/a = cosh^-1(sqrt(2))/pi is approximately 0.281, the one staggered spacing ratio the 1911-12 linear analysis found to be neutrally stable.
explanations.c: 0.5 is not the derived value; it is a plausible-sounding round number a student might guess instead of doing the analysis.
explanations.d: One staggered ratio (about 0.281) is neutrally stable in the theory -- it is the near-square and most other ratios that are unstable.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the vortex-street history in chronological order.

items.text: Strouhal measures the aeolian tone of a wire in wind
Rayleigh links the tone to periodic flow separation
Benard photographs the staggered wake pattern
Karman and Rubach publish the point-vortex stability analysis

questions.explanation: Strouhal's aeolian-tone measurements came in 1878, Rayleigh's explanation followed in 1879-80, Benard photographed the staggered pattern around 1908, and Karman and Rubach's stability theory followed in 1911-12 -- the theory came last, decades after the phenomenon was already being measured and photographed.

questions.prompt: Why do some fluid dynamicists call Karman's 1911-12 result 'fragile' rather than a full explanation of real vortex streets?

options.text: Because it was later shown to give the wrong numerical value of h/a
Because it is an inviscid, idealized point-vortex model that is only neutrally stable at one ratio, and omits viscosity, vortex formation, and three-dimensionality
Because Karman never published the analysis
Because it only applies to wires, not to cylinders

explanations.a: The h/a = 0.281 value itself is not disputed as the output of the idealized model; the critique is about what the model leaves out, not an arithmetic error.
explanations.b: Correct -- the model uses point vortices with no viscosity, no core structure, and no shedding mechanism, and even its stable case is only neutrally (not robustly) stable, which does not by itself explain the strong persistence of real, viscous, three-dimensional wakes.
explanations.c: Karman and Rubach did publish the analysis at Gottingen in 1911-12; the critique concerns its scope, not its existence.
explanations.d: The theory was framed generally for bluff-body wakes, including cylinders, not restricted to wires.

questions.prompt: Why does French-language literature often call the pattern the 'Benard-Karman street'?

options.text: Benard and Karman co-authored the 1911-12 stability paper
Benard photographed the alternating wake pattern around 1908, before Karman's 1911-12 theory, and pressed a priority claim
Benard disproved Karman's spacing ratio
It is a translation error with no historical basis

explanations.a: Benard and Karman never co-authored; they worked independently, which is exactly why a priority dispute arose.
explanations.b: Correct -- Benard's photographic observation of the staggered pattern predates Karman and Rubach's stability theory by several years, and Benard argued the discovery credit should include his name.
explanations.c: Benard's photographs did not address the stability ratio at all; that number came only from Karman and Rubach's later analysis.
explanations.d: The dual naming reflects a real, documented priority dispute, not a translation artifact.

lessons.label: Roshko at Caltech and the Universal Strouhal Number

sections.heading: Mapping the wake into regimes, 1954
sections.body: Anatol Roshko, in two 1954 NACA technical notes (TN 3169, 'On the Drag and Shedding Frequency of Two-Dimensional Bluff Bodies,' and TN 2913, 'On the Development of Turbulent Wakes from Vortex Streets,' the latter later reissued as NACA Report 1191) from his Caltech-era work, ran cylinders across a wide Reynolds-number sweep and found the wake does not behave one way -- it passes through distinct regimes. Below roughly Re = 150-300 the shedding is a stable, laminar, single-frequency street; through an intermediate transition range the wake starts to shed small-scale turbulence into the large vortices; and above that it becomes irregular, with a still-detectable dominant frequency riding on broadband turbulent fluctuation. Roshko fit St-Re relations separately for the stable range, giving the empirical correlation St approximately equal to 0.212*(1 - 21.2/Re) for Re in the low hundreds -- showing St depends measurably on Reynolds number there in a way a single constant like 'St approximately 0.2' hides.

sections.heading: The universal Strouhal number
sections.body: Roshko's more ambitious claim was that shedding frequency should not be judged against the body's diameter at all, but against the wake's own dimensions: the wake width and a velocity scale built from the base (rear) pressure. Defining a universal Strouhal number St* on those wake-based scales, he found circular cylinders, flat plates, and wedges of different frontal shapes collapsed onto nearly the same St* value, near 0.16-0.18 in his subcritical-range data, even though their ordinary diameter-based St values differed. The claim: the wake, not the body's frontal shape, sets the shedding physics -- different bluff bodies are all doing the same thing once measured in the wake's own units.

sections.heading: Bearman, Williamson, and the cylinder as the field's hydrogen atom
sections.body: Bearman's later work sharpened the base-pressure side of Roshko's picture, tying the base (rear-surface) suction coefficient directly to shedding frequency and showing base pressure is a sensitive, physically grounded proxy for wake width across a wide range of bluff shapes. Williamson's comprehensive 1996 Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics survey of cylinder wake dynamics -- transition, three-dimensionality, the full St-Re curve -- consolidated decades of this line of work into the reference every subsequent VIV and wake study cites. Because a plain circular cylinder is geometrically the simplest possible bluff body yet reproduces essentially every qualitative wake behavior seen in engineering flows, the wake-dynamics community treats it the way atomic physicists treat hydrogen: not because cylinders are what anyone ultimately cares about, but because it is the simplest system that still contains the real physics.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher tests a circular cylinder and a flat plate broadside to the flow, both at subcritical Reynolds number. Their ordinary Strouhal numbers (based on frontal width) differ -- roughly 0.2 for the cylinder versus a different value for the plate, because St based on frontal dimension depends on body shape. But when each is rescaled using Roshko's universal St*, built from the measured wake width and a velocity derived from base pressure rather than freestream speed, both bodies land close to the same St* (around 0.16-0.18), demonstrating that the wake, not the upstream-facing shape, governs the shedding frequency -- the collapse Roshko used to argue for one underlying wake mechanism.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'is 0.2 always the Strouhal number for bluff-body shedding?' is checking whether a student has moved past the memorized constant. The strong answer explains that St depends on Reynolds-number regime (Roshko's 1954 stable/transition/irregular ranges) and on how you define the length and velocity scales -- and can describe Roshko's universal St*, built from wake width and base-pressure velocity, that collapses different body shapes onto one curve. That distinction between a diameter-based constant and a physically motivated wake-based scaling is exactly what separates rote recall from understanding why the number holds.

questions.prompt: In Roshko's 1954 NACA reports, which three wake regimes did he identify across a Reynolds-number sweep?

options.text: Laminar, transitional, and turbulent boundary layers
Stable (single-frequency), transition, and irregular shedding
Subsonic, transonic, and supersonic
Attached, separated, and reattached flow

explanations.a: Boundary-layer laminar/transitional/turbulent labels describe the layer on the body surface, not the three wake-shedding regimes Roshko mapped in the near-wake.
explanations.b: Correct -- Roshko's sweep identified a low-Re stable single-frequency range, an intermediate transition range where small-scale turbulence appears within the large vortices, and a higher-Re irregular range with a dominant frequency riding on broadband turbulence.
explanations.c: These are compressibility (Mach-number) regimes, unrelated to Roshko's incompressible-wake Reynolds-number study.
explanations.d: Attached/separated/reattached describes boundary-layer separation behavior, not the three shedding regimes across Reynolds number Roshko reported.

questions.prompt: What made Roshko's 'universal Strouhal number' universal?

options.text: It used the body's frontal diameter and freestream speed, same as the ordinary Strouhal number
It was defined using wake width and a velocity scale from base pressure, which collapsed data from different bluff-body shapes onto nearly one value
It applied only to circular cylinders
It was independent of Reynolds number at all speeds, including supersonic flow

explanations.a: That description is the ordinary, diameter-based Strouhal number, which differs across body shapes -- the opposite of what made Roshko's version universal.
explanations.b: Correct -- by rescaling frequency using wake width and a base-pressure-derived velocity instead of frontal diameter and freestream speed, cylinders, plates, and wedges collapsed onto nearly the same St* value.
explanations.c: The point of the universal number was that it worked across multiple differently shaped bluff bodies, not just cylinders.
explanations.d: Roshko's collapse was demonstrated within a subcritical Reynolds-number range; it was not claimed to hold unchanged into compressible or supersonic regimes.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or reviewer to their contribution to bluff-body wake understanding.

right.text: Mapped stable/transition/irregular wake regimes and proposed the universal Strouhal number
Tied base (rear-surface) pressure directly to shedding frequency across bluff shapes
Wrote the comprehensive Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics survey consolidating cylinder wake dynamics

questions.explanation: Roshko's 1954 NACA reports established the three wake regimes and the universal Strouhal number; Bearman's later work sharpened the base-pressure-to-frequency link; Williamson's 1996 review consolidated decades of cylinder wake research into the field's standard reference.

questions.prompt: Why does the wake-dynamics community call the circular cylinder its 'hydrogen atom'?

options.text: Because cylinders are the only bluff body used in real engineering structures
Because it is the geometrically simplest bluff body that still reproduces essentially every qualitative wake behavior seen in more complex flows
Because Roshko's data only applies to cylinders and not to any other shape
Because cylinder wakes contain hydrogen bonding effects

explanations.a: Engineering structures use many bluff shapes (decks, risers, wedges, plates); the cylinder's importance is as a simplified model system, not the only real-world shape.
explanations.b: Correct -- like hydrogen for atomic physics, the cylinder is the simplest case that still contains the real physics (shedding, transition, three-dimensionality), making it the natural reference case for the whole field.
explanations.c: Roshko explicitly showed the universal Strouhal number collapsed data from plates and wedges as well as cylinders -- the physics is not cylinder-exclusive.
explanations.d: This is a nonsensical literal reading of the analogy; the comparison is about simplicity as a model system, not chemistry.

lessons.label: Feng, Williamson and the VIV Data Wars

sections.heading: Feng's 1968 thesis sets the canonical picture
sections.body: C. C. Feng's 1968 master's thesis at the University of British Columbia measured a spring-mounted circular cylinder, free to vibrate across the flow, at a high mass ratio (the ratio of the oscillating structure's mass to the mass of fluid it displaces, m* approximately 248). Sweeping the reduced velocity U* = U/(fN D), Feng found vibration amplitude rise on an 'initial' branch as the shedding frequency approached the structure's natural frequency, lock-in where the shedding frequency locks to the natural frequency across a range of speeds, then a lower branch with reduced amplitude. For thirty years, Feng's two-branch curve was the reference dataset every vortex-induced-vibration (VIV) model was checked against.

sections.heading: Khalak and Williamson find a third branch
sections.body: In the mid-to-late 1990s, Khalak and Williamson ran the equivalent experiment at low mass and low damping (low combined mass-damping parameter) rather than Feng's high-mass regime, publishing the key results in 1996 and a fuller account in 1999. At low mass-damping they found a distinct upper branch sitting between the initial and lower branches, with peak amplitude to diameter ratio (A*/D) approaching about 1 -- oscillation nearly as large as the cylinder itself, well beyond anything in Feng's high-mass data. The upper branch was not a subtle correction; it was a qualitatively new response regime that high-mass-ratio testing had simply never been able to reach. Lock-in and the upper branch both sit in roughly the same reduced-velocity window, U* approximately 5 to 7, where the shedding frequency stays locked to the structure's natural frequency across the sweep; it is the peak amplitude reached inside that window -- modest for Feng's high-mass branches versus A*/D near 1 for Khalak and Williamson's upper branch -- that marks the qualitative jump, not the reduced-velocity range itself.

sections.heading: The wake-mode map and the mass-ratio argument
sections.body: Williamson and Roshko's 1988 study, mapping vibration amplitude and frequency against a grid of wake patterns visualized downstream, had already shown the wake does not always shed one vortex per cycle. It can shed a single vortex per half-cycle (mode 2S, the ordinary Karman pattern), a pair of vortices per half-cycle (2P), or an asymmetric combination of one single vortex and one pair (P+S) -- and each amplitude branch in the Feng- and Khalak/Williamson-style curves corresponds to a different wake mode. The live argument that followed asked whether a single combined mass-damping parameter fully collapses amplitude data across experiments, as Khalak and Williamson's scaling implied, or whether mass ratio has an independent effect beyond damping alone; Govardhan and Williamson's 2002 study, 'Resonance Forever: Existence of a Critical Mass and an Infinite Regime of Resonance in Vortex-Induced Vibration,' argued the latter, showing mass ratio alone (not just the mass-damping product) shifts the upper-branch response and the critical mass at which galloping-like amplification can occur.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher repeats a VIV experiment twice: once at Feng's high mass ratio (m* approximately 248) and once at a low mass ratio with light damping, sweeping U* in both cases. The high-mass run reproduces Feng's 1968 initial and lower branches with modest peak amplitude. The low-mass-damping run, replicating Khalak and Williamson's setup, shows an upper branch appearing between initial and lower, with A*/D climbing toward 1 -- a response Feng's apparatus, at its much higher mass ratio, was structurally incapable of reaching. Comparing the two curves side by side is the standard way students are shown why 'the' VIV response curve is really a family of curves parameterized by mass-damping.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is there really only one vortex-induced-vibration response curve?' is testing whether a student knows the field's canonical dataset was incomplete for thirty years. The strong answer names Feng's 1968 high-mass thesis as the original two-branch picture, explains that Khalak and Williamson's 1996-99 low-mass-damping experiments revealed a third upper branch invisible at high mass ratio, and can state the live, unresolved-in-detail argument over whether mass-damping alone or mass ratio independently sets the response (per Govardhan and Williamson's 2002 critical-mass study) -- showing the student understands VIV data as parameter-dependent, not as one universal curve.

questions.prompt: What made Feng's 1968 UBC thesis the canonical VIV dataset for decades?

options.text: It was the first study to use a computer simulation instead of a physical model
It measured a spring-mounted cylinder's amplitude across reduced velocity at high mass ratio, establishing the initial and lower response branches
It discovered the upper branch with A*/D near 1
It was the first study to observe lock-in in any oscillating system

explanations.a: Feng's thesis was a physical wind/water-tunnel experiment on a real spring-mounted cylinder, not a simulation.
explanations.b: Correct -- Feng's high-mass-ratio (m* approximately 248) experiment mapped amplitude against reduced velocity U*, establishing the initial and lower branches that became the field's reference curve.
explanations.c: The upper branch was discovered later, by Khalak and Williamson at low mass-damping -- it does not appear in Feng's high-mass data.
explanations.d: Lock-in (shedding frequency locking to structural natural frequency) had been observed before 1968; Feng's contribution was the detailed two-branch amplitude mapping at high mass ratio.

questions.prompt: What did Khalak and Williamson's low-mass-damping experiments (1996-99) add to Feng's picture?

options.text: They disproved lock-in entirely
They revealed a third, upper response branch, with peak amplitude-to-diameter ratio approaching 1
They showed vibration amplitude is independent of mass ratio
They repeated Feng's high-mass conditions and got identical results

explanations.a: Lock-in remained central to their findings; they did not disprove it, they extended the response map beyond it.
explanations.b: Correct -- at low mass-damping, an upper branch appeared between the initial and lower branches, with A*/D approaching about 1, a regime unreachable at Feng's high mass ratio.
explanations.c: The follow-up debate (Govardhan and Williamson, 2002) argued mass ratio does have an independent effect on the response, the opposite of independence.
explanations.d: They deliberately tested a different, low-mass-damping regime, not a repeat of Feng's high-mass conditions -- that contrast is exactly what exposed the new branch.

questions.prompt: Match each wake-mode label from Williamson and Roshko's 1988 map to its description.

right.text: One single vortex shed per half-cycle (ordinary Karman pattern)
A pair of vortices shed per half-cycle
An asymmetric combination of one single vortex and one pair

questions.explanation: Williamson and Roshko's 1988 wake-mode map classified vortex shedding from an oscillating cylinder into 2S (one vortex per half-cycle, the standard Karman street), 2P (a pair per half-cycle), and P+S (an asymmetric mix of one single vortex and one pair), each tied to a different branch of the amplitude response.

questions.prompt: What is the live argument Govardhan and Williamson's 2002 study addressed?

options.text: Whether vortex shedding exists at all in VIV
Whether a single combined mass-damping parameter fully collapses amplitude data, or whether mass ratio has an independent effect beyond damping alone
Whether the Strouhal number changes with cylinder material
Whether Feng's thesis contained a measurement error

explanations.a: Vortex shedding's existence in VIV was well established by 2000; that was never in question.
explanations.b: Correct -- the debate was whether the combined mass-damping parameter alone sets the amplitude response, or whether mass ratio independently shifts the response and the critical mass for amplified vibration, which Govardhan and Williamson's 2002 study argued for.
explanations.c: Cylinder material was not the variable at issue; the argument concerned mass ratio versus the combined mass-damping parameter.
explanations.d: The debate (Govardhan and Williamson, 2002) concerned interpretation and generalization across parameter regimes, not an error in Feng's original measurements.

lessons.label: Tacoma Narrows 1940: The Correction Every Student Needs

sections.heading: A slender deck oscillates for months, then fails
sections.body: The first Tacoma Narrows Bridge, designed under Leon Moisseiff using deflection theory to justify an unusually slender, shallow plate-girder deck, opened on 1 July 1940 and almost immediately earned the nickname 'Galloping Gertie' for the vertical undulations that rippled along its span in ordinary wind. Those vertical oscillations were tolerated as a nuisance for months. On 7 November 1940, in a wind of roughly 42 mph (about 19 m/s), the character of the motion changed: a cable band slipped near midspan, and the deck stopped moving mostly up and down and began twisting -- one edge rising while the other fell, and reversing.

sections.heading: The films and Farquharson's observations: one degree of freedom, one frequency
sections.body: The collapse is unusually well documented. Professor F. B. Farquharson of the University of Washington was on and near the bridge that morning as part of an ongoing study of its motion, and film of the final oscillations was shot from the shore -- the best-known footage by Barney Elliott and Harbine Monroe of a local camera shop. Together the film and Farquharson's observations show the deck settling into a single-degree-of-freedom torsional mode -- the whole span twisting about its centerline as a rigid unit at a frequency near 0.2 Hz -- shortly before the deck tore loose and fell into the Narrows. That torsional frequency is the number that matters for the historical correction: 0.2 Hz, roughly one twist every five seconds, a slow, large-amplitude motion, not a fast buzz.

sections.heading: Why 'resonance with vortex shedding' is the wrong story
sections.body: The version many textbooks told for decades -- that ordinary Karman vortex shedding happened to match the bridge's natural frequency and resonance amplified it to failure -- is the story students most need to unlearn, and Billah and Scanlan's 1991 American Journal of Physics paper laid out why precisely. The key point is that the deck was not a circular cylinder, so the familiar St approximately 0.2 does not apply to it. For the bridge's H-shaped plate-girder cross-section Billah and Scanlan used a Strouhal number of about 0.11, with the deck's roughly 8 ft (about 2.4 m) depth as the characteristic length and the roughly 19 m/s wind. That gives a shedding frequency of about 0.9 Hz -- Billah and Scanlan quote it as roughly 1 Hz -- against an observed torsional frequency of about 0.2 Hz. The forcing is therefore something like four to five times faster than the mode it is supposed to be driving, and a force oscillating four to five times faster than a structural mode cannot excite that mode through simple resonance. Billah and Scanlan instead described the failure as self-excited torsional flutter: once twisting begins, the deck's own oscillating motion reshapes the airflow around it, and beyond a critical wind speed the aerodynamic forces feed energy into the twist faster than structural damping removes it -- a state called negative aerodynamic damping, distinct from forced resonance at a fixed external frequency.

lessons.workedExample: Run the shedding estimate yourself, and watch the choice of Strouhal number do all the work. Take the deck's roughly 8 ft (2.4 m) depth as the characteristic length D and the roughly 42 mph (about 19 m/s) wind recorded that morning as U. Plugging in the textbook circular-cylinder value St approximately 0.2 gives f = 0.2*19/2.4 = 1.6 Hz -- but that value belongs to a smooth round cylinder, not to a bluff H-shaped girder deck, so it is the wrong number to use here. Billah and Scanlan used St approximately 0.11 for this cross-section: f = St*U/D = 0.11*19/2.4 = 0.87 Hz, which they report as roughly 1 Hz. Compare either estimate to the approximately 0.2 Hz torsional frequency seen at collapse: with the deck-appropriate St approximately 0.11 the forcing is about 0.87/0.2, a factor of roughly four to five, above the structural frequency. Whichever Strouhal number you pick, the shedding frequency is several times the torsional frequency, so no resonant match exists, and the real mechanism must generate its own energy input rather than simply being driven at a matching external frequency.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks about Tacoma Narrows is almost always checking whether a student repeats the textbook 'vortex shedding resonance' error or gives the corrected mechanism. The strong answer states the two numbers -- shedding frequency near 0.9 to 1 Hz versus observed torsional frequency near 0.2 Hz -- names Billah and Scanlan's 1991 paper as the source of the correction, and knows why the shedding estimate uses St approximately 0.11 rather than the circular-cylinder 0.2. Then it explains self-excited flutter and negative aerodynamic damping in place of resonance. A student who can produce both numbers and justify the Strouhal number, not just say the word 'flutter,' has clearly gone back to the primary correction rather than repeating a half-remembered physics-class anecdote.

questions.prompt: Approximately what wind speed and torsional mode frequency are documented for the deck just before the 7 November 1940 collapse?

options.text: About 42 mph wind; torsional frequency near 0.2 Hz
About 100 mph wind; torsional frequency near 5 Hz
About 42 mph wind; torsional frequency near 0.9 Hz
About 10 mph wind; torsional frequency near 0.02 Hz

explanations.a: Correct -- the recorded wind was roughly 42 mph (about 19 m/s), and the collapse films and Farquharson's observations put the single-degree-of-freedom torsional mode near 0.2 Hz just before failure.
explanations.b: 100 mph and 5 Hz are both far higher than the documented figures; the collapse occurred in a comparatively moderate wind at a slow torsional rate of about one twist every five seconds.
explanations.c: About 0.9 Hz is the estimated vortex-shedding frequency, not the observed torsional mode frequency -- conflating the two is exactly the error this lesson corrects.
explanations.d: 10 mph and 0.02 Hz are both too low relative to the documented 42 mph wind and 0.2 Hz torsional motion.

questions.prompt: According to Billah and Scanlan's 1991 analysis, why can't ordinary vortex-shedding resonance explain the collapse?

options.text: The bridge deck did not shed vortices at all in that wind speed range
The estimated shedding frequency (about 0.9 to 1 Hz) is several times the observed torsional frequency (about 0.2 Hz), so the frequencies do not match
Vortex shedding only occurs underwater, not in air
The bridge had no natural frequency to resonate with

explanations.a: A bluff deck cross-section in that wind speed range would be expected to shed vortices; the issue is the mismatch in frequency, not the absence of shedding.
explanations.b: Correct -- with St approximately 0.11 for the H-shaped deck, D about 2.4 m and U about 19 m/s, the estimate is 0.11*19/2.4 = 0.87 Hz, which Billah and Scanlan report as roughly 1 Hz. That is about four to five times the observed 0.2 Hz torsional mode, so simple resonance between shedding and the structural mode is not physically supported.
explanations.c: Vortex shedding is a general bluff-body phenomenon in any fluid, including air; this option misstates basic fluid mechanics.
explanations.d: The deck clearly had structural natural frequencies (it oscillated at 0.2 Hz torsionally); the issue is which frequency was driving that mode, not the absence of a natural frequency.

questions.prompt: Why does the shedding estimate for the Tacoma deck use a Strouhal number of about 0.11 instead of the familiar 0.2?

options.text: Because St approximately 0.2 is the circular-cylinder value, and the bridge's H-shaped plate-girder deck is a different bluff shape with its own, lower Strouhal number
Because Strouhal number always drops by half in air compared with water
Because the wind speed was below 20 m/s, and St approximately 0.2 only applies above that speed
Because 0.11 is simply the average of all measured Strouhal numbers for every shape

explanations.a: Correct -- Strouhal number depends on cross-sectional geometry. The approximately 0.2 quoted in textbooks is for a circular cylinder over a wide Reynolds-number range; the deck's H-shaped girder section sheds at a different reduced frequency, and Billah and Scanlan used about 0.11 for it. Using 0.2 here would give 1.6 Hz, a number for a body the bridge did not resemble.
explanations.b: Strouhal number is a dimensionless frequency set by geometry and Reynolds number, not by whether the fluid is air or water; there is no such halving rule.
explanations.c: St approximately 0.2 for a cylinder holds across a broad Reynolds-number range and is not switched on by an absolute wind speed threshold.
explanations.d: Strouhal numbers are shape-specific measured values, not an average across shapes.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the correct chronological order.

items.text: Bridge opens and shows persistent vertical ('Galloping Gertie') oscillation
A cable band slips
Deck settles into a single-degree-of-freedom torsional mode near 0.2 Hz
Deck fails and falls into the Narrows

questions.explanation: The bridge opened on 1 July 1940 and oscillated vertically for months; on 7 November 1940 a cable band slipped near midspan, after which the motion converted to the single-degree-of-freedom torsional mode near 0.2 Hz that the films record, and the deck failed shortly after.

questions.prompt: What mechanism did Billah and Scanlan propose in place of forced resonance?

options.text: Self-excited torsional flutter, in which the deck's own twisting motion reshapes the airflow and, beyond a critical wind speed, feeds energy into the twist faster than damping removes it (negative aerodynamic damping)
Simple resonance between the shedding frequency and the torsional mode
Material fatigue in the steel cables, unrelated to aerodynamics
An earthquake coinciding with high wind

explanations.a: Correct -- Billah and Scanlan described a self-excited instability: the twisting motion itself alters the surrounding airflow, and above a critical wind speed the resulting aerodynamic forces add energy to the twist faster than structural damping can dissipate it, a state termed negative aerodynamic damping.
explanations.b: The frequency mismatch (about 0.9 to 1 Hz shedding versus about 0.2 Hz torsional) is precisely what rules out simple forced resonance as the mechanism.
explanations.c: Cable fatigue was not the proposed aerodynamic mechanism; the corrected story centers on self-excited aerodynamic instability, not a purely material failure.
explanations.d: No earthquake was involved; the failure is a wind-structure aeroelastic event, well documented by the collapse films and wind records.

lessons.label: The Tacoma Debate Is Not Fully Closed

sections.heading: Both schools reject simple resonance -- then split
sections.body: Billah and Scanlan's 1991 correction (that shedding near 1 Hz cannot resonate with a 0.2 Hz torsional mode) is settled and universally accepted. What is not fully settled is exactly which self-excited mechanism took over once shedding-driven resonance was ruled out, and here two technical schools give different accounts. Scanlan's own flutter-derivative tradition treats the 1940 failure as classical aeroelastic flutter: using measured flutter derivatives -- empirical coefficients (Scanlan and Tomko established the method in 1971) that capture how a deck's own motion generates additional aerodynamic force -- for the plate-girder cross-section, the deck's torsional motion is shown to reduce, then reverse, the net aerodynamic damping past a critical wind speed, exactly the negative-damping picture from Billah and Scanlan (1991), extended with quantitative derivatives specific to that deck shape.

sections.heading: Larsen's discrete-vortex alternative
sections.body: Allan Larsen's discrete-vortex simulations, developed through the late 1990s and summarized around 2000, model the flow around the same deck section as discrete vortices shed from the sharp edges of the plate-girder profile. In this account, vortices form at the leading edge and convect downstream across the deck's width, and above a critical wind speed -- Larsen's estimate is on the order of four times the natural frequency times the deck width -- the vortices' convection time synchronizes with the torsional period, so each vortex passage delivers a pressure impulse timed to reinforce the twist already underway. That synchronization, not a fixed external shedding frequency, is what builds and sustains a self-reinforcing limit-cycle oscillation: energy in, cycle after cycle, from vortices whose timing is itself set by the structure's own motion.

sections.heading: Where the accounts agree, and where they are pushed back on
sections.body: Both accounts agree on the essentials a science-fair judge cares about: it is not textbook resonance with an externally fixed shedding frequency, it is a self-excited instability in which the deck's own torsional motion shapes the surrounding flow, and beyond a critical wind speed the aerodynamics feed energy into the twist faster than damping removes it. They differ on mechanism -- classical motion-induced circulatory flutter (Scanlan's derivative approach) versus a vortex-convection limit cycle synchronized to the torsional period (Larsen). Larsen's own model has also drawn direct criticism: other researchers have noted that the specific vortex behavior in Larsen's simulations was never actually observed at Tacoma, and that the discrete-vortex model does not reproduce the data well near the actual failure wind speed. The precise mechanism remains an open, actively studied question -- not the resonance myth, but not fully closed either.

lessons.workedExample: A student presenting on Tacoma Narrows says: 'It wasn't resonance with vortex shedding -- shedding was near 1 Hz and the collapse mode was 0.2 Hz. Structural engineers largely agree it was a self-excited instability, but there are two competing technical pictures of the mechanism: Scanlan's flutter-derivative analysis treats it as classical motion-induced flutter, while Allan Larsen's discrete-vortex simulations propose vortices convecting across the deck synchronized to the torsional period, and that second model has itself been criticized for not matching the observed vortex behavior at Tacoma.' That answer states the settled correction, names both competing accounts with their originators, and flags that the vortex-based alternative is itself contested -- precisely the layered, accurate answer a judge is listening for.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has already heard a student correctly reject the resonance myth will often push further: 'okay, so what was it, exactly?' This lesson exists because a student who answers only 'flutter' has memorized a label, not a mechanism. The strong answer names the two competing technical accounts -- Scanlan's flutter-derivative classical-flutter picture and Larsen's discrete-vortex synchronization picture -- states what they agree on (self-excited, motion-driven, negative-damping instability, not resonance), and is honest that Larsen's specific model has drawn documented criticism, showing the student understands this as an open engineering question rather than a settled fact to recite.

questions.prompt: What do the Scanlan flutter-derivative account and Larsen's discrete-vortex account of the Tacoma Narrows collapse agree on?

options.text: Both agree it was simple resonance between vortex shedding and the torsional mode
Both agree it was a self-excited instability in which the deck's own motion shapes the flow and, past a critical wind speed, feeds energy into the twist faster than damping removes it
Both agree the cable-band slip was the sole structural cause, with no aerodynamic contribution
Both agree no vortices were involved in the failure

explanations.a: Both schools explicitly reject simple resonance -- the settled correction from Billah and Scanlan (1991) that both later accounts build on.
explanations.b: Correct -- despite disagreeing on the specific driving mechanism, both accounts describe a self-excited, motion-driven instability with negative aerodynamic damping past a critical wind speed, not forced resonance.
explanations.c: The cable-band slip is part of the documented sequence of events, but neither technical account treats it as replacing the aerodynamic instability as the driver of the large-amplitude torsional motion.
explanations.d: Larsen's account is specifically vortex-based; only the resonance myth (which both reject) removes vortices from consideration entirely.

questions.prompt: In Larsen's discrete-vortex model, what synchronizes to drive the self-reinforcing torsional motion?

options.text: The vortex-shedding frequency locks to a fixed 1 Hz value
Vortices convecting across the deck width synchronize their timing with the torsional period, delivering pressure impulses that reinforce the twist
The bridge's cables resonate with the local wind's gust frequency
Water currents beneath the Narrows synchronize with the deck motion

explanations.a: Larsen's model does not involve a fixed 1 Hz shedding frequency; the synchronization is between vortex convection time and the (much slower) torsional period.
explanations.b: Correct -- vortices form and convect across the deck section, and above a critical wind speed their convection timing locks to the torsional period, so pressure impulses arrive timed to reinforce the ongoing twist, sustaining a limit cycle.
explanations.c: Cable resonance with gust frequency is not part of either the flutter-derivative or discrete-vortex account; both concern aerodynamic forces on the deck section.
explanations.d: Water currents play no role in either technical account; both are about airflow around the deck.

questions.prompt: What criticism has been raised against Larsen's discrete-vortex model specifically?

options.text: That it still relies on the discredited resonance-with-shedding explanation
That the specific vortex behavior it simulates was never actually observed at Tacoma, and that it does not match data well near the actual failure wind speed
That it has never been published in a peer-reviewed source
That it contradicts Farquharson's films entirely

explanations.a: Larsen's model is explicitly a self-excited, vortex-synchronization account, not a resonance-with-shedding account -- that is not the criticism raised against it.
explanations.b: Correct -- other researchers have noted the specific vortex behavior in Larsen's simulations was never observed at Tacoma, and that the model does not reproduce the data well near the actual collapse wind speed.
explanations.c: Larsen's discrete-vortex work was published (including a 2000 account), which is precisely why it could be scrutinized and criticized by other researchers.
explanations.d: The criticism concerns quantitative matching to wind-speed and vortex data, not a wholesale contradiction of Farquharson's torsional-mode footage, which both accounts accept.

questions.prompt: What is the flutter-derivative method, as established by Scanlan and Tomko (1971), used for in the classical-flutter account of Tacoma Narrows?

options.text: Measuring empirical coefficients that describe how a deck section's own motion generates additional aerodynamic force, used to show aerodynamic damping goes negative past a critical wind speed
Calculating the exact date the bridge would fail
Measuring the tension in the suspension cables
Predicting the shedding frequency from the Strouhal number alone

explanations.a: Correct -- flutter derivatives are empirical, motion-dependent aerodynamic coefficients measured for a given deck cross-section; applying them to the Tacoma deck shows aerodynamic damping turning negative past a critical wind speed, supporting the classical-flutter account.
explanations.b: Flutter derivatives characterize aerodynamic force behavior, not a predictive failure date.
explanations.c: Cable tension is a structural quantity unrelated to flutter derivatives, which describe motion-induced aerodynamic forces.
explanations.d: Shedding frequency from the Strouhal number is a separate, simpler calculation (used in the resonance myth's refutation); flutter derivatives are a distinct, more detailed empirical method describing motion-induced forces.

lessons.label: Founding Aeroelasticity: From Handley Page to Theodorsen

sections.heading: A bomber's tail nearly kills the field before it has a name, 1916
sections.body: The first well-documented case of flutter struck a Handley Page O/400 twin-engine bomber in 1916: the tail began violently oscillating in flight, twisting the rear fuselage and moving the elevators asymmetrically, though the aircraft landed. The incident prompted the first targeted investigations into the phenomenon: Lanchester was consulted and suspected a resonance-like structural cause, while Bairstow and Fage carried out a dedicated wind-tunnel and analytical study of the tail's flutter instability at the National Physical Laboratory, publishing their results as an Aeronautical Research Committee report. Neither had a general theory yet -- what they had was a frightening, repeatable structural failure mode with no name and no predictive calculation.

sections.heading: Frazer and Duncan formalize wing flutter, 1928
sections.body: Frazer and Duncan's 1928 monograph on wing flutter took the scattered post-1916 understanding and organized it into a systematic treatment of how bending and torsion in a wing can couple through aerodynamic forces to produce a self-sustaining, growing oscillation -- flutter as a structural-aerodynamic coupling problem, not a one-off curiosity. Their work set the frame that later analytic theory would fill in with an actual predictive calculation.

sections.heading: Theodorsen makes flutter calculable, 1935
sections.body: Theodore Theodorsen's NACA Report No. 496 (1935), 'General Theory of Aerodynamic Instability and the Mechanism of Flutter,' supplied that calculation. Working from thin-airfoil potential-flow theory for an oscillating plate in plunge, pitch, and control-surface deflection, Theodorsen derived the unsteady aerodynamic forces in closed form, introducing the function C(k) -- the ratio of the actual, wake-affected (circulatory) lift to the quasi-steady lift an airfoil would generate if the flow simply followed its instantaneous angle, expressed as a function of reduced frequency k. C(k) splits into real and imaginary parts, C(k) = F(k) + i*G(k), and is built from Hankel functions of the second kind, H0^(2)(k) and H1^(2)(k) -- specifically C(k) = H1^(2)(k) / [H1^(2)(k) + i*H0^(2)(k)] -- and it is what converts flutter from a qualitative danger into a number an engineer can compute and design against.

sections.heading: Collar's triangle names the whole field, 1946
sections.body: Collar's 1946 aeroelastic triangle gave the field its organizing diagram: aerodynamic forces, elastic (structural stiffness) forces, and inertial forces at the three corners, with every aeroelastic phenomenon -- flutter, divergence, buffeting, and more -- classified by which pairs of forces dominate its coupling. It remains the standard teaching frame for aeroelasticity because it names, in one picture, exactly what makes the subject hard: three physical domains that must be solved together, not separately.

lessons.workedExample: An engineer checking a new airfoil section for flutter risk uses Theodorsen's C(k) at the wing's expected reduced frequency k = omega*b/U (where b is half-chord and U is airspeed) to compute the unsteady circulatory lift, then combines that aerodynamic force with the wing's measured bending and torsional stiffness in a coupled equation of motion -- an explicit application of Collar's triangle, since the calculation only closes once aerodynamic, elastic, and inertial terms are all included together. If instead the wing were a bluff bridge-deck shape rather than a thin airfoil, Theodorsen's thin-airfoil C(k) would not apply directly, and the engineer would need Scanlan and Tomko's empirically measured flutter derivatives for that specific cross-section instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing 'how do engineers actually predict flutter?' is checking whether a student can distinguish the historical arc from a single fact. The strong answer traces the line from the 1916 Handley Page tail incident (Bairstow and Fage) through Frazer and Duncan's 1928 systematic treatment to Theodorsen's 1935 closed-form C(k) that made flutter calculable for thin airfoils, and names Collar's 1946 triangle as the field's organizing concept -- then knows the limit of Theodorsen's analytic theory: it assumes a thin airfoil in potential flow, so bluff, non-airfoil shapes like bridge decks need empirically measured flutter derivatives instead, which is exactly why Scanlan and Tomko built that alternative method in 1971.

questions.prompt: Put these aeroelasticity milestones in chronological order.

items.text: Handley Page O/400 tail flutter incident, investigated by Bairstow and Fage
Frazer and Duncan's wing-flutter monograph
Theodorsen's NACA Report 496 with the C(k) function
Collar's aeroelastic triangle

questions.explanation: The Handley Page tail flutter incident and Bairstow and Fage's investigation came in 1916, Frazer and Duncan's systematic wing-flutter monograph followed in 1928, Theodorsen's calculable C(k) theory appeared in 1935, and Collar's organizing aeroelastic triangle came in 1946.

questions.prompt: What does Theodorsen's function C(k) represent?

options.text: The ratio of actual, wake-affected circulatory lift to the quasi-steady lift, as a function of reduced frequency k
The critical flutter speed of any aircraft
The ratio of structural mass to aerodynamic mass
The Strouhal number for an oscillating airfoil

explanations.a: Correct -- C(k) is the ratio of the actual unsteady circulatory lift (affected by the wake) to the quasi-steady lift the airfoil would produce if the flow instantaneously followed its angle, as a function of reduced frequency k.
explanations.b: C(k) is an aerodynamic force function used within a flutter calculation; it is not itself the critical flutter speed, which depends on combining C(k) with the structure's stiffness and inertia.
explanations.c: C(k) is an aerodynamic lift ratio, not a mass ratio; mass properties enter Theodorsen's flutter equations separately.
explanations.d: The Strouhal number relates shedding frequency to body size and flow speed for bluff-body wakes; C(k) instead describes unsteady circulatory lift on an oscillating thin airfoil in attached potential flow.

questions.prompt: What do the three corners of Collar's 1946 aeroelastic triangle represent?

options.text: Lift, drag, and thrust
Aerodynamic forces, elastic (structural) forces, and inertial forces
Bending, torsion, and shear
Subsonic, transonic, and supersonic flow regimes

explanations.a: Lift, drag, and thrust are steady-flight force components, not the three coupled physical domains Collar's triangle organizes.
explanations.b: Correct -- Collar's triangle places aerodynamic, elastic, and inertial forces at its three corners, classifying aeroelastic phenomena by which pairs of these forces dominate the coupling.
explanations.c: Bending, torsion, and shear are structural deformation modes, not the three force domains at the triangle's corners.
explanations.d: Flow-speed regimes are a separate classification unrelated to Collar's force-domain triangle.

questions.prompt: Why can't Theodorsen's 1935 thin-airfoil theory be applied directly to predict flutter in a bluff bridge deck?

options.text: Because Theodorsen's theory assumes attached potential flow around a thin airfoil, an assumption a bluff, separated-flow deck cross-section violates
Because Theodorsen's theory only applies to helicopter rotors
Because bridge decks do not experience aerodynamic forces
Because Theodorsen's theory has been mathematically disproven

explanations.a: Correct -- Theodorsen's closed-form theory relies on thin-airfoil potential-flow assumptions with attached flow and a Kutta condition at the trailing edge, none of which hold for a bluff, separated-flow bridge-deck section; that gap is exactly why Scanlan and Tomko developed empirically measured flutter derivatives for deck shapes instead.
explanations.b: The theory was developed for oscillating airfoils in general (plunge, pitch, and control-surface motion), not specifically for helicopter rotors.
explanations.c: Bridge decks clearly experience significant aerodynamic forces, as the whole Tacoma Narrows case demonstrates; the issue is which theoretical tool correctly captures those forces for a bluff shape.
explanations.d: Theodorsen's theory remains standard and trusted for its intended domain (thin airfoils in attached flow); it has not been disproven, only shown to have a limited domain of validity.

lessons.label: Bumblebees, Robofly and Today's Open Questions

sections.heading: Killing the myth at its source
sections.body: The claim that 'science proves bumblebees can't fly' traces to a specific, real calculation: entomologist Magnan and a colleague, in the 1934 book Le Vol des Insectes, applied a fixed-wing, steady-state aerodynamic calculation -- comparing the bee to a smooth, flat, non-flapping airplane wing -- and found insufficient lift. The calculation was not wrong arithmetic; it was the wrong model. Insects do not glide on fixed wings, they flap, rotate, and interact with their own wake, and none of that unsteady behavior is captured by a steady-state estimate. The myth survives because the failed calculation is memorable and the correction -- that flapping-wing aerodynamics is a fundamentally unsteady problem -- takes real fluid mechanics to state properly.

sections.heading: Weis-Fogh's clap and fling, and Ellington's leading-edge vortex
sections.body: Weis-Fogh's 1973 study of the tiny wasp Encarsia formosa identified 'clap and fling': the wings clap together at the top of the stroke, then peel apart from the trailing edge like an opening book, a mechanism that generates lift beyond what steady aerodynamics predicts and helps explain flight at the wasp's very low Reynolds number (around 20). Ellington and colleagues' 1996 Nature study went further for larger insects, using a mechanical flapping model ('the flapper') scaled to a hawkmoth (Manduca sexta) and smoke visualization to show a stable, strong leading-edge vortex forms and stays attached along the downstroke, growing from wing base to tip before shedding into the tip vortex near 75% of the wing length -- an attached vortex generating substantially more lift than a conventional airfoil could at the same angle of attack.

sections.heading: Robofly decomposes the mechanism, then gets revised
sections.body: Dickinson, Lehmann and Sane's 1999 Science paper used a scaled-up robotic wing ('Robofly') in mineral oil to isolate three interacting mechanisms across a wingbeat: delayed stall (the leading-edge vortex sustains lift through the translational part of the stroke), rotational circulation (extra force generated as the wing rapidly rotates at stroke reversal), and wake capture (the wing recovers energy from the vortex wake left by the previous stroke as it reverses). That three-part decomposition became the field's standard framework -- but not the final word: Birch and Dickinson's subsequent studies (a 2001 Nature paper on spanwise flow and a 2003 follow-up) complicated the original account, showing spanwise flow's role in stabilizing the leading-edge vortex was more nuanced than first proposed and that wake-capture forces were smaller, or explained differently, than the 1999 study suggested.

sections.heading: What is still genuinely open
sections.body: Unsteady vortex flow has real unresolved engineering problems today. Predicting vortex-induced vibration of long, flexible marine risers is one: industry tools such as SHEAR7, VIVANA, and direct CFD simulation routinely disagree with each other and with field data, because a riser spans many diameters with locally varying current, mode competition, and possible traveling-wave response that no single tool fully captures. Turbulence modeling for massively separated bluff-body flow is another live argument -- URANS, large-eddy simulation (LES), and hybrid detached-eddy simulation (DES) trade cost against fidelity differently, and no single approach is trusted across all regimes. And VIV energy harvesting, exemplified by the VIVACE converter concept, remains disputed as a technology: proponents see a untapped, always-available current-energy source, while skeptics see a niche, low-power-density curiosity that has not demonstrated grid-relevant scale.

lessons.workedExample: A student explaining insect flight at a fair says: 'People think science proved bumblebees can't fly -- that comes from a 1934 calculation by Magnan that modeled a bee like a fixed, non-flapping airplane wing. Real insect flight is unsteady: Weis-Fogh showed the wasp Encarsia gets extra lift from clap-and-fling, and Ellington's 1996 hawkmoth study showed a stable leading-edge vortex sticks to the wing through the downstroke. Dickinson's 1999 Robofly then broke the mechanism into delayed stall, rotational circulation, and wake capture -- though Birch and Dickinson's later work revised how big a role wake capture and spanwise flow actually play.' This answer moves from myth, to its real (flawed-model, not flawed-math) source, through three dated named studies, to the field's own later self-correction.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who raises the bumblebee myth is testing whether a student treats it as trivia or as a real teaching moment about model assumptions -- can they say precisely what the 1934 calculation got wrong (steady, fixed-wing model applied to an unsteady, flapping system) rather than just 'the math was wrong somehow'? A judge who pushes into current insect-flight or VIV research is testing whether the student knows the field still argues with itself: Birch and Dickinson revising their own 1999 Robofly account, and open engineering disputes like riser VIV prediction (SHEAR7 versus VIVANA versus CFD) or whether VIV energy harvesting is real technology, show a student that unsteady fluid dynamics is not a closed textbook subject.

questions.prompt: What was actually wrong with the 1934 calculation (Magnan and colleague) behind the 'bumblebees can't fly' myth?

options.text: The arithmetic contained a sign error
It modeled the bee as a fixed, smooth, non-flapping wing using steady-state aerodynamics, which cannot capture unsteady flapping-flight lift mechanisms
It used the wrong value of air density
It measured the wrong species of bee

explanations.a: The calculation's arithmetic was reportedly consistent with its assumptions; the flaw was in the model, not a numeric slip.
explanations.b: Correct -- the 1934 calculation treated the bee like a fixed, smooth airplane wing under steady-state aerodynamics, missing the unsteady, flapping-wing mechanisms (leading-edge vortices, rotational effects, wake interaction) that actually generate the needed lift.
explanations.c: Air density is a minor, non-central input; the fundamental problem was the steady, fixed-wing modeling assumption, not an atmospheric constant.
explanations.d: The myth is about the modeling approach applied generally to bee-like insects, not a species-identification error.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or study to their contribution to understanding insect flight.

right.text: Identified 'clap and fling' lift enhancement in the wasp Encarsia formosa
Showed a stable, attached leading-edge vortex on a mechanical hawkmoth wing model
Used Robofly to decompose insect-wing lift into delayed stall, rotational circulation, and wake capture

questions.explanation: Weis-Fogh's 1973 study identified clap and fling in the wasp Encarsia formosa; Ellington and colleagues' 1996 Nature study visualized a stable leading-edge vortex on a mechanical hawkmoth model; Dickinson, Lehmann and Sane's 1999 Science paper used Robofly to decompose lift generation into delayed stall, rotational circulation, and wake capture.

questions.prompt: How did Birch and Dickinson's later work relate to the original 1999 Robofly study?

options.text: It confirmed every detail of the 1999 study with no changes
It revised how the field understood spanwise flow's role and the size/explanation of wake-capture forces from the 1999 account
It proved insects cannot generate a leading-edge vortex at all
It replaced Robofly with a live insect for all future testing

explanations.a: The later work specifically complicated and revised parts of the original decomposition, rather than simply confirming it unchanged.
explanations.b: Correct -- Birch and Dickinson's follow-up studies revised the understanding of spanwise flow's role in stabilizing the leading-edge vortex and reassessed the size or explanation of wake-capture forces described in the 1999 paper.
explanations.c: Leading-edge vortices remain a well-supported mechanism across this line of research; the later work refined explanations, not disproved the vortex's existence.
explanations.d: Robofly-style mechanical/robotic wing models remained a standard research tool; the later studies did not abandon that approach for live insects only.

questions.prompt: Which of these is described as a genuinely open, unresolved problem in unsteady vortex flow today?

options.text: Whether vortex shedding occurs behind a circular cylinder at all
Predicting vortex-induced vibration of long flexible marine risers, where tools such as SHEAR7, VIVANA, and CFD routinely disagree
Whether Strouhal's aeolian-tone measurements were accurate
Whether insects use flapping wings to fly

explanations.a: Cylinder vortex shedding is extremely well established, dating back over a century of confirmed observation; it is not an open question.
explanations.b: Correct -- long, flexible marine risers present a genuinely unresolved prediction problem, where established industry tools (SHEAR7, VIVANA) and direct CFD simulation routinely give differing answers and disagree with field data.
explanations.c: Strouhal's 1878 measurements are historically settled and foundational; their accuracy is not a live research dispute.
explanations.d: That insects use flapping-wing, unsteady aerodynamics is well established since Weis-Fogh, Ellington, and Dickinson's work; the open questions concern the finer mechanistic details, not the basic fact of flapping flight.

units.label: Flow-Induced Vibration, Lock-In and Flutter

lessons.label: The Fluid-Structure Feedback Loop

sections.heading: A shedding wake and a compliant body close a loop
sections.body: A rigid cylinder in cross-flow sheds an alternating Karman vortex street and feels a fluctuating lift force at the shedding frequency — but nothing moves, so the story ends there. Make the cylinder compliant (mounted on a spring, or flexible along its span like a riser or a cable) and the loop closes: the fluctuating lift excites motion, that motion changes the relative flow the body sees each cycle, and the retimed separation feeds back into when and how strongly the next vortex sheds. This is flow-induced vibration (FIV) in its most general form — a two-way coupling where fluid forces the structure and structural motion forces the fluid, as opposed to a one-way forced-vibration problem where the flow just imposes a load. Whether the loop grows, saturates, or dies out depends on a single quantity: the phase between the fluctuating fluid force and the structure's velocity. Force in phase with velocity does positive work on the structure each cycle — energy flows fluid-to-structure and amplitude grows. Force out of phase with velocity does negative work — the fluid acts like extra damping and any motion decays.

sections.heading: The non-dimensional groups that govern the loop
sections.body: Four numbers decide where a given structure sits in this loop. Reduced velocity U* = U/(f_n D) compares the flow speed to how fast the structure can respond, scaled by diameter D and natural frequency f_n — it is the master knob, since sweeping U* (by changing flow speed or f_n) is what carries a structure into and out of the excitation ranges covered in the rest of this unit. Mass ratio m* = m/(ρD²), the structure's mass per unit length relative to the mass of fluid it displaces, controls how much a given fluid force can accelerate the structure — heavy structures in air (m* often >100) barely notice the fluid; light structures in water (m* often below 1) are dominated by it. Structural damping ratio ζ is the fraction of critical damping from material and mounting alone, before any fluid effect. Multiplying mass and damping together gives the Scruton number, Sc = 4πm*ζ (equivalently 4πmζ/ρD² per unit length), the single mass-damping parameter that appears throughout the VIV literature because it is what actually collapses response amplitude across very different structures.

sections.heading: Added mass: why underwater natural frequency drops
sections.body: A structure vibrating in a dense fluid must also accelerate the fluid around it, and that fluid inertia acts as added mass — for a circular cylinder in an ideal fluid the added mass per unit length is about ρπD²/4, roughly equal to the mass of fluid the cylinder displaces. Added mass does not change stiffness, so it lowers the natural frequency: f_water = f_air / sqrt(1 + m_added/m_structure). For a heavy steel structure in air this correction is negligible; for a light, low-mass-ratio riser or cable in water it can cut the natural frequency by 30-50%, which matters enormously because U* is defined using that same f_n — get the added-mass correction wrong and every downstream lock-in prediction is wrong too.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.5 m diameter marine riser section has an in-air natural frequency of 1.2 Hz and a structural mass of 400 kg/m. Its added mass per unit length is ρπD²/4 = 1025 × π × 0.25 / 4 ≈ 201 kg/m (seawater ρ ≈ 1025 kg/m³). The in-water natural frequency drops to f_water = 1.2 / sqrt(1 + 201/400) ≈ 1.2 / 1.22 ≈ 0.98 Hz — an 18% reduction that shifts the U* value at any given current speed and moves the riser into (or out of) the lock-in band computed in Lesson 2.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what governs whether this thing vibrates or not?' to separate a student who observed an oscillation from one who can predict it. The tell is whether the student reaches for U*, m*, and Sc unprompted, and whether they can explain the sign of the phase between force and velocity as the actual energy-transfer mechanism rather than saying 'resonance' as a catch-all. A student working with anything submerged who forgets the added-mass correction to natural frequency will mis-predict lock-in by a wide margin — noticing that gap is a strong signal of real understanding versus memorized vocabulary.

questions.prompt: In the fluid-structure feedback loop, what determines whether an oscillation grows or decays?

options.text: The absolute magnitude of the fluctuating lift force
The phase between the fluctuating fluid force and the structure's velocity
Whether the flow is laminar or turbulent upstream
The color/roughness of the cylinder surface

explanations.a: A large force with the wrong phase (out of phase with velocity) still removes energy from the structure; magnitude alone doesn't set the sign of energy transfer.
explanations.b: Correct — force in phase with velocity does positive work each cycle (amplitude grows); force out of phase acts as added damping (amplitude decays).
explanations.c: Upstream turbulence affects shedding details but is not the mechanism that sets growth versus decay of the coupled structural response.
explanations.d: Surface finish can shift the boundary layer and shedding slightly but is a second-order effect, not the governing energy-transfer mechanism.

questions.prompt: Reduced velocity U* = U/(f_n D) is best described as:

options.text: A measure of Reynolds number
The flow speed scaled by how fast the structure can respond, given its diameter and natural frequency
The ratio of structural mass to fluid mass
A damping coefficient

explanations.a: Reynolds number is UD/ν (a viscosity-based ratio); U* uses natural frequency and diameter, not viscosity.
explanations.b: Correct — U* nondimensionalizes flow speed against the structure's own dynamic response scale (f_n D), which is why sweeping it carries a structure through different excitation regimes.
explanations.c: That description is the mass ratio m*, not reduced velocity.
explanations.d: Damping is captured by ζ or the Scruton number, not by U*.

questions.prompt: Why does a light structure vibrating in water have a lower natural frequency than the same structure vibrating in air?

options.text: Water reduces the structure's stiffness
Added mass from the fluid the structure must accelerate increases the effective vibrating mass without adding stiffness
Water increases the structure's damping ratio, which raises natural frequency
Buoyancy cancels part of the structure's weight

explanations.a: Added mass is an inertial effect, not a change in the structure's material or geometric stiffness.
explanations.b: Correct — added mass (about ρπD²/4 per unit length for a cylinder) raises effective mass while stiffness is unchanged, and natural frequency scales as 1/sqrt(mass), so f_water drops.
explanations.c: Higher damping shifts a resonance peak's sharpness, not the underlying undamped natural frequency, and is not the mechanism described here.
explanations.d: Buoyancy affects static loading/weight, not the dynamic added-mass term that governs vibration frequency.

questions.prompt: Match each non-dimensional quantity to what it represents.

right.text: Flow speed scaled by natural frequency and diameter
Structural mass relative to the mass of fluid displaced
Combined mass-damping parameter (mass ratio times damping ratio)

questions.explanation: U* = U/(f_n D) nondimensionalizes flow speed against the structure's dynamics; m* = m/(ρD²) compares structural mass to displaced fluid mass; Sc = 4πm*ζ combines both mass ratio and structural damping into the single parameter that best collapses observed response amplitudes.

lessons.label: Lock-In: When the Wake Obeys the Structure

sections.heading: The wake abandons Strouhal and follows the body instead
sections.body: For a stationary cylinder, shedding frequency obeys the Strouhal relation f_s = St·U/D with St ≈ 0.2 across a wide Reynolds range — shedding frequency tracks flow speed linearly and ignores the structure entirely. Once the cylinder is free to move and reduced velocity U* = U/(f_n D) climbs into roughly the 5-8 range, something qualitatively different happens: the wake stops obeying Strouhal and instead synchronizes to the structure's own natural frequency, f_s locks to f_n over a finite band of flow speeds even as U keeps increasing. This is lock-in (or synchronization), the defining feature of vortex-induced vibration (VIV). Inside the lock-in band, the vortex-shedding process is no longer an independent forcing function — the structure's motion is now controlling when vortices detach, which is exactly the closed feedback loop from Lesson 1 operating at its strongest coupling.

sections.heading: Self-limiting amplitude and branch hysteresis
sections.body: Unlike flutter (Lesson 5), VIV does not diverge. As U* rises into lock-in, cross-flow amplitude grows but saturates near A/D ≈ 1 (about one diameter of peak displacement) rather than continuing to climb — because larger amplitude changes the effective angle of attack and the wake geometry enough to shift the phase between force and velocity back toward zero net work, capping further growth. This self-regulation is why VIV is a fatigue problem, not a catastrophic-failure problem: it bounds itself.
