Portugal and colleagues' 2014 study of phase-matched wingbeats in northern bald ibises

questions.explanation: Triantafyllou's MIT group demonstrated reversed-Karman-street thrust directly on oscillating foils and the RoboTuna; Weihs proposed the theoretical model for fish exploiting a school-mate's vortex wake; and Portugal's 2014 ibis study showed birds phase-matching wingbeats to capture upwash from the bird ahead in a V formation.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps connecting an ordinary drag wake to efficient flapping thrust.

items.text: A bluff body's Karman street has a fixed vortex rotation sense producing a mean velocity deficit in the wake (drag)
An oscillating foil reverses that rotation sense, producing a mean velocity surplus (jet-like wake)
By a momentum argument, a jet-like wake means the foil pushed fluid backward on net, producing thrust
That thrust is most efficient only within the narrow Strouhal number band 0.2\u20130.4

questions.explanation: The reasoning starts from the ordinary drag-producing Karman street, shows how an oscillating foil reverses its vortex sign into a jet-like wake, connects that wake structure to thrust via momentum conservation, and finally notes that this thrust is efficient only inside the narrow Strouhal number band animals are observed to use.

lessons.label: Drafting, Slipstreaming and Platooning

sections.heading: How much a wake is actually worth
sections.body: At race speed, the large majority of a cyclist's resistance is aerodynamic drag, so sitting in someone else's wake is not a minor comfort but the dominant lever available for going faster on the same power. For decades, textbook figures for a rider tucked directly behind another suggested drag reductions in roughly the 50\u201370% range, extrapolated from small-group wind-tunnel and CFD studies. Bert Blocken's 2018 study overturned the scale of that estimate for a real peloton: using CFD simulations of two 121-rider pelotons, on extremely fine meshes on the order of billions of cells each, validated against wind-tunnel tests with full-scale rider models, he found that a rider positioned in the mid-rear of a large, tightly packed pack experiences only about 5\u201310% of an isolated rider's drag \u2014 a 90\u201395% reduction, far beyond the previously assumed 50\u201370%. Motor racing exploits the same physics more aggressively: in NASCAR \u2018bump drafting,\u2019 a trailing car tucked bumper-to-bumper into a leader's wake not only cuts its own drag, it partially fills the low-pressure separated region behind the leader, raising the leader's base pressure and cutting the leader's drag too \u2014 a mutual benefit that is why drafting pairs can out-pace a lone car at high-bank superspeedways.

sections.heading: Slipstreaming at highway scale
sections.body: Freight trucking runs the same trade for fuel economy through automated platooning \u2014 trucks following each other with radar/GPS-linked braking at close, computer-controlled following distances. NREL's 2014 track tests of a two-truck platoon found the lead truck saving up to 5.3% and the trailing truck up to 9.7% at the closest following distances tested; the team average of around 6.4% is a separately measured figure blended across the range of following distances tested, not a simple mean of those two peak numbers. A 2016 PATH/Volvo test of a three-truck platoon found 5.2\u20137.8% savings with standard trailers, rising to as much as 14.2% with aerodynamically streamlined trailers \u2014 in every case the trailing vehicle benefiting more than the vehicle at the front, matching the pattern seen in cycling and motorsport drafting. Speed skaters and open-water swimmers exploit weaker versions of the same effect, tucking into a leader's wake in team pursuit or drafting a faster swimmer, though the savings there are harder to isolate from technique and are typically reported qualitatively rather than as a settled percentage.

sections.heading: What drafting costs, and how the savings get measured
sections.body: None of this is free. A vehicle or rider sitting deep in a wake loses the clean airflow it needs for cooling \u2014 a NASCAR car nose-to-tail with another can overheat its engine within a handful of laps \u2014 and inherits a turbulent, unsteady wake rather than smooth air, which buffets the following body and degrades handling stability exactly when the following distance is smallest and the margin to react to a sudden move up front is thinnest. Engineers quantify the raw aerodynamic benefit with a wake traverse: a rake of pitot-static probes swept across the wake downstream of the leading body measures the local velocity-deficit profile, which is integrated to recover the drag directly from momentum loss, then compared against or extended by CFD for configurations \u2014 like a 121-rider peloton \u2014 too large or expensive to build at full scale in a wind tunnel.

lessons.workedExample: If a peloton cruises at 45 km/h, a rider in the mid-rear experiencing only 5\u201310% of an isolated rider's drag is not merely saving \u2018some\u2019 energy \u2014 since aerodynamic power scales with the cube of speed, that drag reduction converts to an equivalent cycling speed roughly 2.2 to 2.7 times lower than the peloton's actual speed, meaning that sheltered rider's legs are doing work comparable to riding alone at only about 16.6\u201320.9 km/h while still moving at 45 km/h with the group. That gap is exactly why a small breakaway group, without a large pack to hide in, has to work so much harder per rider to hold off a peloton where most riders are paying a fraction of the aerodynamic cost \u2014 and why the break's chances depend heavily on how many riders share the workload at the front.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes drafting because \u2018drafting reduces drag\u2019 is true but nearly content-free without a magnitude and a location \u2014 a student who can say where in a pack the benefit is largest, and by roughly how much, has done real homework rather than repeated folklore. The stronger tell is naming the cost side unprompted: lost cooling airflow, buffeting-driven instability, and a shrunken reaction margin, since these are exactly the safety and reliability trade-offs an engineer or team strategist has to weigh against the energy savings, and a project that only reports the benefit without the cost has not modeled the system, only half of it.

questions.prompt: What did Blocken's 2018 CFD and wind-tunnel study of a 121-rider peloton find that overturned earlier assumptions?

options.text: Riders in the mid-rear of a large peloton experience only about 5\u201310% of an isolated rider's drag, far below the previously assumed 50\u201370%
Drafting provides no measurable drag benefit in a peloton larger than about ten riders
Riders at the very front of a peloton experience the least drag of anyone in the group
Peloton drag reduction depends only on rider height, not on position within the pack

explanations.a: Correct — the study found the mid-rear position dropping to 5\u201310% of isolated-rider drag, a much larger reduction (90\u201395%) than the 50\u201370% figure earlier small-group studies had suggested.
explanations.b: The finding was the opposite: the benefit is large and grows with pack size and position, not absent in a large peloton.
explanations.c: Riders at the front are the most exposed and generally experience the highest drag in the group, not the lowest.
explanations.d: Position within the pack, not rider height, was the key variable the study quantified.

questions.prompt: In NASCAR bump drafting, why does the leading car also gain a benefit from a car drafting closely behind it?

options.text: The trailing car pushes the leader physically forward through direct contact at all times
The trailing car partially fills the leader's low-pressure separated wake, raising the leader's base pressure and cutting the leader's own drag
The trailing car blocks crosswinds that would otherwise slow the leader
There is no benefit to the leader; only the trailing car gains

explanations.a: Bump drafting can include brief contact, but the aerodynamic benefit to the leader comes from wake filling, not sustained pushing.
explanations.b: Correct — the trailing car sits in and partially fills the low-pressure region behind the leader, raising the base pressure there and reducing the pressure-drag component the leader experiences.
explanations.c: Crosswind blocking is not the mechanism behind the leader's benefit in a straight-line drafting pair.
explanations.d: The mutual benefit to both cars is exactly what makes drafting pairs a competitive tactic rather than a one-sided one.

questions.prompt: In NREL's 2014 two-truck platooning tests, roughly what fuel savings did the lead and trailing trucks each achieve?

options.text: Lead truck up to about 5.3%, trailing truck up to about 9.7%
Lead truck up to about 30%, trailing truck up to about 40%
Both trucks saved exactly the same amount, about 6.4% each
Only the trailing truck saved fuel; the lead truck saved none

explanations.a: Correct — NREL's 2014 tests found the lead truck saving up to 5.3% and the trailing truck up to 9.7%, for a team average around 6.4%.
explanations.b: These figures are far too high for the NREL 2014 test results, which were in the single digits of percent.
explanations.c: The two trucks did not save equal amounts; the trailing truck consistently saved more than the lead truck.
explanations.d: The lead truck did save fuel, up to about 5.3%, even though the trailing truck saved more.

questions.prompt: Match each cost of drafting or wake-riding to its description.

right.text: Reduced clean airflow over the radiator or brakes risks overheating
The turbulent, unsteady wake shakes the following vehicle or rider and degrades handling stability
Close following distance leaves less time to react if the leader suddenly moves or brakes

questions.explanation: Wake-riding trades aerodynamic savings for three real costs: lost cooling airflow risking overheating, buffeting from the leader's turbulent wake that degrades handling, and a shrunken reaction margin from following at close distance.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a wake-traverse measurement used to quantify a drafting benefit.

items.text: Sweep a rake of pitot-static probes across the wake downstream of the leading body
Record the local velocity-deficit profile across the wake
Integrate the velocity-deficit profile to recover the drag from the momentum loss
Compare against or extend the result with CFD for configurations too large to test at full scale in a wind tunnel

questions.explanation: A wake traverse starts by placing pitot-static probes across the downstream wake, records the velocity-deficit profile those probes measure, integrates that profile to compute drag directly from the momentum deficit, and is then compared with or extended by CFD when the real configuration, like a large peloton, is impractical to test at full scale.

lessons.label: Living with Vortex Shedding in Engineering

sections.heading: Breaking the correlation before it becomes resonance
sections.body: Vortex shedding only becomes dangerous when it is coherent along the whole span of a structure and its frequency locks onto a structural natural frequency, building large correlated forces cycle after cycle. Most industrial mitigation works by breaking that spanwise coherence rather than eliminating shedding entirely. Tall chimneys and industrial stacks are commonly wrapped in helical strakes \u2014 fins that spiral around the top section \u2014 that force vortices to shed at different phases at different heights, so the net cross-wind force never organizes into one strong resonant push. Offshore, long steel risers carrying oil and gas from seabed wells to a platform face the same problem from ocean currents; operators fit fairings (streamlined shrouds that let the riser weathervane with the flow) or similar strakes to suppress vortex-induced vibration, and because suppression is never perfect, riser fatigue life is explicitly budgeted against the residual VIV stress cycles using industry design guidance such as DNV's riser VIV recommended practice, treating the vibration as a cost to be counted rather than a problem assumed away.

sections.heading: When it wasn't suppressed enough
sections.body: Failures cluster where flow-induced vibration was underestimated. Heat-exchanger and steam-generator tube bundles, where cross-flow past dense rows of tubes can trigger both acoustic resonance and a distinct instability called fluidelastic instability, are a classic case in Blevins's reference text on flow-induced vibration; the San Onofre nuclear plant's replacement steam generators suffered excessive tube wear within roughly a year of startup in 2012, traced to fluidelastic instability from steam velocities higher than the original design assumed, which caused a small tube leak and contributed to the plant's permanent shutdown in 2013. Overhead power lines face two separate flow-induced problems: aeolian vibration, a high-frequency, small-amplitude vortex-shedding response damped out with tuned Stockbridge dampers hung along the span, and galloping, a much larger, low-frequency instability that develops when ice buildup gives the conductor an asymmetric cross-section, governed by the stability criterion Den Hartog published in 1932 after studying sleet-coated line vibration. Cantilevered highway sign and mast structures have suffered fatigue cracking at their base welds from wind-induced vortex shedding, and underwater cables and mooring lines exhibit the marine equivalent, called strumming, both addressed with the same family of fairings and strakes used offshore.

sections.heading: The contrarian move: harvesting the vibration instead of fighting it
sections.body: One line of engineering flips the goal entirely. The VIVACE converter, developed by Bernitsas at the University of Michigan, is deliberately tuned to maximize rather than suppress vortex-induced vibration, adding just enough mechanical damping to extract energy while widening the range of current speeds over which synchronized shedding (lock-in) occurs, so it can harvest power from currents as slow as roughly a quarter meter per second \u2014 speeds too weak for a conventional turbine. Reported output is modest, on the order of tens of watts per cubic meter of water in a few-knot current, and that honest limitation is the center of the debate: proponents argue it opens a niche \u2014 remote sensors, slow rivers, tidal fringes \u2014 that turbines cannot reach, while critics note its power density remains far below wind or tidal turbines, so it is unlikely to scale to grid-relevant power.

lessons.workedExample: San Onofre's two units received replacement steam generators in 2010\u20132011 with a redesigned tube bundle. Within about a year of restart, inspections found unusually rapid wear on thousands of tubes, concentrated where tubes rubbed against their supports and against each other. The cause traced back to fluidelastic instability: the redesign had increased steam velocity through the tube bundle and reduced tube-to-tube support compared to the original generators, pushing the bundle past the critical velocity at which cross-flow forces couple with tube motion and amplify it rather than merely buffeting it. One tube wore through in January 2012, releasing a small amount of radioactive steam; the plant never restarted and was permanently retired in 2013 \u2014 a case where an engineering change that looked minor on paper (velocity and support spacing) crossed a flow-induced-vibration threshold with major consequences.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes vortex-shedding mitigation because \u2018add a damper\u2019 is too generic an answer to show real understanding \u2014 a strong student names the specific fix matched to the specific failure mode: helical strakes or fairings to break spanwise coherence on a stack or riser, Stockbridge dampers for aeolian vibration but a different fix (de-icing, spacers, or a Den Hartog-informed cross-section change) for galloping, since the two power-line problems are different instabilities with different remedies. Citing a real consequence like San Onofre, where a bundle redesign crossed a fluidelastic-instability threshold, shows the student understands this is a fatigue-life and safety budget, not a one-time engineering box to check.

questions.prompt: Why do helical strakes on a chimney or industrial stack suppress vortex-shedding-induced vibration?

options.text: They eliminate vortex shedding entirely along the whole stack
They break the spanwise coherence of shedding, so vortices form at different phases at different heights and the cross-wind force never organizes into one strong resonant push
They increase the natural frequency of the stack so high that wind can never excite it
They add mass to the stack, lowering its natural frequency below any wind speed

explanations.a: Strakes do not stop vortex shedding from occurring; they disrupt how coherently it organizes along the span.
explanations.b: Correct — by forcing vortices to shed out of phase at different heights, strakes prevent the correlated, resonance-driving force that a smooth stack's fully coherent shedding would produce.
explanations.c: Strakes work by disrupting shedding coherence, not by altering the stack's structural natural frequency.
explanations.d: Strakes are aerodynamic fins, not significant added mass, and their function is aerodynamic disruption, not mass tuning.

questions.prompt: What caused the excessive tube wear in San Onofre's replacement steam generators in 2012?

options.text: Corrosion from seawater contamination unrelated to flow
Fluidelastic instability from steam velocities higher than the original design assumed, combined with reduced tube support
A software error in the reactor control system
Ordinary thermal expansion cycling with no flow-vibration component

explanations.a: The documented cause was flow-induced vibration, not corrosion from contamination.
explanations.b: Correct — the redesigned tube bundle ran at higher steam velocity with less tube-to-tube support than the original generators, crossing the critical velocity for fluidelastic instability and driving rapid tube-to-tube and tube-to-support wear.
explanations.c: The failure was a mechanical flow-induced vibration issue in the steam generator tube bundle, not a control-system software fault.
explanations.d: Thermal cycling alone does not explain the rapid, localized wear pattern; the mechanism identified was fluidelastic instability from the flow.

questions.prompt: How does galloping on an ice-coated power line differ from ordinary aeolian vibration on the same line?

options.text: Galloping is a high-frequency, tiny-amplitude vortex-shedding response; aeolian vibration is a low-frequency, huge-amplitude instability

Galloping is a low-frequency, large-amplitude instability driven by an asymmetric iced cross-section, governed by the Den Hartog criterion; aeolian vibration is a higher-frequency, small-amplitude vortex-shedding response
They are the same phenomenon with two different names
Galloping only occurs underwater on marine cables, never on overhead power lines

explanations.a: This reverses the actual characteristics of the two phenomena.
explanations.b: Correct — galloping is the large, low-frequency instability from an ice-asymmetric cross-section, analyzed with the Den Hartog stability criterion, while aeolian vibration is the smaller, higher-frequency response to ordinary vortex shedding.
explanations.c: They are distinct instabilities with different driving mechanisms, frequencies, and amplitudes, requiring different mitigations.
explanations.d: Galloping is specifically an overhead power-line phenomenon tied to ice buildup; the marine analogue described in this lesson is called strumming, not galloping.

questions.prompt: Match each flow-induced vibration problem to its typical mitigation.

right.text: Helical strakes wrapped around the structure to break spanwise shedding coherence
Fairings or strakes, with residual vibration budgeted into fatigue-life design guidance
Tuned Stockbridge dampers hung along the line

questions.explanation: Stacks use helical strakes to disrupt coherent shedding, offshore risers use fairings or strakes with the leftover vibration explicitly budgeted into fatigue-life design, and power-line aeolian vibration is damped with tuned Stockbridge dampers rather than strakes or fairings.

questions.prompt: What is the honest limitation critics raise against VIV/galloping energy harvesters like the VIVACE converter?

options.text: They cannot operate in any flowing water at all
Their power density is far below wind or tidal turbines, making grid-scale power unlikely even though they can harvest very slow currents turbines cannot
They require suppressing vortex shedding entirely to work, contradicting their own design principle
They only function in salt water, never fresh water

explanations.a: VIVACE-type devices are specifically designed to operate in flowing water, including very slow currents.
explanations.b: Correct — the debate centers on power density: these devices can tap currents too slow for turbines, but their output per unit volume remains far below wind or tidal turbines, limiting them to niche rather than grid-scale roles.
explanations.c: The opposite is true; VIVACE is designed to maximize and broaden vortex-induced vibration, not suppress it, to extract energy from it.
explanations.d: Nothing about the vortex-induced-vibration energy-harvesting principle restricts it to salt water specifically.

lessons.label: Designing Your Own Unsteady-Flow Investigation

sections.heading: Two buildable measurements
sections.body: The whole unit collapses into a bench-scale project once you accept that vortex shedding is periodic and therefore has a frequency you can record. Mount a bluff body \u2014 a rod, a dowel, a small plate \u2014 in a steady airflow from a fan, and pick up the shedding with a microphone (the shed vortices generate an audible \u2018Aeolian tone\u2019 at the shedding frequency), a hot-wire anemometer sensing the periodic velocity fluctuation in the wake, or an accelerometer if the body is mounted so it can vibrate slightly. Run the recorded signal through an FFT to find the dominant frequency peak, measure the body's diameter D and the flow speed U, and compute the Strouhal number St = fD/U for several body shapes and speeds. A second, complementary experiment mounts the same rod on a spring so it can move transversely, then sweeps flow speed while recording vibration amplitude: over most speeds the amplitude stays small, but across a narrow band where the shedding frequency approaches the mount's natural frequency, the amplitude jumps sharply \u2014 the lock-in band \u2014 and mapping vibration amplitude against flow speed traces that band directly.

sections.heading: Testing a fix
sections.body: A third project tests suppression rather than just measurement: attach a splitter plate extending downstream from the body's trailing edge, or a helical strake wound around it, and repeat the FFT measurement. Anatol Roshko's studies of cylinder wakes in the 1950s established that a splitter plate placed in the near wake disrupts the interaction between the two shear layers that must communicate across the wake to organize alternating vortex shedding, weakening or eliminating the periodic tone; a successful suppression test should show the clean FFT peak from the bare cylinder become broad and low, or largely disappear, once the plate or strake is added.

sections.heading: Making the numbers defensible
sections.body: Two details separate a convincing result from a shaky one. First, hold everything except the tested variable constant \u2014 same body, same mounting, same tunnel or fan blockage \u2014 when comparing shapes or suppression devices, and report the Reynolds number Re = UD/\u03bd for every run, since both the Strouhal number and the whole character of the wake depend on it. Second, respect the frequency resolution set by how long you record: an FFT of a signal recorded for duration T can only resolve frequencies to within \u0394f = 1/T, so a two-second recording only resolves frequency to 0.5 Hz, and a shorter clip with too few shedding cycles produces a smeared, unreliable peak rather than a sharp one \u2014 the fix is a longer record, not a fancier algorithm.

lessons.workedExample: A student mounts a D = 1 cm rod in front of a box fan producing U \u2248 3 m/s, giving Re = UD/\u03bd \u2248 (3)(0.01)/(1.5\u00d710\u207b\u2075) \u2248 2000 \u2014 solidly inside the subcritical regime where the Strouhal number for a circular cylinder holds close to St \u2248 0.2. That predicts a shedding frequency f = StU/D = (0.2)(3)/(0.01) = 60 Hz. Recording a 2-second accelerometer clip taped to the rod's mount gives a frequency resolution of \u0394f = 1/T = 0.5 Hz, more than sharp enough to confirm or refute the 60 Hz prediction against a clean FFT peak. Repeating the same setup with a splitter plate added behind the rod and watching that peak flatten out demonstrates suppression quantitatively rather than by eye.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about vortex shedding specifically because two questions separate a rehearsed demo from real understanding, and both come up almost every time. \u2018Why isn't this just resonance?\u2019 tests whether the student knows that ordinary vortex shedding on a rigid body is a forced periodic process whose frequency tracks StU/D continuously with speed, unrelated to any structural natural frequency, and that true resonance only appears in the narrow lock-in band on a flexible mount. \u2018What Reynolds number are you at, and does it transfer to full scale?\u2019 tests whether the student can defend a bench-scale result rather than just report it \u2014 the honest answer states the tested Re, notes that St \u2248 0.2 holds fairly flat across the broad subcritical range, and flags that this plateau breaks down near the critical Reynolds number where boundary-layer transition reshapes the wake, so a low-Re bench result does not automatically transfer to a full-scale structure operating in that different regime.

questions.prompt: Why must a student report the Reynolds number for every vortex-shedding measurement, not just the shedding frequency and speed?

options.text: Reynolds number is only a formality with no bearing on the result
Both the Strouhal number and the overall character of the wake depend on Reynolds number, so results are not comparable or transferable without it
Reynolds number replaces the need to measure flow speed at all
Reynolds number only matters for liquids, never for air

explanations.a: Reynolds number directly governs the shedding regime and the Strouhal number's value, so it is far from a formality.
explanations.b: Correct — since St and the wake regime both depend on Re, two measurements at different Reynolds numbers are not directly comparable, and reporting Re is what lets a result be judged transferable or not.
explanations.c: Re is computed from flow speed, not a substitute for measuring it; both quantities are needed.
explanations.d: Reynolds number applies to any fluid, including air; the worked example in this lesson computes it for an airflow.

questions.prompt: A student records a shedding signal for 2 seconds. What frequency resolution does that give their FFT, and why does it matter?

options.text: \u0394f = 1/T = 0.5 Hz; too short a recording gives coarse bins and a smeared, unreliable frequency peak
\u0394f = 2 Hz; longer recordings always make the resolution worse
Frequency resolution does not depend on recording length at all
\u0394f = T = 2 Hz; the units of \u0394f are seconds
Frequency resolution only matters for hot-wire measurements, not for microphones

explanations.a: Correct — the FFT frequency resolution is \u0394f = 1/T, so a 2-second recording resolves frequency only to 0.5 Hz, and a too-short record with too few shedding cycles produces a smeared, unreliable peak rather than a sharp one.
explanations.b: This inverts the relationship; longer recordings improve (shrink) the frequency resolution, they do not worsen it.
explanations.c: Frequency resolution is set directly by recording duration through \u0394f = 1/T.
explanations.d: This mixes up the formula; \u0394f = 1/T, not T, and the units come out in Hz, not seconds.
explanations.e: The \u0394f = 1/T resolution limit applies to any FFT of a time-domain signal, regardless of which sensor produced it.

questions.prompt: A judge asks, 'why isn't this just resonance?' What is the correct distinction to draw for ordinary vortex shedding on a rigid, stationary bluff body?

options.text: It is resonance, because any periodic force is by definition resonance

Shedding on a rigid body is a forced periodic process whose frequency tracks StU/D continuously with flow speed, unrelated to any structural natural frequency; true resonance only appears in the narrow lock-in band on a flexible mount
Vortex shedding and resonance are unrelated phenomena that never interact under any conditions
Resonance only refers to sound, so it cannot apply to vortex shedding at all

explanations.a: A periodic force is not automatically resonance; resonance specifically requires the forcing frequency to coincide with a structural natural frequency.
explanations.b: Correct — on a rigid body, the shedding frequency simply follows f = StU/D as speed changes, with no dependence on a structural natural frequency, while true resonance-like behavior (lock-in) requires a flexible mount and only occurs in a narrow speed band.
explanations.c: The two phenomena do interact, specifically in the lock-in band on a flexible or elastically mounted structure, which this lesson's second experiment is designed to map.
explanations.d: Resonance is a general mechanical and structural concept, not limited to acoustics; it applies directly to flow-induced vibration of structures.

questions.prompt: Match each rehearsed judge question to the correct core of the answer.

left.text: \u2018What Reynolds number are you at, and does it transfer to full scale?\u2019

right.text: State the tested Re; note St \u2248 0.2 holds across the broad subcritical range but the plateau breaks down near the critical Reynolds number where the wake changes character
Explain that rigid-body shedding frequency tracks StU/D continuously with speed, and true resonance-like lock-in only appears in a narrow band on a flexible mount

questions.explanation: The resonance question is answered by distinguishing continuously speed-dependent shedding from the narrow lock-in band where shedding actually synchronizes with a structural natural frequency; the Reynolds-number question is answered by stating the bench-scale Re and being honest about where the St \u2248 0.2 subcritical plateau does and does not hold when scaling up.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the bench-scale Strouhal-number measurement described in this lesson.

items.text: Select the bluff body and measure its diameter D
Set and measure the flow speed U
Record a microphone, hot-wire, or accelerometer signal for a sufficiently long duration T
Run an FFT on the recorded signal to find the shedding frequency peak f
Compute Re = UD/\u03bd and St = fD/U and compare against the expected subcritical value

questions.explanation: The measurement proceeds from fixing the body's diameter and flow speed, through recording a long-enough signal to get adequate frequency resolution, extracting the shedding frequency by FFT, and finally computing Reynolds and Strouhal numbers to compare against the expected subcritical result.

units.label: Hydrostatics, Buoyancy & Floating Stability

lessons.label: Pressure in a Liquid at Rest

sections.heading: The hydrostatic law
sections.body: In a fluid at rest, pressure builds with depth because each layer must support the weight of everything above it. A force balance on a thin horizontal slab gives p = p0 + rho*g*h, where p0 is the pressure at the free surface, rho is fluid density, and h is depth below that surface. The relationship is linear in h and independent of the container's cross-section or shape. That last point is the hydrostatic paradox, sometimes called Pascal's vase problem after experiments popularized in the 1600s: a wide-mouthed flask, a narrow tube, and an inverted cone connected at the same base all show identical pressure, and therefore identical force per unit area, at any given depth, even though the total weight of liquid in each vessel is wildly different. Pressure depends only on depth and density, never on the volume or weight of fluid stacked above a point.

sections.heading: Pascal's principle and the hydraulic press
sections.body: Blaise Pascal formalized the complementary idea around 1653: a pressure change applied anywhere to a confined, incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point in the fluid and to the walls of its container. This is what makes a hydraulic press or a car's braking system work — pushing a small piston of area A1 with force F1 raises pressure by F1/A1 everywhere in the fluid, so a second piston of area A2 feels the same pressure and delivers force F2 = F1*(A2/A1). A small input force on a small piston produces a large output force on a large piston, at the cost of the large piston moving a proportionally smaller distance, since volume displaced is conserved.

sections.heading: Gauge, absolute, and reading a manometer
sections.body: Pressure gauges read relative to local atmospheric pressure (gauge pressure); absolute pressure adds the roughly 101,325 Pa of atmosphere on top. A manometer converts an unknown pressure into a column-height reading using the same hydrostatic law solved backward: h = Delta p/(rho*g). Because mercury is dense (rho = 13,600 kg/m3), a mercury manometer needs only a short column to register large pressures — standard atmospheric pressure balances 760 mm of mercury. The same pressure would need a column of plain water roughly 10.3 m tall (rho = 1000 kg/m3), since water is about 13.6 times less dense. That factor of 13.6 is why barometers and blood-pressure cuffs historically used mercury: a benchtop-sized instrument can register a full atmosphere, whereas a water manometer for the same range would have to run through the ceiling.

lessons.workedExample: A closed water tank sits with its surface exposed to atmosphere (p0 = 101,325 Pa). A pressure gauge is mounted on the tank wall 4 m below the surface. Absolute pressure there is p = 101,325 + (1000)(9.81)(4) = 101,325 + 39,240 = 140,565 Pa, so the gauge itself (which subtracts atmospheric) reads 39,240 Pa, or about 39.2 kPa gauge. Converted to an equivalent mercury-column reading, h = 39,240/(13,600 x 9.81) = 0.294 m, about 294 mm Hg — a fraction of the roughly 760 mm Hg that a full atmosphere would register, confirming the gauge is reading a modest few-meter head, not a vacuum or an over-pressurized line.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about hydrostatic pressure is testing whether a student conflates weight of fluid with pressure at a point — the hydrostatic-paradox trap. A strong answer states plainly that p = p0 + rho*g*h depends only on depth and density, then explains why a manometer works by inverting that same equation, and can convert between fluid columns (why mercury needs only 760 mm to do what water needs 10.3 m to do). A student who says a wider tank exerts more pressure at the bottom because it holds more water has not understood the mechanism; one who can derive the manometer reading from first principles has.

questions.prompt: Two containers, one a narrow tube and one a wide vase, are filled with water to the same height and connected at their bases. How do the pressures at the bottom compare?

options.text: The wide vase has higher pressure because it holds more water
The narrow tube has higher pressure because the water is more concentrated
The pressures are equal, since pressure depends only on depth and density, not container shape
The pressures cannot be compared without knowing each container's volume

explanations.a: This is the hydrostatic-paradox trap: total weight of fluid is irrelevant to pressure at a given depth.
explanations.b: There is no sense in which water is 'concentrated' by a narrow tube; density is unchanged.
explanations.c: Correct — p = p0 + rho*g*h depends only on depth h and density rho, so equal heights of the same fluid give equal bottom pressure regardless of shape.
explanations.d: Volume is exactly the variable that does NOT matter here; depth and density are sufficient.

questions.prompt: Why can a mercury barometer be much shorter than a water barometer measuring the same atmospheric pressure?

options.text: Mercury is roughly 13.6 times denser than water, so it needs a proportionally shorter column to balance the same pressure
Mercury is compressible, so it packs more pressure into less height
Mercury boils at a lower temperature, shrinking the column
Atmospheric pressure is lower when measured with mercury

explanations.a: Correct — since h = Delta p/(rho*g), a denser fluid needs less height for the same pressure; mercury's density of 13,600 kg/m3 versus water's 1000 kg/m3 is why 760 mm Hg equals about 10.3 m of water.
explanations.b: Mercury, like nearly all liquids, is treated as incompressible in this context; compressibility is not the reason.
explanations.c: Boiling point is irrelevant to the static column-height calculation.
explanations.d: Atmospheric pressure is a physical quantity independent of the measuring fluid; only the required column height changes.

questions.prompt: In a hydraulic press, a 0.02 m2 piston is pushed with 200 N of force. What force can a connected 0.5 m2 output piston deliver?

options.text: 200 N, since force is conserved
8 N, from F2 = F1*(A1/A2)
It cannot be determined without knowing the fluid's density

explanations.a: Force is not conserved in a hydraulic press; pressure is transmitted equally, but force scales with piston area.
explanations.b: Correct — pressure equality gives F1/A1 = F2/A2, so F2 = 200*(0.5/0.02) = 5,000 N.
explanations.c: This inverts the area ratio; the larger output piston produces a larger, not smaller, force.
explanations.d: Pascal's principle only requires the fluid be confined and incompressible; density cancels out of the force ratio.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to convert a manometer's mercury-column reading of Delta h into the gauge pressure it represents.

items.text: Read the height difference Delta h between the two mercury columns
Look up or recall mercury's density, rho = 13,600 kg/m3
Compute Delta p = rho * g * Delta h
Report Delta p as the gauge pressure at the measurement point

questions.explanation: The manometer equation h = Delta p/(rho*g) is solved for pressure by first reading the height difference, then supplying the fluid's density, then multiplying by rho*g to get Delta p, which is the gauge pressure (relative to atmosphere).

lessons.label: Forces on Submerged Surfaces

sections.heading: Total force: integrate the pressure prism
sections.body: Because hydrostatic pressure grows linearly with depth (p = rho*g*h), the force on a submerged plane surface is not simply pressure-at-some-point times area — it is the integral of a triangular (or trapezoidal) pressure distribution over that area, a shape engineers call the pressure prism. For a flat panel of area A whose centroid sits at depth h_c below the free surface, that integral collapses to a clean result: the resultant force is F = rho*g*h_c*A. In words, the total force equals the pressure at the centroid multiplied by the area — the same as if the pressure were uniform at the centroid's value — even though the real distribution is triangular, heaviest at the bottom edge and lightest at the top.

sections.heading: Center of pressure sits below the centroid
sections.body: The resultant force's line of action is not through the centroid, because the pressure prism is unevenly weighted toward the deeper (higher-pressure) part of the surface. The center of pressure lies a distance e = I_xx/(h_c*A) below the centroid, where I_xx is the second moment of area of the shape about its own centroidal axis, parallel to the free surface. For a rectangular gate of height d, I_xx = (width*d^3)/12, so a tall, deep gate has its pressure center noticeably lower than its geometric middle, while a small, shallow panel has the two points nearly coincide because e shrinks as h_c grows. This offset is exactly what makes submerged gates and dam faces want to rotate about their base rather than their middle.

sections.heading: Why engineers care: dams, gates, and overturning moment
sections.body: Dam walls, canal lock gates, sluice gates, and even a large aquarium's acrylic panel are all sized using this pair of results. The magnitude F = rho*g*h_c*A tells a designer the total load the structure's hinges, bolts, or foundation must resist; the center-of-pressure depth tells them where that load effectively acts, which sets the overturning moment about the base — the tendency of the wall to rotate outward or the gate to swing open. A dam that only checked total force without locating the center of pressure could under-design the base anchoring, since the moment arm (not just the force) determines whether the structure tips. This is why hydraulic engineers historically treated deep, wide gates with much thicker bases than their shallow counterparts, even at equal panel area.

lessons.workedExample: A rectangular sluice gate, 3 m wide by 2 m tall, is set vertically with its top edge at the water surface. Its centroid is at h_c = 1 m depth, and A = 6 m2, so F = 1000*9.81*1*6 = 58,860 N, about 58.9 kN. The second moment about the centroidal axis is I_xx = (3*2^3)/12 = 2 m4, giving an offset e = I_xx/(h_c*A) = 2/(1*6) = 0.333 m below the centroid. Since the centroid is 1 m deep, the center of pressure sits at 1.333 m depth — exactly 2/3 of the way down the 2 m gate. That is 0.333 m below the panel's geometric middle and still 0.667 m above the bottom hinge, so the resultant acts below center without acting at the base. The skew matters because the triangular pressure distribution puts about 89 percent of the total force on the lower two-thirds of the panel, so the hinge and its supporting wall must be sized for a load concentrated near the bottom rather than one spread evenly over the gate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept wants to see whether a student can distinguish 'how much force' from 'where it acts.' Many students correctly compute F = rho*g*h_c*A and stop, missing that the center of pressure below the centroid is what actually determines the overturning moment on a dam or gate. A strong answer explains why the offset exists (the pressure distribution is triangular, weighted toward the bottom) and can compute e = I_xx/(h_c*A) for a simple shape, connecting it to a real design consequence like base anchoring or hinge placement.

questions.prompt: Why is the resultant hydrostatic force on a submerged vertical panel equal to rho*g*h_c*A, using the centroid depth, rather than the depth of the panel's bottom edge?

options.text: Because pressure is uniform across the panel, equal to the value at the centroid
Because integrating the linearly increasing pressure over the area is mathematically equivalent to using the average pressure, which occurs at the centroid depth
Because the bottom edge experiences zero pressure
Because rho*g*h_c*A is only an approximation and the true force requires numerical integration

explanations.a: Pressure is not uniform — it increases linearly with depth; the centroid formula works despite this, not because of it.
explanations.b: Correct — for a linear pressure distribution, the integral over the area equals the average pressure times area, and the average of a linear function over a shape occurs at its centroid.
explanations.c: The bottom edge has the highest pressure on the panel, not zero.
explanations.d: F = rho*g*h_c*A is an exact closed-form result for a flat surface under hydrostatic pressure, not an approximation.

questions.prompt: A tall, deep gate and a small, shallow panel have the same area, but the centroid depth is much larger for the tall gate. What happens to the offset e between the centroid and the center of pressure as h_c increases (for fixed I_xx and A)?

options.text: e increases, since deeper water pushes the pressure center further down
e decreases, since e = I_xx/(h_c*A) and h_c is in the denominator
e stays constant regardless of depth
e becomes negative, moving the center of pressure above the centroid

explanations.a: This has the dependence backward — e shrinks, not grows, as h_c increases.
explanations.b: Correct — e = I_xx/(h_c*A) has h_c in the denominator, so as a surface is submerged deeper (larger h_c, same shape and area), the pressure distribution across it becomes relatively more uniform and the center of pressure moves closer to the centroid.
explanations.c: e explicitly depends on h_c through the formula; it is not constant.
explanations.d: For a real submerged surface with p0 > 0 at the surface, e is always non-negative — the center of pressure never moves above the centroid.

questions.prompt: A dam's structural engineer computes the total hydrostatic force on a spillway gate correctly but does not locate the center of pressure. What design risk does this create?

options.text: None — knowing the total force is sufficient to size the gate's material thickness
The gate's weight will be miscalculated
The overturning moment about the hinge or base will be unknown, risking under-designed anchoring even though the total force is correct
The water will leak around the gate

explanations.a: Material thickness for bending and the anchoring for rotation both depend on where the force acts, not just its magnitude.
explanations.b: The center of pressure concerns the water's force on the gate, not the gate's own weight.
explanations.c: Correct — the overturning moment is force multiplied by its distance from the pivot (the center of pressure's depth relative to the hinge), so knowing only total force leaves the moment, and therefore the required anchoring strength, undetermined.
explanations.d: Leakage is a sealing/fit issue, unrelated to force distribution analysis.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its role in analyzing force on a submerged plane surface.

right.text: Determines the total resultant hydrostatic force magnitude
Depth of the surface's geometric center below the free surface
Governs how far below the centroid the true force line of action falls
Property of the panel's shape that appears in the center-of-pressure offset

questions.explanation: h_c locates the centroid's depth and feeds directly into F = rho*g*h_c*A, the total force magnitude; I_xx is a shape property (second moment of area about the centroidal axis) that, divided by h_c*A, gives the offset e describing how far below the centroid the center of pressure actually acts.

lessons.label: Archimedes' Principle and Displacement

sections.heading: Buoyancy as a net pressure effect
sections.body: Buoyant force is not a separate mysterious force — it falls straight out of the hydrostatic pressure law applied over a body's whole submerged surface. Pressure pushes inward everywhere, but because pressure increases with depth, the upward push on a body's bottom faces (deeper, higher pressure) exceeds the downward push on its top faces (shallower, lower pressure). Integrating that pressure difference over the entire surface, the horizontal components cancel by symmetry and the vertical components sum to a single net upward force equal to rho*g*V_disp, where V_disp is the volume of fluid the body displaces. This is Archimedes' principle, traditionally dated to the 3rd century BCE and famously tied to the story of Archimedes testing whether a goldsmith had adulterated a crown with silver — but the mechanism is pure pressure calculus, not a special buoyancy law.

sections.heading: Apparent weight and density by displacement
sections.body: A submerged or floating object's apparent weight is its true weight minus the buoyant force: W_apparent = W - rho*g*V_disp. This gives a practical density-measurement technique still used in labs: weigh a sample in air (W_air), then weigh it fully submerged in water (W_water). The difference, W_air - W_water, equals the buoyant force rho_water*g*V, which gives the sample's volume directly, and combined with W_air = rho_sample*g*V, its density follows as rho_sample = rho_water*W_air/(W_air - W_water). This hydrostatic-weighing method is the modern descendant of the crown problem and is precise enough to detect density differences of a percent or less, useful for checking alloy purity or a mineral's identity.

sections.heading: Two classic puzzles
sections.body: Melting ice in a glass of water does not change the water level, because floating ice already displaces a volume of water equal to its own weight, and when it melts it becomes exactly that same weight of water — occupying, by definition, that same volume. The floating-then-melted case leaves level unchanged; this reasoning is the basis for why melting sea ice (which already floats) does not itself raise sea level, unlike land-based ice sheets. The second puzzle: a stone thrown overboard from a floating boat lowers the pond level. While in the boat, the stone's weight is supported by buoyancy, so the boat displaces a volume equal to the stone's weight divided by water density — often much more than the stone's own volume, since rock is denser than water. Once thrown in and sunk, the stone only displaces its own (smaller) volume, so total displacement drops and the water level falls.

lessons.workedExample: A 200 g mineral sample is weighed in air at 1.96 N (using g = 9.8 m/s2) and, fully submerged in water, at 1.35 N. The buoyant force is 1.96 - 1.35 = 0.61 N, which equals rho_water*g*V, so V = 0.61/(1000*9.8) = 6.22 x 10^-5 m3 (62.2 cm3). The sample's density is then mass/volume = 0.200 kg / 6.22 x 10^-5 m3 = 3,215 kg/m3, close to the density of quartz (about 2,650 kg/m3) or a denser silicate — a hydrostatic-weighing student project could compare this measured value against reference densities to identify the mineral, exactly the logic Archimedes is said to have applied to the king's crown.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about Archimedes' principle wants to know whether a student understands buoyancy as a consequence of pressure varying with depth, not as an independent force to memorize. The strongest answers can derive F_B = rho*g*V_disp from the pressure difference between a body's top and bottom, and can resolve the ice-melting and stone-in-boat puzzles by tracking displaced volume before and after, not by guessing. A student who says 'ice floats so it must raise the level when it melts' has not worked through the weight-displacement equivalence that the correct answer depends on.

questions.prompt: What is the physical origin of buoyant force, in terms of pressure?

options.text: A separate force exerted by fluid molecules pushing objects upward
The net result of higher pressure on a body's deeper (bottom) surfaces than on its shallower (top) surfaces
Surface tension acting along the waterline
The weight of air displaced above the fluid surface

explanations.a: Buoyancy is not a distinct fundamental force; it emerges entirely from ordinary hydrostatic pressure.
explanations.b: Correct — because pressure increases with depth, the upward push on a submerged body's bottom exceeds the downward push on its top, and integrating this imbalance over the whole surface yields rho*g*V_disp upward.
explanations.c: Surface tension is a separate, generally much smaller effect relevant at fluid interfaces, not the source of bulk buoyant force.
explanations.d: Buoyancy in a liquid depends on the liquid displaced by the submerged body, not on air above the surface.

questions.prompt: Ice floats in a glass of water and is allowed to melt completely. What happens to the water level?

options.text: It rises, because ice is less dense than water and takes up more volume
It falls, because melting reduces the ice's volume
It stays the same, because the floating ice already displaced a volume of water equal to its own weight, which equals the volume of water it becomes
It depends on the water's temperature

explanations.a: This confuses the ice's own volume with the volume of water it displaces while floating; the displaced volume, not the ice's bulk volume, is what determines the level.
explanations.b: The level does not fall — the melted ice becomes exactly the volume of water that was already displaced.
explanations.c: Correct — a floating object displaces a volume of water equal in weight to itself; when the ice melts, it becomes that same weight of water, occupying that same displaced volume, so the level is unchanged.
explanations.d: Temperature does not change the weight-displacement equivalence that keeps the level constant.

questions.prompt: A dense stone sits in a floating rowboat on a pond. The stone is then thrown overboard and sinks. What happens to the pond's water level?

options.text: It rises, because the stone now displaces water directly
It falls, because the stone in the boat displaced a volume equal to its weight/rho_water (larger, since rock is denser than water), but once sunk it only displaces its own smaller volume
It stays exactly the same regardless of the stone's density
It rises only if the stone is porous

explanations.a: The stone displaces less water once sunk than the boat displaced to carry its weight, so the level falls, not rises.
explanations.b: Correct — while afloat in the boat, the stone's weight is buoyed by displacing weight/rho_water of water; since the stone is denser than water, that displaced volume exceeds the stone's own volume, so removing it and sinking it (displacing only its own smaller volume) reduces total displacement and lowers the level.
explanations.c: The outcome specifically depends on the stone being denser than water; a stone of exactly water's density would produce no level change.
explanations.d: Porosity is not the deciding factor here; density relative to water is.

questions.prompt: A 500 g sample weighs 4.9 N in air and 3.4 N fully submerged in water (g = 9.8 m/s2, rho_water = 1000 kg/m3). What is its approximate density?

explanations.a: This does not follow from the hydrostatic-weighing calculation; it appears to just halve the mass in grams without unit conversion.
explanations.b: 1,000 kg/m3 is water's own density, not the sample's — the sample is denser since it sinks (loses less than half its weight when submerged).
explanations.d: 5,000 kg/m3 overstates the result; carrying through the buoyant-force subtraction correctly gives about 3,267 kg/m3.

lessons.label: Floating Bodies: Draft, Displacement and Reserve Buoyancy

sections.heading: Displacement, deadweight, and draft
sections.body: A floating ship obeys Archimedes' principle directly: at equilibrium, its total weight equals rho*g*V_disp, so naval architects speak of displacement (the weight of water pushed aside, equal to the ship's own weight) rather than a separate 'weight' figure. Displacement splits into lightship weight (the empty hull, machinery, and fittings) and deadweight (cargo, fuel, crew, stores — everything variable that can be loaded or consumed). Draft is how deep the hull sits in the water, measured from the waterline down to the keel; as cargo is loaded, weight increases, so V_disp must increase to match, and since the hull's underwater shape is roughly fixed, draft increases too. The waterplane area — the horizontal cross-section of the hull at the current waterline — governs how much draft changes per unit of added weight.

sections.heading: Tonnes-per-centimeter and freeboard
sections.body: Naval architects quantify that sensitivity as tonnes-per-centimeter immersion (TPC): the mass that must be added to sink the ship one additional centimeter, TPC = (waterplane area x rho_water)/100 when area is in square meters and density in tonnes per cubic meter. A ship with a large waterplane area (a barge) has a high TPC and sinks only slightly per tonne loaded; a narrow-waterplane vessel is far more draft-sensitive. Freeboard is the complementary measurement: the vertical distance from the waterline up to the main deck, essentially the hull's remaining dry height. The volume of hull between the waterline and the point at which the ship would swamp is its reserve buoyancy — the safety margin available to keep floating if a wave washes over the deck or a compartment floods.

sections.heading: The Plimsoll line and density correction
sections.body: Nineteenth-century British shipowners had a financial incentive to overload 'coffin ships' past safe freeboard, and the resulting losses drove Samuel Plimsoll's campaign in Parliament, culminating in the Merchant Shipping Act of 1876, which required British vessels to carry a load-line mark showing the maximum permitted draft. Later legislation fixed the mark's exact position on the hull. The load line is actually a small cluster of marks, because the water a ship floats in is not always the same density: seawater (about 1,025 kg/m3) is denser than fresh water (about 1,000 kg/m3), so the same ship displaces the same weight but a smaller volume, and rides higher, in salt water than in fresh. A ship that transits from a saltwater port to a freshwater river must ride at a shallower salt-water mark on departure, since it will sink lower once it reaches fresh water, even carrying an unchanged cargo weight.

lessons.workedExample: A cargo ship has a waterplane area of 2,400 m2 at its current draft. Its TPC in seawater (rho = 1.025 t/m3) is (2400 x 1.025)/100 = 24.6 tonnes/cm. Loading 1,230 tonnes of cargo therefore increases draft by 1230/24.6 = 50 cm, or 0.5 m. If the same ship then sails from a seawater port into a fresh-water river (rho = 1.000 t/m3) with cargo unchanged, its displaced weight must stay the same, but since it now needs a larger volume of the less-dense fresh water to displace that same weight, its draft increases further — the load-line rules account for exactly this by marking a shallower allowed draft (the 'S' summer saltwater line sits higher on the hull than the freshwater line) so the ship has margin before it reaches the river.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this concept wants to see whether a student treats a ship's displacement as a fixed number or understands it as weight-equals-displaced-water-weight, which shifts with water density even at constant cargo. The strongest answers connect TPC to waterplane area (not overall ship size), explain freeboard and reserve buoyancy as the safety margin against swamping, and can state why the Plimsoll line has multiple marks — because a ship riding safely in salt water can be dangerously low if it later enters fresh water with no correction. A student who thinks load lines are a single fixed depth has missed the density argument entirely.

questions.prompt: A ship's TPC (tonnes-per-centimeter immersion) depends most directly on which quantity?

options.text: The ship's total displacement
The waterplane area at the current draft
The ship's engine power
The lightship weight only

explanations.a: Total displacement is the outcome of loading over time, not the geometric quantity that sets sensitivity to a single added tonne.
explanations.b: Correct — TPC = (waterplane area x rho_water)/100, so a wider waterplane spreads added weight over more area, changing draft less per tonne loaded.
explanations.c: Engine power is unrelated to hydrostatic draft sensitivity.
explanations.d: Lightship weight is a fixed baseline, not the variable governing draft change per added tonne.

questions.prompt: A ship travels from a saltwater port (rho = 1,025 kg/m3) into a freshwater river (rho = 1,000 kg/m3) without changing its cargo. What happens to its draft?

options.text: Draft decreases, because fresh water is 'thinner' and easier to float in
Draft is unchanged, since the ship's weight has not changed
Draft increases, because the less-dense fresh water requires a larger displaced volume to support the same weight
Draft becomes unpredictable without knowing the ship's engine load

explanations.a: Draft moves the opposite direction — the ship sits lower, not higher, in the less dense fresh water.
explanations.b: Weight equals displacement in force terms, but since displaced volume = weight/(rho*g), a lower rho forces a larger volume and thus deeper draft even at constant weight.
explanations.c: Correct — with weight fixed, V_disp = W/(rho*g) grows as rho falls, so the hull must sink deeper to displace the extra volume needed in fresh water.
explanations.d: Engine load is irrelevant to static hydrostatic draft; the density change alone determines the shift.

questions.prompt: What historical problem did the Plimsoll load line, mandated after the Merchant Shipping Act of 1876, address?

options.text: Ships sailing too slowly due to excess cargo weight
Shipowners overloading vessels past a safe freeboard, reducing reserve buoyancy and causing preventable sinkings
Ships being taxed based on their draft
Confusion over nautical mile measurements

explanations.a: Speed loss was not the safety concern driving the legislation; sinking risk was.
explanations.b: Correct — Samuel Plimsoll campaigned against overloaded 'coffin ships' that had too little freeboard and reserve buoyancy, leading to the load-line mark requirement in the 1876 Act.
explanations.c: The load line was a safety marking, not a taxation mechanism.
explanations.d: The load line concerns vertical loading limits, not horizontal distance measurement.

questions.prompt: A ship's waterplane area is 2,000 m2. Using TPC = (waterplane area x rho_water)/100 with rho_water = 1.025 t/m3, how much does draft increase after loading 1,025 tonnes of cargo in seawater?

options.text: 5 cm
50 cm
100 cm

explanations.a: This understates the result substantially; recompute TPC first.
explanations.b: This appears to skip dividing cargo mass by TPC; 20.5 t/cm is the TPC value itself, not the draft increase.
explanations.c: Correct — TPC = (2000 x 1.025)/100 = 20.5 tonnes/cm, so 1,025 tonnes gives 1025/20.5 = 50 cm of additional draft.
explanations.d: This overstates the draft increase by roughly double.

lessons.label: Metacentric Height: Why a Boat Rights Itself

sections.heading: The center of buoyancy moves when a hull heels
sections.body: A floating body's center of buoyancy B is the centroid of its displaced volume, and its center of gravity G is the centroid of its own mass — for stability, both matter, but not the way most people first guess. When a hull heels (tilts) by a small angle, the shape of the submerged volume changes: one side rises out of the water, the other sinks deeper, so B shifts sideways toward the low side even though G stays put in the hull. The key geometric fact is that the vertical line drawn up from the new B intersects the ship's original centerline at a point called the metacenter, M, which for small angles is essentially fixed in place regardless of exactly how far the ship has heeled.

sections.heading: BM, GM, and the righting arm
sections.body: The distance from B up to M is BM = I/V, where I is the second moment of the waterplane area about the ship's centerline (a shape property of the hull at the waterline) and V is the displaced volume. A wide, boxy hull has a large I and thus a high metacenter; a narrow hull has a low one. Metacentric height GM is then found from the keel upward: GM = KB + BM - KG, where KB and KG are the heights of B and G above the keel. If G sits below M (positive GM), heeling creates a righting moment: buoyancy still acts straight up through the shifted B, gravity still acts straight down through G, and the resulting couple, with righting arm GZ approximately equal to GM*sin(theta) for small angles theta, rotates the ship back upright. If G sits above M (negative GM), the same couple pushes the ship further over — the boat is unstable.

sections.heading: Stiff vs tender, and the roll period
sections.body: Real ships operate with GM typically in the range of roughly 0.15 m to 2 m, depending on type. A large GM makes a ship 'stiff': it rights itself quickly and resists heeling, but the fast, jerky righting motion is uncomfortable for passengers and can slam cargo or crew around; naval architects sometimes deliberately keep GM modest on passenger vessels. A small (but still positive) GM makes a ship 'tender': it heels further and rolls more slowly and smoothly, but has less margin against capsizing in heavy weather or from a shifted load. The roll period itself follows T = 2*pi*k/sqrt(g*GM), where k is the ship's radius of gyration about its rolling axis — so, counterintuitively, a stiffer ship (higher GM) rolls with a shorter period, snapping back and forth faster, while a tender ship rolls slowly.

lessons.workedExample: A small research vessel has a waterplane second moment I = 850 m4 and displaces V = 2,100 m3, giving BM = 850/2100 = 0.405 m. Its center of buoyancy is KB = 2.2 m above the keel and its center of gravity, after loading scientific equipment on an upper deck, is KG = 2.5 m above the keel. Then GM = KB + BM - KG = 2.2 + 0.405 - 2.5 = 0.105 m — positive but small, meaning the ship is stable but tender. At a 10-degree heel, the righting arm is approximately GZ ≈ GM*sin(10°) = 0.105*0.174 = 0.018 m, a modest righting lever, which is exactly why loading heavy gear high on deck (raising KG) is the classic way a vessel's stability margin quietly erodes even though it still floats and still rights itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about metacentric height wants to know whether a student can explain WHY a boat rights itself rather than just naming 'stability' as a vague property. The strongest answers trace the mechanism: heeling shifts the center of buoyancy, the metacenter is where the new buoyant line of action crosses the centerline, and the sign of GM (G relative to M) determines whether the resulting couple restores or worsens the heel. A student who can compute BM = I/V for a given hull and explain the stiff-versus-tender tradeoff — and why loading weight higher raises KG and shrinks GM — has demonstrated real understanding, not just vocabulary.

questions.prompt: What physically happens to the center of buoyancy B as a hull heels to a small angle?

options.text: It stays fixed at the hull's geometric center regardless of heel
It shifts sideways, since the submerged volume's shape changes as one side rises and the other sinks
It moves upward toward the deck
It merges with the center of gravity

explanations.a: B is the centroid of the displaced volume, which changes shape as the hull heels, so B moves.
explanations.b: Correct — heeling changes the underwater hull shape (one side rises, the other sinks deeper), shifting the centroid of displaced volume, B, toward the low side.
explanations.c: B moves sideways as displaced volume shifts, not vertically toward the deck.
explanations.d: B and G are distinct points (centroid of displaced volume vs. centroid of mass) and do not merge from heeling alone.

questions.prompt: A ship has GM computed as negative (G above M). What does this predict?

options.text: The ship rights itself faster than a positive-GM ship
The ship is unstable — a small heel produces a couple that increases the heel rather than correcting it
The ship's roll period becomes zero
Negative GM has no effect on stability, only on comfort

explanations.a: Negative GM does the opposite of righting the ship faster; it removes the righting moment entirely.
explanations.b: Correct — when G is above M, the buoyancy-gravity couple that forms during a heel acts to increase the tilt rather than oppose it, meaning the ship is statically unstable at that condition.
explanations.c: The roll-period formula assumes positive GM; a zero or negative GM does not correspond to a normal oscillatory roll.
explanations.d: Negative GM is a fundamental stability problem, not merely a comfort issue — it can lead to capsize or an angle of loll.

questions.prompt: Loading heavy cargo higher on a ship's deck (raising KG, with KB and BM unchanged) does what to GM and to stiffness?

options.text: GM increases, making the ship stiffer
GM decreases, making the ship more tender (less stable margin)
GM is unaffected by KG
GM increases only if the cargo is heavier than the ship itself

explanations.a: Raising KG works against GM, not for it, since GM = KB + BM - KG.
explanations.b: Correct — since GM = KB + BM - KG, increasing KG directly decreases GM, shrinking the ship's stability margin and making it more tender (or, in the extreme, unstable).
explanations.c: GM depends explicitly on KG through the subtraction in the formula.
explanations.d: The effect on GM follows directly from the height at which weight is added (KG), not from the cargo's total weight relative to the ship.

questions.prompt: Comparing two ships with the same radius of gyration k but different GM, which one has the SHORTER roll period, according to T = 2*pi*k/sqrt(g*GM)?

options.text: The one with the smaller GM ('tender')
The one with the larger GM ('stiff')
Roll period is independent of GM
They always have identical roll periods if k is the same

explanations.a: A smaller GM makes the denominator sqrt(g*GM) smaller, which lengthens, not shortens, the period.
explanations.b: Correct — GM sits in the denominator under a square root, so a larger GM (stiffer ship) produces a shorter roll period, meaning stiff ships roll quickly and tender ships roll slowly.
explanations.c: GM directly appears in the roll-period formula, so period is very much dependent on it.
explanations.d: Equal k with different GM gives different periods, per the formula.

lessons.label: When Stability Fails: Free Surface Effect, Loll and Capsize

sections.heading: Free surface effect: a virtual rise of G
sections.body: A tank that is completely full or completely empty holds its liquid fixed as the ship heels, contributing nothing extra to instability beyond its weight. A partially (slack) filled tank is a different problem: as the ship tilts, the liquid inside sloshes toward the low side, and that shift moves the tank's own center of mass sideways in the same direction the ship is already heeling — worsening the tilt rather than resisting it. The effect behaves mathematically as if the ship's center of gravity had risen, even though no weight actually moved vertically; naval architects quantify it as a virtual GM loss of rho_liquid*i/displacement for each slack tank, where i is the tank's own waterplane second moment (about its centerline, in the direction of tilt) and displacement is the ship's total weight. This is why tanks on real ships are subdivided with baffles and why cargo decks are partitioned — halving a tank's width can cut its contribution to i, and thus its destabilizing effect, by roughly a factor of eight, since i scales with the cube of breadth.

sections.heading: Negative GM, angle of loll, and the GZ curve
sections.body: If free-surface losses, high cargo, or flooding push GM negative, a ship does not necessarily capsize outright — it can settle at a stable angle of loll, tilted to one side, where the righting arm GZ happens to return to zero from a non-upright position rather than from upright. This is deceptive: the ship looks like it has 'found' a resting angle, but it has zero or negative stability at zero heel and can easily be pushed past its new balance point by a wave or wind gust. The full picture is captured in the GZ curve, a plot of righting arm against heel angle: GZ rises from zero, ideally stays large through a broad range of angles, then falls back to zero at the angle of vanishing stability — beyond which no righting moment exists at all and the ship will continue to capsize.

sections.heading: Three case studies
sections.body: The Swedish warship Vasa sank in Stockholm harbor in 1628 on her maiden voyage, having gone barely a nautical mile: too little ballast relative to a tall, heavily armed upper hull left inadequate GM, and a modest gust was enough to heel her past recovery. The ferry Herald of Free Enterprise capsized in 1987 shortly after leaving Zeebrugge with her bow doors left open; water flooding onto the vehicle deck created a massive, largely unrestrained free surface, and the vessel rolled over in roughly ninety seconds, killing 193 people. The cruise ship Costa Concordia struck rocks off Isola del Giglio in 2012, tearing open the hull; progressive flooding through multiple compartments shifted weight and displacement asymmetrically, producing a growing heel that ended with the ship grounded on its side. All three losses trace back to the same underlying quantity, GM, being eroded past zero by a mechanism the crew did not control in time.

lessons.workedExample: A ferry has displacement 8,000 tonnes and GM = 0.9 m before loading. Its car deck floods to a shallow depth after a wave washes over a low freeboard opening, creating a free surface 20 m long by 15 m wide. The tank's second moment about its long centerline is i = (length*breadth^3)/12 = (20*15^3)/12 = 5,625 m4. With seawater density 1.025 t/m3, the virtual GM loss is (1.025*5625)/8000 = 0.72 m. The ship's effective GM drops from 0.9 m to about 0.18 m — still positive, but the ship is now far more tender, and if a second wave adds more water or the deck is left unbaffled, a wide, shallow flood like this can erase the remaining margin entirely, which is exactly the free-surface mechanism behind the Herald of Free Enterprise capsize.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing stability failure wants to see whether a student understands that free-surface loss is a shift in effective GM caused by liquid movement, not simply 'extra weight from flooding.' The strongest answers can explain why the loss scales with the cube of the free surface's breadth (making subdivision so effective), distinguish angle of loll from a genuinely capsized state, and can name at least one real incident with the correct mechanism attached — not just the ship's name. A student who says 'the Titanic sank from free surface effect' has confused an iceberg-gash flooding scenario with the specific free-surface and open-door mechanisms of Vasa, Herald of Free Enterprise, or Costa Concordia.

questions.prompt: Why does a partially filled (slack) tank reduce a ship's effective stability more than a completely full tank of the same liquid weight?

options.text: A slack tank weighs more than a full one
The liquid in a slack tank shifts toward the low side as the ship heels, moving that mass in the same direction as the tilt and behaving as a virtual rise in G
A full tank cannot be pumped out in an emergency
Slack tanks increase the ship's total displacement

explanations.a: A full tank of the same liquid actually weighs more, not less, than a partially filled one; weight is not the mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct — the liquid surface in a slack tank redistributes toward the low side during a heel, and this shift acts as if the ship's center of gravity had virtually risen, reducing effective GM.
explanations.c: Pumpability is an operational detail unrelated to the physical free-surface mechanism.
explanations.d: Free surface effect changes stability (effective GM), not the ship's total displaced weight.

questions.prompt: Why does subdividing a slack tank with baffles reduce free-surface loss so effectively?

options.text: Because the loss is proportional to i, and i scales with the cube of the tank's breadth, so narrowing each subdivided section sharply cuts the loss
Because baffles reduce the total volume of liquid in the tank
Because baffles increase the tank's overall weight, adding stability
Because baffles prevent the liquid from being pumped out

explanations.a: Correct — free-surface loss is rho*i/displacement, and i for a rectangular free surface scales with breadth cubed, so subdividing a wide tank into narrower sections sharply reduces the destabilizing effect even though total liquid weight is unchanged.
explanations.b: Baffles do not remove liquid; the same volume remains, just constrained from sloshing across the full breadth.
explanations.c: Baffles are lightweight structural partitions, not a meaningful stability contribution through added weight.
explanations.d: Baffles are unrelated to pumping capability; they physically limit lateral sloshing distance.

questions.prompt: A ship settles at a fixed tilt angle away from upright and appears to stop rotating further. What does an 'angle of loll' actually indicate?

options.text: The ship has fully recovered its stability and is safe
The ship has negative GM at upright, and has found a non-upright angle where GZ returns to zero — it remains fragile and can be pushed past this point by a wave or gust
The ship's engines have failed
The ship is at its angle of vanishing stability and about to right itself

explanations.a: An angle of loll signals compromised, not recovered, stability — the ship has zero or negative GM at upright.
explanations.b: Correct — a loll angle is a deceptive resting point that appears stable but reflects negative GM at zero heel; the ship's margin against a further disturbance is minimal.
explanations.c: Engine status has no bearing on this geometric stability condition.
explanations.d: The angle of vanishing stability is the upper limit of the GZ curve where righting arm falls to zero on the way toward capsize, not a settled resting angle.

questions.prompt: Match each historical capsize/loss to its primary stability-failure mechanism.

right.text: Open bow doors let water onto the vehicle deck, creating a large free surface that capsized the ship within about ninety seconds
Insufficient ballast for a tall, heavily armed upper hull left inadequate GM from the outset
A hull gash from grounding caused progressive, asymmetric flooding that produced a growing heel

questions.explanation: Vasa sank from too little ballast relative to her top-heavy design; Herald of Free Enterprise capsized when open bow doors let seawater flood the car deck, creating a severe free-surface effect; Costa Concordia's hull was torn open on rocks, and the resulting progressive, uneven flooding produced the heel that ended with her grounded on her side.

lessons.label: Settling: Buoyancy, Drag and Terminal Velocity

sections.heading: The three-way force balance
sections.body: A particle sinking through a fluid is governed by three forces at once: weight pulling it down, buoyancy pushing it up (Archimedes' principle again, F_B = rho*g*V), and drag resisting its motion, growing with speed. Initially weight exceeds buoyancy plus drag and the particle accelerates, but as speed increases so does drag, until the three forces balance and acceleration stops — the particle has reached terminal (settling) velocity. For a small sphere moving slowly enough through a viscous fluid, George Gabriel Stokes derived the drag force in 1851 as F = 6*pi*mu*R*V, where mu is the fluid's dynamic viscosity, R the sphere's radius, and V its velocity — linear in velocity, unlike the velocity-squared drag familiar from fast-moving objects in air.

sections.heading: Stokes' law and the settling velocity formula
