sections.body: Setting weight minus buoyancy equal to Stokes drag and solving for V gives the settling velocity w_s = (2/9)*(rho_s - rho)*g*r^2/mu, where rho_s is the particle's density and rho the fluid's. The r^2 dependence is the dominant feature: halving a particle's radius cuts its settling speed by a factor of four, which is why fine sediment takes drastically longer to settle than coarse sediment of the same material. A 0.1 mm quartz sand grain (radius 0.05 mm, rho_s about 2,650 kg/m3) settling in water works out to roughly 9 mm/s — reaching the bottom of a beaker in seconds. A 1 micron clay particle of the same material settles thousands of times slower, on the order of a micron per second, meaning it can take hours to days to fall even a modest column height, which is exactly why muddy water stays cloudy long after sand has settled out.

sections.heading: Where Stokes' law breaks down
sections.body: Stokes' law is only valid at low Reynolds number, conventionally Re < 1, where Re = rho*V*d/mu compares inertial to viscous forces. The 0.1 mm sand grain above sits right around Re ≈ 0.9 — close to the edge of Stokes' regime, which is why sand settling calculations are often treated as an approximate boundary case. Above roughly Re ≈ 1, the drag-coefficient-versus-Reynolds-number curve departs from the simple Stokes line, entering an intermediate regime and eventually the Newton regime (roughly 1,000 < Re < 200,000) relevant to coarser particles like gravel, where drag coefficient is approximately constant and settling velocity scales with the square root of particle diameter rather than its square. A separate complication is hindered settling: in a concentrated suspension, particles interfere with each other's flow fields and displace fluid that must return past neighboring particles, so settling velocity drops well below the dilute-suspension Stokes prediction as concentration rises — a correction engineers must apply when designing sedimentation tanks handling real slurries rather than single isolated particles.

lessons.workedExample: A geology student wants to estimate how long a sediment sample takes to separate by grain size in a 20 cm settling column. Using w_s = (2/9)*(rho_s - rho)*g*r^2/mu with quartz (rho_s = 2,650 kg/m3), water (rho = 1,000 kg/m3, mu = 0.001 Pa*s) and r = 0.05 mm (a 0.1 mm grain), w_s = (2/9)*(1650)*(9.8)*(0.05e-3)^2/0.001 ≈ 9 mm/s, so the sand reaches the bottom of the 20 cm column in about 22 seconds. Checking validity, Re = rho*w_s*d/mu = 1000*0.009*1e-4/0.001 ≈ 0.9, just inside the Re < 1 window, so Stokes' law is a reasonable (if borderline) approximation here — a coarser gravel-sized particle would need the Newton-regime relation instead, since its Re would be far above 1.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about settling wants to see whether a student can state the force balance (weight, buoyancy, drag) and knows Stokes' law has a validity range rather than treating it as universally true. The strongest answers can compute w_s from the r^2 relationship, explain why fine particles take dramatically longer to settle than coarse ones of the same density, and check the resulting Reynolds number to confirm Stokes' law actually applies — flagging when a problem has left the Re < 1 regime and needs the Newton relation instead. A student who applies Stokes' law to a gravel-sized particle without checking Re has memorized a formula without understanding its limits.

questions.prompt: According to w_s = (2/9)*(rho_s - rho)*g*r^2/mu, if a particle's radius is halved (all else unchanged), what happens to its settling velocity?

options.text: It is halved
It is cut to one quarter, since velocity depends on r squared
It is unchanged
It doubles

explanations.a: This would be true for a linear dependence on r, but the formula depends on r^2, not r.
explanations.b: Correct — since w_s scales with r^2, halving the radius reduces settling velocity by a factor of (1/2)^2 = 1/4.
explanations.c: Settling velocity is strongly radius-dependent, not constant.
explanations.d: Reducing radius decreases, not increases, settling velocity.

questions.prompt: Why does Stokes' law require checking that Reynolds number Re < 1 before it can be trusted?

options.text: Because Stokes' law was derived assuming viscous forces dominate inertial forces, an assumption that breaks down as Re grows past roughly 1
Because Re < 1 is required for buoyancy to act on the particle at all
Because Stokes' law only applies to particles denser than 5,000 kg/m3
Because Reynolds number determines the fluid's viscosity

explanations.a: Correct — Stokes drag (linear in velocity) is a low-Re approximation; once inertial effects become significant (Re above roughly 1), the drag-coefficient curve departs from the Stokes line and the formula overpredicts or underpredicts drag.
explanations.b: Buoyancy acts on any submerged particle regardless of Reynolds number; it is unrelated to this validity condition.
explanations.c: Stokes' law's validity is about flow regime (Re), not a specific density threshold.
explanations.d: Reynolds number is a ratio that depends on viscosity among other things, but it does not determine viscosity itself.

questions.prompt: A concentrated slurry (many particles close together) settles more slowly than the dilute-suspension Stokes prediction for a single isolated particle. What causes this hindered settling?

options.text: The particles chemically bond together in concentrated suspension
Neighboring particles interfere with each other's flow fields, and displaced fluid must return past nearby particles, slowing the whole assembly
Concentrated suspensions have lower viscosity, which paradoxically slows settling
Hindered settling only occurs above Re = 1,000

explanations.a: Chemical bonding is not the general mechanism behind hindered settling; it is a hydrodynamic interference effect.
explanations.b: Correct — in a concentrated suspension, particles are close enough that their individual flow fields interact, and fluid displaced by one particle must flow back past its neighbors, reducing the effective settling speed of the group below the single-particle Stokes prediction.
explanations.c: Concentration typically raises effective suspension viscosity or interference, not lowers it, and that is not the primary mechanism described here.
explanations.d: Hindered settling is a concentration effect, not a Reynolds-number threshold phenomenon.

questions.prompt: Order the events in a particle's motion from being released at rest in a fluid to reaching terminal (settling) velocity.

items.text: Particle is released at rest; weight exceeds buoyancy plus drag
Particle accelerates downward, gaining speed
As speed increases, drag (proportional to velocity under Stokes' law) grows
Weight, buoyancy, and drag reach balance; acceleration stops at terminal velocity

questions.explanation: The particle starts at rest with a net downward force (weight exceeding buoyancy plus the initially small drag), accelerates and gains speed, which increases drag since Stokes drag grows with velocity, until drag plus buoyancy exactly balances weight and the particle continues at a constant terminal (settling) velocity.

units.label: Critical Flow: Froude, Specific Energy & the Hydraulic Jump

lessons.label: Gravity Waves and the Free Surface

sections.heading: A surface that can deform is a surface that can send signals
sections.body: A pipe full of water has no free surface, so a disturbance at one end shows up everywhere else almost instantly, limited only by fluid compressibility. An open channel is different: the top of the flow is free to bulge up or dip down, and gravity is the restoring force that pulls a bulge back toward flat. That restoring action propagates as a gravity wave — the same physics as an ocean swell, just shrunk to a puddle or a river. In shallow water, where the wavelength is long compared to the depth y, every wave travels at the same speed regardless of its length: c = sqrt(g*y). Drop a pebble in a 0.2 m deep gutter and the ring expands at sqrt(9.8*0.2) ≈ 1.4 m/s no matter how tight or broad the ripple is. This non-dispersive speed is the single most important number in open-channel hydraulics, because it is the rate at which information about a downstream obstruction — a rock, a gate, a drop — can travel back upstream.

sections.heading: Deep water breaks the rule: waves become dispersive
sections.body: Once the water is deep relative to the wavelength, the orbital motion of a wave dies out with depth before it ever feels the bottom, and the bed no longer matters. Speed then depends on wavelength itself: c = sqrt(g*lambda/(2*pi)), so long ocean swells outrun short wind chop — the classic dispersive behavior sailors use to judge an approaching storm's distance. Hydraulic engineers draw the line using the ratio of depth to wavelength, y/lambda: below about 0.05 the shallow-water formula c = sqrt(g*y) is accurate to within a couple percent, and above about 0.5 the deep-water formula takes over cleanly. Between those cutoffs is a transitional zone where the full dispersion relation, c = sqrt((g*lambda/(2*pi))*tanh(2*pi*y/lambda)), is needed to blend the two limits.

sections.heading: Where gravity stops being the only restoring force
sections.body: Gravity is not the only thing that flattens a bump on a free surface — surface tension does too, and for short enough wavelengths it dominates. The crossover for water occurs near lambda ≈ 1.7 cm, where the phase speed of a capillary-gravity wave actually reaches a minimum (around 23 cm/s) before rising again for both shorter, tension-dominated ripples and longer, gravity-dominated waves. This is why the fine cat's-paw texture on a pond looks and moves differently from the broad swells feeding it — they are governed by different physics, not just different sizes.

lessons.workedExample: A drainage channel carries water 0.45 m deep. Estimate how fast a warning of a downstream gate closure can reach a point 20 m upstream. Shallow-water celerity: c = sqrt(9.8 * 0.45) = sqrt(4.41) ≈ 2.10 m/s. If the flow itself moves at only 0.8 m/s, the disturbance's net upstream propagation speed relative to the ground is c - V = 2.10 - 0.80 = 1.30 m/s, so the wavefront reaches the 20 m mark in about 15.4 seconds — the flow is subcritical, and upstream points genuinely feel downstream changes. Repeating the calculation with V = 3.0 m/s (net speed c - V is negative) shows the same disturbance would instead be swept downstream, never reaching that upstream point at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how does information travel through a flowing fluid with a free surface?' is testing whether a student understands that c = sqrt(g*y) is not a decorative formula but the mechanism behind every upstream/downstream control question in the rest of the unit. A strong answer explains that the wave speed sets a finite signal speed relative to the water, so whether that signal can climb back upstream against the current depends on comparing it to the flow speed — which is exactly the Froude number waiting one lesson away. A weak answer recites the formula without connecting it to why some channels 'know' about a downstream gate and others do not.

questions.prompt: Why can a disturbance on a free surface propagate as a wave at all, while a disturbance in a full pipe essentially cannot deform the boundary?

options.text: Because pipes are always turbulent and channels are always laminar
Because the free surface can move up and down under gravity's restoring force, while a rigid pipe wall cannot deform
Because water in pipes is always colder
Because pipes have no viscosity

explanations.a: Turbulence/laminarity is unrelated to whether a boundary can deform under gravity.
explanations.b: Correct — a free surface is the deformable boundary; gravity pulls a bulge back toward flat, and that restoring action is exactly what propagates as a gravity wave.
explanations.c: Temperature is irrelevant to whether a boundary can support a gravity wave.
explanations.d: Viscosity affects wave damping, not whether the boundary can deform in the first place.

questions.prompt: A 0.2 m deep gutter carries a shallow-water disturbance. Approximately what is its celerity?

options.text: 14 m/s

explanations.a: This is just the depth value in meters, not a speed computed from c = sqrt(g*y).
explanations.b: Correct — c = sqrt(9.8 * 0.2) = sqrt(1.96) ≈ 1.4 m/s, matching the lesson's gutter example.
explanations.c: This is g itself, not sqrt(g*y).
explanations.d: This overshoots by roughly a factor of 10; check the square root.

questions.prompt: In deep water, why do long ocean swells outrun shorter wind-driven chop?

options.text: Because deep-water waves are dispersive: c = sqrt(g*lambda/(2*pi)) increases with wavelength
Because shallow-water celerity c = sqrt(g*y) always applies in the ocean
Because longer waves have less surface tension acting on them, which is the only difference
Because chop is always moving against the current

explanations.a: Correct — in deep water the bed is irrelevant, and the dispersion relation makes speed depend on wavelength, so longer swells travel faster than shorter chop.
explanations.b: The shallow-water formula applies only when y/lambda is below about 0.05; the open ocean is deep-water territory.
explanations.c: Surface tension only dominates near the ~1.7 cm crossover, far shorter than ocean swells or wind chop; it is not the reason swells outrun chop.
explanations.d: Current direction is not mentioned or required to explain the dispersive speed difference.

questions.prompt: Match each free-surface wave regime to its governing description.

right.text: c = sqrt(g*y), independent of wavelength
c = sqrt(g*lambda/(2*pi)), the bed no longer matters
Surface tension rivals gravity; phase speed reaches a minimum

questions.explanation: Below y/lambda ≈ 0.05 the shallow-water formula holds because every wavelength travels at the same depth-set speed; above y/lambda ≈ 0.5 the bottom no longer influences the wave and the deep-water dispersion relation takes over; near lambda ≈ 1.7 cm surface tension becomes comparable to gravity, producing the capillary-gravity minimum phase speed.

lessons.label: The Froude Number and Flow Regimes

sections.heading: A race between the flow and its own messenger
sections.body: The previous lesson established that a gravity wave carries information at celerity c = sqrt(g*y) relative to the water. But the water itself is moving at speed V, so the question that actually matters is a race: can the wave outrun the current and climb back upstream, or does the current sweep it downstream no matter what? William Froude, a 19th-century British engineer better known for towing-tank ship-hull testing in the 1860s-70s, gave hydraulics its name for this ratio: Fr = V / sqrt(g*y). Fr is dimensionless, and it is the single number that tells you which way information can travel in open-channel flow. Note that Froude's own work was on ship resistance and wave-making, not river hydraulics directly — the number was named for him later because his wave-speed reasoning applies identically to channels.

sections.heading: Three regimes, and who controls whom
sections.body: When Fr < 1 (subcritical), the flow is relatively deep and slow, and V < c, so a wave generated anywhere can still propagate upstream against the current — a downstream gate, weir, or channel narrowing can reach back and set the depth upstream of it. This is why subcritical flow is said to be controlled from downstream. When Fr > 1 (supercritical), the flow is shallow and fast, V > c, and no disturbance can climb back upstream at all — depth downstream is dictated entirely by what happens upstream. Fr = 1 is critical flow, the exact knife-edge where wave speed equals flow speed, explored in depth in the next lesson through the specific-energy diagram. The regimes are not symmetric in how much they 'know': subcritical flow is aware of what's coming, supercritical flow is not.

sections.heading: The Mach number analogy is exact, not loose
sections.body: This upstream/downstream distinction is precisely the compressible-flow problem restated in a liquid: the Froude number plays the role the Mach number plays for gas, with the gravity-wave celerity sqrt(g*y) standing in for the speed of sound. Subcritical (Fr<1) is the open-channel analog of subsonic flow; supercritical (Fr>1) is the analog of supersonic flow; and, as later lessons show, the hydraulic jump that abruptly raises depth and dissipates energy in supercritical flow is the direct analog of a normal shock wave. You can see the regimes by eye: water sheeting thin and fast down a spillway chute or over a driveway during a storm is supercritical; the same water pooling deep and slow in a gutter puddle is subcritical; and the V-shaped wake spreading behind a canoe paddle or a duck marks the critical-speed boundary, the same geometric signature as a Mach cone.

lessons.workedExample: A spillway chute carries water 0.08 m deep at 4.5 m/s. Wave celerity: c = sqrt(9.8 * 0.08) = sqrt(0.784) ≈ 0.885 m/s. Froude number: Fr = 4.5 / 0.885 ≈ 5.1, strongly supercritical — nothing downstream (not even a wall) can send a depth signal back up the chute. Compare a reservoir outlet channel 2.0 m deep flowing at 0.6 m/s: c = sqrt(9.8*2.0) = sqrt(19.6) ≈ 4.43 m/s, so Fr = 0.6/4.43 ≈ 0.14, deeply subcritical — a downstream gate closure would be felt far upstream almost immediately.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes the Froude number because it is the cleanest test of whether a student memorized 'Fr = V over root(gy)' or actually understands what the number means physically. The tell is asking a student to predict, without doing arithmetic, whether a given control (a gate, a weir, a channel step) will affect the flow upstream of it — a student who reasons from 'can the wave get back upstream?' answers instantly and correctly, while one who only has the formula has to compute Fr for every case. Naming the exact Mach-number analogy, including that a hydraulic jump is the shock-wave analog, is a strong signal of transfer rather than rote recall.

questions.prompt: What does the Froude number Fr = V/sqrt(g*y) physically compare?

options.text: The flow speed to the speed a gravity wave can travel relative to the water
The flow's temperature to its viscosity
The channel's width to its depth
The flow rate to the channel's roughness coefficient

explanations.a: Correct — Fr compares the current's speed V to the gravity-wave celerity sqrt(g*y), determining whether disturbances can propagate upstream against the flow.
explanations.b: Fr has nothing to do with temperature or viscosity.
explanations.c: That ratio is the channel's aspect ratio, not the Froude number.
explanations.d: Roughness governs energy loss via friction, a separate concept from the wave-speed race Fr describes.

questions.prompt: A spillway chute has depth 0.08 m and velocity 4.5 m/s. What flow regime is this?

options.text: Subcritical, Fr ≈ 0.2
Critical, Fr = 1.0
Supercritical, Fr ≈ 5.1
Cannot be determined without the channel width

explanations.a: This underestimates Fr by roughly a factor of 25; recompute c = sqrt(9.8*0.08) and divide V by it.
explanations.b: Fr = 1 would require V ≈ c ≈ 0.885 m/s, far below the chute's 4.5 m/s.
explanations.c: Correct — c = sqrt(9.8*0.08) ≈ 0.885 m/s, so Fr = 4.5/0.885 ≈ 5.1, strongly supercritical, matching the worked example.
explanations.d: Fr depends only on velocity and depth (per unit width), not on channel width directly.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the asymmetry between subcritical and supercritical control?

options.text: Supercritical flow is controlled from downstream; subcritical flow is controlled from upstream
Subcritical flow can be controlled from downstream because waves can climb upstream against it; supercritical flow cannot, so it is controlled only from upstream
Both regimes are controlled equally from upstream and downstream
Neither regime can be controlled by gates or weirs

explanations.a: This reverses the correct relationship.
explanations.b: Correct — in subcritical flow V < c so a downstream disturbance's wave can propagate back upstream and set depth there; in supercritical flow V > c so no disturbance can climb upstream, leaving it entirely upstream-controlled.
explanations.c: The regimes are explicitly asymmetric, not equal, in which direction information can travel.
explanations.d: Gates and weirs are exactly the controls hydraulic engineers use; the question is only which direction their influence reaches.

questions.prompt: Match each open-channel flow concept to its compressible-flow (aerodynamics) analog.

right.text: Mach number
Speed of sound
Normal shock wave

questions.explanation: The Froude number plays the role the Mach number plays in gas dynamics; the gravity-wave celerity sqrt(g*y) is the liquid analog of the speed of sound; and the hydraulic jump, which abruptly raises depth and dissipates energy when supercritical flow decelerates, is the direct analog of a normal shock wave in supersonic flow.

lessons.label: Specific Energy and the E-y Diagram

sections.heading: Energy measured from the channel bed, not from sea level
sections.body: Bernoulli's equation gives total head as elevation plus pressure head plus velocity head. In open-channel work it is far more useful to measure energy relative to the local channel bed rather than an absolute datum, because the bed itself may slope. That bed-referenced quantity is called specific energy: E = y + V^2/(2*g), where y is depth (which, for hydrostatic pressure in a channel, also equals the pressure head) and V^2/(2*g) is the velocity head. Writing velocity in terms of the discharge per unit width, q = V*y, gives the form used for analysis: E = y + q^2/(2*g*y^2). For a fixed discharge q, E is a function of depth alone, and plotting E against y produces one of the most useful diagrams in hydraulics.

sections.heading: The two-limbed curve and alternate depths
sections.body: The E-y curve has two branches meeting at a point. As y grows large, the q^2/(2gy^2) term vanishes and E approaches y itself — the upper branch is nearly a 45-degree line, representing deep, slow, subcritical flow where velocity head is negligible. As y shrinks toward zero, the q^2/(2gy^2) term blows up and E rises steeply — the lower branch represents shallow, fast, supercritical flow dominated by velocity head. Critically, for almost any value of E above the curve's minimum, a horizontal line crosses the curve at two points: two different depths, one on each branch, that carry the same discharge q with the same total specific energy. These are called alternate depths, and they are the same two depths that appear on either side of a hydraulic jump or a channel transition — same E, same q, different y, different Fr.

sections.heading: The nose of the curve is critical flow
sections.body: The curve's minimum is not arbitrary — differentiating E with respect to y at constant q and setting dE/dy = 0 gives 1 - q^2/(g*y^3) = 0, which rearranges to y_c = (q^2/g)^(1/3), the critical depth. Substituting back shows the velocity head at that point is exactly half the depth, so E_min = y_c + y_c/2 = 1.5*y_c. At this single depth, V^2 = g*y_c, which is exactly the condition V = sqrt(g*y), i.e., Fr = 1. So the nose of the E-y curve is critical flow: the depth that minimizes the energy needed to pass a given discharge. Any depth above y_c sits on the subcritical branch (Fr<1); any depth below sits on the supercritical branch (Fr>1). Reading a flow's branch off the diagram — not just computing Fr numerically — is the core skill this lesson builds, because the next two lessons use the same diagram to explain what bumps, gates, and jumps do to a flow.

lessons.workedExample: A rectangular channel carries q = 2.0 m^2/s (discharge per unit width). Critical depth: y_c = (q^2/g)^(1/3) = (4.0/9.8)^(1/3) = (0.408)^(1/3) ≈ 0.742 m. Minimum specific energy: E_min = 1.5 * 0.742 ≈ 1.11 m. Now suppose the actual flow runs at E = 1.40 m. Solving y + q^2/(2*g*y^2) = 1.40 for y gives two roots: a subcritical alternate depth near y ≈ 1.27 m (V = 2.0/1.27 ≈ 1.57 m/s, Fr ≈ 0.44) and a supercritical alternate depth near y ≈ 0.47 m (V = 2.0/0.47 ≈ 4.27 m/s, Fr ≈ 2.00) — the same q, the same E, two physically distinct flows on opposite branches of the curve.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge draws the E-y diagram and asks a student to point to a depth and identify its branch because it separates students who treat critical flow as 'a formula to plug into' from those who see it as the geometric minimum of a real curve. The strong answer explains why the minimum exists (velocity head trades off against depth for fixed discharge) and can immediately read off that any point on the left branch is supercritical, any point on the right branch is subcritical, and points at equal height are alternate depths — without recomputing Fr from scratch. That fluency is exactly what lets a student reason qualitatively about bumps and gates in the next lesson.

questions.prompt: Specific energy E = y + q^2/(2*g*y^2) is measured relative to what reference?

options.text: Sea level
The local channel bed
The water surface at the channel's downstream end
Atmospheric pressure

explanations.a: Sea level is an absolute datum; specific energy is deliberately bed-referenced so it works on sloped channels too.
explanations.b: Correct — specific energy is defined relative to the local channel bed, which is why depth y appears directly as one of its terms.
explanations.c: The downstream end is not the reference; E is defined locally at each cross-section relative to that section's own bed.
explanations.d: Atmospheric pressure sets the zero for gauge pressure but is not the specific-energy reference.

questions.prompt: A channel carries q = 2.0 m^2/s. What is the critical depth?

explanations.a: This is too small; recompute (q^2/g)^(1/3) with q=2.0, g=9.8.
explanations.b: Correct — y_c = (q^2/g)^(1/3) = (4.0/9.8)^(1/3) ≈ 0.742 m, matching the worked example.
explanations.c: 1.40 m is the specific energy E used in the worked example's alternate-depth calculation, not the critical depth.
explanations.d: 2.00 m is just the numeric value of q, not a depth derived from the critical-depth formula.

questions.prompt: At critical depth y_c, how does E_min relate to y_c, and what is Fr there?

options.text: E_min = 2*y_c and Fr = 0
E_min = y_c and Fr < 1
E_min = 1.5*y_c and Fr = 1
E_min = 0.5*y_c and Fr > 1

explanations.a: E_min is not double y_c; this overstates the velocity head's share.
explanations.b: This describes the deep, subcritical limit of the upper branch far from the minimum, not the critical point itself.
explanations.c: Correct — at the curve's minimum, velocity head equals y_c/2, so E_min = y_c + y_c/2 = 1.5*y_c, and this is exactly where V = sqrt(g*y), i.e., Fr = 1.
explanations.d: This understates E_min and misassigns the Froude number; critical flow is exactly Fr = 1, not greater.

questions.prompt: In the E-y diagram, two 'alternate depths' at the same specific energy E represent:

options.text: Two different discharges q passing through the same depth
The same discharge q and same E, but one depth on the subcritical branch and one on the supercritical branch
Measurement error, since a real flow only has one depth for a given E
Two channels of different width carrying unrelated flows

explanations.a: Alternate depths share the same q, not different discharges; the curve is drawn for a single fixed q.
explanations.b: Correct — for a fixed q, a horizontal line at a given E (above E_min) crosses both branches, giving a subcritical depth and a supercritical depth that carry the same discharge with the same specific energy.
explanations.c: This is a real, expected feature of the E-y curve, not an error — it is the same pair of depths that appears across a hydraulic jump or a channel transition.
explanations.d: Both alternate depths belong to the same channel and same q; width is not the variable being compared.

lessons.label: Controls and Transitions: Bumps, Gates and Choking

sections.heading: A smooth bump on the bed does opposite things to the two regimes
sections.body: Consider a smooth, gentle rise of height Δz on an otherwise flat channel bed, with discharge q held constant. Energy is conserved (no losses over a smooth bump), but total head measured from a fixed datum stays constant while the bed itself has risen, so specific energy over the bump must drop by exactly Δz: E2 = E1 - Δz. On the E-y diagram this is just a horizontal step to the left, toward lower E. If the approach flow is subcritical (upper branch), moving left along that branch means the depth y must decrease — the water surface actually dips over the bump, a result that surprises most people the first time they see it. If the approach flow is supercritical (lower branch), moving left along that branch means y must increase — the water surface rises over the same bump. The single diagram predicts both, opposite, correct behaviors just by knowing which branch you started on.

sections.heading: A sluice gate is an upstream control that manufactures supercritical flow
sections.body: A sluice gate — a flat plate lowered partway into the flow — forces water to squeeze under it, and because the gate opening is set by the operator rather than by the flow itself, it fixes the depth immediately downstream of the gate independent of what is happening farther downstream. That forced shallow depth combined with the same discharge q means high velocity, so the jet emerging from under a sluice gate is characteristically supercritical, regardless of whether the approach flow upstream of the gate was subcritical. This is why a sluice gate is called an upstream control: it sets conditions for the flow leaving it, and everything downstream must adjust to what the gate delivers, up until something else (like a hydraulic jump, covered next lesson) intervenes.

sections.heading: Choking: when the bump asks for more than the flow can give
sections.body: The leftward shift E2 = E1 - Δz only works if E2 stays at or above E_min for that discharge — the E-y curve simply does not exist below its nose. If the bump height Δz exceeds the margin (E1 - E_min) available in subcritical approach flow, the flow cannot pass that discharge over the bump at the original upstream depth. The channel responds by damming up: the upstream depth rises until the available specific energy is large enough that E1(new) - Δz just reaches E_min at critical depth on the bump crest. This is called choking, and the bump crest becomes a control section — a specific location where depth and discharge are uniquely tied together (critical depth y_c = (q^2/g)^(1/3)) regardless of what is happening upstream or downstream, making it a natural place to gauge flow, as in a Venturi flume or broad-crested weir.

lessons.workedExample: A wide channel carries q = 1.5 m^2/s at a subcritical approach depth y1 = 1.0 m. Critical depth for this q: y_c = (1.5^2/9.8)^(1/3) = (0.2296)^(1/3) ≈ 0.612 m, so E_min = 1.5*0.612 ≈ 0.918 m. Approach specific energy: E1 = 1.0 + 1.5^2/(2*9.8*1.0^2) = 1.0 + 0.115 ≈ 1.115 m, giving a margin of E1 - E_min ≈ 0.197 m. A bump of Δz = 0.10 m (below the margin) simply dips the surface over the crest, staying subcritical throughout. A bump of Δz = 0.30 m exceeds the 0.197 m margin, so the flow chokes: depth backs up upstream of the bump until a new, higher E1 makes the arithmetic work, and the crest itself runs at exactly critical depth, becoming a control section that fixes the stage-discharge relation there.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the bump problem because 'water dips over a bump in a stream but a car's air rises over a hill in a shock-free supersonic flow' sounds paradoxical until a student can trace both cases through the same E-y (or equivalent compressible) diagram and explain the sign of dy/dz on each branch. The strongest answers go further and explain choking: that a control section is not just 'critical flow happened here' but the direct consequence of the upstream depth being forced to rise because the bump demanded more specific-energy drop than the approach flow could supply. A student who can predict when a given obstruction will choke a channel, not just describe the qualitative dip/rise, has genuinely internalized the diagram.

questions.prompt: Subcritical flow passes over a smooth bump of modest height (no choking). What happens to the water surface directly over the bump?

options.text: It rises, tracking the bed
It dips, because E must drop and moving left on the upper (subcritical) branch means y decreases
It stays perfectly flat regardless of the bump
It oscillates unpredictably

explanations.a: This is the supercritical-flow behavior, not the subcritical case.
explanations.b: Correct — E2 = E1 - Δz shifts the state left on the E-y curve; on the subcritical (upper) branch, lower E corresponds to lower y, so the surface dips.
explanations.c: The surface does respond to the bump; specific energy must drop by exactly the bump height, which forces a depth change.
explanations.d: The response is a deterministic shift on the E-y curve, not an oscillation.

questions.prompt: Why is a sluice gate called an 'upstream control'?

options.text: Because it is always installed at the upstream end of a canal
Because it fixes the depth (and hence the supercritical jet) leaving the gate, and downstream conditions must adjust to what the gate delivers
Because water flows upstream through it
Because it only works when the approach flow is already supercritical

explanations.a: Physical location in a canal is not what defines 'upstream control' in this technical sense.
explanations.b: Correct — the gate opening sets the downstream depth independent of what is farther downstream, producing a supercritical jet that downstream conditions must accommodate.
explanations.c: Flow still moves downstream through a sluice gate; 'upstream control' describes which direction the control's influence propagates, not the flow direction.
explanations.d: A sluice gate produces a supercritical jet regardless of whether the approach flow upstream of the gate was subcritical or supercritical.

questions.prompt: A channel carries q=1.5 m^2/s at subcritical depth y1=1.0 m, giving E1 ≈ 1.115 m and E_min ≈ 0.918 m (margin ≈ 0.197 m). What happens for a bump of Δz = 0.30 m?

options.text: The flow passes smoothly, just dipping slightly more than for a smaller bump
The flow chokes: upstream depth rises until the bump crest reaches exactly critical depth
The bump has no effect because q is held constant
The flow becomes supercritical everywhere upstream of the bump

explanations.a: 0.30 m exceeds the available 0.197 m margin, so the bump demands more E-drop than the approach flow can supply without hitting the curve's nose — smooth passage at the original depth is not possible.
explanations.b: Correct — since Δz exceeds the margin E1 - E_min, the upstream depth must rise (increasing E1) until the crest can just reach critical depth, making the crest a control section.
explanations.c: Holding q constant is exactly why the bump forces E to change; it does not exempt the flow from the bump's effect.
explanations.d: Only the crest reaches critical depth; the upstream approach flow remains subcritical, just at a greater (backed-up) depth than before.

questions.prompt: Order the sequence of events as a subcritical flow encounters a bump tall enough to choke the channel.

items.text: Approach flow is subcritical with specific energy E1 and margin E1 - E_min above critical
The bump's height Δz exceeds the available margin
Upstream depth rises, increasing E1 until the crest can just supply enough drop
The bump crest settles at exactly critical depth, becoming a control section

questions.explanation: The channel starts with some subcritical margin above E_min; when the bump demands more specific-energy drop than that margin allows, the only way to satisfy conservation of q is for the upstream depth (and thus E1) to rise; once E1 is large enough, the crest reaches exactly critical depth and becomes a fixed control section for the discharge.

lessons.label: The Hydraulic Jump

sections.heading: Why the jump needs momentum, not energy
sections.body: A hydraulic jump is the sudden, turbulent transition from supercritical to subcritical flow — a rolling, foaming wall of water where a fast, shallow sheet abruptly becomes a slow, deep pool. It is tempting to analyze it with the E-y diagram, but the jump itself is a violently turbulent, energy-dissipating process, so specific energy is not conserved across it — the entire point of a jump is that it destroys energy. What is conserved is momentum, or more precisely the momentum function (also called specific force), M = q^2/(g*y) + y^2/2, which balances the momentum flux against the hydrostatic pressure force per unit width. Setting M1 = M2 for the same discharge per unit width q and solving for the depth ratio gives the relation named for the French engineer Jean-Baptiste Belanger, who studied the jump in the early nineteenth century: y2/y1 = 0.5*(sqrt(1 + 8*Fr1^2) - 1), where y1 and Fr1 are the supercritical approach depth and Froude number and y2 is the resulting subcritical sequent depth.

sections.heading: How much energy the jump throws away
sections.body: Once y2 is known from Belanger's relation, the energy lost follows directly from the two specific energies, and it collapses to a clean closed form: dE = (y2-y1)^3 / (4*y1*y2). The loss scales steeply with the approach Froude number: at Fr1 ≈ 1.7 the jump is barely dissipative, losing only a few percent of the approach energy; by Fr1 ≈ 9 the loss has climbed to roughly 70% of the incoming specific energy, and only around Fr1 ≈ 20, deep in the strong-jump band, does it reach roughly 85%, converted almost entirely into turbulence, air entrainment, and ultimately heat. This is precisely why engineers deliberately trigger jumps at the base of dams and spillways — a jump is one of the few structures that can destroy an enormous amount of kinetic energy within a channel length of a few jump-heights, protecting the streambed and downstream structures from a supercritical jet that would otherwise scour everything it touched.

sections.heading: The USBR classification and stilling basins
sections.body: The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation catalogued jump appearance against Fr1 into five bands: undular (Fr1 = 1-1.7, barely a jump at all, just a train of standing surface waves with no real turbulent roller), weak jump (1.7-2.5, a low roller with a smooth downstream surface), oscillating jump (2.5-4.5, an unstable jet that intermittently darts along the bed and then the surface, producing troublesome irregular waves that can travel far downstream), steady jump (4.5-9.0, a well-behaved, stable jump that is the design target for most spillway stilling basins because its position barely moves with tailwater fluctuations), and strong jump (Fr1 > 9.0, highly turbulent and effective but rough, often requiring a longer basin). Real stilling basins, such as the USBR's standard Type III design, add chute blocks at the entrance to split and lift the incoming jet, and baffle piers partway down the basin to force additional turbulence and pin the jump in place within a shorter length than a plain concrete apron would need; the higher-velocity Type II design uses chute blocks and a dentated end sill instead, omitting baffle piers because they are prone to cavitation damage at those velocities — deliberately engineering the same mechanism this lesson analyzes.

lessons.workedExample: A spillway delivers water at y1 = 0.4 m and V1 = 8.0 m/s into a stilling basin. First, Fr1 = V1/sqrt(g*y1) = 8.0/sqrt(9.8*0.4) = 8.0/1.98 ≈ 4.04. Because 4.04 is below 4.5, this sits in the USBR 'oscillating jump' band (2.5-4.5), near its upper edge — it has not reached the steady-jump band, which a designer would notice immediately. Belanger's relation gives the sequent depth: y2/y1 = 0.5*(sqrt(1+8*4.04^2) - 1) = 0.5*(sqrt(131.6) - 1) = 0.5*(11.47-1) ≈ 5.24, so y2 ≈ 0.4*5.24 ≈ 2.09 m. Energy loss: dE = (2.09-0.4)^3 / (4*0.4*2.09) = (1.69)^3/3.34 ≈ 4.83/3.34 ≈ 1.45 m, dissipated against an approach specific energy of E1 = 0.4 + 8.0^2/(2*9.8) ≈ 0.4+3.27 = 3.67 m — a loss of roughly 40% of the incoming energy, consistent with an oscillating jump near the top of its Fr1 range. A designer who wanted the stable, wave-free steady jump instead would have to raise Fr1 past 4.5, for example by delivering the same discharge on a shallower, faster approach.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to explain a hydraulic jump is checking for exactly the switch this lesson teaches: recognizing that momentum (specific force), not specific energy, is the conserved quantity across the jump itself, because the jump is precisely where energy is destroyed on purpose. A student who reaches for Bernoulli or the E-y diagram to analyze the jump has missed the point; one who reaches for the momentum balance, computes Fr1, places the jump in the correct USBR band by reading the numeric limits literally, and can explain why the steady band (Fr1 = 4.5-9.0) is the design target for a stilling basin shows real command of the topic, not memorized vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Why is the momentum function (specific force), not specific energy, used to relate depths across a hydraulic jump?

options.text: Because specific energy is easier to measure in the field
Because the jump is a violently turbulent process that destroys energy on purpose, so energy is not conserved across it, while momentum is
Because momentum and energy are always interchangeable in fluid mechanics
Because Belanger only worked with momentum, never energy

explanations.a: Ease of field measurement is not the reason; the physical conservation law is what matters.
explanations.b: Correct — a hydraulic jump dissipates energy by design (turbulence, air entrainment), so specific energy is not conserved across it, whereas the momentum balance (specific force) still holds and gives the sequent-depth relation.
explanations.c: Momentum and energy are distinct conserved quantities that coincide only in loss-free cases; a jump is specifically not loss-free.
explanations.d: The choice is dictated by which physical law actually holds across the jump, not by any one engineer's personal preference.

questions.prompt: A jump has approach depth y1 = 0.4 m and Fr1 ≈ 4.04. Using Belanger's equation, what is the sequent depth y2?

explanations.a: This is far too small a ratio for Fr1 ≈ 4; recompute y2/y1 = 0.5*(sqrt(1+8*Fr1^2)-1).
explanations.b: Still too small; the ratio y2/y1 at Fr1 ≈ 4 is above 5, not 3.
explanations.c: Correct — y2/y1 = 0.5*(sqrt(1+8*4.04^2)-1) ≈ 5.24, so y2 ≈ 0.4*5.24 ≈ 2.09 m, matching the worked example.
explanations.d: This overshoots; check the arithmetic inside the square root before multiplying by y1.

questions.prompt: According to the USBR classification, an approach Froude number Fr1 = 3.0 produces which jump type?

options.text: Undular jump
Weak jump
Oscillating jump
Strong jump

explanations.a: Undular jumps occur at Fr1 = 1-1.7, well below 3.0.
explanations.b: Weak jumps occupy Fr1 = 1.7-2.5, below 3.0.
explanations.c: Correct — the oscillating jump band is Fr1 = 2.5-4.5, and 3.0 falls within it; this is the least desirable band for a stilling basin because the darting jet produces irregular downstream waves.
explanations.d: Strong jumps require Fr1 > 9.0, far above 3.0.

questions.prompt: The worked example's spillway gives Fr1 ≈ 4.04. A designer wants the stable 'steady jump' the USBR recommends for stilling basins. What does Fr1 ≈ 4.04 tell them?

options.text: It is already a steady jump, since 4.04 is close to 4.5
It is an oscillating jump — below the 4.5 threshold — so the approach conditions must change to reach the steady band
It is a strong jump, because the loss is about 40% of the incoming energy
It is an undular jump, because no roller forms below Fr1 = 4.5

explanations.a: The bands are read literally: the steady band starts at Fr1 = 4.5, and 4.04 is below it, so this is not a steady jump no matter how close the number looks.
explanations.b: Correct — 2.5 < 4.04 < 4.5 puts it in the oscillating band, the one that sends irregular waves downstream; reaching the steady band requires pushing Fr1 above 4.5, for instance with a shallower, faster approach.
explanations.c: Strong jumps require Fr1 > 9.0; the ~40% energy loss here is consistent with an oscillating jump, not a strong one.
explanations.d: Undular jumps are confined to Fr1 = 1-1.7, and a well-developed roller certainly forms at Fr1 ≈ 4.

questions.prompt: Why do engineers add chute blocks and baffle piers to a spillway stilling basin?

options.text: To smooth the flow and prevent a hydraulic jump from forming at all
To deliberately force additional turbulence and pin the jump in place, letting the basin be shorter than a plain apron would need
To increase the approach Froude number as much as possible
To convert supercritical flow into critical flow without any energy loss

explanations.a: The basin is designed to encourage, not prevent, a jump — the jump is the energy-dissipating mechanism the structure relies on.
explanations.b: Correct — chute blocks split and lift the incoming jet and baffle piers add turbulence, stabilizing the jump's location and shortening the basin length needed compared to a plain concrete apron.
explanations.c: Raising Fr1 would only make the incoming jet faster and more erosive; the basin's job is to dissipate the energy already present, not to add to it.
explanations.d: The entire mechanism relies on the energy loss dE across the jump; a loss-free transition to critical flow is not what a stilling basin does.

lessons.label: The Circular Jump in Your Sink

sections.heading: Same physics, radial geometry
sections.body: Turn on a kitchen tap over a flat sink or plate and watch the thin, fast, glassy disk of water spreading out from the impact point — then, at some radius, it abruptly thickens into a slower, rougher, deeper annular ring. That ring is a hydraulic jump, the same subcritical/supercritical transition from the previous lesson, just wrapped into a circle instead of laid out across a straight channel. Inside the ring the film is thin and moving fast (supercritical, Fr>1); outside it the water is deeper and slower (subcritical, Fr<1). The everyday version of this was noted qualitatively decades before a real predictive account arrived.

sections.heading: Watson's boundary-layer theory of the jump radius
sections.body: E.J. Watson published the definitive analysis in 1964 ('The radial spread of a liquid jet over a horizontal plane'), treating the thin outward-spreading film as a growing viscous boundary layer superimposed on an inviscid outer flow, then locating the jump where that boundary layer's momentum deficit forces the abrupt thickening. Watson's theory predicts the jump radius R scales with the volumetric flow rate Q and the kinematic viscosity nu roughly as R ∝ Q^(5/8) * nu^(-3/8) — notably independent of gravity in the regime where surface tension and gravity are both secondary to viscous stresses within the thin film. The 5/8 power on Q means the jump radius grows a good deal slower than flow rate itself: doubling the tap's flow rate roughly 1.5x's the radius, not doubles it, a prediction a sink and a stopwatch can actually check.

sections.heading: Not always a clean circle: polygons and undulations
sections.body: At low flow rates the circular jump can lose its symmetry entirely. Ellegaard and coworkers reported in a 1998 study that under certain depth and flow conditions the jump front distorts into a stable polygon — a triangle, square, pentagon, or hexagon of standing corners rotating slowly or holding still — driven by an instability in the separated flow at the jump rather than any asymmetry in the tap or sink. Very low, gentle flows can instead show an undular circular jump, echoing the undular straight jump from the previous lesson's USBR classification: a train of smooth standing ripples around the jump radius rather than one sharp turbulent step. Both effects mean 'the jump radius' is only cleanly defined for the ordinary, higher-flow circular case a student is most likely to measure at home.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test Watson's Q^(5/8) scaling with kitchen equipment: a 1-liter measuring jug, a stopwatch, a ruler, and a flat dinner plate held level in the sink. Procedure: fill the jug, time how long it takes to empty at a fixed tap opening to get Q (liters per second), pour onto the plate's center from a fixed, low height to minimize impact-splash effects, let the jump stabilize for a few seconds, then measure the jump radius with the ruler at four points around the ring and average them (the ring is rarely perfectly circular in practice). Repeating at three or four different tap openings (three or four different Q values) and plotting log(R) against log(Q) should give a line with a slope near 5/8 = 0.625 if Watson's scaling holds — a genuinely testable, quantitative science-fair result from equipment already in the kitchen. A second, qualitative test: slowly raise the plate's edge or add water to the sink basin to raise the downstream (outer) water level, and watch the jump radius shrink inward as the deeper tailwater reduces the sequent-depth ratio needed to sustain it, the same downstream-control idea from the controls lesson.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots a 'circular hydraulic jump in a sink' project is checking whether the student sees it as the exact same physics as the straight jump earlier in the unit, applied in radial geometry, rather than as an unrelated curiosity. The strongest students can state Watson's scaling law, explain that it comes from treating the spreading film as a growing boundary layer (not from a simple force balance), and have actually measured a log-log slope against flow rate rather than just photographed the ring. A student who additionally demonstrates that raising the downstream water level pulls the jump inward — connecting circular jump position to the same downstream-control concept as a straight-channel jump — shows the concept transferred, not just replicated in a novel container.

questions.prompt: What is the flow regime just inside versus just outside the circular hydraulic jump ring in a sink?

options.text: Inside is subcritical and thick; outside is supercritical and thin
Inside is supercritical and thin; outside is subcritical and thicker
Both sides are supercritical, differing only in temperature
The ring marks a boundary between laminar and turbulent flow only, with no Froude-number change

explanations.a: This reverses the actual regimes; the fast, thin film is closest to the tap's impact point, inside the ring.
explanations.b: Correct — inside the ring the film is thin and fast (supercritical, Fr>1); outside it thickens and slows abruptly (subcritical, Fr<1), the same regime change as a straight-channel jump.
explanations.c: The defining change across the jump is depth/speed (and hence Fr), not temperature.
explanations.d: The jump is specifically a supercritical-to-subcritical (Fr) transition, the same physics as the straight hydraulic jump, not merely a laminar/turbulent boundary.

questions.prompt: Watson's 1964 analysis modeled the spreading film's radial growth using what approach?

options.text: A simple hydrostatic pressure balance, ignoring viscosity entirely
A growing viscous boundary layer within the thin film, with the jump located where its momentum deficit forces abrupt thickening
A direct analogy to sound waves in air
Measurement of surface tension alone, with viscosity treated as negligible

explanations.a: Watson's treatment is explicitly a boundary-layer (viscous) analysis, not a purely hydrostatic one.
explanations.b: Correct — Watson treated the outward film as a growing viscous boundary layer under an inviscid outer flow, locating the jump where the boundary layer's momentum deficit forces the thickening.
explanations.c: The analysis is a fluid boundary-layer theory, not an acoustic analogy.
explanations.d: Viscosity is central to Watson's scaling (R ∝ nu^(-3/8)); it is not treated as negligible.

questions.prompt: A student doubles the tap's flow rate Q while holding viscosity fixed. Per Watson's scaling R ∝ Q^(5/8), roughly what happens to the jump radius R?

options.text: R stays exactly the same
R roughly doubles
R increases by a factor of about 1.5, less than doubling
R decreases

explanations.a: R does depend on Q; it is not constant.
explanations.b: A full doubling would require R ∝ Q^1, but the exponent is 5/8, not 1.
explanations.c: Correct — 2^(5/8) ≈ 1.54, so doubling Q increases R by roughly 1.5x, not a full doubling, exactly as the lesson describes.
explanations.d: R increases with Q since the exponent 5/8 is positive; it does not decrease.

questions.prompt: What did Ellegaard and coworkers (1998) report about circular hydraulic jumps at certain low flow conditions?

options.text: The jump front can distort into a stable rotating or stationary polygon shape
The jump disappears entirely below a critical flow rate
The jump radius becomes independent of flow rate at low Q
The jump only forms in zero gravity

explanations.a: Correct — under certain conditions the jump loses circular symmetry and forms a stable polygon (triangle through hexagon and beyond), an instability in the separated flow at the jump itself.
explanations.b: The lesson describes altered shapes (polygonal, undular) at low flow, not disappearance of the jump.
explanations.c: No such independence from flow rate is described; Watson's Q-dependence is the general scaling result discussed in this unit.
explanations.d: The jump is a gravity/viscosity-dependent phenomenon studied at ordinary sink conditions, not a zero-gravity effect.

units.label: Open-Channel Flow: Manning, Roughness & Water-Surface Profiles

lessons.label: Uniform Flow: Chezy and Manning

sections.heading: Normal depth: gravity down the slope versus friction on the bed
sections.body: In steady, uniform open-channel flow the depth stops changing along the channel because two forces exactly balance: the downslope component of gravity pulling the water forward, and the shear resistance the bed and banks exert backward. For a channel of slope S carrying a flow of cross-sectional area A, wetted perimeter P, and hydraulic radius R = A/P, that balance reduces to a strikingly simple result: the average bed shear stress is tau_0 = rho*g*R*S. The depth at which this balance holds for a given discharge is called the normal depth, and it is the flow condition a channel settles into far from any gate, weir, or slope break.

sections.heading: Chezy's formula and its French-canal origins
sections.body: The first working resistance law for open channels came from Antoine Chezy, a French engineer who derived V = C*sqrt(R*S) in 1769 while sizing a canal to supply water to Paris. The Chezy coefficient C absorbed all the friction physics into one empirical number, and for over a century engineers had to guess C from tables of prior canals with roughly similar beds.

sections.heading: Manning's power-law refinement, and the hydraulic radius
sections.body: In 1889 the Irish engineer Robert Manning presented a refinement to the Institution of Civil Engineers of Ireland, proposing that C should scale as R^(1/6)/n, which turns Chezy's law into the now-standard Manning equation: V = (k/n)*R^(2/3)*S^(1/2), where n is the Manning roughness coefficient and k is a unit-conversion constant equal to 1.0 in SI units (meters, seconds) and 1.486 in US customary units (feet, seconds) — the 1.486 exists purely to convert R from feet into the meters Manning's empirical R^(2/3) was fit against, not a different physical law. Hydraulic radius R = A/P is the geometric heart of both formulas: it measures how much cross-sectional area is available per unit of wetted, friction-generating boundary. In a very wide, shallow channel the two banks contribute almost nothing to the wetted perimeter compared with the wide bed, so P approaches the top width and R collapses to approximately the flow depth y — a useful shortcut for wide rivers and floodplains. For a trapezoidal channel, A and P are both functions of depth y, so Q(y) = (k/n)*A(y)*R(y)^(2/3)*S^(1/2) has no closed-form inverse; engineers find the normal depth by iterating a guessed y until Q(y) matches the design discharge.

lessons.workedExample: Size a trapezoidal drainage channel with bottom width b = 3 m, side slopes 2:1 (horizontal:vertical), bed slope S = 0.001, and n = 0.025, to carry Q = 10 m^3/s. Guess y = 1.5 m: A = (3 + 2*1.5)*1.5 = 9.0 m^2, P = 3 + 2*1.5*sqrt(5) = 9.71 m, R = 0.927 m, giving Q = (1/0.025)*9.0*0.927^(2/3)*0.001^0.5 = 10.8 m^3/s — slightly too much. Try y = 1.45 m: A = 8.56 m^2, P = 9.48 m, R = 0.902 m, Q = 10.1 m^3/s. Normal depth is therefore about 1.45 m — found by iterating the Manning equation, not by solving it directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does that depth stay the same downstream?' to check whether a student understands normal depth as a force balance rather than a formula to plug numbers into. The tell of real understanding is explaining that tau_0 = rho*g*R*S is bed shear balancing gravity, and that R = A/P is why a wide, shallow channel behaves almost like an infinite flat bed (R ≈ y) while a narrow deep one does not. A student who can also say why they had to iterate — because A and P both depend on the unknown y — rather than treating the Manning equation as directly solvable, has shown they understand the geometry, not just memorized the formula.

questions.prompt: At normal (uniform) depth, what two things are in balance?

options.text: The downslope component of gravity and the bed/bank shear resistance
The channel's inlet velocity and outlet velocity
Atmospheric pressure and hydrostatic pressure
The Manning n of the bed and the Manning n of the banks

explanations.a: Correct — uniform flow occurs when the downslope pull of gravity on the water exactly equals the frictional shear resistance from the wetted boundary, giving tau_0 = rho*g*R*S.
explanations.b: Uniform flow means velocity is constant along the reach, not that inlet and outlet velocities are separately balancing anything.
explanations.c: Pressure balance describes hydrostatics, not the force balance that defines normal depth in open-channel flow.
explanations.d: n is a single roughness coefficient assigned to the wetted perimeter, not two separate balancing values for bed and bank.

questions.prompt: Why does the Manning equation use k = 1.486 instead of k = 1.0 when working in feet and seconds?

options.text: Because friction physically increases in US customary units
It is purely a unit-conversion factor for R^(2/3) between feet and the meters the formula was empirically fit against
Because Robert Manning worked exclusively with imperial canals
It corrects for gravity being different in feet versus meters

explanations.a: Friction is a physical property of the boundary and flow, not something that changes with the unit system used to describe it.
explanations.b: Correct — since R^(2/3) is a fractional power, converting feet to meters does not cancel out with a simple 1:1 factor, so 1.486 is the residual conversion constant, not new physics.
explanations.c: Manning's formula and its constant are unit-system artifacts of the R^(2/3) exponent, unrelated to which canals he personally studied.
explanations.d: Gravitational acceleration g does not appear explicitly in the Manning equation at all; the constant is about converting R's units, not g.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in uniform-flow calculations.

left.text: Behavior of R in a very wide, shallow channel

right.text: Cross-sectional area divided by wetted perimeter
Approaches the flow depth y, since banks contribute little to P
Empirical single number absorbing all resistance physics in V = C*sqrt(R*S)
Empirical coefficient scaling resistance as R^(1/6)/n in Manning's refinement

questions.explanation: R = A/P is the geometric ratio at the core of both formulas; in a wide channel the wetted perimeter is dominated by the bed so R approaches y; Chezy's C is a single empirical resistance number from 1769; Manning's n plays the analogous role in the 1889 refinement V = (k/n)*R^(2/3)*S^(1/2).

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding the normal depth of a trapezoidal channel by iteration.

items.text: Guess a trial depth y
Compute A(y) and P(y) from the trapezoid geometry
Compute R = A/P and evaluate Q(y) with the Manning equation
Compare Q(y) to the target discharge and adjust y
Repeat until Q(y) converges to the design discharge

questions.explanation: Because A and P both depend on the unknown depth, Q(y) cannot be inverted algebraically — you guess y, compute the geometry and resulting Q, compare against the target, adjust, and repeat until convergence.

lessons.label: Choosing n: Roughness, Vegetation and Compound Channels

sections.heading: n is a resistance coefficient, not a material property
sections.body: Manning's n is often taught as if it were looked up like a density, but it is really a lumped resistance coefficient standing in for grain friction, bedforms, vegetation drag, and channel irregularity all at once. Typical published values span a huge range: about 0.010 for smooth glass or PVC, 0.013 for finished concrete, roughly 0.030 for a natural gravel-bed stream, and anywhere from 0.05 to 0.15 for a floodplain thick with brush or trees, since standing stems generate form drag far beyond what grain size alone predicts.

sections.heading: Cowan's method: building n from its parts
sections.body: Because no single lookup table captures a real channel, Cowan proposed in 1956 an additive method still used today: n = (n0 + n1 + n2 + n3 + n4) * m5, where n0 is a base value for the bed material, n1 adds for surface irregularity, n2 for variation in cross-section shape along the reach, n3 for obstructions like debris or piers, n4 for vegetation, and m5 is a multiplier correcting for channel meandering. Each term is chosen from a table of qualitative severity (minor, moderate, severe), so two engineers looking at the same reach can still assemble noticeably different n values — the method disciplines the estimate without eliminating judgment. Representative increments make the additive formula concrete rather than just qualitative: n0 runs about 0.02-0.03 for a sand or gravel bed, each of n1 through n4 typically adds roughly 0.005-0.020 depending on whether the severity is judged minor or severe, and the meander multiplier m5 runs about 1.0 for a straight reach up to roughly 1.3 for a strongly sinuous one — so a moderately irregular, lightly vegetated gravel reach might sum to n0 0.025 + n1 0.010 + n2 0.005 + n3 0.005 + n4 0.010 = 0.055, then times m5 1.15 for a meandering channel, giving n ≈ 0.063.

sections.heading: n changes with stage and season — and Q is directly proportional to it
sections.body: A single n value is a snapshot, not a constant: submerged grass flattens and its drag drops as flow rises, while a dry-season channel choked with summer vegetation can have double the n of the same channel in winter. Because Manning's equation gives Q = (k/n)*A*R^(2/3)*S^(1/2), discharge is directly, linearly proportional to 1/n — a 20% error in the assumed n produces a 20% error in the predicted discharge, with no cushioning exponent to shrink the mistake. For a compound channel — a deep main channel flanked by a shallow, rougher floodplain — using one averaged n and one averaged R badly misrepresents the flow, since velocities in the two zones differ sharply. The standard fix, the divided-channel method, splits the cross-section into main-channel and floodplain panels at the break in depth, computes each panel's conveyance K = (1/n)*A*R^(2/3) separately, and sums the panel conveyances before multiplying by sqrt(S) to get total discharge.

lessons.workedExample: A flooding river has a main channel with A = 40 m^2, R = 1.8 m, n = 0.035, plus a brushy floodplain panel with A = 60 m^2, R = 0.6 m, n = 0.08, on a slope S = 0.0009. Divided-channel method: K_main = (1/0.035)*40*1.8^(2/3) = 1691, K_floodplain = (1/0.08)*60*0.6^(2/3) = 534. Total conveyance K = 2225, so Q = K*sqrt(0.0009) = 2225*0.03 = 66.7 m^3/s — computed by summing two panels rather than forcing one blended n across the whole irregular section.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how did you choose your Manning n?' is testing whether a student treated n as a single confident lookup or as the genuinely uncertain input it is. The strong answer names a method — Cowan's additive breakdown, or at least acknowledging vegetation and season change n — and states the consequence: since Q is directly proportional to 1/n, an unjustified n choice propagates one-for-one into the discharge estimate. A student who also knows a compound channel needs to be split into panels, rather than averaged into one R, shows they understand why real rivers resist a single-number treatment.

questions.prompt: Why is n for a dense vegetated floodplain (0.05-0.15) so much higher than n for finished concrete (0.013)?

options.text: Vegetated floodplains always have steeper bed slopes
Standing stems generate form drag far beyond what grain-size friction alone would predict
Floodplains are always shallower, and n depends directly on depth
Concrete channels are always artificially widened

explanations.a: Bed slope is a separate term (S) in Manning's equation; it is not what n represents.
explanations.b: Correct — vegetation adds form drag from flow separating around stems and branches, a resistance mechanism grain-size-based roughness values do not capture.
explanations.c: Depth affects R, a separate variable from n; n itself is meant to describe the boundary's resistance character, not the depth.
explanations.d: Channel width is unrelated to why n differs between a smooth lining and a vegetated surface.

questions.prompt: If your assumed Manning n is 20% too low, what happens to your predicted discharge using Q = (k/n)*A*R^(2/3)*S^(1/2)?

options.text: Predicted Q is roughly 20% too high, since Q is directly proportional to 1/n
Predicted Q is roughly 40% too high, since n enters squared
Predicted Q is unaffected, since A and R absorb the error
Predicted Q is roughly 20% too low

explanations.a: Correct — n appears to the first power in the denominator, so Q scales as 1/n directly; a 20% low n gives a 20% high Q.
explanations.b: n is not squared in Manning's equation; only R carries a fractional exponent (2/3), and A, S carry their own separate exponents.
explanations.c: A and R are independent geometric quantities; they do not compensate for an error in the separately estimated n.
explanations.d: An n that is too low means less assumed resistance, which increases predicted Q, not decreases it.

questions.prompt: Match each Cowan (1956) term to what it accounts for in n = (n0 + n1 + n2 + n3 + n4) * m5.

right.text: Base value for the bed material
Surface irregularity
Variation in cross-section shape along the reach
Obstructions such as debris or piers
Vegetation

questions.explanation: Cowan's additive method decomposes n into a base material value (n0) plus four correction terms for irregularity, cross-section variation, obstructions, and vegetation, then applies a meander multiplier m5 to the sum.

questions.prompt: Why does the divided-channel method split a compound section into main-channel and floodplain panels instead of using one averaged n and R?

options.text: Because Manning's equation cannot be applied to any composite shape
Because the main channel and floodplain have sharply different depths, roughness, and velocities, so one blended R misrepresents the flow
Because floodplains never actually convey any discharge
Because n0 in Cowan's method requires separate panels by definition

explanations.a: Manning's equation can be applied to any single panel; the issue is that a single blended R across dissimilar zones distorts the result, not that the equation is inapplicable.
explanations.b: Correct — the main channel is typically deep and smoother while the floodplain is shallow and rougher, so summing separate panel conveyances captures the real velocity contrast that one averaged R would hide.
explanations.c: Floodplains do convey real discharge during floods, which is exactly why they need their own conveyance term rather than being ignored.
explanations.d: Cowan's method estimates n for a single panel; it does not itself require splitting a compound channel — that requirement comes from the conveyance geometry, not from Cowan's formula.

lessons.label: Channel Geometry and Design

sections.heading: The best hydraulic section: minimizing wetted perimeter
sections.body: For a fixed cross-sectional area A and slope S, Manning's equation shows conveyance rises as R^(2/3) = (A/P)^(2/3) — so for a given area, the shape that minimizes the wetted perimeter P maximizes conveyance and lets you move the design discharge through the smallest, cheapest excavation. Among all shapes, a semicircle is the theoretical optimum: no other shape encloses a given area with less perimeter. Open channels are rarely built as semicircles because vertical or near-vertical banks are unstable in earth, so engineers instead use the best hydraulic trapezoid: geometrically, this is half of a regular hexagon, with side slopes set at 60 degrees from horizontal. That shape has the elegant property that its hydraulic radius equals exactly half the depth, R = y/2 — the closest an excavatable trapezoid can get to the semicircle's efficiency.

sections.heading: Freeboard and side-slope stability
sections.body: Freeboard is the extra wall or bank height built above the design water surface, protecting against wind waves, superelevation on bends, wall settlement, and the inevitable uncertainty in the n and Q used for design; it is not extra conveyance capacity, and typical practice adds anywhere from a few tenths of a meter up to a fraction of the design depth. Side-slope choice is separately governed by soil mechanics: an unlined earth channel in sandy loam typically cannot stand steeper than about 2:1 (horizontal:vertical) without slumping, while a rock-cut or lined channel can go far steeper, even vertical.

sections.heading: Design methods, and the modern tension with naturalized channels
sections.body: Two classical methods keep an erodible channel from washing itself out. The permissible-velocity method, formalized in tables like Fortier and Scobey's 1926 compilation, simply caps the mean channel velocity below a threshold the bed material can withstand — around 0.6 m/s for a sandy loam, higher for cohesive clay or riprap. The tractive-force method is more rigorous: rather than capping an average velocity, it limits the local boundary shear stress (which is not uniform around the wetted perimeter) to a permissible tractive force for the lining material, catching erosion risk near the toe of the banks that a single average velocity would miss. Modern channel design increasingly pulls against pure conveyance efficiency: stream restoration projects deliberately reintroduce meanders, riffle-pool sequences, and bank vegetation — raising n and reducing hydraulic efficiency on purpose — to restore habitat, sediment transport balance, and geomorphic stability that a straightened, smooth-lined channel destroys.

lessons.workedExample: A drainage engineer compares a standard trapezoidal channel to the best hydraulic trapezoid for the same discharge. For depth y = 2 m, the best hydraulic trapezoid uses side slopes at 60 degrees (z = 1/sqrt(3) horizontal:vertical) and bottom width b = 2y/sqrt(3) = 2.31 m, giving A = 6.93 m^2 and, by the shape's defining property, R = y/2 = 1.0 m exactly — noticeably better than a conventional b = 3 m, z = 1.5 trapezoid of similar area, which typically yields R around 0.85-0.9 m for the same footprint, meaning more excavation is needed to carry the same flow.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why that cross-section shape?' is testing whether a student picked dimensions arbitrarily or understood that shape controls hydraulic radius, and hydraulic radius controls conveyance for a given excavation cost. The strongest answer names the best-hydraulic-trapezoid property (R = y/2, half-hexagon side slopes) and can also explain why a real design does not chase pure efficiency — freeboard, side-slope stability, and increasingly the deliberate trade of efficiency for habitat value in naturalized channels. A student who conflates freeboard with extra capacity, or cannot say which design method (permissible-velocity vs. tractive-force) they used to size an erodible channel, has not internalized the difference between an efficient shape and a stable one.

questions.prompt: Why does a semicircle minimize the wetted perimeter for a given cross-sectional area?

options.text: It is a geometric property: among all shapes enclosing a fixed area, the semicircle uses the least boundary length
Because water naturally seeks a circular cross-section under gravity
Because n is always lowest for curved surfaces
Because a semicircle always has the steepest bed slope

explanations.a: Correct — this is a pure geometric optimization result, independent of the material or roughness: no shape encloses a given area with a shorter perimeter than a circle (or half-circle, for an open channel).
explanations.b: Gravity governs flow depth and slope, not the cross-sectional shape a channel is excavated into.
explanations.c: n is a property of the surface material and irregularity, not of the geometric curvature of the shape.
explanations.d: Bed slope S is an independent design variable set by topography, unrelated to why the semicircle minimizes perimeter.

questions.prompt: What defines the 'best hydraulic trapezoid'?

options.text: A trapezoid with vertical side walls and no bottom width
Half of a regular hexagon: 60-degree side slopes, giving R = y/2
A trapezoid whose bottom width equals its depth
Any trapezoid lined with concrete

explanations.a: Vertical walls are unstable in earth and are exactly what the trapezoidal compromise avoids; that is not the best hydraulic trapezoid.
explanations.b: Correct — the best hydraulic trapezoid is geometrically half of a regular hexagon, with 60-degree side slopes, and it has the defining property R = y/2.
explanations.c: That relationship is not the defining property; the best hydraulic trapezoid's defining feature is R = y/2, tied to the 60-degree side slopes.
explanations.d: Lining material affects n and erosion resistance, not the geometric optimum shape being described here.

questions.prompt: What is freeboard for?

options.text: To increase the channel's design discharge capacity
To accommodate waves, superelevation on bends, settlement, and uncertainty above the design water surface
To reduce Manning's n
To replace the need for side-slope stability analysis

explanations.a: Freeboard is extra wall/bank height above the design water surface — it is a safety margin, not part of the flow capacity calculation itself.
explanations.b: Correct — freeboard protects against waves, bend superelevation, settlement, and the inherent uncertainty in n and Q used to set the design depth.
explanations.c: Freeboard is a geometric height allowance; it has no direct effect on the roughness coefficient n.
explanations.d: Side-slope stability is a separate soil-mechanics question about how steep the banks can safely stand; freeboard does not substitute for it.

questions.prompt: Match each design approach to what it directly limits or achieves.

right.text: Caps the mean channel velocity below an erosion threshold for the bed material
Limits the local boundary shear stress around the wetted perimeter
Deliberately raises n and lowers conveyance efficiency to restore habitat and geomorphic function

questions.explanation: The permissible-velocity method (e.g., Fortier and Scobey, 1926) caps an average velocity; the tractive-force method is the more rigorous approach limiting local boundary shear stress; naturalized channel restoration intentionally sacrifices conveyance efficiency for ecological and geomorphic benefits.

lessons.label: Gradually Varied Flow and Backwater Curves

sections.heading: The GVF equation and its singularity at critical depth
sections.body: When depth changes gradually along a channel — because of a dam, bridge, weir, or slope break — the flow is no longer uniform, but it is close enough to steady, one-dimensional, and hydrostatic that an energy balance still applies at each cross-section. That balance yields the gradually varied flow (GVF) equation: dy/dx = (S0 - Sf) / (1 - Fr^2), where S0 is the bed slope, Sf is the friction slope (the energy grade line's slope, from Manning's equation), and Fr is the Froude number. As Fr approaches 1 — flow passing through critical depth — the denominator goes to zero and dy/dx mathematically blows up. Physically this signals that the GVF approximation itself is breaking down: near critical depth the water surface curves so sharply that vertical accelerations, which GVF assumes are negligible, are no longer small, and the transition is better described as rapidly varied flow.

sections.heading: Classifying profiles: M and S curves
sections.body: Profiles are classified by the channel's slope type and where the actual depth sits relative to normal depth yn and critical depth yc. On a mild slope (yn > yc), an M1 curve lies above both — the classic backwater profile piling up behind a dam or weir, asymptotically approaching normal depth far upstream. M2 lies between yn and yc, a drawdown curve typically seen where a mild channel steepens or approaches a free overfall. M3 lies below yc, a rare, rapidly rising profile downstream of a sluice gate on a mild slope. On a steep slope (yn < yc), the labels flip: S1 lies above yc (a backwater from a downstream control forcing subcritical flow onto a steep bed), S2 lies between yc and yn (drawdown), and S3 lies below yn (an accelerating profile downstream of a gate).

sections.heading: The standard step method, and how it becomes a floodplain map
sections.body: Computing a profile numerically uses the standard step method: the channel is divided into cross-sections, and the energy equation is solved between adjacent sections for the unknown depth, marching outward from a known control. Because subcritical flow (M1, M2, S1) is controlled from downstream — a weir or channel constriction sets the depth there and the effect propagates upstream — computation marches upstream from that known point. Supercritical flow (M3, S2, S3) is controlled from upstream, so computation marches downstream instead. This is exactly the computation the US Army Corps of Engineers' HEC-RAS software performs at hundreds of surveyed cross-sections along a real river reach, stepping the standard-step method through each one to build the water-surface profile that becomes a FEMA-style floodplain inundation map.

lessons.workedExample: A river with bed slope S0 = 0.0004 (mild) and n = 0.03 has normal depth yn = 1.8 m and critical depth yc = 1.0 m for its design discharge. A highway bridge constricts the channel and forces the water surface up to 2.8 m right at the bridge. Since 2.8 m > yn (1.8 m) > yc (1.0 m), this is an M1 backwater curve.
