Because it is subcritical, the standard step method marches upstream from the bridge: stepping upstream, the computed depth decays from 2.8 m toward normal depth, reaching about 1.83 m — within a few centimeters of yn — roughly 4 km upstream, which defines the effective length of the bridge's backwater influence.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes GVF profile classification to see whether a student can predict the shape of a real backwater rather than just naming 'M1' from a table. The strong answer explains the mechanism: dy/dx = (S0-Sf)/(1-Fr^2) means the profile's curvature depends on how far the flow sits from both normal and critical depth, and that the denominator's behavior near Fr = 1 is a real physical warning sign, not a computational bug. Knowing that subcritical profiles are computed marching upstream from a downstream control (and supercritical the reverse) — and that this is literally what HEC-RAS does at every cross-section to build a floodplain map — distinguishes a student who understands the physics from one who has only memorized the M1-M2-M3 labels.

questions.prompt: What happens to dy/dx in the GVF equation as the Froude number Fr approaches 1?

options.text: It approaches zero, meaning the profile becomes perfectly flat
The denominator (1 - Fr^2) approaches zero, so dy/dx becomes very large — the GVF approximation breaks down near critical depth
It has no special behavior; Fr does not appear in the denominator
S0 and Sf both become zero simultaneously

explanations.a: A vanishing denominator drives dy/dx toward very large values, not zero — this is the opposite of a flat profile.
explanations.b: Correct — as Fr -> 1, (1 - Fr^2) -> 0, causing dy/dx to become very steep, which signals that the gradually varied flow assumption (negligible vertical acceleration) is failing near critical depth.
explanations.c: Fr is exactly the term in the denominator that drives this behavior; it is central to the equation, not absent from it.
explanations.d: S0 is a fixed bed slope and Sf depends on friction and depth; neither is forced to zero by Fr approaching 1.

questions.prompt: Match each profile label to its defining condition.

right.text: Mild slope, depth above both normal and critical depth (backwater, e.g. behind a dam)
Mild slope, depth between critical and normal depth (drawdown)
Steep slope, depth above critical depth (backwater forced by a downstream control)
Steep slope, depth below normal depth (accelerating flow below a gate)

questions.explanation: On a mild slope, M1 sits above yn and yc (a classic dam backwater), M2 sits between yc and yn (drawdown). On a steep slope, S1 sits above yc (a downstream control forcing subcritical flow), and S3 sits below yn (accelerating flow below a gate).

questions.prompt: In the standard step method, why does computation for a subcritical (M1) profile march upstream starting from a downstream control like a weir?

options.text: Because subcritical flow information propagates upstream, so the downstream control depth determines the whole backwater shape
Because it is computationally simpler regardless of the physics
Because supercritical flow requires marching upstream instead
Because normal depth is always found downstream of critical depth

explanations.a: Correct — in subcritical flow, disturbances travel upstream, so a downstream control like a weir sets the depth there and its influence must be marched upstream from that known point.
explanations.b: The marching direction is dictated by which way flow information physically propagates, not by computational convenience.
explanations.c: Supercritical flow is controlled from upstream, so its standard-step marching direction is downstream, the opposite of the subcritical case.
explanations.d: The relative position of normal and critical depth defines the slope type (mild vs. steep), not the marching direction, which depends on subcritical vs. supercritical flow.

questions.prompt: How does software like HEC-RAS build a floodplain inundation map?

options.text: By interpolating satellite flood photographs from past storms
By computing the standard-step GVF profile at many surveyed cross-sections along the reach
By assuming uniform (normal-depth) flow everywhere along the river
By solving the Shields equation at each cross-section

explanations.a: Satellite imagery may validate a model but is not how the water-surface elevations themselves are computed for a design event.
explanations.b: Correct — HEC-RAS steps the standard-step method through each surveyed cross-section to compute the gradually varied water-surface profile, which is then mapped onto terrain to show inundation extent.
explanations.c: Assuming uniform flow would ignore exactly the backwater effects (bridges, weirs, constrictions) that GVF and the standard step method are built to capture.
explanations.d: The Shields equation concerns sediment incipient motion, not water-surface elevation computation for flood mapping.

lessons.label: Incipient Motion: Shields and Hjulstrom

sections.heading: The Shields parameter: when does a grain start to move?
sections.body: A sediment grain resting on a streambed stays put as long as the driving force from bed shear is smaller than the resisting force from its submerged weight and friction with neighboring grains. Shields nondimensionalized this competition in a 1936 doctoral dissertation at the Prussian civil engineering research institute in Berlin, defining the Shields parameter tau* = tau_0 / ((rho_s - rho)*g*d), where tau_0 is the bed shear stress, rho_s and rho are sediment and fluid density, and d is grain diameter. Motion begins once tau* exceeds a critical value tau*_c, and for fully rough turbulent flow — coarse grains at high grain Reynolds number — tau*_c is commonly cited as approximately 0.06.

sections.heading: A band, not a line: the real scatter in Shields' data
sections.body: That single number 0.06 hides substantial scatter. Shields' original curve was already a wide band, and later reanalyses — notably Buffington and Montgomery's 1997 review — found that published critical values for the same grain conditions range roughly from 0.03 to 0.07, largely because 'incipient motion' is inherently subjective: different researchers used different visual criteria for when a bed counted as 'moving,' from the first occasional grain wobble to a measurable transport rate. The lesson for a science-fair project is not to treat 0.06 as a precise constant but to report it as a threshold estimate with an honest uncertainty band.

sections.heading: Hjulstrom's diagram, cohesion, and dam-downstream armouring
sections.body: In 1935 the Swedish geographer Hjulstrom, working from a doctoral dissertation at Uppsala, published a different but complementary picture: a diagram plotting velocity against grain size, with separate curves for erosion, transport, and deposition. Its most striking feature is that the minimum velocity needed to erode a bed occurs for fine sand — roughly 0.1 to 0.3 mm — around 20 cm/s. Coarser material needs more velocity because it is heavier; but finer material, silt and clay, also needs more velocity to erode than fine sand does, because cohesive electrochemical bonds between clay particles resist detachment even though each particle is individually tiny and light. Once entrained, particles keep moving at velocities below the erosion threshold, which is why the diagram's transport zone extends to lower velocities than the erosion curve, with deposition only below the still-lower settling-velocity curve. A related field phenomenon is bed armouring downstream of a dam: the dam traps the river's natural sediment supply, so the clear-water releases below it winnow away fine material from the bed while leaving the coarser grains behind as a resistant armor layer, changing the channel's erosion behavior for years afterward.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate the critical shear stress to move d = 20 mm gravel (rho_s = 2650 kg/m^3, rho = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.81 m/s^2) using tau*_c = 0.06: tau_c = 0.06 * (2650-1000) * 9.81 * 0.02 = 0.06 * 1650 * 9.81 * 0.02 = 19.4 Pa. On the Hjulstrom diagram, a 20 mm particle sits well into the coarse-gravel range, consistent with needing a comparatively high velocity (well above the fine-sand minimum around 20 cm/s) to erode — the two frameworks, one in shear stress and one in velocity, agree qualitatively that coarse material resists entrainment.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing incipient motion wants to see whether a student treats Shields' tau*_c = 0.06 as an exact law or understands it as an empirically band-limited threshold — citing Buffington and Montgomery's 1997 reanalysis showing 0.03-0.07 scatter shows real depth. On the Hjulstrom side, the give-away question is 'why does fine sand erode more easily than clay, even though clay grains are smaller and lighter?' A student who can explain cohesion — that clay's electrochemical bonding resists detachment despite low particle weight — has understood the mechanism, not just memorized a U-shaped curve. Naming dam-downstream armouring as a real consequence shows the concept connects to an actual river management problem, not just a lab curve.

questions.prompt: What does the Shields parameter tau* = tau_0 / ((rho_s - rho)*g*d) physically represent?

options.text: The ratio of driving bed shear stress to the grain's submerged-weight-based resisting stress
The absolute velocity required to erode any grain
The settling velocity of a grain in still water
The Manning roughness coefficient of the bed material

explanations.a: Correct — tau* nondimensionalizes the driving shear stress against the grain's submerged weight per unit area, making it comparable across grain sizes and densities.
explanations.b: Shields' parameter is a dimensionless stress ratio, not a velocity; Hjulstrom's diagram addresses velocity thresholds separately.
explanations.c: Settling velocity is a different quantity, used later in the Rouse number for suspended sediment, not in the Shields incipient-motion criterion.
explanations.d: Manning's n describes bulk channel resistance to flow, an entirely different concept from the grain-scale force balance Shields describes.

questions.prompt: Why should tau*_c = 0.06 be treated as a band rather than a precise constant?

options.text: Because Shields never actually published a numerical value
Because reanalyses, including Buffington and Montgomery (1997), found published critical values ranging roughly 0.03-0.07, reflecting subjective criteria for 'incipient motion'
Because tau*_c depends only on water temperature
Because it only applies to grains smaller than clay

explanations.a: Shields did publish a curve with a specific commonly-cited value near 0.06; the issue is the scatter around it, not an absence of a number.
explanations.b: Correct — different researchers defined 'motion begins' differently (first grain wobble vs. measurable transport rate), producing a genuine range in reported critical values rather than one precise universal constant.
explanations.c: Temperature affects viscosity and thus the grain Reynolds number, but it is not the primary reason tau*_c is reported as a scattered range.
explanations.d: The Shields curve is built around coarse, non-cohesive grains at high Reynolds number; it is not restricted to clay-sized particles.

questions.prompt: On the Hjulstrom diagram, why does fine sand require the lowest velocity to erode, while both coarser gravel and finer clay require higher velocities?

options.text: Coarser grains are heavier and resist detachment by weight, while finer clay resists via cohesive electrochemical bonding, so both extremes need more force than the middle
Fine sand has no measurable settling velocity
Clay particles are actually larger than sand particles
Gravel is chemically identical to clay

explanations.a: Correct — the U-shaped erosion threshold arises because coarse grains resist erosion through sheer weight, while cohesive fine sediments resist through electrochemical bonding between particles, leaving fine sand (large enough to lack strong cohesion, light enough to move easily) as the easiest to erode.
explanations.b: Fine sand does have a measurable settling velocity; that is not why it sits at the erosion-threshold minimum.
explanations.c: Clay particles are by definition smaller than sand particles; size ordering is not reversed on the diagram.
explanations.d: Gravel and clay differ fundamentally in composition and cohesive behavior; they are not chemically identical.

questions.prompt: What causes bed armouring downstream of a dam?

options.text: The dam increases sediment supply to the downstream channel
Clear-water releases from the dam winnow away fine bed material without resupply, leaving a coarse lag layer that resists further erosion
Downstream velocity always drops to zero below a dam
The Shields parameter becomes undefined below dams

explanations.a: A dam traps the river's natural sediment supply upstream; it reduces, not increases, sediment reaching the downstream channel.
explanations.b: Correct — with sediment supply cut off, the clear-water release still has enough shear to move finer bed particles but not the coarsest ones, so fines are progressively winnowed away, leaving a coarse, resistant armor layer.
explanations.c: Downstream velocity remains nonzero (dams still release flow); it is the sediment supply, not the velocity, that is fundamentally altered.
explanations.d: The Shields parameter remains well defined below a dam; armouring is a physical consequence of the incipient-motion balance shifting as fines are removed, not a breakdown of the concept.

lessons.label: Bed Load, Suspended Load and the Rouse Profile

sections.heading: Three modes of sediment transport
sections.body: A river moves sediment in three distinct ways. Bed load is material that rolls, slides, or bounces (saltates) along the bed, staying in near-continuous contact with it. Suspended load is material lifted off the bed and carried within the water column, held up by turbulent eddies against its own tendency to settle. Wash load is a special case of suspended sediment — very fine silt and clay whose settling velocity is so small compared to turbulent mixing that it stays suspended essentially all the time and is rarely found sitting on the bed at all; wash load supply usually comes from hillslope erosion in the watershed rather than from the channel bed itself.

sections.heading: Bedload formulas that disagree by an order of magnitude
sections.body: Meyer-Peter and Muller published an empirical bedload transport formula in 1948, based on flume experiments at ETH Zurich, relating dimensionless bedload transport to the excess of the Shields stress above its critical threshold. It remains one of the most widely used bedload equations, but it is only one of many — Einstein's, Engelund and Hansen's, and van Rijn's formulas are among the alternatives — and a well-known, uncomfortable fact in sediment transport engineering is that different formulas applied to the same measured discharge and grain size can predict bedload transport rates differing by an order of magnitude. This is not a sign that the formulas are careless; transport rate is extremely sensitive to how far shear stress sits above the critical threshold, and each formula was calibrated against its own limited range of flume or field data.

sections.heading: The Rouse number and the suspended-sediment profile
sections.body: Whether a given grain rides as bed load, suspended load, or wash load is captured by the Rouse number, P = w_s / (kappa * u_star), where w_s is the grain's settling velocity, kappa is the von Karman constant (approximately 0.4), and u_star is the shear velocity — a measure of the turbulence available to keep the grain aloft. Rouse derived in 1937 the equilibrium concentration profile this ratio predicts, C/Ca = [(y_a*(h-y)) / (y*(h-y_a))]^P, balancing upward turbulent diffusion against downward settling. Large P (greater than about 2.5) means settling dominates: the grain effectively cannot be lifted into suspension and travels as bed load. Small P (less than about 0.8) means turbulence dominates so completely that the grain is mixed nearly uniformly through the depth — wash load. Between those thresholds, P produces the classic graded suspended-load profile: concentration highest near the bed and decreasing toward the surface. Field sediment rating curves (plots of suspended sediment discharge against water discharge) show hysteresis across a single flood: the rising limb often carries more sediment at a given discharge than the falling limb, because the readily available supply is exhausted or hillslope connectivity to the channel changes as the flood progresses.

lessons.workedExample: Compute the Rouse number for a medium sand grain with settling velocity w_s = 0.02 m/s in a flow with shear velocity u_star = 0.05 m/s, using kappa = 0.4: P = 0.02 / (0.4*0.05) = 0.02/0.02 = 1.0. Since 0.8 < 1.0 < 2.5, this grain travels as classic suspended load with a graded concentration profile. Compare a fine silt grain with w_s = 0.0005 m/s in the same flow: P = 0.0005/0.02 = 0.025, well under 0.8, so it behaves as wash load, mixed nearly uniformly through the water column regardless of local bed conditions.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is this bed load or suspended load?' to test whether a student can classify transport mechanistically rather than by eyeballing turbidity. The strong answer computes or at least reasons through the Rouse number, w_s/(kappa*u_star), and states the thresholds (P > 2.5 bed load, P < 0.8 wash load). A student who also knows that competing bedload formulas like Meyer-Peter-Muller can disagree by an order of magnitude on the same river shows scientific maturity — they are reporting an estimate with real uncertainty rather than treating one formula's output as ground truth. Naming rating-curve hysteresis explains why a single sediment-discharge relationship measured on one flood limb can mislead if applied blindly to another.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes wash load from ordinary suspended load?

options.text: Wash load is coarser and settles faster than typical suspended sediment
Wash load's settling velocity is so low relative to turbulence that it stays suspended almost all the time and is rarely found on the bed
Wash load only exists in bed load formulas like Meyer-Peter and Muller's
Wash load is defined by having a Rouse number above 2.5

explanations.a: Wash load is finer, not coarser, than typical suspended sediment, which is why it settles more slowly, not faster.
explanations.b: Correct — wash load's very low settling velocity relative to turbulent mixing keeps it in suspension continuously, and it is generally supplied from outside the channel bed (hillslope erosion) rather than exchanged with it.
explanations.c: Meyer-Peter and Muller's formula addresses bedload transport specifically; wash load is a suspended/near-uniformly-mixed transport category, not part of that bedload formula.
explanations.d: A Rouse number above 2.5 indicates bed load, the opposite classification from wash load, which corresponds to P below about 0.8.

questions.prompt: Why do different bedload transport formulas (Meyer-Peter-Muller, Einstein, others) often predict rates differing by an order of magnitude for the same conditions?

options.text: Because sediment transport rate is highly sensitive to how far shear stress exceeds the critical threshold, and each formula is calibrated to its own limited data range
Because only one of the formulas is actually correct and the others contain simple arithmetic errors
Because bedload transport does not actually depend on shear stress at all
Because the formulas were all derived from the exact same flume dataset

explanations.a: Correct — transport rate rises steeply and nonlinearly once shear stress exceeds the Shields critical threshold, so small differences in assumed threshold or calibration range can cascade into large differences in predicted transport.
explanations.b: The formulas are not simple arithmetic errors; they are legitimate empirical fits, each reasonably accurate within the range of conditions it was calibrated against.
explanations.c: Shear stress (via the excess above the Shields critical threshold) is exactly the driving variable these formulas are built around.
explanations.d: Each formula, including Meyer-Peter and Muller's 1948 equation, was calibrated against its own distinct set of flume or field experiments, not a shared dataset.

questions.prompt: A grain has settling velocity w_s = 0.02 m/s in a flow with shear velocity u_star = 0.05 m/s (kappa = 0.4). What transport mode does its Rouse number predict?

options.text: P = 1.0, suspended load with a graded profile
P = 2.5, wash load
P = 0.4, bed load
P = 4.0, wash load

explanations.a: Correct — P = w_s/(kappa*u_star) = 0.02/(0.4*0.05) = 1.0, which falls between the 0.8 and 2.5 thresholds, predicting suspended load with the classic graded concentration profile.
explanations.b: P = 2.5 would be the bed-load threshold, not the value computed here, and 2.5 corresponds to bed load, not wash load.
explanations.c: 0.02/(0.4*0.05) does not equal 0.4, and a P near 0.4 would actually fall in the wash-load range (below 0.8), not bed load.
explanations.d: The correct computation gives P = 1.0, not 4.0; a P of 4.0 would indicate bed load, not wash load.

questions.prompt: Order these Rouse-number ranges from least easily suspended to most easily suspended.

items.text: P > 2.5: settling dominates, travels as bed load
0.8 < P < 2.5: suspended load with a graded concentration profile
P < 0.8: turbulence dominates, nearly uniform mixing (wash load)

questions.explanation: A larger Rouse number means settling velocity dominates over turbulent mixing (harder to suspend, bed load); as P falls, turbulence increasingly wins out, moving through graded suspended load and finally to wash load, which is mixed almost uniformly through the depth.

questions.prompt: What does hysteresis in a sediment rating curve refer to?

options.text: Sediment discharge is identical at a given water discharge regardless of whether the flood is rising or falling
The rising limb of a flood often carries more sediment at a given discharge than the falling limb, because available sediment supply or hillslope connectivity changes through the event
Rating curves only apply to bed load, never to suspended load
Sediment discharge always exceeds water discharge in a flood

explanations.a: That would describe the absence of hysteresis; hysteresis specifically means the relationship differs between the rising and falling limbs.
explanations.b: Correct — because readily mobilized sediment can be exhausted or hillslope-to-channel connectivity can change as a flood progresses, the same water discharge often corresponds to different sediment discharges on the rising versus falling limb.
explanations.c: Rating curves are typically built for suspended sediment discharge versus water discharge, not restricted to bed load.
explanations.d: Sediment discharge is a mass or volume flux of a different quantity than water discharge; there is no general rule that one must exceed the other.

units.label: Measuring Free-Surface Flow: Weirs, Flumes & Gauging

lessons.label: Sharp-Crested Weirs

sections.heading: The rectangular weir: an orifice that free-falls into a nappe
sections.body: A sharp-crested weir is a thin plate set across a channel with a machined edge; water backs up behind it and spills over as a free-falling sheet called the nappe. Because the flow accelerates over the crest under gravity, integrating velocity across the sheet gives the Poleni formula: Q = (2/3)*Cd*sqrt(2g)*b*H^(3/2), where b is crest length and H is head measured above the crest. The base discharge coefficient Cd ≈ 0.62 comes from real nappes contracting slightly as they leave the sharp edge, not the ideal frictionless value of 1.0. Because real Cd depends weakly on H and crest height P (approach velocity grows as the pool gets shallow relative to head), Rehbock's 1929 formula refined it to Cd = 0.611 + 0.075*(H/P), letting one coefficient track the approach-velocity effect instead of forcing a single constant onto every setup. Kindsvater and Carter (1957) went further, adding small empirical corrections to both H and b (effective head and effective width) rather than to Cd alone, which fit lab data better across a wider range of head-to-crest ratios and is the version most hydraulics labs and USGS manuals now specify.

sections.heading: The V-notch: trading capacity for sensitivity at low flow
sections.body: For small or highly variable flows, a triangular (V-notch) weir is preferred because head grows faster than in a rectangular notch as flow rises — Q = (8/15)*Cd*sqrt(2g)*tan(theta/2)*H^(5/2). For the standard 90-degree notch (tan 45° = 1) with Cd near 0.58-0.60, this collapses to the practical SI rule Q ≈ 1.4*H^2.5 (H in meters, Q in m3/s). The H^2.5 exponent versus the rectangular weir's H^1.5 means a V-notch's opening grows with depth, giving much better resolution at low flow — a doubling of H roughly quintuples Q instead of tripling it, so a gauge reading swings more per unit of actual flow change, which is exactly what you want when trying to resolve a trickle.

sections.heading: What makes the coefficient trustworthy
sections.body: Every published Cd assumes the nappe springs clear and is ventilated — air must reach the space beneath the falling sheet, or subatmospheric pressure pulls it into a lower, 'clinging' profile that invalidates the rating. The crest itself must be machined to a knife edge (under roughly 2 mm thick, beveled downstream) so the flow separates cleanly rather than following a rounded or thick lip. Approach velocity must stay small, which is why the head is measured 3-4H upstream of the plate, ahead of the drawdown curve the weir itself creates. Because Q scales as H^1.5 or H^2.5, a small head-reading error is magnified: dQ/Q ≈ 1.5*(dH/H) for rectangular weirs and 2.5*(dH/H) for V-notch weirs, so the same 1 mm gauge error costs a V-notch weir noticeably more accuracy than it costs a rectangular one.

lessons.workedExample: A 90-degree V-notch weir reads H = 120 mm during a low-flow test. Q ≈ 1.4*(0.12)^2.5 = 1.4*0.00499 = 0.00699 m3/s ≈ 7.0 L/s. If the staff gauge is misread by 2 mm (H = 122 mm instead of 120), dH/H ≈ 1.67%, and the discharge error is amplified to about 2.5*1.67% ≈ 4.2%, versus only 2.5% had the same absolute misreading occurred on a rectangular weir with the same H. This is why V-notch installations demand a precise point gauge (a hook or vernier gauge reading to 0.5 mm), not a coarse painted staff scale, even though the notch itself is simple to build.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a weir in a project immediately asks which shape was chosen and why, because the answer reveals whether the student understands the H-exponent tradeoff rather than having copied a formula. A student who says 'I used a V-notch because my flows were small and I needed head sensitivity, so I used a point gauge to control the amplified error' has connected the exponent to an instrument choice. A student who cites Cd = 0.62 without mentioning nappe ventilation or where they measured H has a formula but not an understanding of why the coefficient is only valid under specific conditions.

questions.prompt: Why is a V-notch (triangular) weir preferred over a rectangular weir for measuring small, low flows?

options.text: It has a larger discharge coefficient, so it passes more water
Its H^2.5 head-discharge relationship makes head change faster per unit of flow, improving resolution at low flow
It does not require nappe ventilation
It eliminates the need to measure head upstream of the plate

explanations.a: Cd for a V-notch (~0.58-0.60) is not larger than a rectangular weir's (~0.62); capacity is not the reason it is chosen.
explanations.b: Correct — because Q scales with H^2.5 rather than H^1.5, the notch opening widens with depth, so head changes more per unit of discharge, giving finer resolution at low flow.
explanations.c: V-notch weirs still require a ventilated, freely-falling nappe just like rectangular weirs; the physics of nappe separation is the same.
explanations.d: Head is still measured 3-4H upstream of a V-notch plate to avoid the approach drawdown curve, exactly as with a rectangular weir.

questions.prompt: The Rehbock (1929) formula Cd = 0.611 + 0.075*(H/P) improves on a fixed Cd = 0.62 mainly by accounting for:

options.text: Water temperature effects on viscosity
The growing influence of approach velocity as head becomes large relative to crest height
Wind loading on the nappe
The color and material of the weir plate

explanations.a: The Rehbock refinement is a geometric/hydraulic correction (H/P ratio), not a viscosity or temperature correction.
explanations.b: Correct — as H grows relative to the pool depth P, approach velocity becomes non-negligible, which the H/P term captures instead of forcing one constant coefficient onto every setup.
explanations.c: Wind effects on a small lab or field nappe are not what this empirical correction addresses.
explanations.d: Plate material only matters insofar as the crest is thin and sharp; it is not part of the H/P correction.

questions.prompt: A rectangular sharp-crested weir's nappe is observed clinging to the downstream face of the plate instead of springing clear. What does this indicate, and what is the consequence?

options.text: The crest is too thin; thickening it will fix the problem
The nappe is not ventilated, air beneath it is subatmospheric, and the standard Cd no longer applies
Nothing — clinging nappes are the normal, expected condition
The approach channel is too wide

explanations.a: A thin, sharp crest is required and correct; thickening it would create a different, also-invalid flow condition (a broad-crested-like profile).
explanations.b: Correct — published Cd values assume a freely ventilated, springing nappe; without an air vent beneath it, negative pressure pulls the sheet in and the calibration is invalidated.
explanations.c: A clinging nappe is a known failure mode, not the expected or acceptable condition for a rated sharp-crested weir.
explanations.d: Approach channel width affects approach velocity, not nappe ventilation, which is a separate requirement (an air vent behind the plate).

questions.prompt: Order these steps for correctly commissioning a new sharp-crested V-notch weir installation, from first to last.

items.text: Machine the plate to a thin (under ~2 mm), beveled crest at the desired notch angle
Install the plate and confirm the space beneath the nappe is vented to atmosphere
Position a point/hook gauge 3-4H upstream of the plate, ahead of the drawdown curve
Record H and compute Q from the rated formula

questions.explanation: The crest geometry must be built correctly first, then the nappe's ventilation confirmed so the flow condition matches the rating assumptions, then the head gauge positioned where the approach flow is undisturbed, and only then is a head reading meaningful for computing discharge.

lessons.label: Broad-Crested Weirs and Critical-Depth Structures

sections.heading: A long crest forces the flow to choose its own control section
sections.body: A broad-crested weir is a raised, flat-topped block long enough (relative to the head over it) that the flow has room to accelerate and pass through critical depth while still on the crest, rather than falling free like a sharp-crested weir's nappe. At critical depth, specific energy is at a minimum for the given discharge, so the flow over the crest settles into yc = (2/3)*H, where H is the upstream total head above the crest. Substituting that critical condition into continuity gives a rating derived from first principles rather than curve-fit alone: Q = 1.705*Cd*b*H^(3/2) in SI units, where 1.705 = (2/3)^1.5*sqrt(g). Because that constant falls directly out of the critical-flow condition, a broad-crested weir's discharge coefficient Cd is a small, near-unity correction for crest roughness and boundary-layer losses rather than the whole story of the rating, unlike a sharp-crested weir where Cd absorbs the entire departure from ideal flow.

sections.heading: Why forcing critical depth is self-calibrating
sections.body: The key hydraulic property is that once flow passes through critical depth on the crest, information cannot propagate upstream against it — small disturbances downstream (a partly closed gate, a rising tailwater) cannot travel back through the critical section to affect the approach flow, so discharge depends only on the upstream head. This is the same choking principle that governs compressible flow through a converging-diverging nozzle at sonic conditions. A structure that manufactures its own critical control section is called modular (or free-flowing), and it is more trustworthy than a device rated purely by an empirical coefficient because the H-Q relationship is derived from open-channel energy principles first and only lightly tuned by Cd, so it degrades gracefully and predictably rather than depending entirely on matching a lab calibration exactly.

sections.heading: The modular limit and what happens beyond it
sections.body: That self-calibration only holds while the structure stays modular. If the downstream (tailwater) level rises enough to drown the crest, the critical section is submerged, the flow can no longer accelerate freely through it, and the simple upstream-head-only rating breaks down. The modular limit is expressed as the submergence ratio h2/h1 (downstream head over upstream head above the crest) below which the structure remains free-flowing; broad-crested weirs typically stay modular up to roughly 0.66-0.85 depending on crest shape and approach geometry. Past that ratio, a submergence correction factor (reducing computed Q from the free-flow value) must be applied, or a second, downstream head measurement is needed to correct the rating — the same two-head problem that motivates flume design.

lessons.workedExample: A rectangular broad-crested weir with crest length b = 1.5 m and Cd = 0.93 registers an upstream head H = 0.35 m during a free-flow check. Q = 1.705*0.93*1.5*0.35^1.5 = 1.705*0.93*1.5*0.2071 ≈ 0.494 m3/s. A field technician then notices the downstream water surface has risen until h2/h1 ≈ 0.9, well past the roughly 0.8 modular limit expected for this crest shape; the crest is now drowned, so the same head reading of 0.35 m no longer corresponds to 0.494 m3/s — the true discharge is lower, and the site now needs a submergence correction (or a second head gauge downstream) rather than the plain free-flow formula.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe broad-crested weirs to see whether a student can explain why the device works, not just recite Q = 1.705*Cd*b*H^1.5. The concept a judge is fishing for is choking: that forcing critical depth on the crest makes discharge insensitive to downstream conditions, which is why the structure is called self-calibrating and why its rating is trusted with only a small empirical coefficient instead of an entirely curve-fit one. A student who can state the modular limit and describe what happens if the crest is drowned demonstrates they understand the structure's operating envelope, not just its formula.

questions.prompt: In the broad-crested weir formula Q = 1.705*Cd*b*H^(3/2), where does the constant 1.705 come from?

options.text: It is an empirically fitted constant with no theoretical basis
It falls out of the critical-flow condition, equal to (2/3)^1.5*sqrt(g)
It is the value of Cd averaged across many lab weirs
It converts feet to meters

explanations.a: Unlike the sharp-crested weir's empirical Cd, this constant is derived analytically from critical-depth theory, not just curve-fit.
explanations.b: Correct — substituting yc = (2/3)H (the critical-depth condition) into continuity produces exactly this constant, which is why Cd only needs to be a small correction factor.
explanations.c: Cd is a separate, near-unity correction applied after this constant, not folded into it as an average.
explanations.d: It is a dimensional constant from the critical-flow derivation in SI units, not a unit-conversion factor.

questions.prompt: Why is a broad-crested weir described as 'self-calibrating' compared to a device rated purely by an empirical coefficient?

options.text: It requires no maintenance once installed
Forcing critical depth on the crest means discharge depends only on upstream head, derived from energy principles rather than curve-fitting alone
It automatically adjusts its own crest height to match any flow
It never needs a discharge coefficient
It works identically whether submerged or free-flowing

explanations.a: Self-calibrating refers to the hydraulics of the rating, not to physical maintenance requirements.
explanations.b: Correct — because critical flow is a choke point that blocks downstream disturbances from propagating upstream, the H-Q relationship comes from first-principles energy analysis, with Cd only a minor tuning factor.
explanations.c: The crest is a fixed, rigid structure; it does not physically adjust.
explanations.d: It still uses Cd, just as a small correction rather than as the entire empirical basis of the rating.
explanations.e: The self-calibrating property holds only while flow stays modular (free-flowing); once submerged past the modular limit, the simple rating breaks down.

questions.prompt: A broad-crested weir's tailwater rises until the submergence ratio h2/h1 exceeds its modular limit. What is the correct response?

options.text: Keep using the free-flow formula since the crest geometry has not changed
Apply a submergence correction or add a downstream head measurement, since the crest is now drowned and discharge depends on tailwater too
Increase Cd to compensate
Ignore it since broad-crested weirs cannot be submerged

explanations.a: Once submerged, critical depth no longer occurs on the crest, so the free-flow formula (which assumes upstream head alone controls Q) is no longer valid.
explanations.b: Correct — past the modular limit the structure is no longer choked, so a submergence correction factor or a two-head (upstream and downstream) rating is required, echoing the same problem flumes solve.
explanations.c: Cd is a small correction for crest friction, not a tool for compensating for a fundamentally different (submerged) flow regime.
explanations.d: Broad-crested weirs absolutely can be drowned if tailwater rises high enough; the modular limit exists precisely because this can happen.

questions.prompt: Match each hydraulic concept to what it describes for a broad-crested weir.

right.text: yc = (2/3)*H, the minimum-specific-energy depth reached on a sufficiently long crest
Downstream conditions cannot influence discharge; Q depends on upstream head alone
Tailwater has risen past the modular limit, and a correction or second head reading is needed
A near-unity correction for crest friction and boundary-layer losses, not the whole rating

questions.explanation: Critical depth is the specific depth (2/3 of head) the crest forces flow through; while that critical section stays un-drowned (modular/free flow), discharge depends only on upstream head; once drowned (submerged flow) past the modular limit, a correction is required; and Cd remains only a small tuning factor because the bulk of the rating comes from the critical-flow derivation itself.

lessons.label: Flumes: Parshall, Venturi and Cutthroat

sections.heading: Why gauge with a throat instead of a dam
sections.body: A flume measures discharge the same way a broad-crested weir does — by forcing flow through critical depth at a control section — but does it by narrowing the channel walls instead of raising the bed with a dam. That distinction matters operationally: a weir ponds water and traps sediment behind it, while a flume's contraction passes sediment and debris through with only a modest, gradually-recovering head loss. That combination — self-calibrating critical flow, low head loss, and self-cleaning — is why flumes dominate wastewater treatment plants and irrigation canals, where a silting weir pool would be a maintenance disaster and where head is often too precious to spend.

sections.heading: The Parshall flume and its empirical rating
sections.body: Ralph Parshall developed the flume that bears his name in 1922 at the Colorado Agricultural Experiment Station, giving it a converging inlet, a constricted throat, and a diverging outlet with a specific floor drop through the throat. It comes in a standard family of throat widths, from a few inches up to 50 feet, and each size is rated empirically as Q = C*Ha^n, where Ha is the head measured in the converging (upstream) section at a fixed gauging point. For the widely used 1-foot throat, n ≈ 1.522 and C ≈ 4 (US customary units, Ha in feet, Q in cfs) — an exponent close to, but not exactly, the 1.5 that pure critical-depth theory would predict, reflecting the flume's specific converging geometry rather than a plain broad-crested weir. Every standard throat size has its own calibrated C and n from the original Parshall lab tests, so a builder must use tables for the specific size, not extrapolate one size's coefficients to another.

sections.heading: Free flow, submergence, and the cutthroat alternative
sections.body: The single-head rating only holds in free flow, where the throat stays at critical depth undisturbed by the tailwater. Beyond a submergence ratio (Hb/Ha, downstream over upstream head) of roughly 0.5 for the smallest throats up to about 0.8 for the largest, the throat drowns and a second head reading (Hb) plus a submerged-flow correction table is required — the same two-head problem broad-crested weirs face past their modular limit. The Parshall flume's converging and diverging floor sections make it precise but expensive and fussy to form correctly; the cutthroat flume, developed at Utah State University in the late 1960s, uses a flat bottom with only the side walls contracting, trading a little accuracy for a shape any contractor can pour, and is rated the same free-flow/submerged-flow way from two head measurements.

lessons.workedExample: A 1-foot-throat Parshall flume registers Ha = 0.80 ft in free flow. Q = 4.00*(0.80)^1.522 ≈ 4.00*0.712 ≈ 2.85 cfs. A week later, algae growth downstream raises the tailwater until Hb/Ha climbs to 0.75, above the roughly 0.7 free-flow limit typical for this throat size; the throat is now submerged, so plugging the same Ha into the free-flow formula would overstate the true discharge. The operator now must record both Ha and Hb and apply the manufacturer's submerged-flow correction curve, which subtracts a correction that grows with submergence ratio, rather than trusting the single-head equation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a flume design wants to hear why a flume was chosen over a weir for a specific site — the answer should be sediment passage and low head loss, not just 'it's more accurate.' The tell of real understanding is a student who can state their throat's free-flow submergence limit and describe what changes operationally (a second head gauge, a correction table) once it is exceeded, rather than treating Q = C*Ha^n as valid at every tailwater condition. Naming Parshall's 1922 origin or the cutthroat's flat-bottom simplification shows the student engaged with why the geometry looks the way it does, not just that a lookup table exists.

questions.prompt: Why do flumes dominate gauging in wastewater and irrigation settings compared to weirs?

options.text: They are always cheaper to construct than any weir
Their throat contraction passes sediment and debris with lower head loss instead of ponding water behind a dam
They never require calibration
They eliminate the need to measure head at all

explanations.a: Parshall flumes especially are precise, formed structures that can be more expensive to build correctly than a simple weir plate.
explanations.b: Correct — narrowing the walls instead of raising the bed avoids ponding sediment behind the structure and costs less head, which matters in flat wastewater or irrigation systems.
explanations.c: Flumes still rely on calibrated coefficients (C and n per throat size); they are not calibration-free.
explanations.d: Flumes still require at least one head measurement (Ha), and two under submerged conditions.

questions.prompt: In the Parshall flume rating Q = C*Ha^n, the exponent n ≈ 1.522 for the 1-foot throat is:

options.text: Exactly equal to the 1.5 exponent predicted by pure critical-depth theory
Close to, but empirically distinct from, the 1.5 value, reflecting the specific converging/diverging throat geometry
The same exponent used for every Parshall throat size regardless of width
A unit-conversion artifact with no hydraulic meaning

explanations.a: It is close to 1.5 but not exactly equal — Parshall's converging inlet and floor drop shift it slightly from the plain critical-depth prediction.
explanations.b: Correct — the exponent comes from Parshall's original lab calibration for that specific throat size and geometry, near but not identical to the theoretical 1.5.
explanations.c: Each standard throat width has its own calibrated C and n from Parshall's original tests; they are not interchangeable across sizes.
explanations.d: It reflects real hydraulic behavior of the converging throat, not a units artifact.

questions.prompt: A Parshall flume's submergence ratio Hb/Ha rises above its free-flow limit. What must the operator do?

options.text: Continue using Q = C*Ha^n unchanged
Record both Ha and Hb and apply a submerged-flow correction, since the single-head rating no longer holds
Switch to the broad-crested weir formula instead
Increase C to compensate

explanations.a: Once submerged, the throat is no longer at undisturbed critical depth, so the free-flow single-head equation overstates true discharge.
explanations.b: Correct — this mirrors the broad-crested weir's modular-limit problem: a second head reading downstream plus a correction table is required once submergence exceeds the free-flow limit.
explanations.c: The broad-crested weir formula does not apply to a flume's throat geometry; a flume-specific submerged-flow correction is needed instead.
explanations.d: C is a fixed calibration constant for the throat size, not a knob to compensate for a different flow regime.

questions.prompt: Match each flume-related term to its correct description.

right.text: Developed by Parshall in 1922, with a converging inlet, constricted throat, and diverging outlet with a floor drop
A flat-bottomed, side-wall-only contraction developed at Utah State University in the late 1960s, easier to construct
Upstream head measured at the fixed gauging point in the converging section
The submergence ratio (roughly 0.5-0.8 depending on throat size) above which a second head and correction are needed

questions.explanation: The Parshall flume is Ralph Parshall's 1922 converging-throat-diverging design; the cutthroat flume is the simpler, flat-bottomed Utah State alternative; Ha is the standard upstream head reading used for the free-flow rating; and the submergence limit is the tailwater ratio beyond which the single-head rating breaks down and a two-head correction is required.

lessons.label: Measuring Stage

sections.heading: From a painted plate to a continuous recorder
sections.body: Stage is simply the water-surface elevation at a gauging site, and every discharge estimate — weir, flume, or rating curve — is only as good as the stage reading behind it. The simplest instrument is a staff gauge, a graduated plate fixed to a wall or pile and read by eye; its entire value depends on datum control, tying its zero to a stable, independently surveyed benchmark, because a staff gauge that has shifted a centimeter silently biases every reading taken against it afterward. Continuous records historically came from a stilling well: a vertical pipe or shaft connected to the river through a small-diameter inlet that damps waves and turbulence, inside which a float rides the water surface and drives a tape or shaft-encoder recorder that traces stage against time, the classic USGS approach for over a century of gauge records.

sections.heading: Pressure-based and non-contact sensors
sections.body: A submerged pressure transducer converts hydrostatic pressure at a fixed depth into stage. A vented transducer runs a small tube from the sensor to the surface open to atmosphere, so it measures gauge pressure directly and needs no further correction. An absolute transducer measures total pressure (water plus atmosphere) and therefore requires a separate barometric correction — subtracting a concurrent atmospheric-pressure record, often from a nearby barologger — before the reading means only water depth; skip that correction and a passing weather system reads as a flow event. Bubbler (gas-purge) systems purge a slow stream of gas through a submerged orifice and read the back-pressure needed to push bubbles out, which equals the hydrostatic head, avoiding a wetted electronic sensor entirely. Non-contact options read the surface from above: ultrasonic sensors time a sound pulse's round trip, but the speed of sound in air depends on air temperature, so an uncompensated sensor drifts as the day warms; radar sensors avoid that temperature dependence but can still be fooled by foam, dense weed growth breaking up the reflecting surface, or multipath echoes off nearby structure.

sections.heading: Fast-response probes and the quiet failure mode
sections.body: For wave or hydraulic-jump work where the surface moves faster than a float or an averaged acoustic return can track, capacitance and resistance wave probes use a thin wire partially submerged in the flow, whose measured capacitance or resistance changes with submerged depth; these need a static calibration (dry, staged submersion at known depths before use) and are prone to drift, so re-zeroing matters. Across every technology, the most dangerous failure is not a broken sensor but a silent datum shift — a stilling well that has silted, a staff gauge nudged out of level, a benchmark that has settled — because the record keeps looking smooth and plausible while being uniformly wrong, and it can take a full season of otherwise-normal-looking data before anyone re-levels the gauge and discovers it.

lessons.workedExample: A site runs an absolute pressure transducer without a barometric correction. Over three days, atmospheric pressure drops by about 1.5 kPa as a low-pressure system moves through — equivalent to roughly 150 mm of water. The uncorrected stage record shows the river rising 150 mm and then falling back with no corresponding change in discharge at the downstream gauge, because the transducer cannot distinguish a falling barometer from rising water. Once the technician pulls concurrent barometric data and subtracts it, the artificial 'rise and fall' disappears entirely, confirming the river stage was flat the whole time — the storm was in the air, not the channel.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about stage instrumentation is testing whether a student understands that every discharge number rests on a stage reading with its own error sources — vented versus absolute transducers is a favorite because it reveals whether the student actually installed and corrected the sensor or just downloaded a datasheet number. A student who explains why an absolute transducer needs a barometric correction, or why a stilling well is damped rather than open to the river directly, shows they understand instrumentation as a system with failure modes, not a black box that outputs a trustworthy number.

questions.prompt: Why does an absolute pressure transducer require a barometric correction while a vented transducer does not?

options.text: Absolute transducers are less accurate in general
An absolute transducer measures water pressure plus atmospheric pressure, so atmospheric changes must be subtracted; a vented transducer already reads gauge pressure directly
Vented transducers cannot be submerged
Barometric correction is only needed at high elevation sites

explanations.a: The issue is what physical quantity is measured (absolute vs. gauge pressure), not a general accuracy difference between sensor types.
explanations.b: Correct — an absolute sensor cannot separate atmospheric pressure from water pressure on its own, so a concurrent barometric record must be subtracted; a vented sensor's atmospheric-reference tube does that subtraction mechanically.
explanations.c: Vented transducers are fully submersible; the vent tube runs to the surface for atmospheric reference, not to keep the sensor dry.
explanations.d: Barometric correction is needed anywhere atmospheric pressure varies with weather, which happens at essentially every elevation.

questions.prompt: An ultrasonic stage sensor mounted above the water reads erroneously higher stage on a hot afternoon than a nearby radar sensor at the same site, with no real change in water level. What explains this?

options.text: The radar sensor is broken
The speed of sound in air changes with temperature, and an uncompensated ultrasonic sensor's timed round-trip is thrown off; radar is largely unaffected by air temperature
Ultrasonic sensors cannot operate in daylight
Radar sensors do not measure stage

explanations.a: Radar's insensitivity to air temperature is a known advantage, not evidence of a fault.
explanations.b: Correct — ultrasonic ranging depends on the speed of sound in air, which rises with temperature, so an uncompensated sensor misjudges distance as the day warms; radar (an electromagnetic, not acoustic, signal) does not have this temperature dependence.
explanations.c: Ultrasonic ranging works regardless of light; the described error is thermal, not optical.
explanations.d: Radar is one of the standard non-contact stage-measurement technologies, alongside ultrasonic.

questions.prompt: Why is a silent datum shift (e.g., a nudged staff gauge or a settled benchmark) considered the most dangerous failure mode in stage measurement?

options.text: It typically causes the sensor to stop recording entirely, which is easy to notice
It produces a record that still looks smooth and plausible while being uniformly biased, so it can go undetected for a long time
It only affects capacitance wave probes
It is immediately obvious from the discharge computed downstream

explanations.a: A datum shift typically does not stop the sensor from recording; it keeps producing plausible-looking numbers, which is exactly the danger.
explanations.b: Correct — because the shift is a constant offset, the record still varies smoothly with real changes in flow, so nothing looks obviously wrong until someone re-surveys the datum against the benchmark.
explanations.c: Any stage technology tied to a fixed reference — staff gauges, stilling wells, pressure transducers — can suffer a datum shift, not only wave probes.
explanations.d: A uniformly offset stage record produces a uniformly offset discharge record, which can look like a real hydrologic shift rather than an instrument fault.

questions.prompt: Match each stage-measurement technology to its defining feature or requirement.

right.text: Damps waves and turbulence through a small inlet so a float can drive a continuous mechanical/electronic record
Reads gauge pressure directly via an atmosphere-referenced tube, no barometric correction needed
Reads back-pressure needed to purge gas through a submerged orifice, avoiding a wetted electronic sensor
A thin submerged wire whose capacitance or resistance tracks fast surface fluctuations; needs static calibration before use

questions.explanation: A stilling well physically damps turbulence for a float-driven record; a vented transducer's atmosphere-referenced tube gives gauge pressure directly; a bubbler infers hydrostatic head from purge back-pressure without a wetted electronic sensor; and capacitance/resistance wave probes track fast surface motion but need dry, staged calibration first.

lessons.label: Velocity-Area Gauging and the Rating Curve

sections.heading: The mid-section method: summing many small pieces
sections.body: Where no weir or flume exists, discharge is measured directly by wading or boating a cross-section and summing velocity times area. The USGS mid-section method divides the channel into roughly 20-30 vertical subsections, chosen so no single vertical carries more than about 5-10% of total flow; at each vertical, width and depth are measured and a velocity sample is taken with a current meter. In shallow flow (depth under about 0.76 m / 2.5 ft), a single reading at 0.6 of the depth below the surface is used because that point closely approximates the mean velocity in a typical logarithmic vertical profile. In deeper flow, a two-point method averages readings at 0.2 and 0.8 depth, which better represents a profile where near-bed and near-surface velocities diverge more. Each vertical's discharge is that velocity times the subsection's width times depth, and summing across all verticals gives total Q.

sections.heading: Instruments, from spinning cups to sound
sections.body: The classic tool is a mechanical current meter — a Price AA meter (cup-type) or the smaller Price pygmy meter for shallow water — whose rotation rate converts to velocity via a calibration equation. Electromagnetic current meters measure velocity from the voltage induced as flowing water crosses a magnetic field, with no moving parts to foul on debris. For an entire cross-section at once, an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP), mounted on a boat or tethered platform, measures a full velocity profile via the Doppler shift of sound reflecting off suspended sediment and bubbles as it transects the channel, producing a discharge estimate in minutes instead of the hour or more a wading survey takes.

sections.heading: Turning gaugings into a rating curve, and where it fails
sections.body: A single velocity-area measurement gives one (stage, discharge) point. Repeating it across many stages builds a rating curve, typically fit as Q = a*(h - h0)^b, where h0 is the stage of effectively zero flow (a small offset, not always the streambed elevation) and a, b are found by regression. Plotting log(Q) against log(h - h0) should trace a straight line if the power-law form holds; a curving or kinked plot signals that h0 is wrong or that the channel control changes shape at some stage (e.g., water spreads onto a floodplain). Two conditions defeat a clean single-valued rating. During unsteady flood flow, the rising limb carries more discharge than the falling limb at the same stage — a loop or hysteresis rating — because the flood wave's water-surface slope adds to (or subtracts from) the normal energy gradient a steady-flow rating assumes. And after a flood reshapes the channel bed through scour or deposition, the whole rating shifts and must be redefined by new gaugings; using an old rating on a changed channel, or extrapolating any rating above the highest flow it was ever gauged at, is a well-documented source of large discharge errors, since a channel's control can change shape entirely once flow leaves the main channel.

lessons.workedExample: A gauging crew measures 24 verticals across a 30 m wide channel. In the 1.1 m deep center verticals they average velocities at 0.2 and 0.8 depth (two-point method); at the 0.4 m deep edges they use a single 0.6-depth reading. Summing width*depth*velocity across all 24 verticals gives Q = 18.4 m3/s at a gauged stage of 2.10 m. Plotted with 14 other gaugings spanning stages of 0.8-2.4 m, log(Q) vs log(h - h0) with h0 = 0.35 m falls on a straight line with slope b ≈ 2.1, giving a usable rating Q = 6.7*(h-0.35)^2.1 — but a flood the following spring reaches stage 3.6 m, well above the highest gauged point (2.4 m), so the rating is extrapolated with no verification that the channel control still behaves the same way at that height.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about rating curves to test whether a student understands that a stage-discharge relationship is a fitted model built from real point measurements, not a law of nature — and specifically whether they know its weak points: hysteresis during floods, shifts after channel-reshaping events, and the danger of trusting a rating above its highest gauged flow. A student who plots log(Q) vs log(h-h0) to check linearity, or who flags that their highest flow was extrapolated beyond gauged data, is demonstrating exactly the skepticism a working hydrologist applies to their own rating curve.

questions.prompt: In the mid-section velocity-area method, why does deeper flow (over about 0.76 m) typically use velocity readings at both 0.2 and 0.8 depth instead of a single 0.6-depth reading?

options.text: Current meters cannot physically be lowered to 0.6 depth in deep water
In deeper flow the vertical velocity profile diverges more between near-bed and near-surface, so averaging two points better approximates the mean
The two-point method requires less time than a single reading
Regulations forbid single-point readings in navigable channels

explanations.a: Meters can be lowered to any practical depth; the choice is about profile representativeness, not equipment limits.
explanations.b: Correct — as depth increases, a single 0.6-depth point becomes a less reliable proxy for the mean of a more fully developed logarithmic profile, so averaging two points captures the shape better.
explanations.c: The two-point method takes longer, not less time, since it requires two readings per vertical instead of one.
explanations.d: The choice of single- vs two-point method is a hydraulic accuracy decision, not a navigation regulation.

questions.prompt: Why does the rising limb of a flood typically carry more discharge than the falling limb at the same measured stage (a 'loop' or hysteresis rating)?

options.text: The current meter reads differently depending on time of day
The flood wave's water-surface slope adds to the normal energy gradient on the rising limb and subtracts from it on the falling limb, changing velocity at a given stage
Sediment concentration is always higher on the rising limb
Loop ratings only occur in artificial channels, never in natural rivers

explanations.a: Instrument behavior does not vary with time of day; the effect is hydraulic, tied to the unsteady flood wave itself.
explanations.b: Correct — a single-valued rating assumes a steady-flow energy gradient, but during a flood the wave's own surface slope adds extra driving force on the rise and removes it on the recession, so the same stage corresponds to different velocities (and discharges) at different times.
explanations.c: Sediment load can vary but is not the mechanism behind the discharge difference at matched stage; the energy-gradient effect is.
explanations.d: Loop ratings are a well-documented natural-river phenomenon during unsteady flood flow, not an artifact limited to engineered channels.

questions.prompt: A rating curve Q = a*(h-h0)^b was built from gaugings between stage 0.8 m and 2.4 m. A flood later reaches stage 3.6 m. What is the primary danger of using the fitted equation to estimate discharge at 3.6 m?

options.text: There is no danger; a power-law fit is valid at any stage once a, b, and h0 are known
The channel control governing the stage-discharge relationship may behave differently above the highest gauged flow (e.g., floodplain spreading), so the extrapolated rating is unverified
The equation becomes undefined mathematically above the gauged range
Current meters cannot measure flows above 2.4 m of stage

explanations.a: A power-law fit is only validated across the range where it was tested against real gaugings; nothing guarantees the same relationship holds beyond that range.
explanations.b: Correct — if the channel's hydraulic control changes shape at high stage (for instance, flow spreading onto a floodplain activates a wider, different control), the fitted exponent and coefficient no longer describe the true relationship, making extrapolated high-flow estimates unreliable.
explanations.c: The formula remains mathematically computable at any stage; the problem is physical validity, not a mathematical breakdown.
explanations.d: Current meters can be used at higher stages in principle; the issue described is about the rating curve, not instrument range.

questions.prompt: Match each instrument or method to what it is best suited for.

right.text: Classic mechanical velocity measurement via rotating cups, calibrated to a velocity equation
Velocity from induced voltage as water crosses a magnetic field, no moving parts to foul
A full cross-section velocity profile from a single boat transect via Doppler-shifted sound
Dividing the channel into ~20-30 verticals, each contributing a width*depth*velocity subsection to total discharge

questions.explanation: The Price AA meter is the classic rotating-cup mechanical meter; electromagnetic meters sense velocity from induced voltage with no moving parts; an ADCP profiles the whole cross-section acoustically in one transect; and the mid-section method is the overall framework of dividing the channel into many verticals and summing their individual discharges.

lessons.label: Tracer and Volumetric Methods

sections.heading: Salt dilution: measuring flow without touching velocity
sections.body: Dilution gauging sidesteps velocity and cross-section measurement entirely by using conservation of mass: add a known amount of tracer, measure how much it was diluted downstream, and back out the discharge that must have diluted it. Common salt (NaCl) is the standard tracer because its concentration is read cheaply and continuously with a conductivity probe. In the constant-rate (plateau) method, a solution is injected at a steady, known rate q until the downstream conductivity reading flattens into a stable plateau; discharge follows directly from Q = q*(Ci - Cb)/(Cp - Cb), where Ci is injected concentration, Cb is background, and Cp is the plateau concentration. In the gulp (integral, or slug) method, a known mass M is dumped instantaneously and the entire concentration-time curve is recorded as the tracer cloud passes the downstream probe; discharge is Q = M / integral of (C - Cb) dt over the whole passage, so a wider, more dilute passage curve corresponds to a smaller Q for the same injected mass.

sections.heading: Why boulder streams need dilution, not current meters
sections.body: Both dilution methods require the tracer to become fully mixed laterally and vertically across the channel before it reaches the sampling point — the mixing-length requirement — because a probe reading a still-stratified plume would not see the true cross-sectional average concentration. This is precisely where dilution gauging earns its keep: steep, boulder-strewn mountain streams are exactly the setting where turbulence mixes a tracer fast (giving a short required mixing length) while simultaneously defeating velocity-area methods, since chaotic, plunging flow around boulders makes wading, current-metering, or even locating a clean cross-section impractical. Practitioner guides such as Moore (2004-2005) codify how to size the injection, choose an adequate mixing reach, and correct for a non-flat conductivity background in these settings, which is why salt dilution became the standard low-cost method for small mountain catchments worldwide.

sections.heading: The volumetric reference standard and dye for travel time
sections.body: For very small flows, the timed bucket (volumetric) method is the ultimate primary standard: catch the entire flow in a container of known volume and time the fill with a stopwatch. It has almost no theoretical uncertainty beyond timing and volume-reading precision, which is exactly why it is used to calibrate other devices — a lab weir, a flume, or a dilution-gauging setup — against a trusted reference rather than against another indirect method. Beyond discharge, fluorescent dyes serve a different purpose: fluorescein and rhodamine WT, read with a fluorometer, are used for travel-time and dispersion studies rather than routine discharge gauging, tracking how fast and how spread-out a pollutant slug would move downstream. Rhodamine WT resists photodecay and adsorption onto sediment better than fluorescein, which is why USGS travel-time methodology (Kilpatrick and Wilson, 1989) and tracer-discharge technique reports (Kilpatrick and Cobb, 1985) both treat it as the more field-robust choice for longer reaches.

lessons.workedExample: A crew injects 2.0 L of a concentrated salt solution (mass M = 800 g NaCl) instantaneously into a steep, boulder-choked stream where wading with a current meter is impossible. A conductivity probe 150 m downstream — chosen to give adequate mixing length in the turbulent reach — records a concentration-time curve that, after subtracting background, integrates to 40 g*s/L. Discharge is Q = M / integral(C-Cb)dt = 800 g / 40 g*s/L = 20 L/s. The same week, a technician checks a small lab flume by timing a 10.0 L bucket fill at 25.3 seconds, giving Q = 10.0/25.3 ≈ 0.395 L/s, used as the trusted reference against which the flume's own head-discharge rating is verified.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge hearing about dilution gauging is checking whether a student understands it as a mass-balance technique, not magic — and specifically whether they know why it is chosen: turbulent mixing (which dilution gauging needs) and impossible wading conditions (which defeat velocity-area methods) co-occur in exactly the steep streams where dilution shines. A student who can state the mixing-length requirement, distinguish constant-rate from gulp injection, and explain why the bucket-and-stopwatch method is the reference standard used to calibrate everything else shows they understand the hierarchy of trust among gauging methods, not just one formula in isolation.

questions.prompt: In the gulp (slug) salt-dilution method, why is discharge computed as Q = M / integral(C - Cb)dt rather than from a single concentration reading?

options.text: Because the entire tracer cloud passes the probe over time, and the total dilution experienced by the whole injected mass is captured only by integrating the full concentration-time curve
Because conductivity probes cannot take more than one reading
Because the mass M is unknown until the integral is computed
Because background concentration is always zero in gulp injections

explanations.a: Correct — a slug injection produces a rising-then-falling concentration pulse as it passes; only integrating the excess concentration over the whole pulse duration accounts for all of the injected mass and yields the correct discharge.
explanations.b: Conductivity probes readily take continuous readings; a full time-series is exactly what the method requires and uses.
explanations.c: The mass M is the known, precisely weighed or measured injected quantity, set before injection, not derived from the integral.
explanations.d: Background concentration (Cb) is measured beforehand and subtracted; it is not assumed to be zero.

questions.prompt: Why is salt dilution gauging particularly well suited to steep, boulder-strewn mountain streams?

options.text: Boulders have no effect on either method, so the choice is arbitrary
The same turbulence that mixes tracer quickly (shortening the required mixing length) also makes wading and current-metering impractical, so dilution succeeds exactly where velocity-area fails
Salt is cheaper to buy at high elevation
Boulder streams have no background conductivity to correct for

explanations.a: Boulder-choked, highly turbulent flow strongly affects both methods, just in opposite directions: it helps dilution and hurts velocity-area.
explanations.b: Correct — high turbulence gives fast, thorough mixing (a short mixing-length requirement) at the same time that chaotic flow around boulders defeats wading and current-metering, making dilution gauging the practical choice.
explanations.c: Salt cost is unrelated to elevation and is not the reason dilution gauging is favored in these streams.
explanations.d: Background conductivity still needs to be measured and subtracted regardless of stream type.

questions.prompt: Why is the timed bucket (volumetric) method used as a reference standard to calibrate other flow-measurement devices?

options.text: It is the fastest method available for any flow rate
It directly captures the entire flow in a known volume over a timed interval, so its uncertainty is limited mainly to timing and volume precision rather than an indirect hydraulic or tracer model
It requires a conductivity probe, making it comparable to dilution gauging
It works at any flow rate including large rivers

explanations.a: It is only practical at small flows where the entire discharge can be diverted into a container; it is not a general-purpose fast method.
explanations.b: Correct — because it measures volume and time directly rather than inferring discharge through a rating equation or dilution model, its error sources are minimal and well understood, making it the trusted primary standard other devices are checked against.
explanations.c: The bucket method uses no conductivity probe at all; it relies purely on volume and a stopwatch.
explanations.d: It is limited to small flows that can physically be captured in a container; it does not scale to large rivers.

questions.prompt: Match each tracer or method to its primary use.

right.text: Injecting at a steady known rate until downstream concentration flattens into a plateau, giving Q from the plateau concentration
Instantaneously injecting a known mass and integrating the full concentration-time curve downstream
Fluorometer-read dye used for travel-time and dispersion studies, resistant to photodecay and sediment adsorption
The primary reference standard for small flows, used to calibrate other discharge-measurement devices

questions.explanation: Constant-rate injection reads discharge from a stable downstream plateau concentration; gulp injection integrates the whole passing concentration pulse; rhodamine WT is the field-robust dye of choice for travel-time and dispersion work; and the timed bucket method is the primary volumetric standard used to check other devices.

lessons.label: Building a Bench Flume: Rig, Errors and Uncertainty

sections.heading: A bathtub-scale flume from hardware-store parts
sections.body: A serviceable open-channel flume for a science-fair bench can be built from a length of vinyl or aluminum rain gutter as the channel, a small recirculating pump lifting water from a sump reservoir to a head tank at the inlet, and a V-notch cut into a discharge box at the outlet to measure the flow leaving the system. The head tank needs a honeycomb flow straightener — a bundle of drinking straws or a perforated baffle plate works — to kill the turbulent jet coming off the pump and deliver calm, uniform flow into the gutter channel; skip that and the approach flow to any measurement point downstream is turbulent and unrepeatable. The gutter is typically hinged or jacked at one end so slope (S0) can be set and read with a simple level and a ruler over a known horizontal run, letting the same rig test multiple bed slopes.

sections.heading: Establishing zero and tracing the flow
sections.body: Before any head reading means anything, the rig needs a still-water zero: with the pump off and the channel at rest, the head gauge (a point gauge or a ruler against the V-notch crest) is read and recorded as the true zero datum, since any offset between the physical crest and the gauge's zero mark becomes a constant bias in every subsequent head reading. Flow can then be visualized cheaply — food-coloring dye streaks reveal streamlines and separation zones, yarn tufts taped to a probe rod show local flow direction and reversal, and small floating particles (puffed rice or light plastic beads) tracked frame-by-frame on video give surface velocity — all standard, low-cost hydraulics-teaching techniques that turn an otherwise invisible flow field into something a judge can see in a photo or video.

sections.heading: The error budget, and why head dominates it
sections.body: A rig like this has several honest error sources that should be named and combined, not ignored. A head-zero offset directly biases the discharge computed from the V-notch reading, and because that box's rating scales as Q ∝ H^2.5, a small absolute offset is amplified into a much larger discharge error at low heads. Surface tension becomes non-negligible below roughly 30 mm of head, distorting the nappe's profile away from the shape the standard Cd assumes — most weir standards (including the Kindsvater-Carter approach) recommend staying above about 30-50 mm of head for exactly this reason. A narrow, shallow gutter channel has a small aspect ratio (width to depth), so sidewall friction claims a disproportionate share of the wetted perimeter and skews the velocity profile away from what a wide-channel assumption predicts. A pulsing pump output — common with small centrifugal or diaphragm pumps — creates head oscillation that the head tank's volume and baffling must be sized to damp out, and probe blockage from debris or trapped air bubbles in a small-bore pressure tap can silently corrupt readings. Combined properly (added in quadrature, not simply summed), these sources make clear that head-measurement precision, amplified by the H^2.5 exponent, dominates the total uncertainty far more than any timing or geometric error in the rig.

lessons.workedExample: A student's bench flume uses a V-notch box with a still-water zero later found to be off by 1.5 mm (the gauge read H = 0 when the true crest was 1.5 mm higher). At a working head of H = 40 mm, the true head was actually 38.5 mm, a 3.75% error in H. Because Q ∝ H^2.5 for the V-notch, that becomes roughly 2.5*3.75% ≈ 9.4% error in every discharge value computed for the session — larger than the roughly 3% timing uncertainty from a stopwatch-and-bucket check run alongside it. Re-zeroing the gauge against the true crest and re-running the trials cuts the dominant error source, while the timing check confirms the corrected V-notch readings now agree with the bucket-and-stopwatch reference within about 4%.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge examining a bench flume wants to see an uncertainty budget, not just a clean-looking dataset — the giveaway of real understanding is a student who identifies head-zero offset as the dominant error specifically because of the H^2.5 exponent, rather than listing every possible error with equal weight. A student who re-zeroed against a still-water datum, stayed above the ~30 mm surface-tension threshold, and cross-checked a few points against a bucket-and-stopwatch reference has built a rig they can defend under questioning; one who reports a single trial with no zero check or cross-validation has not.

questions.prompt: Why does a 1.5 mm head-zero offset cause a disproportionately large discharge error on a V-notch discharge box at low heads?

options.text: Because V-notch weirs have no established discharge coefficient at low head
Because Q scales as H^2.5, so a given percentage error in H is amplified by roughly 2.5x in the computed discharge
Because 1.5 mm offsets only matter for rectangular weirs, not V-notches
Because pumps cannot deliver flow accurately below 40 mm of head
