explanations.a: V-notch weirs do have an established Cd at low head; the issue here is a zero-offset error, not a missing coefficient.
explanations.b: Correct — because Q ∝ H^2.5, dQ/Q ≈ 2.5*(dH/H), so the same absolute offset becomes a larger fraction of a small head, producing an amplified discharge error, as shown in the worked example (3.75% head error becoming ~9.4% discharge error).
explanations.c: The H-exponent amplification effect applies to V-notch weirs specifically because of their H^2.5 relationship; it is not a rectangular-weir-only phenomenon.
explanations.d: The error described is a zero-datum calibration issue, not a limitation of pump delivery accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why should a bench flume's V-notch discharge readings be kept above roughly 30 mm of head?

options.text: Below that head, surface tension distorts the nappe profile away from the shape the standard discharge coefficient assumes
Below that head, the pump cannot maintain steady flow
Below that head, the honeycomb flow straightener stops working
There is no lower limit; any head down to zero gives a valid reading

explanations.a: Correct — at low heads, surface tension forces become comparable to gravitational/inertial forces shaping the nappe, invalidating the assumptions behind the standard Cd, which is why weir standards recommend staying above roughly 30-50 mm.
explanations.b: Pump steadiness is a separate issue (addressed by the head tank and honeycomb straightener), not the reason for the minimum-head recommendation.
explanations.c: The flow straightener's job is calming turbulence in the head tank, unrelated to the surface-tension limit at the discharge box.
explanations.d: There is a real practical lower limit; below it, the standard weir rating is known to become invalid due to surface-tension distortion.

questions.prompt: Why does a narrow, shallow bench-flume channel (small aspect ratio) skew results away from wide-channel assumptions?

options.text: Sidewall friction claims a disproportionate share of the wetted perimeter, altering the velocity profile compared to a wide channel where sidewalls matter less
Narrow channels always have higher discharge coefficients
Small aspect ratios eliminate the need for a still-water zero
Narrow channels are immune to surface-tension effects

explanations.a: Correct — in a narrow, shallow channel, the walls make up a larger fraction of the wetted perimeter relative to the flow area, so wall friction has an outsized effect on the velocity profile compared to a wide channel where the bed dominates.
explanations.b: Aspect ratio changes the velocity distribution, not a general rule about the discharge coefficient's magnitude.
explanations.c: The still-water zero is an unrelated calibration step required regardless of channel aspect ratio.
explanations.d: Aspect ratio and surface-tension sensitivity are separate error sources; a narrow channel is not protected from surface tension.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for correctly commissioning and running a bench flume test session.

items.text: Assemble the rig: gutter channel, pump and sump, head tank with honeycomb straightener, V-notch discharge box
With the pump off, record the still-water zero at the head gauge
Set the channel slope and turn on the pump to establish steady flow
Record head readings and cross-check discharge against a timed bucket-and-stopwatch measurement

questions.explanation: The rig must be built first, then a true zero datum established while the water is still (before any flow-induced bias is possible), then slope set and flow started, and only then are head readings meaningful — with a bucket-and-stopwatch check providing an independent reference against the dominant head-amplified uncertainty.

units.label: Landmark Work & Open Debates

lessons.label: Archimedes: The Crown, the Book, and What He Actually Proved

sections.heading: The legend versus the record
sections.body: The story everyone knows — Archimedes leaping from his bath shouting "eureka" after realizing he could detect gold adulterated with silver in King Hiero II's crown by the water it displaced — comes from a single source: the Roman engineer Vitruvius, writing roughly two centuries after the fact, in the preface to Book IX of De Architectura. Vitruvius is not a physics text; it is an anecdote used to illustrate a point about intellectual honesty. Nowhere in Archimedes' own surviving works does he describe a crown, a bath, or a king's suspicion of a goldsmith. What Archimedes did leave is On Floating Bodies (Peri okhoumenon), a two-book treatise that survives mostly through a 13th-century Latin translation of a lost Greek original, and it is far more rigorous — and far more interesting — than the bath story suggests.

sections.heading: What On Floating Bodies actually proves
sections.body: Book I states and proves what is now called the Archimedes principle: a body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of fluid displaced, derived from postulates about fluid pressure increasing with depth and fluids seeking their lowest state — essentially an early hydrostatics from first principles, not an empirical rule of thumb. Book II goes further and is the genuinely startling part: Archimedes analyzes the floating equilibrium and stability of paraboloid segments (solids of revolution shaped like a parabola rotated about its axis) at varying densities and degrees of tilt, working out exactly when such a solid returns upright after being disturbed versus when it capsizes. This is floating-body stability theory — the ancestor of the metacentric-height analysis naval architects would not formalize again until the 18th century — worked out geometrically, without calculus, roughly 2,000 years before Bouguer.

sections.heading: Why the crown test doesn't actually work
sections.body: The popularized version — dunk the crown, read the water-level rise, compare to an equal-weight lump of pure gold — is real physics but a poor instrument. Gold's density (about 19.3 g/cm3) is so far above silver's (10.5 g/cm3) that even a moderately debased crown displaces only a little more volume than pure gold of the same weight; the volume difference for a plausible adulteration is a few percent of the total, well within the measurement error of reading a water line by eye in an irregularly shaped vessel. The Renaissance polymath Galileo Galilei recognized this problem and, in a short 1586 treatise called La Bilancetta ("The Little Balance"), proposed a more plausible reconstruction: a hydrostatic balance that weighs the crown against a pure-gold counterweight first in air and then both submerged in water, converting a hard-to-read volume difference into a directly readable difference in balance tilt — a method with far better sensitivity, and the one most historians of science now think comes closer to whatever Archimedes may have actually done.

lessons.workedExample: A goldsmith is suspected of substituting silver for some of the gold in a 1.0 kg crown while keeping the weight exact. Pure gold at that weight displaces about 51.8 cm3 of water; a crown that is 90% gold by weight and 10% silver by weight displaces about 56.2 cm3 — a difference of only about 4.3 cm3, easy to miss in a splashing basin. Galileo's balance method instead hangs the crown on one arm and a pure-gold reference of equal air-weight on the other, then submerges both: because the crown is less dense than pure gold, it displaces more water, loses more apparent weight, and the balance visibly tips toward the gold reference — converting a few-percent volume discrepancy into a directly observable rotation of the balance arm, a far more sensitive readout than eyeballing a water line.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "what did Archimedes actually prove, and could his bath test have worked?" is testing whether a student can separate a charming legend from a citable primary result and reason about measurement sensitivity rather than just repeating the story. The strong answer names On Floating Bodies specifically, distinguishes Book I's buoyancy principle from Book II's stability analysis of floating solids, and can explain quantitatively why a displacement test is too insensitive for a real adulteration — then knows Galileo's La Bilancetta as the better-instrumented alternative. A student who only knows "eureka" has memorized folklore, not the physics.

questions.prompt: Which ancient source is the origin of the "eureka" bathtub crown story, and what is its evidentiary status?

options.text: Archimedes' own On Floating Bodies, which opens with the anecdote
Vitruvius's De Architectura, written roughly two centuries later as an illustrative anecdote, not a physics account
Galileo's La Bilancetta, which invented the story to justify his balance method
A contemporary inscription commissioned by King Hiero II

explanations.a: On Floating Bodies contains no mention of a crown, a bath, or King Hiero; it is a purely mathematical treatise.
explanations.b: Correct — Vitruvius tells the story in De Architectura's Book IX preface, writing about two hundred years after Archimedes, as a moral illustration rather than a technical report.
explanations.c: Galileo's 1586 pamphlet works from the legend to propose a better method; it does not originate the story.
explanations.d: No such contemporary inscription survives or is referenced by any historian of the episode.

questions.prompt: What is the key result of Book II of On Floating Bodies?

options.text: A restatement of the buoyancy principle already given in Book I
A stability analysis of floating paraboloid segments, determining when they return upright versus capsize
A method for measuring the density of silver alloys
A proof that ships are more stable when loaded with cargo

explanations.a: The buoyancy principle (displaced-fluid weight equals buoyant force) is Book I's result; Book II goes further.
explanations.b: Correct — Book II works out the equilibrium and stability of floating paraboloid segments across densities and tilts, an early ancestor of metacentric stability theory.
explanations.c: Density measurement of alloys is the folklore crown application, not the content of Book II.
explanations.d: Book II is a geometric stability analysis of a specific solid shape, not a general statement about cargo loading.

questions.prompt: Why is the naive displacement test (dunk the crown, read the water-level rise) an impractical way to detect gold adulterated with silver?

options.text: Water does not displace when a solid is submerged
Gold and silver have nearly identical densities, so no volume difference exists
Gold and silver densities differ enough that even a modest adulteration produces only a small volume difference, hard to read accurately off a water line
The method only works for spherical objects

explanations.a: Displacement is real and is exactly the physical basis of Archimedes' principle; the issue is sensitivity, not existence of the effect.
explanations.b: Gold (about 19.3 g/cm3) and silver (about 10.5 g/cm3) differ substantially in density — the problem is the opposite of identical densities.
explanations.c: Correct — because gold is so much denser than silver, even a crown a few percent silver by weight has a volume only slightly larger than pure gold of equal weight, producing a water-level change too small to read reliably by eye.
explanations.d: Archimedes' principle applies to any submerged shape; geometry is not the limiting factor here.

questions.prompt: Match each figure to their contribution regarding the crown problem.

right.text: Proved the buoyancy principle and paraboloid floating-body stability in On Floating Bodies
Recorded the eureka bathtub anecdote roughly two centuries after the fact, in De Architectura
Proposed a more sensitive hydrostatic balance reconstruction in La Bilancetta (1586)

questions.explanation: Archimedes' own mathematical legacy is On Floating Bodies; Vitruvius supplies the popular legend long after Archimedes' death; Galileo, recognizing the legend's test was too crude, proposed the hydrostatic balance method in his 1586 pamphlet La Bilancetta as a more plausible and sensitive reconstruction.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Archimedes writes On Floating Bodies, proving buoyancy and paraboloid stability
Vitruvius records the eureka crown anecdote in De Architectura
Galileo publishes La Bilancetta, proposing the hydrostatic balance method

questions.explanation: Archimedes' treatise dates to the 3rd century BCE; Vitruvius wrote in the 1st century BCE, about two centuries later; Galileo's La Bilancetta followed in 1586, over a millennium after both.

lessons.label: Bouguer, Euler and the Invention of Metacentric Stability

sections.heading: A century-late theory
sections.body: On 10 August 1628 the Swedish warship Vasa capsized and sank less than a mile into her maiden voyage in Stockholm harbor, killed by top-heaviness from extra decks and armament added without any way to compute their effect on stability. No such computation existed yet. The mathematical tool that would have caught the error — the metacenter — was not introduced until 1746, when the French mathematician and hydrographer Pierre Bouguer published Traite du navire, defining the metacenter as the point where the vertical line of buoyant force, as a hull heels through a small angle, crosses the ship's centerline. If that point sits above the center of gravity, the ship rights itself; if below, it capsizes further. Bouguer's metacentric height (GM) reduced stability to a single, calculable number.

sections.heading: Euler's independent route
sections.body: Leonhard Euler reached equivalent stability criteria independently, publishing them in Scientia Navalis (1749), a treatise developed from his work at the St. Petersburg Academy. Euler approached the problem through the general theory of rigid-body equilibrium and small rotations rather than Bouguer's more geometric, ship-specific derivation, and the two men's near-simultaneous, independently-derived results are now treated as parallel foundations of naval hydrostatics rather than a priority dispute — each solved the same problem from a different mathematical direction within three years of the other. Together they turned "will this hull capsize" from a question answered by experience and superstition into one answered by measuring hull geometry, weight distribution, and a trigonometric small-angle calculation.

sections.heading: From theory to shipyard practice, and its limits
sections.body: The practical descendant of Bouguer and Euler's work is the inclining experiment: a set of known weights is shifted a known distance across a moored, otherwise-complete ship's deck, and the resulting small heel angle is measured, letting engineers back-calculate the actual height of the center of gravity and hence GM — still standard practice today. But metacentric height is only valid for small heel angles; real stability across a full range of tilt requires the righting-arm curve, or GZ curve, which the low-angle metacenter approximates only near upright. That gap between an adequate GM and an adequate full-range GZ curve is exactly what proved fatal in 1870, when the Royal Navy's low-freeboard turret ship HMS Captain capsized in a gale after her righting moment, as later calculation showed, peaked near 21 degrees of heel and collapsed thereafter — a case the theory could have flagged in advance, and very nearly did.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a hull with its center of gravity fixed but its metacenter computed at two different heel ranges. Near upright, the metacentric height GM is a healthy 2 feet, meaning small disturbances are righted — the ship passes a simple inclining-experiment check. But a full GZ curve, plotting righting arm against heel angle from 0 to 90 degrees, can still show the righting arm rising only briefly and then collapsing to zero well before capsizing angle if the hull's freeboard is low and its topside weight (turrets, armor, rigging) is heavy — exactly the shape of curve later reconstructed for HMS Captain, whose righting moment peaked around 21 degrees versus roughly 40 degrees for her more conventional sister design HMS Monarch. A single GM number at small angles looked fine; the full curve did not.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about ship stability wants to see whether a student can name the actual mechanism — metacenter above or below center of gravity — rather than gesturing at "balance." The distinguishing move is knowing that GM is a small-angle approximation, that the inclining experiment is how it gets measured on a real hull, and that a full GZ curve is the tool that catches failures GM alone would miss. Naming Bouguer (1746) and Euler (1749) as independent originators, and being able to explain concretely why a positive GM is not the same guarantee as a well-shaped GZ curve, is what separates rote memorization of "metacenter" from understanding why the concept had to be invented at all.

questions.prompt: What does the metacentric height (GM) measure, and what does a positive value indicate?

options.text: The distance between the keel and the waterline; positive means the ship is fully loaded
The height of the metacenter above the center of gravity; positive means the ship tends to right itself at small heel angles
The ship's total displacement in tons; positive means the ship is seaworthy
The speed at which the hull generates waves; positive means excess drag

explanations.a: That describes draft, an unrelated hull-geometry measurement.
explanations.b: Correct — GM is the metacenter's height above the center of gravity; when positive, the buoyant force line crosses above the center of gravity as the hull heels slightly, producing a righting moment.
explanations.c: Displacement measures weight/volume of water displaced, not stability.
explanations.d: That describes resistance or wave-making, a separate topic from static stability.

questions.prompt: How did Bouguer and Euler arrive at metacentric stability theory?

options.text: Bouguer copied Euler's Scientia Navalis after its 1749 publication
They co-authored a single joint treatise
They developed equivalent stability criteria independently — Bouguer in Traite du navire (1746), Euler in Scientia Navalis (1749) — using different mathematical approaches
Euler's result predates Bouguer's by several decades

explanations.a: The chronology runs the other way if anything — Bouguer's 1746 publication came first — but there is no evidence either copied the other; the results were independent.
explanations.b: The two works were separate publications by separate authors, not a joint treatise.
explanations.c: Correct — Bouguer's more geometric, ship-specific derivation appeared in 1746; Euler's derivation from general rigid-body rotation appeared in 1749, arrived at independently.
explanations.d: Bouguer's 1746 publication actually precedes Euler's 1749 one, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: Why is a positive GM alone not sufficient to guarantee a ship won't capsize in a real gale?

options.text: GM only applies to submarines, not surface ships
GM is a small-angle approximation; the full righting-arm (GZ) curve can still collapse well before large heel angles even if GM near upright is positive
GM changes randomly with weather and cannot be measured
GM only matters for wooden hulls, not iron ones

explanations.a: Metacentric height applies to surface ships (and floating bodies generally); it is not submarine-specific.
explanations.b: Correct — as shown by HMS Captain, a hull can have a reassuring small-angle GM yet a GZ curve whose righting arm peaks at a low angle and collapses to zero well before capsize, a danger GM alone does not reveal.
explanations.c: GM is measurable directly via the inclining experiment; it is not unmeasurable or purely random.
explanations.d: The physics of metacentric stability is hull-material-independent; it depends on geometry and weight distribution, not the material.

questions.prompt: What does the inclining experiment measure on a real ship?

options.text: The ship's top speed under full power
The height of the center of gravity, back-calculated from the small heel angle produced by shifting known weights a known distance
The wave-making resistance at various speeds
The fuel efficiency of the ship's engines

explanations.a: Speed trials are a separate test entirely unrelated to stability measurement.
explanations.b: Correct — moving known weights a known distance across the deck of a moored ship and measuring the resulting small heel angle lets engineers back-calculate the actual center-of-gravity height and hence GM.
explanations.c: Wave-making resistance is measured via towing-tank or full-scale towing trials (as with Froude), not the inclining experiment.
explanations.d: Fuel efficiency has nothing to do with the weight-shift/heel-angle method of the inclining experiment.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Vasa capsizes on her maiden voyage in Stockholm harbor
Bouguer publishes Traite du navire, defining the metacenter
Euler publishes Scientia Navalis with independently-derived stability criteria
HMS Captain capsizes in a gale after a GZ curve that peaked near 21 degrees

questions.explanation: Vasa sank in 1628, over a century before stability theory existed. Bouguer's Traite du navire followed in 1746, Euler's Scientia Navalis in 1749, and HMS Captain's capsize came over a century after the theory was available, in 1870, when a low-freeboard design was approved despite the danger the theory could reveal.

lessons.label: William Froude and the Torquay Towing Tank

sections.heading: Building the case for models
sections.body: In the 1860s naval architecture had no reliable way to predict a full-size ship's resistance from a small model — informal model trials had never given results that tracked the full-scale ships they were meant to predict, and the dominant professional opinion was that model tests would never prove a useful guide to full-scale behavior. William Froude disagreed, and set out to prove it with his own money and reputation before the Admiralty would fund him. Testing two hull forms he had built — named Swan and Raven — first as models towed in the River Dart in 1867 and then at larger scale, he found that resistance did not scale simply with size, but separated into two physically distinct components: skin friction (scaling with wetted surface area and a velocity-dependent friction coefficient he measured directly by towing thin planks of varying length and surface finish through calm water in 1872-74) and wave-making resistance (scaling with a dimensionless speed-to-length relationship now called the Froude number).

sections.heading: The Torquay tank and the law of comparison
sections.body: Convinced by his plank and model results, Froude persuaded the Admiralty to fund a dedicated testing facility; the tank at Torquay was approved around 1870 and began operating in 1871, roughly 278 feet long (about 85 meters), using a constant-speed pulley system and Froude's own dynamometers to tow wax hull models and record resistance directly. From the plank-friction data and the model tests, Froude formulated his law of comparison: if two geometrically similar hulls, model and full-size, are towed at speeds whose ratio equals the square root of their length ratio (equal Froude number), their wave-making resistance coefficients match, while skin-friction resistance — measured separately via the planks — can be added back in by calculation. This let Froude predict a full-size ship's total resistance from a small model's wave pattern plus a computed friction correction, rather than needing to guess at a single blanket scaling rule.

sections.heading: The Greyhound trial and the reception
sections.body: Skepticism did not vanish with the tank's opening. William Rankine, a leading figure at the Institution of Naval Architects and a proponent of competing streamline theory, remained doubtful that small tank models could stand in for full-size hulls in a turbulent sea. The decisive test came in 1874: the Royal Navy sloop HMS Greyhound, towed by HMS Active at a series of speeds from about 3 to 12.5 knots and instrumented to measure the towline pull directly, produced a resistance curve of the same shape as Froude's model predictions — somewhat higher in absolute terms, which Froude attributed correctly to greater hull roughness on the real ship than assumed in his friction planks. Froude wrote that the trial substantially verified his law of comparison, and the result is generally treated as the founding demonstration of experimental naval architecture: a quantitative prediction, made from a small model in a tank, confirmed against a full-size ship at sea.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a 6-foot model of a hull, towed in the Torquay tank, shows a particular wave-making resistance at a model speed of 2 knots. To predict the wave-making resistance of the real 100-foot ship at the corresponding condition, Froude's law of comparison says to test (or compare) at a full-scale speed where the Froude number matches: since speed scales with the square root of length, the full-size ship's corresponding speed is 2 times the square root of (100/6), or roughly 8.2 knots. The wave-making coefficient measured on the model at 2 knots should then match the full ship's wave-making coefficient at 8.2 knots; skin-friction resistance, which does not scale the same way, is instead computed separately from the plank-friction data and added to get total predicted resistance — precisely the two-step method the HMS Greyhound trial at speeds up to 12.5 knots was built to check.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing model-testing methodology wants to know whether a student understands that Froude's contribution was not just "build a tank" but a physical decomposition — separating resistance into two components that scale differently — plus a validated scaling rule connecting model speed to full-scale speed. The tell of real understanding is being able to state the law of comparison's actual claim (matching Froude number preserves wave-making behavior, while friction is corrected separately) and naming the Greyhound trial as the empirical check against real skepticism, rather than treating "tow a small model" as self-evidently sufficient. A student who cannot say why friction and wave-making need different scaling has missed the actual insight.

questions.prompt: What two physically distinct components did Froude's plank and model experiments separate total hull resistance into?

options.text: Wind resistance and current resistance
Skin friction (scaling with wetted area and speed) and wave-making resistance (scaling with the Froude number)
Engine efficiency and propeller cavitation
Buoyant force and gravitational force

explanations.a: Froude's tank tests were towed in calm conditions specifically to isolate hull resistance from wind and current effects.
explanations.b: Correct — his 1872-74 plank experiments isolated skin friction as a function of wetted surface and velocity, while his model tests isolated wave-making resistance scaling with the Froude number.
explanations.c: Propulsion machinery was not the subject of the plank and hull-model experiments, which addressed passive resistance.
explanations.d: Buoyancy and gravity determine floating equilibrium, not the drag a moving hull experiences through water.

questions.prompt: According to Froude's law of comparison, at what model speed does a model's wave-making resistance coefficient match the full-size ship's?

options.text: The same absolute speed as the full-size ship
A speed whose ratio to the full-size speed equals the square root of the length ratio (equal Froude number)
Any speed, since wave-making resistance does not depend on speed
A speed proportional to the cube of the length ratio

explanations.a: Testing at the same absolute speed would give a wildly mismatched Froude number for a much smaller model.
explanations.b: Correct — matching Froude number (speed proportional to the square root of length) is the scaling condition that preserves wave-making resistance coefficients between geometrically similar hulls.
explanations.c: Wave-making resistance is strongly speed-dependent; this is exactly the effect the Froude number scaling captures.
explanations.d: A cube-of-length-ratio scaling is not the relationship Froude derived; his law uses a square-root relationship.

questions.prompt: What did the 1874 HMS Greyhound trial demonstrate, and how did the result compare to Froude's model prediction?

options.text: The full-scale resistance curve had a completely different shape than the model prediction, disproving Froude's law
The full-scale resistance curve matched the model prediction's shape but ran somewhat higher, which Froude attributed to greater hull roughness than assumed in the friction-plank data
The trial measured only top speed, not a resistance curve, so it could not test the law of comparison
The trial showed wave-making resistance was negligible at all tested speeds

explanations.a: The trial's resistance curve matched the model's shape, which is why it was taken as verification rather than refutation.
explanations.b: Correct — towed by HMS Active across a range of speeds, Greyhound's measured resistance curve had the same character as the model prediction but somewhat higher values, attributed to real hull roughness exceeding the friction-plank assumption.
explanations.c: The trial measured towline pull across a range of speeds from about 3 to 12.5 knots, producing a full resistance curve, not just a single top-speed figure.
explanations.d: Wave-making resistance was a central, not negligible, part of what the trial and Froude's law addressed.

questions.prompt: Which figure at the Institution of Naval Architects remained skeptical that small tank models could reliably predict full-scale hull behavior?

options.text: Bouguer
Rankine
Euler
Manning

explanations.a: Bouguer worked a century earlier on metacentric stability, an unrelated question from ship resistance.
explanations.b: Correct — Rankine, a proponent of competing streamline theory, was among the prominent skeptics of using small-scale models to predict full-size ship resistance.
explanations.c: Euler worked on stability theory in the 18th century, not on 19th-century resistance-scaling debates.
explanations.d: Manning is associated with open-channel flow formulas, unrelated to ship-model testing.

questions.prompt: Order these events in Froude's program chronologically.

items.text: Swan and Raven models first towed in the River Dart
Admiralty-funded towing tank at Torquay begins operating
Plank experiments isolate skin-friction resistance from wave-making resistance
HMS Greyhound full-scale towing trial verifies the law of comparison

questions.explanation: Froude's early Swan and Raven river tests in 1867 built the case for Admiralty funding; the Torquay tank opened in 1871; the plank experiments isolating friction ran through 1872-74 alongside tank operations; the Greyhound full-scale trial in 1874 came last, as the empirical check against real skepticism.

lessons.label: Chezy, Manning and the Fight Over an Empirical Formula

sections.heading: Chezy's canal-derived starting point
sections.body: In 1769, the French engineer Antoine de Chezy, tasked with sizing a supply canal for Paris drawing from the river Yvette, worked out a relationship between a channel's mean flow velocity, its hydraulic radius (cross-sectional flow area divided by wetted perimeter), and its slope, tying the three together through a single resistance coefficient. Chezy's formula, v = C times the square root of (R times S), was derived empirically by comparing the Yvette project to an existing canal and to Seine River flow data rather than from first-principles fluid mechanics, and it became the starting template for open-channel flow calculations for the next century — with the coefficient C left as a number to be found by experience for a given channel, not predicted from channel properties alone.

sections.heading: Manning's paper, and Manning's own discomfort with it
sections.body: On 4 December 1889, the Irish engineer Robert Manning, then 73, presented a paper to the Institution of Civil Engineers of Ireland (published 1891) reviewing existing open-channel formulas and proposing a refinement in which Chezy's coefficient C is replaced by a function of hydraulic radius raised to the one-sixth power divided by a roughness coefficient n — yielding the now-familiar v = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2). The awkward historical fact, often left out, is that Manning himself was not fully satisfied with the formula that came to bear his name and continued to favor other formulations he considered more physically justified; the version popularized after him is also dimensionally inhomogeneous — the constant 1/n only works in specific unit systems (metric or U.S. customary, with different numeric conversion factors), unlike a truly dimensionless physical law, a flaw modern hydraulics texts note but the formula's practical convenience has never displaced.

sections.heading: Priority: Gauckler, Strickler, and a name that outran its history
sections.body: Manning was not first. The French engineer Philippe-Gaspard Gauckler had already published an essentially equivalent power-law relationship in 1867, over two decades earlier, and the Swiss engineer Albert Strickler independently proposed a similar roughness-based formulation in 1923. Because of this layered priority, the formula is known in much of Europe as the Gauckler-Manning formula or the Gauckler-Manning-Strickler formula, while U.S. practice largely credits Manning alone — a naming asymmetry that reflects which country's engineering tradition popularized the formula locally rather than genuine chronological priority. The live modern critique goes beyond naming: Manning's n is routinely treated in textbooks as a fixed property of a channel's bed material, but in real rivers n measurably shifts with flow stage (rising with overbank vegetation at high flow, falling as bedforms smooth out at high velocity) and with seasonal vegetation growth, meaning a single tabulated n value is at best a rough average, not a channel constant.

lessons.workedExample: An engineer sizing a trapezoidal drainage channel with hydraulic radius R = 1.2 m and bed slope S = 0.001 looks up a roughness coefficient n = 0.030 for a clean earth channel and computes velocity as v = (1/0.030) times 1.2^(2/3) times 0.001^(1/2), giving roughly 1.19 m/s in SI units. But if that same channel grows dense summer vegetation along its banks, n might realistically rise to 0.05-0.06, cutting predicted velocity by nearly half for the identical geometry and slope — illustrating why treating n as a fixed lookup-table constant, rather than a seasonally and stage-dependent quantity, is the single most common real-world source of error when applying the formula to natural channels rather than to a fixed concrete culvert.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks about Manning's formula is testing whether a student treats textbook equations as historical artifacts with a real, messy priority chain, or as handed-down truths. The strong answer names Chezy's 1769 canal work as the template, credits Gauckler's 1867 priority and Strickler's 1923 contribution alongside Manning's 1889 paper, and volunteers two specific weaknesses: the formula's dimensional inhomogeneity, and n's real dependence on flow stage and vegetation rather than being a fixed channel property. A student who cites the formula but cannot say where n actually comes from, or that it drifts with conditions, has memorized a lookup table rather than understood a model's limits.

questions.prompt: What was the empirical basis of Chezy's 1769 formula?

options.text: Laboratory experiments with scaled pipe models
Comparison of the proposed Yvette canal project to an existing canal and to Seine River flow data
A first-principles derivation from the Navier-Stokes equations
Tidal measurements taken in the English Channel

explanations.a: Chezy's work was tied to a specific real canal project, not scaled laboratory pipe models.
explanations.b: Correct — Chezy derived his velocity-slope-hydraulic radius relationship by comparing the planned Yvette supply canal against an existing canal and Seine River data, an empirical rather than first-principles approach.
explanations.c: The Navier-Stokes equations were not formulated until the 19th century, decades after Chezy's 1769 work.
explanations.d: Chezy's work concerned a freshwater supply canal for Paris, unrelated to tidal or Channel measurements.

questions.prompt: What is the awkward historical fact about Robert Manning's relationship to the formula bearing his name?

options.text: Manning never worked in hydraulics and the formula was misattributed to him by later engineers
Manning presented the formula in 1889 but was not fully satisfied with it and preferred other formulations he considered more physically justified
Manning plagiarized the formula directly from Strickler's 1923 paper
Manning refused to publish his formula, and it was reconstructed posthumously from his notes

explanations.a: Manning did present a genuine paper on open-channel formulas to the Institution of Civil Engineers of Ireland in 1889; the misattribution issue is about priority (Gauckler), not authorship.
explanations.b: Correct — despite presenting the formula in his 1889 paper, Manning himself continued to favor other formulations he found more physically justified, and was not the formula's enthusiastic champion.
explanations.c: The chronology runs the other way: Manning's paper (1889) predates Strickler's work (1923) by decades, so plagiarism in that direction is chronologically impossible.
explanations.d: Manning presented the paper himself in 1889, in his own lifetime; it was not posthumously reconstructed.

questions.prompt: Why is the Manning formula considered dimensionally inhomogeneous?

options.text: Because hydraulic radius cannot be measured in real channels
Because the 1/n coefficient only produces correct units in specific unit systems, unlike a truly dimensionless physical law
Because it uses slope, which has no physical meaning
Because it was derived without any reference to a real channel

explanations.a: Hydraulic radius is a standard, measurable channel-geometry quantity; that is not the source of the dimensional issue.
explanations.b: Correct — the formula's 1/n term is calibrated to work correctly only within a specific unit system (metric or U.S. customary, with different conversion constants), a hallmark of a dimensionally inhomogeneous empirical relationship rather than a scale-invariant physical law.
explanations.c: Slope (a ratio of rise to run) is dimensionless and physically meaningful; it is not the source of the inhomogeneity.
explanations.d: The formula descends from Chezy's canal-derived relationship and Manning's own channel-flow paper, both grounded in real channel data.

questions.prompt: What is the live modern critique of treating Manning's roughness coefficient n as a fixed channel property?

options.text: n cannot be measured at all, even in a laboratory flume
n varies with flow stage and vegetation, so a single tabulated value is only a rough average rather than a true constant
n only applies to circular pipes, not open channels
n was never actually defined by Manning or Gauckler

explanations.a: n is routinely measured and tabulated for many channel and bed-material types; the critique is about its stability as a value, not its measurability.
explanations.b: Correct — real rivers show n shifting with flow stage (overbank vegetation effects, bedform smoothing at higher velocity) and seasonal vegetation growth, so a single lookup-table n is at best an approximation.
explanations.c: The formula and its roughness coefficient were developed specifically for open-channel flow, not pipe flow.
explanations.d: Both Gauckler's 1867 work and Manning's 1889 paper defined a roughness-related coefficient central to their respective formulas.

questions.prompt: Match each figure to their contribution to the open-channel flow formula.

right.text: 1769: empirical velocity-slope-hydraulic-radius relationship from the Yvette canal project
1867: earliest publication of an essentially equivalent power-law roughness formula
1889: paper to the Institution of Civil Engineers of Ireland refining the coefficient into a roughness term
1923: independent proposal of a similar roughness-based formulation

questions.explanation: Chezy's 1769 canal work is the template; Gauckler's 1867 publication has priority over the roughness-based power-law form; Manning's 1889 paper (published 1891) is the version that became eponymous in U.S. practice; Strickler's independent 1923 formulation completes the Gauckler-Manning-Strickler naming used in much of Europe.

lessons.label: The Hydraulic Jump: Bidone, Belanger and the Kitchen-Sink Controversy

sections.heading: The classical channel jump
sections.body: A hydraulic jump is the abrupt, turbulent transition a fast, shallow flow makes to a slower, deeper flow — the standing wall of churning water you see below a spillway or a weir. The Italian hydraulician Giorgio Bidone gave the phenomenon its first systematic experimental study in 1818, observing and measuring jumps in Turin, documenting how the jump's height and the energy it dissipated depended on the upstream flow's speed and depth. A decade later, the French engineer Jean-Baptiste Belanger supplied the theoretical backbone in 1828, applying momentum conservation across the jump (rather than energy conservation, which is not conserved through the turbulent jump itself) to derive the relationship between the depths upstream and downstream — the same momentum-balance logic still taught today as the Belanger equation for conjugate depths.

sections.heading: From open channels to a circular jump on a plate
sections.body: The version of the jump familiar from a kitchen sink — the roughly circular ring where a fast, thin sheet of water spreading out from a falling jet abruptly thickens — is geometrically different from Bidone's channel jump but was long treated as governed by the same underlying physics. Lord Rayleigh gave the circular hydraulic jump a hydrodynamic treatment in 1914, and the physicist Watson developed a more complete boundary-layer theory of the thin-film flow leading up to the jump in 1964, modeling the radial spreading jet's viscous boundary layer growth to predict where the jump would form. For roughly a century after Rayleigh, the standard assumption — echoing the channel case — was that gravity, resisting the outward-spreading flow once the film thins enough, is what sets the jump's radius.

sections.heading: The 2018 challenge and the fight since
sections.body: In 2018, Bhagat, Jha, Linden and Wilson published a paper in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics arguing that for the everyday kitchen-sink-scale circular jump, gravity is not the dominant force at all — instead, surface tension and viscous forces alone balance the flow's momentum at the jump, with the jump radius staying essentially unchanged even when the whole setup is tilted or inverted, which would not be true if gravity were doing the work. This directly challenged over a century of assumed gravity-driven theory descending from Rayleigh and Watson. The claim did not stand unchallenged: researchers including Duchesne, Andersen and Bohr published a rebuttal within about a year arguing the interpretation was flawed, and Duchesne and Limat followed with a more detailed 2022 Journal of Fluid Mechanics paper, "Circular hydraulic jumps: where does surface tension matter?", arguing gravity remains essential except in a narrow regime — while earlier work by Bush and Aristoff (2003) had already shown surface tension's curvature effects matter for the jump radius at small scale, meaning the live argument is not whether surface tension matters at all, but how large a role it plays relative to gravity, and where the crossover sits.

lessons.workedExample: A student running a kitchen-sink experiment sets a steady faucet flow to form a stable circular jump on a flat plate, measures its radius, then re-runs the identical flow rate with the plate tilted 20 degrees from horizontal. Under the classical gravity-driven picture (Rayleigh, Watson), tilting the plate should change the balance of forces resisting the outward flow and measurably shift the jump radius; Bhagat and colleagues reported in 2018 that for their thin-film jumps the radius stayed essentially the same regardless of orientation, which they read as evidence gravity was not the controlling force at that scale. A student redoing this test today, aware of the Duchesne-Limat rebuttal, should expect the actual outcome to depend on exactly which flow-rate and film-thickness regime they land in — the tilt test is genuinely diagnostic, but the field disagrees on what a given result implies.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the rare landmark topics where a judge can ask a student to describe an experiment they could run in their own kitchen and get a real, currently-disputed research question. The strong answer distinguishes the classical channel jump (Bidone 1818, Belanger's 1828 momentum analysis) from the circular plate jump (Rayleigh 1914, Watson 1964), then names the actual 2018 controversy — Bhagat and colleagues' surface-tension claim versus the gravity-defends rebuttals from Duchesne, Limat, and others — without overclaiming that either side has definitively won. A student who presents the 2018 paper as settled fact, rather than as one side of an active dispute, has missed exactly the nuance the topic is meant to teach.

questions.prompt: What conservation principle did Belanger apply in his 1828 analysis of the channel hydraulic jump, and why not the alternative?

options.text: Energy conservation, because momentum is not conserved through a turbulent jump
Momentum conservation, because energy is not conserved through the turbulent, dissipative jump itself
Mass conservation only, ignoring both energy and momentum
Angular momentum conservation, treating the jump as a rotating flow

explanations.a: Momentum is conserved across the jump control volume; energy is the quantity that is not conserved due to turbulent dissipation.
explanations.b: Correct — Belanger applied momentum conservation across the jump, because the turbulence within the jump dissipates mechanical energy, making energy conservation invalid there, while momentum balance still holds.
explanations.c: Mass conservation (continuity) is used alongside momentum, but the distinguishing theoretical move Belanger made was applying momentum balance specifically because energy conservation fails.
explanations.d: The classical channel jump is analyzed with linear momentum balance across the flow direction, not angular momentum.

questions.prompt: What was the standard assumption about the circular kitchen-sink-type hydraulic jump for roughly a century following Rayleigh's 1914 treatment?

options.text: That surface tension alone, with no role for gravity, sets the jump radius
That gravity, resisting the outward-spreading thinning film, is the dominant force setting the jump radius
That the jump forms due to a temperature gradient in the water
That no theoretical model could describe the circular jump at all

explanations.a: The surface-tension-dominant view is the 2018 challenge, not the century-long prior assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — following Rayleigh (1914) and later Watson's 1964 boundary-layer theory, the standard picture treated gravity's resistance to the thinning, spreading film as what sets the jump radius, paralleling the channel-jump logic.
explanations.c: Temperature gradients are not part of the classical or the 2018-challenged hydrodynamic treatment of the circular jump.
explanations.d: Both Rayleigh (1914) and Watson (1964) developed working theoretical treatments; the field was not without a model, just a gravity-centered one.

questions.prompt: What did the 2018 Bhagat, Jha, Linden and Wilson paper argue, and what was their key evidence?

options.text: That gravity dominates the jump, evidenced by the jump radius shrinking sharply when the plate is tilted
That surface tension and viscous forces, not gravity, dominate the thin-film jump, evidenced by the jump radius staying essentially unchanged when the setup is tilted or inverted
That the jump does not occur at all in thin liquid films
That Belanger's 1828 momentum equation applies unchanged to the circular jump

explanations.a: This is closer to the century-old gravity-dominant assumption the 2018 paper was challenging, not its own claim.
explanations.b: Correct — Bhagat and colleagues argued surface tension and viscous forces balance the momentum at the jump, supporting this with the observation that jump radius was essentially independent of the plate's orientation relative to gravity.
explanations.c: The paper's whole subject is explaining the origin of an observed thin-film circular jump, not denying its existence.
explanations.d: Belanger's equation is a channel-jump (rectilinear, momentum-based) result; the 2018 paper's contribution is specifically about the different circular thin-film case.

questions.prompt: How did the field respond to the 2018 surface-tension claim?

options.text: It was immediately and universally accepted with no published disagreement
Researchers including Duchesne, Andersen and Bohr, and later Duchesne and Limat, published rebuttals arguing gravity remains essential, making it a genuinely open, still-argued question
The claim was retracted by its own authors within a year
No further research has been published on the topic since 2018

explanations.a: The claim provoked published disagreement rather than uniform acceptance.
explanations.b: Correct — rebuttals from Duchesne, Andersen and Bohr and a more detailed 2022 Duchesne and Limat paper argued gravity remains essential except in a narrow regime, making the relative roles of gravity and surface tension a live, actively debated question rather than a settled one.
explanations.c: The original authors did not retract the paper; the disagreement played out through published rebuttals and counter-analyses by other researchers.
explanations.d: Multiple papers, including Bush and Aristoff's earlier 2003 work and the Duchesne-Limat 2022 paper, show the topic remained actively researched well past 2018.

questions.prompt: Order these contributions to hydraulic jump theory chronologically.

items.text: Bidone's systematic experimental observations of the channel jump in Turin
Belanger's momentum-balance derivation of conjugate depths
Rayleigh's hydrodynamic treatment of the circular jump
Watson's boundary-layer theory of the radial thin-film flow
Bhagat, Jha, Linden and Wilson's surface-tension challenge to gravity-driven theory

questions.explanation: Bidone's observations came first in 1818, followed by Belanger's momentum analysis in 1828. Rayleigh's circular-jump treatment followed much later in 1914, Watson's boundary-layer theory in 1964, and the surface-tension challenge to the gravity-driven consensus arrived in 2018, itself followed by ongoing rebuttals.

lessons.label: Open Questions Today

sections.heading: Sediment transport: formulas that disagree by an order of magnitude
sections.body: Predicting how much sediment a river carries along its bed (bedload) remains one of hydraulics' least settled quantitative problems. Dozens of competing formulas exist — descendants of early 20th-century work culminating in relationships like the Meyer-Peter and Muller formula (1948) — and it is routine, not exceptional, for two well-regarded formulas applied to the same measured reach, same flow, and same grain size to disagree by an order of magnitude in predicted transport rate. Underlying nearly all of them is the Shields parameter, introduced by Albert Shields in 1936 to define a dimensionless threshold at which flow first mobilizes bed grains; the Shields curve plotting that threshold against grain Reynolds number is a foundational reference in every sediment-transport course, but the original dataset behind it was sparse, and nearly a century of subsequent measurement has produced a scatter band around the curve wide enough that engineers routinely apply safety factors of two or more rather than trusting a single threshold value.

sections.heading: Roughness that will not hold still
sections.body: Manning's n, treated in textbooks as a lookup-table property of a channel bed, is known to drift with flow stage and vegetation density — and that drift is no longer a purely academic footnote. Climate-driven shifts in growing seasons and invasive vegetation are changing the seasonal roughness cycle of managed and natural channels in ways flood models calibrated on older data increasingly miss, meaning a flood-risk map built on a fixed roughness assumption can be measurably stale within years rather than decades, an active concern in current hydraulic engineering practice rather than a settled input.

sections.heading: When a scaled model lies: scale effects, and the towing-tank-versus-CFD argument
sections.body: Froude-scaling a physical model (matching Froude number between model and full scale, per Froude's own law of comparison) reproduces wave-making behavior faithfully but distorts other physics: surface tension does not scale down with geometry, so a small enough model can show capillary effects with no full-scale counterpart, and a model's boundary layer can stay laminar at a Reynolds number where the full-size hull's boundary layer is turbulent, changing the skin-friction physics being compared — exactly the roughness-driven gap Froude himself had to correct for with HMS Greyhound. Modern naval architecture increasingly substitutes or supplements physical towing-tank tests with computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and the live argument is not whether CFD is useful but whether it can be trusted to extrapolate beyond the flow regimes it has been validated against, given that towing tanks carry a century-plus validation record CFD solvers do not yet match. Related is the persistent 'hull speed' myth: the popular claim that a displacement hull has a hard speed limit near 1.34 times the square root of its waterline length in feet is not a physical law but a rule-of-thumb marking where wave resistance begins rising steeply — a distinction that separates students who can name the actual physics (Froude number, wave-making resistance) from those repeating a folk ceiling as if it were unbreakable.

lessons.workedExample: A civil engineering team models a proposed flood channel at 1:50 scale in a laboratory flume, matching Froude number to the full-size design flow. The model correctly reproduces the free-surface wave pattern and overall flow depth, matching the century-old logic of Froude's law of comparison. But at 1:50 scale the model's flow depth is shallow enough that its boundary layer stays laminar at the tested flow rate, while the real channel's boundary layer would be fully turbulent — meaning the model's friction losses, and hence its predicted velocity and depth at the design flow, are systematically off in a way pure Froude scaling cannot catch, the same category of scale effect that forced Froude himself to correct HMS Greyhound's predicted resistance for hull roughness in 1874.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "what does the field still not know" is checking whether a student can name a genuinely live, quantitative dispute rather than reciting settled textbook material as if the field were finished. The strongest answers are concrete: naming that competing bedload formulas can disagree by an order of magnitude on an identical reach, that the Shields curve carries real scatter rather than being a precise threshold, or that Froude-scaled models distort surface tension and boundary-layer state even while getting wave-making right. Debunking the hull-speed myth by name — explaining it is a rule of thumb about rising wave resistance, not a hard physical ceiling — is a reliable signal a student has understood Froude scaling rather than memorized a number.

questions.prompt: How much can well-regarded bedload transport formulas disagree when applied to the same measured river reach, flow, and grain size?

options.text: They typically agree within about 5 percent
It is routine for them to disagree by an order of magnitude
They always agree exactly, since bedload transport is fully solved
Disagreement only occurs for grain sizes below 1 millimeter

explanations.a: Real-world comparisons of competing bedload formulas show far larger disagreement than a small percentage-level gap.
explanations.b: Correct — it is routine, not exceptional, for two well-regarded bedload formulas applied to the same reach and flow to disagree by an order of magnitude in predicted transport rate.
explanations.c: Bedload transport prediction remains one of hydraulics' least settled quantitative problems, not a fully solved one.
explanations.d: The order-of-magnitude disagreement problem is general across grain sizes, not confined to a specific fine-grain regime.

questions.prompt: What does the Shields parameter, introduced by Shields in 1936, define?

options.text: The exact volume of sediment a river will transport per year
A dimensionless threshold at which flow first mobilizes bed grains
The roughness coefficient n for a given channel
The metacentric height of a floating sediment particle

explanations.a: Annual sediment volume is a downstream quantity computed from transport formulas, not what the Shields parameter itself defines.
explanations.b: Correct — the Shields parameter defines a dimensionless critical threshold at which bed grains begin to move under a given flow, plotted against grain Reynolds number as the Shields curve.
explanations.c: Manning's n is a separate roughness coefficient from open-channel flow formulas, unrelated to the Shields threshold concept.
explanations.d: Metacentric height concerns floating-body stability, an unrelated topic from sediment mobilization thresholds.

questions.prompt: Why does Froude-scaling a physical model faithfully reproduce wave-making behavior but potentially distort other physics?

options.text: Because Froude scaling matches speed to the square root of length, but surface tension does not scale down with geometry and a model's boundary layer can remain laminar where the full-scale flow would be turbulent
Because Froude scaling only works for round pipes, not open channels or hulls
Because Froude scaling was never validated against any full-scale test
Because Froude scaling ignores gravity entirely

explanations.a: Correct — matching Froude number preserves wave-making behavior, but surface tension and the laminar-versus-turbulent state of the boundary layer do not scale the same way, so a small enough model can show physics (capillary effects, laminar friction) absent at full scale.
explanations.b: Froude scaling applies broadly to free-surface flows including channels and ship hulls, not narrowly to pipe flow.
explanations.c: Froude scaling was directly validated against a full-scale test, the 1874 HMS Greyhound trial.
explanations.d: Froude scaling is explicitly built around gravity-driven wave-making behavior (the Froude number itself involves gravitational acceleration), not a gravity-free approach.

questions.prompt: What is the accurate description of the popular 'hull speed' rule (about 1.34 times the square root of waterline length in feet)?

options.text: A hard physical law that a displacement hull can never exceed under any circumstances
A rule-of-thumb marking where wave-making resistance begins rising steeply, not an unbreakable physical ceiling
A precise formula derived directly from Belanger's 1828 momentum equation
A measure of a hull's metacentric height

explanations.a: Displacement hulls can and do exceed the traditional hull-speed figure, particularly with sufficient power or favorable hull form; it is not an absolute ceiling.
explanations.b: Correct — the figure marks roughly where wave-making resistance, governed by the Froude number, begins rising steeply, making further speed increasingly costly rather than physically impossible.
explanations.c: Belanger's equation concerns conjugate depths across a hydraulic jump, an unrelated open-channel result, not ship hull speed.
explanations.d: Metacentric height concerns stability, not the speed-resistance relationship the hull-speed rule addresses.

questions.prompt: What is the current live argument regarding CFD versus towing-tank testing in naval architecture?

options.text: Whether CFD is useful at all, since it has never produced a correct prediction
Whether CFD can be trusted to extrapolate beyond flow regimes it has been validated against, given towing tanks' much longer validation record
Whether towing tanks should be abandoned entirely in favor of Froude's original plank experiments
Whether ships should be tested at full scale only, with no models of any kind

explanations.a: CFD is a legitimately useful and widely used tool; the debate is about the limits of its extrapolation, not its basic usefulness.
explanations.b: Correct — the dispute centers on whether CFD's predictions remain trustworthy outside the specific flow regimes it has been validated against, since physical towing tanks carry a century-plus track record CFD solvers have not yet matched.
explanations.c: The argument concerns CFD versus modern towing-tank practice broadly, not a return to Froude's specific 19th-century plank apparatus.
explanations.d: Full-scale-only testing (abandoning models altogether) is not the position either side of the CFD-versus-towing-tank debate holds; both accept some form of scaled or computational prediction.

units.label: Surface Tension, Capillarity & Small-Scale Free Surfaces

lessons.label: What Surface Tension Is

sections.heading: Unbalanced cohesion at an interface
sections.body: A molecule deep inside a liquid is pulled equally in every direction by its neighbors, so the net intermolecular force on it averages to zero. A molecule sitting at the liquid-vapor interface has neighbors only below and to the sides — the vapor phase is far too dilute to pull back — so it feels a net inward force toward the bulk. The liquid responds by pulling surface molecules inward and packing the interface as tightly as its geometry allows, which behaves macroscopically like a stretched elastic membrane resisting any increase in its own area. Surface tension is not a literal membrane; it is the bulk bookkeeping of that molecular imbalance.

sections.heading: Two equivalent readings of gamma
sections.body: Surface tension gamma has two equally valid unit readings for the same physics. Read as energy per unit area (J/m^2), gamma is the work needed to drag a molecule from the bulk to the surface and create new interface — this is why forming many small droplets, which have high surface-area-to-volume, costs extra energy. Read as force per unit length (N/m, numerically identical to J/m^2), gamma is the force a stretched surface exerts along any line drawn on it — the mechanical definition behind a wire-frame soap-film experiment, where a sliding wire of length L is pulled by a force 2*gamma*L, doubled because the film has two faces. Water at 20 C has gamma = 72.8 mN/m, unusually high because of extensive hydrogen bonding; ethanol, which hydrogen-bonds less and packs less densely, sits near 22 mN/m; liquid mercury, held by strong isotropic metallic bonding, reaches roughly 480 mN/m.

sections.heading: Temperature and contamination both attack gamma
sections.body: Surface tension falls roughly linearly as temperature rises, because thermal agitation weakens the cohesive bonds holding the surface together, and it extrapolates to zero at the liquid's critical temperature, where the liquid-vapor distinction disappears (captured empirically by the Eotvos and Guggenheim-Katayama relations). Contamination attacks gamma even faster: surfactant molecules — soap, detergent, biological lipids — have a polar head and a nonpolar tail, so they adsorb at the interface, disrupt water's hydrogen-bond network there, and can cut gamma to well under half, down toward 25-30 mN/m. A grease film does similar damage by coating the interface with nonpolar molecules that barely attract each other, which is why a needle floating on clean water sinks the instant a drop of dish soap touches it.

sections.heading: Where surface tension starts to beat gravity
sections.body: Gravity's contribution to pressure grows with size (rho*g*L), while a curved surface's capillary pressure (gamma/L) grows as size shrinks, so the two forces balance at a characteristic length — for water, close to 2-3 mm. Below that scale (a water strider's leg, a small droplet, a thin tube's meniscus) surface tension rules and droplets stay round; above it, gravity flattens the free surface and surface tension becomes a minor edge correction.

lessons.workedExample: A wire frame 8 cm wide dips into a soapy solution whose surfactant has lowered gamma to about 25 mN/m and forms a film with a free sliding wire along one edge. Holding the wire against the film's pull requires F = 2*gamma*L = 2 * 0.025 N/m * 0.08 m = 4.0 mN, measurable with a sensitive force gauge or a small counterweight. That factor-of-two, two-surfaces geometry is exactly what reappears as the 4*gamma/R soap-bubble pressure in the next lesson.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks what surface tension physically is is testing whether a student can move past the membrane metaphor to the molecular cause, and can state both the energy-per-area and force-per-length readings of gamma without treating them as different quantities. The tell of shallow understanding is quoting the 72.8 mN/m water figure without being able to explain why soap collapses it or why mercury sits an order of magnitude higher — both follow directly from hydrogen bonding versus metallic bonding and from surfactant disruption of the interface, and tracing effect back to molecular cause is what separates recitation from understanding.

questions.prompt: Which molecular fact explains why a liquid surface behaves as if it were under tension?

options.text: Surface molecules move faster than bulk molecules
Surface molecules feel a net inward force because they have neighbors on only one side
Surface molecules carry a net electric charge
Gravity pulls surface molecules down more strongly than bulk molecules

explanations.a: Thermal speed does not systematically differ between surface and bulk molecules at the same temperature; that is not the source of surface tension.
explanations.b: Correct — surface molecules lack neighbors on the vapor side, so the net intermolecular pull is inward, which macroscopically resists any increase in surface area.
explanations.c: Ordinary liquids like water and ethanol are electrically neutral at the surface; the imbalance is in intermolecular attraction, not charge.
explanations.d: Gravity acts on mass, not on molecular position at an interface, and does not distinguish surface molecules from bulk ones over such short distances.

questions.prompt: By what mechanism does soap cut water's surface tension to well under half?

options.text: It heats the water, weakening cohesive bonds
It increases hydrogen bonding between water molecules
Surfactant molecules adsorb at the interface and disrupt water's hydrogen-bond network there
It raises the atmospheric pressure pressing on the surface

explanations.a: Adding soap does not heat the water; the effect is chemical, not thermal.
explanations.b: Surfactants disrupt hydrogen bonding at the surface, they do not increase it.
explanations.c: Correct — soap's polar-head, nonpolar-tail molecules adsorb at the liquid-vapor interface and break up the hydrogen-bond network that gives water its high gamma, cutting it to well under half, down toward 25-30 mN/m.
explanations.d: Atmospheric pressure is unrelated to surfactant chemistry and is unchanged by adding soap.

questions.prompt: Match each liquid (at 20 C, or as noted) to its approximate surface tension.

right.text: About 72.8 mN/m
About 22 mN/m
About 480 mN/m
About 25-30 mN/m

questions.explanation: Water's extensive hydrogen bonding gives it a high gamma of 72.8 mN/m; ethanol hydrogen-bonds less and sits near 22 mN/m; mercury's strong metallic bonding pushes it to roughly 480 mN/m; dissolved soap disrupts water's surface hydrogen-bond network, dropping gamma to roughly 25-30 mN/m.

questions.prompt: In the wire-frame soap-film experiment, why is the force pulling the sliding wire equal to 2*gamma*L rather than gamma*L?

options.text: The film has two air-liquid surfaces, front and back, each contributing gamma*L
The wire has two ends, each contributing gamma*L
Soap film gamma is always exactly double water's gamma
The factor of two corrects for gravity acting on the film

explanations.a: Correct — a soap film is a thin sheet with two exposed liquid-vapor surfaces, so the wire feels a force of gamma*L from each face, totaling 2*gamma*L.
explanations.b: The two ends of the wire are not the source of the factor of two; the doubling comes from the film's two surfaces, not the wire's geometry.
explanations.c: Soap-film gamma is simply the surfactant solution's own surface tension; it is not defined as double any other liquid's value.
explanations.d: Gravity is not part of the horizontal force balance being described here; the doubling is purely geometric, from two surfaces.

questions.prompt: Below the capillary length scale (roughly 2-3 mm for water), which force dominates the shape of a free surface?

options.text: Gravity
Surface tension
Viscosity
Atmospheric pressure gradients

explanations.a: Gravity's contribution grows with size and only dominates above the capillary length, not below it.
explanations.b: Correct — below the capillary length, capillary pressure (which grows as size shrinks) outweighs gravitational pressure, so surface tension controls the shape, keeping small droplets round.
explanations.c: Viscosity affects how fast a surface reaches its shape, not which force sets the equilibrium shape itself.
explanations.d: Atmospheric pressure is essentially uniform over these small scales and does not set the surface's curvature.

lessons.label: Young-Laplace: Curvature Sets Pressure

sections.heading: The general law: curvature sets the pressure jump
sections.body: Any curved liquid surface supports a pressure difference across it, higher on the concave side, because surface tension pulls the interface toward its center of curvature. The Young-Laplace equation states this generally as dp = gamma*(1/R1 + 1/R2), where R1 and R2 are the two principal radii of curvature of the surface at a point. For a sphere, R1 = R2 = R, so the jump simplifies to dp = 2*gamma/R — this is the excess pressure inside a spherical liquid drop or gas bubble suspended in a liquid, relative to the outside. Flatten the curvature (R to infinity) and the pressure jump vanishes, which is why a flat pool has essentially uniform pressure across its free surface.

sections.heading: Why a soap bubble needs double: 4*gamma/R
sections.body: A soap bubble in air is not one curved surface but a thin liquid film with two air-liquid interfaces, inner and outer, each nearly the same radius R since the film is thin. Each interface individually obeys dp = 2*gamma/R, and because the two surfaces are effectively in series, their pressure jumps add, giving a total dp = 4*gamma/R between the bubble's inside and the surrounding air. This factor of two produces a genuinely counterintuitive result when two bubbles of different size are connected by a tube and valve: because pressure scales as 1/R, the smaller bubble has the higher internal pressure and empties into the larger one, shrinking further as it does, until it collapses or a shared meniscus forms — the opposite of what most people guess before trying it.

sections.heading: Minimal surfaces and Plateau's rules
sections.body: A soap film spanning a wire frame, with no pressure difference across it, minimizes its own surface area, which mathematically means its mean curvature is zero everywhere — a minimal surface. Finding the minimal surface spanning a given boundary is Plateau's problem, named for Belgian physicist Joseph Plateau, who ran extensive soap-film experiments in the 1800s despite eventually going blind from earlier optics research. Plateau found empirically that films always meet in threes along an edge at 120-degree angles, and that edges themselves meet four at a vertex at the tetrahedral angle of about 109.47 degrees — Plateau's rules, later proven rigorously using geometric measure theory by mathematician Jean Taylor in 1976.

sections.heading: Nucleation: why tiny bubbles need extreme superheat
sections.body: Forming a new vapor bubble inside boiling liquid requires creating a tiny bubble of radius R, and the Laplace pressure 2*gamma/R needed to hold it against the surrounding liquid balloons as R shrinks toward molecular scale. Homogeneous nucleation of a sub-micron bubble in perfectly clean, smooth water therefore requires many degrees of superheat above 100 C. Real kettles boil right at 100 C because they cheat: scratches, dissolved gas pockets, and boiling chips provide pre-existing gas pockets with an effectively large R, lowering the pressure barrier — heterogeneous nucleation — which is also why a smooth, clean, microwaved mug of water can superheat and then suddenly and dangerously erupt when disturbed.

lessons.workedExample: A soap bubble of radius 1 cm, with gamma about 25 mN/m from the surfactant, has an internal pressure excess dp = 4*0.025/0.01 = 10 Pa above atmospheric. A much smaller bubble of radius 2 mm, blown from the same solution, has dp = 4*0.025/0.002 = 50 Pa — five times higher, purely from being smaller. If the two are connected by a tube, the 2 mm bubble's higher internal pressure pushes air into the 1 cm bubble, and the small one keeps shrinking rather than growing, exactly as the 1/R scaling predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the curvature-pressure relationship because the common intuition — that a bigger bubble must be under more pressure — is backwards, and correcting it in real time distinguishes a student who has internalized dp is proportional to 1/R from one reciting a formula. A strong answer also connects the same 2*gamma/R term to nucleation: explaining why boiling water needs either superheat or nucleation sites shows the student sees curvature-driven pressure as a single unifying idea across bubbles, drops, and phase change, not three separate facts to memorize.

questions.prompt: A spherical liquid drop has pressure jump dp = 2*gamma/R, but a soap bubble in air has dp = 4*gamma/R. Why the extra factor of two?

options.text: A soap bubble's film has two air-liquid interfaces (inner and outer), each contributing its own 2*gamma/R jump
Soap solution's gamma is always exactly twice that of pure water
Bubbles are always exactly twice the radius of comparable drops
The factor of two accounts for atmospheric humidity around the bubble

explanations.a: Correct — the thin film has two curved liquid-vapor surfaces of nearly the same radius, and their pressure jumps add in series, doubling the single-surface result.
explanations.b: Soap solution's gamma (roughly 25 mN/m) is lower than water's, not double it; the factor of two is geometric, not about gamma's value.
explanations.c: Radius is whatever the bubble happens to be; the doubling has nothing to do with a fixed size ratio to drops.
explanations.d: Humidity is not part of the Young-Laplace derivation; the doubling comes strictly from the film having two surfaces.

questions.prompt: Two soap bubbles of different sizes are connected by a tube with an open valve. What happens, and why?

options.text: The larger bubble shrinks into the smaller one, because pressure increases with radius
The smaller bubble shrinks into the larger one, because its internal pressure is higher (dp scales as 1/R)
Nothing happens; bubble pressure does not depend on radius
Both bubbles grow equally until they merge into one sphere

explanations.a: This inverts the actual scaling; pressure increases as radius decreases, not increases, for a bubble.
explanations.b: Correct — because dp = 4*gamma/R, the smaller bubble has the higher internal pressure and pushes air into the larger bubble through the connecting tube, shrinking further as it empties.
explanations.c: Bubble pressure depends directly on radius through the 1/R term; it is not radius-independent.
explanations.d: The two bubbles do not grow symmetrically; the pressure imbalance drives air specifically from the smaller bubble to the larger one.

questions.prompt: Order these soap bubbles from highest to lowest internal (Laplace) pressure.

items.text: Bubble A, radius 1 mm
Bubble B, radius 5 mm
Bubble C, radius 10 mm

questions.explanation: Since dp = 4*gamma/R, pressure is inversely proportional to radius, so the smallest bubble (1 mm) has the highest internal pressure and the largest bubble (10 mm) has the lowest.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: dp = gamma*(1/R1 + 1/R2), the pressure jump across any curved interface
Finding the minimal-area surface that spans a given wire boundary
Films meet in threes at 120 degrees; edges meet four at a vertex at about 109.47 degrees
Vapor bubbles form at existing gas pockets or surface scratches, lowering the pressure barrier to boiling

questions.explanation: The Young-Laplace equation gives the general curvature-pressure relation; Plateau's problem is the search for the minimal surface spanning a boundary; Plateau's rules describe the specific angles soap films form at junctions; heterogeneous nucleation explains why real boiling starts at defects and gas pockets rather than requiring extreme superheat.

lessons.label: Contact Angle and Wetting

sections.heading: Young's equation: three tensions in balance
sections.body: Where a liquid drop meets a solid, three interfacial tensions pull on the three-phase contact line at once: solid-vapor (gamma_SV), solid-liquid (gamma_SL), and liquid-vapor (gamma_LV). Thomas Young argued in 1805 that at equilibrium these must balance horizontally, giving cos(theta) = (gamma_SV - gamma_SL)/gamma_LV, where theta is the contact angle measured through the liquid. A surface is called hydrophilic when theta is below 90 degrees (the liquid spreads, favoring solid-liquid contact) and hydrophobic when theta exceeds 90 degrees (the liquid beads up); surfaces reaching theta above roughly 150 degrees, with drops nearly spherical and barely touching, are called superhydrophobic.

sections.heading: Roughness changes the story: Wenzel versus Cassie-Baxter
sections.body: Young's equation assumes an ideally smooth, chemically uniform surface, but real surfaces are rough, and roughness amplifies whatever wetting tendency was already there — sometimes through two very different physical states.
