In the Wenzel model, proposed by Robert Wenzel in 1936, liquid fully penetrates the surface grooves, and the apparent contact angle follows cos(theta*) = r*cos(theta), where r is the roughness factor (actual surface area divided by projected area, always greater than 1); this makes a hydrophilic surface more wetting and a hydrophobic one more beading. In the Cassie-Baxter model, published by Cassie and Baxter in 1944, the drop instead sits partly on solid and partly on trapped air pockets in the grooves, giving cos(theta*) = f1*cos(theta) - f2, where f1 and f2 are the solid and air area fractions beneath the drop. Trapped air is what produces true superhydrophobicity: the lotus leaf's roughly 160-degree contact angle, characterized by Wilhelm Barthlott and Christoph Neinhuis in 1997 as arising from micrometer-scale papillae topped with nanoscale wax crystals, works by holding the Cassie-Baxter air-cushion state. That state is metastable — enough pressure, from droplet impact or evaporation, can collapse it into the fully wetted Wenzel state, and the leaf's self-cleaning effect is lost until the air pockets re-form.

sections.heading: Measuring contact angle, and why it hysteresis-shifts
sections.body: Contact angle is measured with the sessile-drop method: a small drop is placed on the surface and photographed in profile, and a tangent line is drawn to the drop's outline at the point where it touches the solid, giving theta directly (goniometer instruments or image-analysis software automate the tangent fit). A single static number understates the real behavior, though, because contact angle shows hysteresis: the advancing angle theta_A, measured as the front of a growing drop moves over dry surface, is larger than the receding angle theta_R, measured as the drop's edge retreats over already-wetted surface. The gap theta_A - theta_R comes from surface roughness and chemical heterogeneity pinning the contact line, and it is what determines whether a drop on a tilted surface rolls off cleanly (small hysteresis, as on a lotus leaf) or stays pinned in place (large hysteresis, as water on a dusty windshield).

lessons.workedExample: A student photographs a water droplet on a waxy leaf in profile and measures theta = 155 degrees from the tangent line — a Cassie-Baxter superhydrophobic state, since the leaf's papillae plus wax crystals trap an air layer beneath the drop. Tilting the leaf slightly, the drop rolls off at just a few degrees of tilt because the advancing and receding angles differ by only about 5 degrees (low hysteresis). Repeating the measurement on a smooth, rough-etched hydrophilic ceramic tile, theta drops to around 40 degrees and the same tilt leaves the drop pinned in place — evidence of a fully wetted Wenzel state with much larger hysteresis.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe contact angle because 'rougher equals more hydrophobic' is a common but wrong shortcut — roughness amplifies an existing tendency, and whether that amplification looks like Wenzel or Cassie-Baxter depends on whether liquid fills the grooves or air is trapped beneath it. A student who can name both models, predict which one explains lotus-leaf behavior, and describe how the Cassie state collapses under pressure has grasped wetting as a physical mechanism; one who can only report a measured angle number has not connected the measurement to the surface structure producing it.

questions.prompt: Young's equation, cos(theta) = (gamma_SV - gamma_SL)/gamma_LV, balances forces at the contact line using which three tensions?

options.text: Solid-vapor, solid-liquid, and liquid-vapor interfacial tensions
Gravity, buoyancy, and viscous drag
Atmospheric pressure, hydrostatic pressure, and vapor pressure
Solid-vapor tension only, measured at three different points

explanations.a: Correct — the equilibrium contact angle balances the solid-vapor, solid-liquid, and liquid-vapor interfacial tensions pulling on the three-phase contact line.
explanations.b: These are bulk forces relevant to drop shape under gravity, but Young's equation is specifically a surface-tension force balance, not a gravity balance.
explanations.c: Young's equation concerns interfacial tensions, not pressures; pressure differences are handled separately by the Young-Laplace equation.
explanations.d: Young's equation requires three distinct interfacial tensions (solid-vapor, solid-liquid, liquid-vapor), not repeated measurements of one.

questions.prompt: What is the key physical difference between the Wenzel and Cassie-Baxter wetting states on a rough surface?

options.text: Wenzel involves the liquid fully filling the surface grooves; Cassie-Baxter involves air trapped beneath the drop in the grooves
Wenzel applies only to hydrophobic surfaces; Cassie-Baxter applies only to hydrophilic surfaces
Wenzel is measured with a goniometer; Cassie-Baxter is measured by weighing the drop
There is no physical difference; they are two names for the same state

explanations.a: Correct — in the Wenzel state liquid penetrates the grooves completely, while in the Cassie-Baxter state the drop rests on a composite of solid tips and trapped air pockets.
explanations.b: Both models can in principle apply to either wetting tendency; the distinguishing factor is whether liquid fills the grooves or air is trapped, not the underlying hydrophilicity.
explanations.c: Both states are measured the same way, typically by the sessile-drop method; the measurement technique does not distinguish them.
explanations.d: They describe genuinely different physical configurations with different formulas (cos theta* = r cos theta for Wenzel versus cos theta* = f1 cos theta - f2 for Cassie-Baxter) and different consequences for hysteresis.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: cos(theta*) = r*cos(theta); liquid fully wets the surface grooves
cos(theta*) = f1*cos(theta) - f2; air pockets trapped beneath the drop
The gap between advancing and receding contact angles, caused by pinning
Photographing a drop's profile and fitting a tangent line at the contact point

questions.explanation: The Wenzel model describes full groove wetting with roughness factor r; the Cassie-Baxter model describes a composite solid-air interface; hysteresis is the advancing-minus-receding angle gap caused by pinning at surface defects; the sessile-drop method is the standard way to measure contact angle from a drop photograph.

questions.prompt: Why does a drop roll easily off a lotus leaf but stay pinned on a dusty windshield at the same tilt angle?

options.text: The lotus leaf has low contact-angle hysteresis (small gap between advancing and receding angles); the windshield has high hysteresis
The lotus leaf's contact angle is measured differently, using weight instead of a tangent line
The windshield has a higher gamma_LV for water than the leaf does
Rolling off depends only on drop volume, not on the surface at all

explanations.a: Correct — low hysteresis means the contact line is not strongly pinned, so a small tilt is enough to overcome the small angle gap and let the drop roll; high hysteresis on a rougher, dirtier surface pins the drop in place.
explanations.b: Both surfaces are measured the same way; the difference is in the physical pinning behavior, not the measurement method.
explanations.c: gamma_LV is a property of the liquid (water), not the solid surface, so it does not differ between the leaf and the windshield.
explanations.d: Drop volume affects the gravitational force available to overcome pinning, but the surface's hysteresis is what sets the threshold tilt in the first place.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the sessile-drop method for measuring contact angle.

items.text: Place a small liquid drop on the test surface
Photograph the drop in profile (side-on)
Identify the three-phase contact point where the drop's outline meets the solid
Fit a tangent line to the drop outline at that point and read the angle

questions.explanation: The drop must first be placed on the surface, then photographed from the side so its profile is visible, then the contact point located, and finally the tangent line fit at that point to extract the contact angle itself.

lessons.label: Capillary Rise and the Bond Number

sections.heading: Jurin's law: balancing a ring of tension against a column's weight
sections.body: When a narrow tube is dipped into a wetting liquid, surface tension pulls the liquid up the tube wall until the upward force balances the weight of the raised column. The upward pull acts around the tube's circumference, 2*pi*r*gamma*cos(theta), where r is the tube radius and theta the contact angle; the weight being lifted is rho*g*pi*r^2*h. Setting these equal and canceling pi*r gives Jurin's law: h = 2*gamma*cos(theta)/(rho*g*r). The law is named for James Jurin, who published quantitative capillary-rise experiments in 1718, among the earliest careful measurements in fluid mechanics. Because h scales as 1/r, halving the tube radius doubles the rise — which is why capillary rise is dramatic in hair-thin tubes and negligible in a drinking glass.

sections.heading: The capillary length: where curvature and gravity trade places
sections.body: Jurin's law implies a natural length scale at which capillary pressure and hydrostatic pressure are equal: the capillary length, sqrt(gamma/(rho*g)). For water at room temperature this works out to roughly 2.7 mm. A tube with radius much smaller than the capillary length shows a nearly hemispherical meniscus and Jurin's law applies cleanly; a container much larger than the capillary length has a meniscus confined to a thin ring near the walls, with the bulk free surface staying essentially flat under gravity's control.

sections.heading: The Bond number: gravity versus capillarity as a single ratio
sections.body: The capillary length can be generalized into a dimensionless ratio, the Bond number (also called the Eotvos number), Bo = rho*g*L^2/gamma, comparing gravitational to capillary forces at any length scale L. Bo much less than 1 means capillarity dominates — drops stay spherical, capillary rise is significant, menisci are strongly curved. Bo much greater than 1 means gravity dominates — surfaces flatten, curvature effects become a minor correction. Bo = 1 occurs exactly at L equal to the capillary length, so the Bond number is simply Jurin's threshold recast as a general design check applicable to any free-surface problem, not just tubes.

sections.heading: Practical consequences of getting the scale wrong
sections.body: Reading a liquid level in a narrow manometer or burette tube introduces a systematic error if the tube bore is not well above the capillary length: water's concave meniscus (theta near 0) makes the level look higher than it is if read at the meniscus edge instead of consistently at its center, while mercury's convex meniscus (theta greater than 90 degrees, since mercury does not wet glass) depresses the apparent reading — both effects shrink but do not vanish as bore increases, which is why precision manometry favors tubes with a bore well above roughly 10-12 mm or applies an explicit correction. The same physics drives wicking in paper, cloth, and soil, where a fine capillary network pulls water upward against gravity through countless tube-like pores, and it is why any free-surface experiment run in narrow tubing — a homemade manometer, a thin glass wave channel — needs a bore correction or a switch to wider tubing before the data can be trusted.

lessons.workedExample: A hair-thin capillary tube with a 0.2 mm diameter (r = 0.0001 m) is dipped in water, which wets glass completely (theta about 0, cos theta = 1). Jurin's law gives h = 2*0.0728/(1000*9.81*0.0001) = 0.1456/0.981 = about 0.148 m, nearly 15 cm of rise from a tube barely visible to the eye. The Bond number for this tube, using L = r, is Bo = rho*g*L^2/gamma = 1000*9.81*(0.0001)^2/0.0728, about 0.0013 — far below 1, confirming capillarity utterly dominates gravity at this scale and explaining why the rise is so dramatic.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe capillary rise because it is the single most common source of silent measurement error in a home-built fluids rig — a narrow manometer or graduated tube reads wrong by an amount the student never suspects. A strong answer states Jurin's law, names the roughly 2.7 mm capillary length or Bond number as the actual threshold for when the effect matters, and proposes a concrete fix (wider bore, or a documented correction) rather than just noting that 'surface tension might be a factor.'

questions.prompt: Jurin's law, h = 2*gamma*cos(theta)/(rho*g*r), predicts that halving the tube radius r does what to the capillary rise height h?

options.text: Doubles h
Halves h
Leaves h unchanged
Quarters h

explanations.a: Correct — h is inversely proportional to r, so halving r doubles h, which is why fine tubes show dramatic capillary rise.
explanations.b: This inverts the actual relationship; h grows, not shrinks, as r shrinks.
explanations.c: r appears explicitly in the denominator of Jurin's law, so changing it does change h.
explanations.d: h scales as 1/r, a linear inverse relationship, not 1/r^2, so halving r doubles rather than quadruples h.

questions.prompt: What does the capillary length, sqrt(gamma/(rho*g)) (about 2.7 mm for water), represent?

options.text: The maximum possible height of capillary rise in any tube
The length scale at which capillary pressure and hydrostatic pressure are equal
The diameter of a water molecule
The minimum tube radius at which Jurin's law applies at all

explanations.a: Jurin's law shows rise height can exceed the capillary length itself in sufficiently narrow tubes; the capillary length is not a rise-height cap.
explanations.b: Correct — it is the length at which capillary and gravitational pressure contributions are equal (Bond number = 1), marking the crossover between capillarity-dominated and gravity-dominated free surfaces.
explanations.c: Molecular diameters are on the order of nanometers, roughly a million times smaller than the millimeter-scale capillary length.
explanations.d: Jurin's law applies at any small radius; the capillary length is a reference scale for comparison, not a validity cutoff for the formula.

questions.prompt: A free-surface problem has Bond number Bo much greater than 1. What does that indicate?

options.text: Surface tension dominates and the surface will be strongly curved
Gravity dominates and the surface will be essentially flat except near boundaries
Viscosity dominates and flow will be laminar
The liquid is close to its critical temperature

explanations.a: This is backwards; a large Bond number means gravity, not surface tension, dominates and the surface flattens rather than curving strongly.
explanations.b: Correct — Bo = rho*g*L^2/gamma compares gravitational to capillary forces, and Bo much greater than 1 means gravity's contribution dominates, flattening the bulk free surface with curvature confined to a thin edge region.
explanations.c: The Bond number contains no viscosity term; it compares gravity to surface tension only, not to viscous forces.
explanations.d: Critical temperature relates to gamma approaching zero as a substance-specific property, not to the length-scale comparison the Bond number expresses.

questions.prompt: Order these water-filled capillary tubes from greatest to least capillary rise height.

items.text: Tube A, radius 0.05 mm
Tube B, radius 0.5 mm
Tube C, radius 5 mm

questions.explanation: Jurin's law gives h inversely proportional to radius r, so the narrowest tube (0.05 mm) produces the greatest rise and the widest tube (5 mm, well above the capillary length) produces the least.

questions.prompt: Why does precision manometry avoid very narrow tubes, or apply a correction if it must use them?

options.text: Narrow tubes break more easily under pressure
Capillary rise or depression systematically shifts the apparent liquid level away from the true pressure-indicated level
Narrow tubes have higher viscosity than wide ones
Narrow tubes cannot hold mercury at all

explanations.a: Mechanical fragility is a real practical concern but is not the reason tied to surface tension and Jurin's law.
explanations.b: Correct — in a tube whose radius is not well above the capillary length, the meniscus rise (wetting liquids like water) or depression (non-wetting liquids like mercury) shifts the reading by an amount unrelated to the actual pressure being measured, requiring a wide bore or an explicit correction.
explanations.c: Viscosity is a fluid property independent of the tube's radius; narrow tubes do not have inherently different viscosity.
explanations.d: Mercury can be held in narrow tubes; its behavior is a depressed, convex meniscus (theta greater than 90 degrees), not an inability to be contained.

lessons.label: The Weber Number: Drops, Jets and Splashes

sections.heading: Inertia versus surface tension: We = rho*V^2*L/gamma
sections.body: The Weber number, We = rho*V^2*L/gamma, compares a flow's inertial force to the surface tension holding its free surface together, where V is a characteristic velocity, L a characteristic length, rho the liquid density, and gamma its surface tension. At low We, surface tension wins and a liquid mass — a jet, a falling drop — stays coherent or even rebounds off an impact surface. At high We, inertia overwhelms surface tension and the liquid tears apart into smaller drops or a spreading, disintegrating sheet. This single ratio is the organizing idea behind jet breakup, droplet impact, and spray atomization alike.

sections.heading: Rayleigh-Plateau instability: why a jet becomes drops
sections.body: A smooth cylindrical liquid jet is inherently unstable: any small sinusoidal perturbation in its radius grows over time because breaking the cylinder into separate spheres reduces the total surface area for the same volume, and surface tension always favors less area. Lord Rayleigh's 1878 stability analysis found that perturbations grow fastest at a specific wavelength, lambda_max, of about 4.51 times the jet's diameter (equivalently about 9.02 times its radius); that fastest-growing wavelength sets the spacing, and therefore the size, of the drops a jet naturally breaks into. This Rayleigh-Plateau instability governs everything from a dripping faucet to the regular droplet trains produced by inkjet nozzles and garden-hose streams.

sections.heading: Droplet impact regimes
sections.body: When a drop strikes a solid or liquid surface, its fate depends on We (and on the Reynolds number, which brings in viscosity). At low We, the drop simply spreads and stays — deposition. At higher We, the drop flattens into a thin outward-spreading sheet that can lift off its own edge and break into a ring of secondary droplets — corona splash, first captured photographically by Arthur Worthington in the late 1800s and later systematically categorized into named regimes, including deposition, splash, and rebound, by Rioboo, Tropea, and Marengo in 2001. At very low We on a superhydrophobic or Leidenfrost (vapor-cushioned, superheated) surface, the drop can instead bounce cleanly off — rebound — because there is too little inertia to break through the surface tension holding the drop's shape together. Empirically, splashing tends to onset once a combined inertia-viscosity parameter crosses a threshold, an idea formalized by Mundo, Sommerfeld, and Tropea in 1995.

sections.heading: Applied cases: printing, spraying, and rain
sections.body: Inkjet printers must land single, well-formed droplets without producing satellite droplets or splash-back, which constrains them to a narrow printability window balancing inertia, viscosity, and surface tension. Spray atomizers — fuel injectors, agricultural sprayers — want the opposite: deliberately high We to shatter a liquid stream into the finest possible mist for even coverage or combustion. Falling raindrops face an upper size limit for the same reason a jet breaks apart: as a drop grows, the aerodynamic pressure from falling through air raises its effective Weber number until it approaches the threshold for aerodynamic breakup, flattening and then shattering the drop into smaller ones — which is why raindrops rarely exceed roughly 5-6 mm even when ample condensation is available to keep feeding them.

lessons.workedExample: A raindrop 4 mm in diameter falls at its terminal velocity of roughly 9 m/s. Using air density (rho_air = 1.2 kg/m^3, since aerodynamic pressure against the falling drop is what threatens to break it apart) and water's gamma = 0.0728 N/m: We = rho_air*V^2*D/gamma = 1.2*(9^2)*0.004/0.0728, about 5.3. Published critical Weber numbers for aerodynamic 'bag breakup' of falling drops sit in the range of roughly 10-20, so a 4 mm raindrop is already a substantial fraction of that threshold — and because terminal velocity also keeps rising with drop size, We grows faster than linearly with diameter, which is exactly why raindrops rarely grow much larger before aerodynamic drag deforms and shatters them into smaller drops.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the Weber number because it is the cleanest one-ratio explanation for why some drops splash and others bounce, why a jet is doomed to break into drops of a predictable size rather than staying a smooth stream, and why raindrops have a natural size ceiling. A strong answer correctly names inertia and surface tension as the two forces in the ratio, states which regime (deposition, splash, rebound) corresponds to which end of the We scale, and applies the same reasoning to a real system — inkjet, spray, or rain — rather than treating each application as an unrelated fact.

questions.prompt: The Weber number We = rho*V^2*L/gamma compares which two forces?

options.text: Gravity and viscosity
Inertial force and surface tension
Buoyancy and atmospheric pressure
Viscosity and surface tension

explanations.a: Gravity and viscosity are not part of the Weber number's construction; those ratios are captured by the Bond number and Reynolds number respectively.
explanations.b: Correct — We compares the inertial force (rho*V^2*L, roughly dynamic pressure times area) to the surface-tension force (gamma), telling whether a flow's momentum can overcome the surface holding it together.
explanations.c: Buoyancy and atmospheric pressure do not appear in the Weber number's definition.
explanations.d: That ratio is the Ohnesorge or capillary number territory; the Weber number specifically involves inertia, not viscosity, against surface tension.

questions.prompt: Why does a smooth cylindrical liquid jet spontaneously break into a train of drops (the Rayleigh-Plateau instability)?

options.text: Breaking into spheres reduces the total surface area for the same volume, which surface tension favors
Gravity always pulls cylindrical jets apart at regular intervals
The jet's viscosity increases as it travels, forcing it to solidify into drops
Air resistance cuts the jet into segments

explanations.a: Correct — a sphere has less surface area per unit volume than a cylinder, so surface tension drives any small perturbation in the jet's radius to grow until the cylinder pinches off into separate drops, minimizing total surface energy.
explanations.b: Gravity affects the jet's trajectory but is not the mechanism driving the instability itself, which is a surface-tension-area effect.
explanations.c: The instability is a surface-energy effect at constant liquid state, not a phase change or viscosity increase.
explanations.d: Air resistance can influence the process but the fundamental instability, identified by Rayleigh, exists even in the idealized case without air effects.

questions.prompt: Match each droplet-impact regime to its description.

right.text: Low We; drop simply spreads and stays on the surface
Higher We; drop flattens into a spreading sheet that breaks into a ring of secondary droplets
Very low We on a superhydrophobic or Leidenfrost surface; drop bounces off intact

questions.explanation: Deposition occurs at low We where the drop simply spreads and stays; corona splash occurs at higher We where the drop's inertia drives a spreading sheet that breaks apart at its edge; rebound occurs at very low We on non-wetting or vapor-cushioned surfaces where surface tension holds the drop together and it bounces off intact.

questions.prompt: Why do raindrops rarely exceed roughly 5-6 mm in diameter even with abundant condensation?

options.text: Larger drops freeze before reaching the ground
As drops grow, their effective Weber number rises toward the aerodynamic breakup threshold, and they flatten and shatter into smaller drops
Air pressure prevents water molecules from condensing past that size
Surface tension increases sharply once a drop exceeds 5 mm

explanations.a: Freezing is unrelated to the size-limiting mechanism described here, which is a mechanical breakup process, not a phase change.
explanations.b: Correct — as a falling drop grows, the aerodynamic pressure against it (captured in We using air density) rises until it approaches the critical Weber number for bag breakup, deforming and shattering the drop into smaller pieces.
explanations.c: Condensation itself is not limited by air pressure in this way; the limit comes from mechanical instability of the falling drop, not from a barrier to further condensation.
explanations.d: Surface tension (gamma) is a material property of water and does not change with drop size; what changes is the aerodynamic force acting against it.

questions.prompt: Order these applications from lowest to highest Weber number typically needed for their intended outcome.

items.text: A drop bouncing cleanly off a superhydrophobic coating
An inkjet nozzle depositing a single well-formed droplet
A fuel injector atomizing liquid into a fine mist

questions.explanation: Rebound requires very low We so surface tension keeps the drop's shape intact through impact; inkjet printing needs a moderate, tightly controlled We to form one clean droplet without satellites or splashing; spray atomization deliberately uses high We to shatter the liquid into the finest possible mist.

lessons.label: When Surface Tension Ruins the Model

sections.heading: Small hydraulic models don't scale surface tension
sections.body: Physical scale models of rivers, spillways, and weirs are typically built using Froude similarity, which preserves the ratio of inertial to gravitational forces between model and prototype. Surface tension, however, does not shrink along with the model — gamma is a fixed material property of water, not a length — so a small model systematically exaggerates the relative importance of surface tension compared to the full-scale structure it represents. This mismatch is a scale effect, and for a weir (an overflow structure used to measure discharge from the height of water flowing over its crest) it shows up as a practical minimum: below roughly 30 mm of head over the crest, surface tension distorts the shape of the falling sheet (the nappe) enough that the calibrated head-discharge rating curve becomes unreliable. Flumes need an equivalent minimum flow depth for the same reason, so a model that shrinks a real structure by a large factor can fail specifically at the low-flow conditions students often care most about testing.

sections.heading: Wave tanks need Weber-number similarity and clean water
sections.body: A laboratory wave tank modeling ocean or coastal waves at reduced scale must also satisfy a Weber-number criterion — the model's We has to stay high enough that surface tension does not disproportionately damp or distort the short-wavelength ripples relative to what the full-scale prototype would show. Contamination compounds the problem: even trace surfactants from dust, skin oils, or residue from a previous test lower gamma unevenly across the tank's surface, damping capillary-scale ripples and skewing how waves break. This is why careful wave-tank protocols specify surfactant-free water, kept clean and frequently skimmed, rather than treating water as an interchangeable, inert working fluid.

sections.heading: Marangoni flows: surface-tension gradients drive their own current
sections.body: A surface with a gamma gradient pulls liquid along itself from low-tension regions toward high-tension regions — a Marangoni flow. The classic example is tears of wine: alcohol evaporates faster than water from the thin film that climbs a wine glass's wall, locally raising that film's water fraction and, since water's gamma exceeds ethanol's, locally raising gamma there too; the resulting tension gradient pulls more liquid up the wall via Marangoni stress until gravity overcomes it and the excess falls back down as a visible tear. James Thomson described the tears-of-wine effect in 1855, and Carlo Marangoni's 1865 doctoral thesis worked out the general theory of surface-tension-gradient-driven flow that now carries his name. The same mechanism, unwanted, can distort a wave tank or a small hydraulic model wherever evaporation or contamination creates an uneven surface-tension field.

sections.heading: Practical fixes model labs actually use
sections.body: Rather than fighting surface tension directly, hydraulic model labs work around it with explicit rules: a documented minimum head, depth, or dimension below which results are flagged unreliable; rigorously clean, surfactant-free water to keep gamma at its intended value (since deliberately adding wetting agents is done only in the rare case where suppressing surface tension is the actual goal); and distorted models, which use a different horizontal scale than vertical scale, so a spillway can shrink enough to fit in a lab while its critical heads and depths stay comfortably above the roughly 30 mm capillary-effect threshold, at the accepted cost of a geometric distortion that must itself be corrected for in the results.

lessons.workedExample: A student scales a real spillway down 1:100 to test it in a lab flume. The prototype's design head over the weir crest is 3 m, which scales down to just 30 mm in the model — right at the threshold where surface tension begins distorting the nappe and biasing the head-discharge rating curve, so the model cannot faithfully reproduce low-flow behavior even though it performs well at the design head. The standard fix is a distorted model: keeping the horizontal scale at 1:100 but using a less-aggressive vertical scale, say 1:50, so the modeled head becomes 60 mm, comfortably clear of the capillary-effect threshold, at the cost of accepting a known geometric distortion between the model's horizontal and vertical proportions.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because student-built rigs — bathtub spillways, DIY wave tanks — routinely violate Froude or Weber similarity without the builder ever suspecting surface tension is the culprit. A student who diagnoses 'my model's head is below the capillary-effect threshold, so my rating curve doesn't scale to the prototype' is naming the actual error source rather than blaming vague instrument noise, and recognizing Marangoni flows or the need for surfactant-free water shows they understand surface tension as an active distorting force in a model, not just a passive nuisance to wave away.

questions.prompt: Why does a small-scale hydraulic model of a weir become unreliable at very low flow, even though it was calibrated with Froude similarity?

options.text: Because surface tension (gamma) does not shrink with the model, so at small heads it distorts the nappe shape and biases the rating curve
Because gravity is weaker in a laboratory setting
Because Froude similarity is only valid for turbulent flow
Because small models always have less friction than the prototype

explanations.a: Correct — Froude similarity preserves the inertia-to-gravity ratio but not the ratio involving surface tension, so a fixed gamma becomes relatively more important as the model's head shrinks toward the roughly 30 mm capillary-effect threshold.
explanations.b: Gravity in a lab is the same as everywhere else on Earth's surface; Froude scaling accounts for gravity correctly, it is surface tension that is left unscaled.
explanations.c: Froude similarity is used across a range of flow regimes for gravity-inertia scaling; the limitation described here is specifically about surface tension, not turbulence.
explanations.d: Friction scaling is a separate, real concern in hydraulic modeling, but it is not the mechanism causing the specific low-head rating-curve distortion described here.

questions.prompt: In the tears-of-wine effect, what actually pulls liquid up the glass and produces the falling 'tears'?

options.text: Capillary rise through pores in the glass
A surface-tension gradient: faster alcohol evaporation raises the local water fraction and gamma in the climbing film, pulling more liquid up via Marangoni stress
Static electricity building up on the glass surface
Convection currents driven by the wine's temperature alone

explanations.a: Glass is not porous in the way paper or soil is; this is not a capillary-wicking effect through the material.
explanations.b: Correct — as alcohol evaporates faster than water from the thin climbing film, the film's water fraction and thus its gamma rise locally, and that surface-tension gradient drags more liquid up the wall (a Marangoni flow) until gravity pulls the excess back down as a tear.
explanations.c: Static electricity plays no role in this effect; it is a surface-tension-gradient phenomenon.
explanations.d: Temperature alone does not explain the effect; the key gradient is compositional (water fraction), which changes gamma, not a separately imposed temperature field.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the model-lab fix used to address it.

left.text: A model weir's head drops below the capillary-effect threshold
A wave tank's surface is contaminated with trace surfactants
A prototype is too large to fit a lab at a single uniform scale without shrinking below capillary thresholds

right.text: Flag results below the documented minimum head/depth as unreliable
Keep water rigorously clean and surfactant-free, skimmed between tests
Use a distorted model with different horizontal and vertical scales

questions.explanation: Labs handle a too-small head by flagging results below a documented threshold as unreliable, handle contamination by keeping the water clean and surfactant-free, and handle the competing need to shrink a large prototype while keeping heads above the capillary threshold by using a distorted model with separate horizontal and vertical scales.

questions.prompt: Who is credited with the 1865 doctoral thesis that developed the general theory of surface-tension-gradient-driven flow now called the Marangoni effect?

options.text: James Jurin
Joseph Plateau
Carlo Marangoni
Thomas Young

explanations.a: James Jurin is credited with early 18th-century capillary-rise experiments (Jurin's law), not the surface-tension-gradient flow theory.
explanations.b: Joseph Plateau is known for 19th-century soap-film and minimal-surface experiments (Plateau's rules), not the gradient-driven-flow theory.
explanations.c: Correct — Carlo Marangoni's 1865 doctoral thesis worked out the general theory of surface-tension-gradient-driven flow, which now bears his name.
explanations.d: Thomas Young is credited with the 1805 contact-angle relation (Young's equation), not the Marangoni-flow theory.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: James Thomson describes the tears-of-wine effect
Carlo Marangoni's doctoral thesis develops the general surface-tension-gradient-flow theory
Modern wave-tank labs adopt formal Weber-number similarity criteria and surfactant-free water protocols

questions.explanation: James Thomson observed and described the tears-of-wine effect in 1855, Carlo Marangoni developed the general theory of surface-tension-gradient-driven flow in his 1865 thesis, and formal Weber-number similarity and surfactant-free protocols for wave-tank modeling are a later, twentieth-century engineering development building on that earlier physics.

units.label: Ship Resistance, Wave-Making & Froude Scaling

lessons.label: Decomposing Ship Resistance

sections.heading: One number, several physical fights
sections.body: A ship's total resistance R is usually reported as a dimensionless total resistance coefficient, Ct = R / (0.5 * rho * S * V^2), where S is the wetted surface area and V the ship speed — the same normalization used for a flat plate or an airfoil, so different hull sizes and speeds can be compared on one curve. But Ct is not one physical mechanism; it is a sum. Naval architects split it into frictional (skin-friction) resistance from the turbulent boundary layer dragging along the wetted hull, viscous pressure resistance (form drag) from the way that boundary layer separates and thickens around a non-streamlined hull shape, wave-making resistance from the surface waves the hull permanently radiates away, plus smaller appendage resistance (rudders, shafts, bilge keels) and air resistance on the above-water hull and superstructure. Each term obeys different physics and scales with a different dimensionless group — friction and form drag are governed by Reynolds number Re = VL/nu, wave-making by Froude number Fr = V / sqrt(g*L) — which is precisely why the total cannot be captured by one scaling law.

sections.heading: Why the split matters more than the total
sections.body: Knowing only Ct tells a designer nothing about where to intervene. If friction dominates, the lever is wetted-surface area and hull roughness/coating; if wave-making dominates, the lever is hull shape and length-to-beam ratio, because friction is largely insensitive to hull lines while wave-making is almost entirely determined by them. This is why resistance is decomposed before it is optimized — a hull redesigned to cut wave-making by 20% can be nearly worthless on a ship that only ever operates in the friction-dominated regime, and vice versa.

sections.heading: The split moves with Froude number
sections.body: The frictional/wave-making balance depends almost entirely on Fr, which is why a ship's design speed decides what its designer optimizes. A slow bulk tanker cruising near Fr ~ 0.15 barely disturbs the free surface; roughly 80-90% of its resistance is skin friction, so tanker design chases low wetted surface, hull smoothness, and anti-fouling coatings. A fast ferry or naval combatant pushed to Fr ~ 0.5 is a different problem: it can lose close to half its propulsive power to wave-making alone, so its hull lines (fine entrance angle, transom shape, bulbous bow) matter far more than surface finish. The same total-Ct curve, decomposed, tells two designers to optimize almost opposite things.

lessons.workedExample: A 300 m tanker with 25,000 m^2 of wetted surface cruises at 15 knots, giving Fr ~ 0.15; measured Ct at that point splits roughly 85% frictional/viscous and 15% wave-making, so a coating that cuts frictional resistance 5% saves close to 4% of total power — a real fuel-bill number over a year of steaming. Contrast a 150 m fast ferry at 35 knots, Fr ~ 0.47: at that Froude number the same 5% friction improvement barely moves total resistance, because roughly half the resistance curve there is wave-making, so the ferry's real gains come from re-lining the bow and stern, not from hull coating.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "where does your ship's resistance actually come from?" is testing whether a student decomposed the problem or just quoted a single drag number off a spec sheet. A strong answer names the components (friction, form, wave-making, at minimum) and states which one dominates at the design speed and why — tying that dominance to Froude number rather than treating resistance as one monolithic force. A student who proposes a hull-shape change to fix a slow, friction-dominated vessel, or a surface-coating fix for a fast, wave-dominated one, has not understood that the fix must match the regime.

questions.prompt: The total resistance coefficient Ct = R / (0.5 * rho * S * V^2) uses which area in its normalization?

options.text: The waterplane area (deck-level footprint)
The wetted surface area S
The maximum cross-sectional (midship) area
The projected frontal area above the waterline

explanations.a: Waterplane area describes the hull's footprint at the water surface, not the submerged surface friction acts on.
explanations.b: Correct — Ct is normalized by wetted surface area S, mirroring how a flat-plate or airfoil drag coefficient is defined, so hulls of different size and speed can be compared on one curve.
explanations.c: Midship section area is used in some hull-form coefficients (like block coefficient) but not in the resistance-coefficient normalization.
explanations.d: Above-water frontal area matters for air resistance specifically, not for the total hydrodynamic resistance coefficient.

questions.prompt: Frictional and wave-making resistance are governed by different dimensionless groups. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Friction by Froude number, wave-making by Reynolds number
Friction by Reynolds number, wave-making by Froude number
Both are governed by the same number, Froude number
Both are governed by the same number, Reynolds number

explanations.a: This reverses the correct pairing.
explanations.b: Correct — skin friction (a viscous boundary-layer effect) scales with Reynolds number Re = VL/nu, while wave-making (a gravity-wave, free-surface effect) scales with Froude number Fr = V/sqrt(g*L). This mismatch is the whole reason ship resistance cannot be captured by one scaling law.
explanations.c: If both scaled the same way, the classic model-testing scaling problem in ship hydrodynamics would not exist.
explanations.d: Wave-making is a gravity-driven free-surface phenomenon, not a viscous one, so Reynolds number alone cannot govern it.

questions.prompt: A slow tanker cruising near Fr ~ 0.15 gets roughly what share of its resistance from friction, per this lesson?

options.text: About 10-20%
About 50%
About 80-90%
Essentially 100%, wave-making is zero

explanations.a: That range describes the wave-making share at low Froude number, not the frictional share.
explanations.b: A roughly even 50/50 split describes a fast vessel near Fr ~ 0.5, not a slow tanker.
explanations.c: Correct — at Fr ~ 0.15 the tanker barely disturbs the free surface, so roughly 80-90% of its resistance is frictional/viscous.
explanations.d: Wave-making is small but not literally zero at Fr ~ 0.15; the lesson gives an 80-90% frictional share, implying a small nonzero wave component.

questions.prompt: Match each resistance component to the design lever that most directly addresses it.

right.text: Wetted-surface area, hull roughness and anti-fouling coating
Hull lines: entrance angle, transom shape, bulbous bow
Rudder, shaft, and bilge-keel design

questions.explanation: Frictional resistance responds to wetted area and surface smoothness because it is a boundary-layer effect largely insensitive to hull shape; wave-making responds to hull-line changes because it is set by how the hull displaces the free surface; appendage resistance is addressed by streamlining the appendages themselves.

lessons.label: Wave-Making Resistance and the Kelvin Wake

sections.heading: Two wave systems, permanently radiated
sections.body: A hull moving across a free surface generates two coupled wave systems: transverse waves that ride roughly perpendicular to the direction of travel and divergent waves that fan out obliquely from the bow and stern. Both are gravity waves, generated because the hull must push water aside and let it fall back, and both carry away energy that the ship's engines supplied and can never recover — this permanent energy loss is what wave-making resistance actually is, distinct from friction, which merely converts kinetic energy to heat in the boundary layer. Lord Kelvin worked out the geometry of this radiated pattern in 1887: for any object moving steadily across deep water, the whole wave system stays confined inside a wedge trailing behind the disturbance, bounded by a cusp line at a half-angle of arcsin(1/3), approximately 19 degrees 28 minutes — a result that, remarkably, does not depend on the object's speed at all. A duck, a canoe, and a supertanker in deep water all produce the same 19.47-degree wake angle, because the angle comes from the ratio of group velocity to phase velocity of deep-water gravity waves, not from the disturbance itself.

sections.heading: A 2013 correction: wakes that look narrower
sections.body: Kelvin's angle held unchallenged for over a century, but in 2013 Rabaud and Moisy re-examined satellite images of ship wakes and found that fast, slender modern hulls often show an apparent wake noticeably narrower than 19.47 degrees. Their explanation was not that Kelvin was wrong — the full wave pattern is still bounded by the classic cusp line — but that for a hull whose length is large relative to the wavelength of the waves it generates (roughly Fr above ~0.5, where Fr uses hull length), the wave energy concentrates along an inner angle that shrinks with speed, in a pattern resembling a Mach cone for supersonic flow rather than Kelvin's constant angle. The visible, energetic part of the wake narrows even though the outer geometric boundary does not move.

sections.heading: Interference and the resistance curve's humps and hollows
sections.body: A hull is not one wave source but at least two — a diverging/transverse system generated at the bow and another generated at the stern (and, on a real hull, additional systems at shoulders and other curvature changes). These systems interfere: at some speeds bow and stern wave crests reinforce, and at others they cancel. Because wavelength is set by speed while the bow-to-stern distance is fixed, this interference oscillates as speed rises, producing the characteristic humps and hollows visible on a resistance-vs-Froude-number curve, with a prominent hump near Fr ~ 0.3 and another near Fr ~ 0.5. A designer choosing a cruising speed that lands in a hollow rather than a hump gets meaningfully lower wave resistance for the same hull, which is why the resistance curve, not just its overall trend, drives speed selection.

lessons.workedExample: A 200 m naval vessel is being evaluated at two candidate cruising speeds that both satisfy mission range requirements: one lands near Fr ~ 0.30 (a resistance hump, where bow and stern wave systems partly reinforce) and the other near Fr ~ 0.38 (a hollow between the Fr ~ 0.3 and Fr ~ 0.5 humps, where they partly cancel). Even though the higher speed option seems less favorable by a naive 'faster costs more' intuition, its position in a resistance hollow can give it lower wave resistance than the nominally slower option sitting on a hump — which is exactly why naval architects plot the full Ct-versus-Fr curve rather than assuming resistance rises smoothly with speed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge asks about the Kelvin wake angle to check whether a student understands that wave-making resistance is a genuine energy loss with real geometry, not a vague 'water resistance' catch-all. The tell of real understanding is citing the 19.47-degree (arcsin 1/3) result as speed-independent in the classic deep-water case, while also being able to explain the 2013 narrowing observation as an apparent, near-field effect rather than a contradiction — a student who treats the two facts as conflicting rather than complementary has memorized a number without understanding the mechanism generating it.

questions.prompt: In deep water, Kelvin's 1887 result for the wake half-angle behind a moving object is:

options.text: arcsin(1/3), about 19 degrees 28 minutes, independent of the object's speed
45 degrees, independent of speed
A half-angle that increases linearly with speed
A half-angle that depends on the object's mass, not its speed

explanations.a: Correct — Kelvin showed the wave pattern is confined to a wedge with half-angle arcsin(1/3), about 19.47 degrees, regardless of the moving object's speed in deep water.
explanations.b: 45 degrees is not the Kelvin angle; it does not match the geometry derived from deep-water gravity-wave dispersion.
explanations.c: The classic Kelvin result is precisely that the outer geometric angle does NOT change with speed.
explanations.d: The angle comes from the ratio of group to phase velocity of deep-water waves, a wave property, not from the moving object's mass.

questions.prompt: What did Rabaud and Moisy's 2013 study add to Kelvin's classic result?

options.text: It disproved Kelvin's 19.47-degree geometric boundary entirely
It showed that for fast, slender hulls, the energetic (apparent) wake can look narrower than 19.47 degrees, without overturning the outer geometric limit
It showed the wake angle depends only on water depth, not on speed at all
It proved the Kelvin angle applies only to canoes, not ships

explanations.a: The full wave pattern's outer geometric boundary is still bounded by Kelvin's classic cusp line; Rabaud and Moisy did not overturn that.
explanations.b: Correct — for fast, slender modern hulls the visible, energy-concentrated part of the wake narrows with speed in a Mach-cone-like way, even though the outer Kelvin boundary is unchanged.
explanations.c: The lesson describes a speed-dependent narrowing effect, not a depth-only effect.
explanations.d: Nothing in the finding restricts the classic result to small craft; it concerns fast, slender hulls generally.

questions.prompt: The humps and hollows in a ship's resistance-versus-Froude-number curve are caused mainly by:

options.text: Random measurement noise in towing-tank data
Interference between the bow and stern wave systems as their wavelength shifts with speed
Changes in water temperature during testing
The engine's power curve, not the hull's hydrodynamics

explanations.a: The humps and hollows are a repeatable hydrodynamic feature, not noise.
explanations.b: Correct — as speed changes, the wavelength of the radiated waves changes while bow-to-stern distance is fixed, so the two wave systems alternately reinforce and cancel, producing the humps (around Fr ~ 0.3 and ~ 0.5) and hollows on the curve.
explanations.c: Water temperature is not the driver described in this lesson's interference mechanism.
explanations.d: This is a hull hydrodynamics effect (wave interference), independent of what engine drives the ship.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the historical development of wave-making wake understanding.

items.text: Kelvin derives the constant 19.47-degree deep-water wake half-angle
Fast, slender modern hulls become common, prompting satellite-image wake studies
Rabaud and Moisy publish the 2013 finding of an apparently narrower wake at high speed

questions.explanation: Kelvin's geometric result came first (1887); modern fast, slender hulls later gave researchers real-world cases where the apparent wake visibly narrowed; Rabaud and Moisy's 2013 study then explained that narrowing using satellite imagery and modeling.

lessons.label: Hull Speed and Speed Regimes

sections.heading: Three ways to be supported by water
sections.body: As Froude number rises, a hull passes through qualitatively different regimes of how it is held up. In the displacement regime (Fr below about 0.4) the hull is supported entirely by buoyancy — Archimedes' principle — and simply pushes a wave system ahead of and alongside itself as it moves; this is where essentially all large commercial ships (tankers, container ships, bulk carriers) live. In the semi-planing (or semi-displacement) regime, roughly 0.4 to 1.0, the hull still displaces its weight in water but dynamic pressure on the after-body begins contributing meaningful lift, partially unloading the buoyant support and changing the hull's trim and wave pattern. Above roughly Fr ~ 1.0, a hull can enter true planing, where dynamic (hydrodynamic) lift off a mostly flat after-body does most or all of the supporting work, wetted surface collapses dramatically, and the wave-making picture changes entirely — a planing hull rides on top of the water rather than pushing through it.

sections.heading: The 1.34*sqrt(L) rule is a resistance hump, not a wall
sections.body: Recreational boaters often cite a 'hull speed' rule of thumb, V (knots) = 1.34 * sqrt(LWL in feet), as if it were a hard physical limit a displacement hull cannot exceed. It is not a wall; it is simply the speed at which Fr (using waterline length) reaches about 0.4 — the wavelength of the ship's self-generated bow wave becomes comparable to the waterline length, producing one of the resistance humps described in the wave-interference picture. Below that speed a hull's own bow and stern waves interfere favorably; near and above it, resistance rises steeply for typical hull proportions, which is what generates the barrier's economic character: pushing through it costs disproportionate power, not that it is impossible. A hull with the power-to-weight ratio to pay that toll does exceed it — hull speed is a statement about typical displacement-hull economics at typical proportions, not a hard ceiling in the physics.

sections.heading: Slenderness, not just length, is the real lever
sections.body: The parameter that actually controls how easily a hull crosses that hump is a slenderness ratio, roughly L / (displaced volume)^(1/3) — waterline length divided by the cube root of displacement volume, a length-to-'effective diameter' comparison rather than length alone. Long, slender hulls generate much smaller wave systems for a given displacement than short, beamy ones, so they can push well past Fr ~ 0.4 with comparatively modest extra power. Racing rowing shells (extremely slender, very light) and offshore multihulls (catamarans and trimarans, whose narrow demihulls carry the same total displacement as a single wider hull) both operate routinely at Froude numbers where a conventional monohull would be paying a steep resistance penalty, precisely because slenderness — not brute engine power — is what buys passage through the hump.

lessons.workedExample: Two 40-foot-waterline boats target 10 knots: a beamy displacement monohull and a narrow rowing-shell-proportioned hull. The rule of thumb gives 'hull speed' at 1.34*sqrt(40) ~ 8.5 knots for both, so both are asking to run above their nominal hull speed. But the beamy monohull, with a low slenderness ratio, sits deep in the Fr ~ 0.4 resistance hump at 10 knots and needs a large power increase to hold that speed; the slender hull, with a high L/(displacement volume)^(1/3), generates a much smaller wave system at the same speed and length, so it reaches 10 knots with only a modest power penalty over its 8.5-knot hull speed — the same rule-of-thumb number, two very different real costs.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why can some boats go faster than their hull speed?' is testing whether a student treats 1.34*sqrt(L) as folklore or as a physical statement they can unpack. The strong answer identifies the rule as marking Fr ~ 0.4, a resistance hump from bow/stern wave interference, not an impassable limit, and names slenderness (L over the cube root of displacement volume) as the parameter that actually determines how expensive crossing that hump is — citing rowing shells or multihulls as real craft that exceed it routinely. A student who says a displacement hull 'physically cannot' go faster than hull speed has mistaken an economic barrier for a physical one.

questions.prompt: Order these hull speed regimes from lowest to highest Froude number.

items.text: Displacement regime (buoyancy-supported)
Semi-planing / semi-displacement regime
Planing regime (dynamic lift dominates)

questions.explanation: Displacement mode holds below roughly Fr ~ 0.4, semi-planing spans roughly 0.4 to 1.0 as dynamic lift begins contributing, and true planing appears above roughly Fr ~ 1.0 where hydrodynamic lift dominates over buoyancy.

questions.prompt: The traditional 'hull speed' rule V(knots) = 1.34*sqrt(LWL in feet) corresponds physically to:

options.text: The absolute maximum speed any displacement hull can ever reach
The speed at which waterline-length Froude number reaches about 0.4, a resistance hump from bow/stern wave interference
The speed at which the hull's engine reaches maximum RPM
The speed at which frictional resistance becomes zero

explanations.a: It is not an absolute maximum; sufficiently slender or powerful hulls exceed it routinely, which is why it is described as an economic rather than physical barrier.
explanations.b: Correct — the coefficient 1.34 corresponds to roughly Fr ~ 0.4 for length in feet, marking a resistance hump where the self-generated wave system becomes costly, not a hard limit.
explanations.c: The rule is a hydrodynamic (hull-and-water) relationship, unrelated to any specific engine's RPM.
explanations.d: Frictional resistance never goes to zero and is not what this rule describes; the rule concerns wave-making interference.

questions.prompt: Which parameter is described in this lesson as the real control on how easily a hull crosses the Fr ~ 0.4 resistance hump?

options.text: Waterline length alone
Engine horsepower alone
Slenderness, roughly L divided by (displacement volume)^(1/3)
Hull color and paint finish

explanations.a: Length alone appears in the hull-speed rule, but two hulls of the same length can have very different wave resistance depending on how slender they are.
explanations.b: Horsepower determines whether a given hull CAN pay the cost of the hump, but the lesson identifies slenderness as the parameter that determines how large that cost is.
explanations.c: Correct — slenderness (length over the cube root of displaced volume) compares length to an 'effective diameter,' and it is what determines how large a wave system a hull generates for its displacement.
explanations.d: Paint finish affects frictional resistance and roughness, not the wave-making hump this question concerns.

questions.prompt: Which two types of craft does this lesson name as routinely operating past the Fr ~ 0.4 hump because of high slenderness?

options.text: Beamy tankers and bulk carriers
Racing rowing shells and offshore multihulls (catamarans/trimarans)
Anchored barges and floating docks
Submarines running fully submerged

explanations.a: Tankers and bulk carriers are cited elsewhere as low-Fr, friction-dominated, displacement-regime vessels, not slender hulls crossing the hump.
explanations.b: Correct — rowing shells (very slender, light) and multihulls (narrow demihulls sharing the total displacement) both routinely operate at Froude numbers past the hump that would penalize a conventional monohull.
explanations.c: Anchored or stationary craft are not relevant to a speed-regime discussion at all.
explanations.d: A submerged submarine does not generate a free-surface wave system, so the Fr ~ 0.4 hump does not apply to it in that state.

lessons.label: Froude's Law of Comparison: Why Models Are Froude-Scaled

sections.heading: Two dimensionless numbers, one model, no fluid that satisfies both
sections.body: A scale model of a ship exists to predict full-scale resistance cheaply, but ship resistance depends on two dimensionless groups — Froude number Fr (governing wave-making) and Reynolds number Re (governing viscous friction) — and a single physical model in a single fluid cannot match both simultaneously. Matching Fr requires model speed V_model = V_ship / sqrt(lambda), where lambda is the geometric scale ratio (ship length over model length); at a typical lambda of 20-40, that model speed is a modest fraction of full scale. Matching Re at that same reduced model speed requires a fluid whose kinematic viscosity is nu_model = nu_ship * lambda^(-3/2) — for lambda = 40, roughly 1/253 of water's viscosity, a fluid that simply does not exist in any practical liquid. The alternative — abandon Froude scaling and match Re directly at model size — is just as unworkable: for a 5 m model of a 200 m ship (lambda = 40), matching Re in the same fluid requires the model to run at V_ship times lambda, roughly 40 times the full-scale speed, which would destroy the model and bears no relation to how the real ship's waves behave anyway.

sections.heading: William Froude's split: separate the physics, don't force one model to do both
sections.body: William Froude, running early experiments in the 1860s-70s from what became the first purpose-built towing tank (Torquay, 1871), resolved the impasse not by finding a magic fluid but by refusing to treat total resistance as one quantity. His law of comparison splits total resistance into a frictional component Rf and a residuary component Rr (chiefly wave-making, plus viscous pressure drag): Rt = Rf + Rr. The residuary coefficient, Froude argued, is essentially the same for model and ship when tested at the same Froude number (the two hulls are 'geosims' — geometrically similar and dynamically similar in their wave pattern), so Rr scales with the cube of the linear scale ratio, Rr proportional to lambda^3, once measured on the model at the corresponding Fr-matched speed.

sections.heading: Friction gets computed, not modeled
sections.body: The frictional component is handled separately and is not read directly off the model, because a model tested at Fr-matched (i.e., much lower Re) speed has proportionally thicker, more laminar-prone boundary-layer behavior than the full-scale ship. Instead, Rf is computed from a standard flat-plate friction formula (originally Froude's own data, later replaced by the ITTC-1957 line) evaluated at each hull's own actual Reynolds number, model and ship separately. The measured model Rr is then scaled up by lambda^3 and added to the computed full-scale Rf to predict the ship's total resistance — extrapolating the wave physics geometrically while computing the viscous physics analytically, rather than forcing one tank test to represent both.

lessons.workedExample: A 200 m ship is represented by a 5 m model, so lambda = 40. To match Froude number, the model runs at 1/sqrt(40) ~ 1/6.3 of the ship's speed — a manageable, sub-2-m/s tow. Trying instead to match Reynolds number directly would require the model to run at 40 times the ship's speed, physically impossible for a towed model and irrelevant to reproducing the ship's actual wave pattern. Froude's method sidesteps both problems: the tank measures Rr at the Fr-matched low speed, scales it by lambda^3 = 64,000 to predict the ship's wave resistance, and separately computes Rf for the model (at its own low Re) and for the ship (at its own much higher Re) from a flat-plate formula, adding the ship-scale Rf to the scaled-up Rr.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing 'why don't you just build a smaller ship and time it?' is checking whether a student understands that Fr and Re cannot both be matched at reduced scale, and why. The strong answer states the actual conflict — Froude-matched speed goes as 1/sqrt(lambda) while Reynolds-matched speed would go as lambda, pulling in opposite directions — and can explain Froude's fix as splitting resistance into a geometrically-scaled residuary term and a separately computed frictional term, rather than reading total resistance straight off the model. A student who scales the model's total measured resistance by lambda^3 without separating friction has silently over-scaled the frictional part and will mispredict full-scale power.

questions.prompt: Why can a single scale model in water not match both Froude number and Reynolds number simultaneously?

options.text: Matching Fr requires model speed to scale as 1/sqrt(lambda), while matching Re at that same size requires a fluid of viscosity nu*lambda^(-3/2), which does not exist
Froude number and Reynolds number are actually the same dimensionless group, so matching one automatically matches the other
Model tanks are not long enough to reach the required speed for either number
Reynolds number does not apply to free-surface flows at all

explanations.a: Correct — the two scaling requirements pull in incompatible directions; satisfying both would require an impossible fluid viscosity at Fr-matched speed.
explanations.b: Fr (V/sqrt(gL)) and Re (VL/nu) are distinct groups governing different physics (gravity waves vs. viscosity); matching one does not match the other.
explanations.c: Tank length is a practical constraint but not the fundamental reason — the fundamental reason is the incompatible fluid-viscosity requirement.
explanations.d: Reynolds number applies to any viscous flow, including free-surface flow around a hull; it governs the frictional/boundary-layer part of resistance.

questions.prompt: For a 5 m model of a 200 m ship (lambda = 40), matching Reynolds number directly (instead of Froude-scaling) would require the model to run at roughly:

options.text: 1/40 of the ship's speed
The same speed as the ship
About 40 times the ship's speed
About 6.3 times slower than the ship, matching Fr instead

explanations.a: 1/40 the ship's speed is roughly the Froude-matched speed's neighborhood inverted incorrectly; Reynolds matching requires a much higher, not lower, model speed.
explanations.b: Matching Re at a 40x smaller length requires compensating with much higher speed, not equal speed.
explanations.c: Correct — since Re = VL/nu with the same nu, matching Re at 1/40 the length requires roughly 40 times the speed, an impractical and physically unrepresentative test.
explanations.d: 6.3x slower (1/sqrt(40)) describes the Froude-matched speed, not the Reynolds-matched speed, which is the opposite regime described here.

questions.prompt: In Froude's law of comparison, the residuary resistance coefficient measured on the model is assumed to equal the ship's residuary coefficient when:

options.text: Model and ship are run at the same Reynolds number
Model and ship are run at the same Froude number
Model and ship are run at the same absolute speed
Model and ship have the same wetted surface area

explanations.a: Matching Re is the Reynolds-scaling approach Froude's method deliberately avoids for the residuary (wave) term.
explanations.b: Correct — Froude's law of comparison assumes the residuary coefficient matches between geometrically similar hulls tested at the same Fr, because that reproduces dynamically similar wave patterns.
explanations.c: Absolute speed matching would badly mismatch both Fr and Re between a small model and a large ship.
explanations.d: Equal wetted surface area is not the similarity condition; geometric similarity plus matched Fr is.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Froude's method for predicting full-scale ship resistance from a model test.

items.text: Tow the geometrically similar model at the Froude-matched speed
Measure the model's total resistance and subtract its computed frictional resistance to isolate Rr
Scale the model's residuary resistance Rr up by lambda^3 to predict the ship's residuary resistance
Compute the ship's own frictional resistance at full-scale Reynolds number and add it to the scaled Rr

questions.explanation: The model is towed at the speed matching the ship's Froude number, its measured total resistance is separated into friction and residuary components (friction computed from a flat-plate formula at the model's own Re), the residuary part is scaled geometrically by lambda^3, and the ship's own frictional resistance (computed at the ship's much higher Re) is added to get predicted full-scale total resistance.

lessons.label: Inside the Towing Tank

sections.heading: The carriage, the model, and a boundary layer that lies
sections.body: A towing tank is a long, narrow basin spanned by an overhead carriage that tows a hull model at precisely controlled speed while a strain-gauge dynamometer records resistance. Models are traditionally carved from paraffin wax (cheap, easily reshaped between test runs) or built from foam-and-wood composites for reusable, more durable series testing; both are machined to hull-form offsets and finished smooth. But a small model run at Froude-matched speed sits at a far lower Reynolds number than the ship, and a smooth model hull at that low Re can keep a laminar boundary layer over much of its length — something the real, turbulent-flow ship never experiences. Left uncorrected, that laminar patch would make the model look artificially low-drag in a way that has nothing to do with the ship. The standard fix is turbulence stimulation: a line of small studs, sand strips, or a thin trip wire fixed near the bow forces the boundary layer to transition to turbulent flow at a known, repeatable location, so the model's flow regime actually resembles the ship's, just at model scale.

sections.heading: Standard formulas so every tank agrees
sections.body: Because the frictional component is computed rather than read off the model, the industry needs one agreed formula for it. Since 1957 the ITTC (International Towing Tank Conference) has used a single model-ship correlation line, Cf = 0.075 / (log10(Re) - 2)^2, applied identically at model and ship Reynolds numbers so results from different tanks and different countries are comparable. A refinement Hughes proposed in 1954 splits viscous resistance further into flat-plate friction and a form factor (1+k) that accounts for the extra viscous pressure drag a real, non-flat hull shape adds beyond a flat plate; (1+k) is typically found by the Prohaska (1966) method, extrapolating a series of very low-speed runs (roughly Fr 0.12-0.20) where wave-making is negligible, so the residual viscous effect can be isolated cleanly before the wave-dominated higher-speed runs are analyzed.

sections.heading: What the tank itself gets in the way of measuring correctly
sections.body: A finite tank is not open ocean, and two artifacts must be corrected for: blockage, where the tank's walls and floor constrict flow around the model and artificially raise measured resistance (worse for a wide or deep model relative to the tank's cross-section), and shallow-water interference, where wave propagation itself changes once water depth is comparable to the wavelength the model generates, distorting the wave pattern the test is trying to measure. Tanks correspondingly specify a minimum depth-to-draft and model-size-to-tank-cross-section ratio before results are trusted. A correlation allowance is also added when scaling predictions to real ships, accounting for hull roughness and other full-scale effects a smooth wax model cannot capture. Separately, many basins have a wavemaker at one end, used not for resistance testing but for seakeeping trials, generating controlled regular or irregular waves to test a hull's motions in a seaway rather than its calm-water resistance.

lessons.workedExample: A 6 m wax model of a container ship is towed at Fr-matched speed for a resistance series. Left smooth, its bow region would stay laminar over the first meter or so — a Reynolds number regime the real 300 m ship never sees — so technicians fix a row of turbulence studs a short distance aft of the bow to force early transition. Runs are conducted in two speed bands: several very low-Fr runs (0.12-0.20) used with the Prohaska method to extract the form factor (1+k), and the full range of design-speed runs used to measure total resistance, from which the ITTC-57 line-based frictional prediction is subtracted to isolate residuary resistance for lambda^3 scaling.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how do you know your tank result isn't an artifact of the model itself?' is testing whether a student understands that a towing tank measurement is not a direct readout of ship physics but a carefully corrected proxy. The strong answer names turbulence stimulation (studs or a trip wire) as forcing a realistic turbulent boundary layer despite low model-scale Reynolds number, cites the standard ITTC-57 friction line so results are comparable across tanks, and can explain blockage or shallow-water interference as basin-geometry artifacts requiring correction — distinguishing genuine hull physics from tank-induced error is exactly what separates a rigorous model-test result from a number pulled off a dynamometer with no context.

questions.prompt: Why do towing-tank technicians add turbulence stimulation (studs or a trip wire) near the bow of a model?

options.text: To reduce the model's total wetted surface area
To force early transition to a turbulent boundary layer, because a smooth model at low model-scale Reynolds number would otherwise stay artificially laminar unlike the real ship
To make the model's paint finish more durable between runs
To simulate ocean waves for seakeeping tests

explanations.a: Studs and trip wires do not change wetted area meaningfully; they trigger a flow-regime change.
explanations.b: Correct — at Froude-matched (low) model speed, Reynolds number is low enough that a smooth model hull could stay laminar over much of its length, unlike the turbulent-flow ship, so stimulation forces a representative turbulent boundary layer.
explanations.c: Durability is unrelated; studs are a flow-transition device, not a protective coating.
explanations.d: Wave simulation for seakeeping is the job of a basin's wavemaker, a separate piece of equipment from bow-mounted turbulence studs.

questions.prompt: The ITTC-1957 model-ship correlation line for frictional resistance coefficient is:

options.text: Cf = 1.34 * sqrt(Re)
Cf = Re / (0.5 * rho * S)
Cf = arcsin(1/3)

explanations.a: Correct — this is the standard ITTC-1957 line, applied identically at model and ship Reynolds numbers so results from different tanks are comparable.
explanations.b: This resembles the hull-speed rule of thumb, an unrelated relationship about wave-making resistance humps, not a friction-coefficient formula.
explanations.c: This is not a real friction formula; it garbles the definition of a resistance coefficient with Reynolds number.
explanations.d: This is the Kelvin wake half-angle in radians-equivalent form, unrelated to frictional resistance.

questions.prompt: Hughes' form factor (1+k), extrapolated using the Prohaska (1966) method, is typically determined from:

options.text: A series of very low-Froude-number runs (roughly Fr 0.12-0.20) where wave-making is negligible
Runs conducted only at the ship's full design speed
The tank's wavemaker output alone, with the carriage stationary
A single high-speed run near the Fr ~ 0.5 resistance hump

explanations.a: Correct — running at very low Fr keeps wave-making negligible, isolating the viscous form-drag effect the form factor is meant to capture, then extrapolating per Prohaska's method.
explanations.b: Design-speed runs are dominated by wave-making, which would contaminate a measurement meant to isolate viscous form drag.
explanations.c: The wavemaker is used for seakeeping tests, not for form-factor determination, which requires towing the model.
explanations.d: The Fr ~ 0.5 hump is a wave-making-dominated regime, the opposite of where form factor is cleanly isolated.

questions.prompt: Match each towing-tank artifact or correction to what it addresses.

right.text: Tank walls/floor constricting flow and artificially raising measured resistance
Water depth comparable to the model's wavelength, distorting the wave pattern being measured
Full-scale hull roughness effects a smooth wax model cannot reproduce

questions.explanation: Blockage is a finite-tank-geometry artifact from the walls and floor constricting flow; shallow-water interference occurs when depth becomes comparable to generated wavelength, distorting the measured wave pattern; the correlation allowance is added when scaling to full scale to account for real hull roughness a smooth model cannot capture.

lessons.label: From Tank to Sea: Trials, CFD and Where They Disagree

sections.heading: Sea trials measure the real ship, in weather that isn't calm water
sections.body: The final check on any resistance prediction is a full-scale speed/power sea trial: the actual ship runs measured courses at several engine settings while speed, shaft power, and torque are logged. Unlike a towing tank, the ocean does not hold wind, waves, and current at zero, so raw trial data must be corrected back to the equivalent calm-water, no-current condition before it can be compared to a tank prediction. The standard framework for this is ISO 15016, which specifies how to correct measured speed and power for added wind resistance, added wave resistance, current, and even water temperature/density and shallow-water effects, so that trials run on different days in different weather remain comparable to each other and to the model-scale extrapolation. A trial run in a stiff headwind that is not corrected will look like a slower, higher-resistance ship than it actually is in calm water.

sections.heading: CFD: excellent in calm water, weaker once waves enter
sections.body: Free-surface Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) CFD solves the flow around a full hull directly, resolving both the turbulent boundary layer and the free-surface wave pattern without needing the model-scale-to-full-scale extrapolation a towing tank requires. For calm-water resistance prediction, modern RANS CFD routinely agrees with towing-tank or trial results to within a few percent — good enough to guide hull-form design decisions and, increasingly, to substitute for some tank testing. That accuracy degrades once realistic sea states are added: resolving a hull's motions and added resistance in irregular waves, breaking-wave effects, and slamming loads is a much harder computational problem, and CFD predictions in waves carry noticeably larger uncertainty than the calm-water case — which is why seakeeping work still leans heavily on physical basin testing with a wavemaker rather than CFD alone.

sections.heading: A live argument, and effects no small model reproduces
sections.body: Even within pure model-scale extrapolation there is a standing methodological disagreement: plain ITTC-1957-line extrapolation (treating all viscous resistance as flat-plate friction, scaled the same way at every speed) versus form-factor methods (Hughes' 1+k, from Prohaska (1966) low-speed runs) that separate out the extra viscous pressure drag from hull shape before scaling. The two methods can give different full-scale predictions for the same tank data, particularly for full-form hulls where viscous pressure drag is a larger share of total resistance, and different tanks and class societies have historically favored one over the other. Beyond that argument, full-scale hulls also carry real-world effects no small wax or foam model can reproduce at all: actual hull roughness from steel plating and welds, and biofouling — marine growth accumulating between drydockings — both of which measurably raise full-scale friction beyond what a smooth model or a clean-hull correlation allowance predicts, which is exactly why ships are periodically hull-cleaned and why trial results drift upward in resistance over a ship's time between drydockings.

lessons.workedExample: A newly built 300 m container ship runs sea trials showing higher fuel consumption at design speed than the tank prediction promised.
